top10_weekly.title: Septin partitioning between microtubules and actin is regulated by GSK3-dependent septin 9 phosphorylation.
top10_weekly.abstract: Septins are cytoskeletal filaments that associate with the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton but the mechanisms that govern septin crosstalk and function with these networks are largely unknown. Here, we show that glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) directly phosphorylates Septin 9 (SEPT9) and regulates bidirectionally septin distribution between actin and microtubules. We show that GSK3 inhibition redistributes endogenous SEPT9 toward microtubules in multiple cell types. Phosphomimetic mutations at serines 82 and 85 reduce microtubule binding and enhance actin association in cells and in vitro, while phosphonull mutations promote microtubule binding and growth. In primary hippocampal neurons, GSK3β inactivation promotes SEPT9-microtubule association, and phosphomimetic SEPT9 expression impairs asymmetric neurite growth during neuronal polarization. These findings reveal a phosphorylation-dependent mechanism of septin partitioning between actin and microtubules, placing the cytoskeletal functions of septins under the control of GSK3-a kinase linked to multiple signaling pathways of cell physiology and metabolism.

top10_weekly.title: Dynein-dependent positioning of multiple organelles regulates adaptive gene expression during oxidative stress.
top10_weekly.abstract: Cells respond to environmental insults through well-characterized changes to their transcriptome and proteome. The contribution that reorganization of intracellular architecture makes to the adaptive stress response is much less understood. Here, we reveal a conserved spatial response to oxidative stress in which the microtubule motor dynein enhances perinuclear clustering of multiple membrane-bound organelles. These events are triggered by reactive oxygen species and protein kinase C and occur without increased association of dynein with its activator dynactin, pointing to a noncanonical mechanism for stimulating retrograde transport. Using a chemically inducible system for dispersing individual organelles, we show that perinuclear localization of multiple compartments potentiates oxidative stress-induced gene expression, with distinct genes depending on inputs from either combinations of organelles or individual compartments. Together, these findings implicate positioning of multiple membrane-bound compartments in gene expression regulation and identify coordinated organelle trafficking by dynein as an additional regulatory layer in the cellular stress response.

top10_weekly.title: Drp-1 Participates in LPS-Induced Neuroinflammation and Microglia-Neuron Interaction Through mtDNA-cGAS-STING Axis.
top10_weekly.abstract: To investigate the role of dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp-1) in the process of LPS-induced microglial injury and its initiated neuroinflammation. C57BL/6J mice or BV2 microglia were challenged with LPS, and the behavioral performance and the cell viability were tested, respectively. The expression of Drp-1, inflammatory factors, and key molecules of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway was measured in the mouse hippocampus or in microglia in vitro, together with the abundance of mtDNA. Moreover, the effect of Drp-1 was further explored by siRNA in vitro and its selective inhibitor Mdivi-1 in vivo. Furthermore, a co-culture system of microglia and neurons was used to observe the potential role of cell-free mtDNA in the microglia-neuron crosstalk. Meanwhile, the plasma levels of cell-free mitochondrial DNA (cf-mtDNA) were detected in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). In vivo, intraperitoneal injection of LPS could result in anxious-like and depression-like behaviors in mice, together with a significant microglial activation and its related neuroinflammation, mtDNA release, and the imbalanced expression of synaptic plasticity, Drp-1, cGAS, STING, p-STING, and IRF3 in the hippocampus. All these behavioral and neuropathological changes could be reversed by treatment with Mdivi-1. Moreover, LPS-induced behavioral dysfunction and neuropathological injuries were also observed in mice that received hippocampal stereotactic injection of mtDNA. In vitro, besides the detrimental effect of LPS on microglia, our results indicated a crucial role of microglia-derived mtDNA in linking Drp-1-associated mitochondrial dysfunction to LPS-induced microglial injury and neuroinflammation, and in the crosstalk between HT22 and BV2 cells. Additionally, the plasma concentration of cf-mtDNA was increased in MDD patients, with a significant positive correlation with plasma levels of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IFN-γ. As a key regulator of mitochondrial fission, the imbalanced expression of Drp-1 participates in LPS-induced microglial injury and neuroinflammation via the Drp-1-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis.

top10_weekly.title: Distinct regulatory logic controls recruitment and membrane dynamics of ESCRT-III subunit Vps60.
top10_weekly.abstract: Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery drives membrane remodeling and scission events essential for multivesicular body (MVB) biogenesis. The accessory ESCRT-III subunit Vps60 (mammalian CHMP5) shares structural features with the major polymerizing subunit Snf7, including the capacity to form homopolymers in vitro. Here, we demonstrate in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that Vps60 recruitment and polymerization require conditions that permit Snf7 polymer turnover: Vps60 is largely excluded when Snf7 assembly is absent and when Snf7 disassembly is blocked, consistent with recruitment of Vps60 late in the ESCRT-III cycle to Snf7 assemblies that undergo normal turnover. Structure-function analysis reveals that Vps60 regulation diverges fundamentally from core ESCRT-III subunits: while occlusion of the Vps60 C-terminus by a GFP tag drives constitutive membrane association and polymer assembly, C-terminal truncation impairs endosomal recruitment, indicating that the Vps60 C-terminus is required for membrane recruitment, in contrast to the autoinhibitory C-terminal domains of core ESCRT-III subunits. A C-terminally tagged Vps60 that constitutively associates with membranes phenocopies loss of Vps60 function in both intralumenal vesicle (ILV) formation and cargo sorting. These findings indicate that despite structural similarity to Snf7, Vps60 functions as a late-arriving accessory factor whose recruitment and assembly are tightly coupled to Snf7 dynamics.

top10_weekly.title: Motor neuron disease due to a novel PIK3R1 mutation.
top10_weekly.abstract: Mutations in PIK3R1, which encodes the regulatory subunit (p85α) of class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), are associated with immunologic and developmental disorders, but their effects on the nervous system have not been studied. We identified a novel heterozygous frameshift mutation (PIK3R1 c.1710dup) in a patient with common variable immunodeficiency who developed adult-onset, slowly progressive ALS-like motor-neuron disease. Studies of patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) demonstrated PIK3R1 haploinsufficiency with selective AKT activation. Investigation of patient's iPSC-derived motor neurons (iMNs) showed reduced neuronal electrical activity, and markedly increased apoptosis. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed coordinated up-regulation of differentiation and apoptosis programs across neuronal and glial clusters. Engineering the PIK3R1 c.1710dup mutation into healthy-control iPSCs reproduced the impaired electrical activity, increased apoptosis, and transcriptional vulnerability, confirming the variant's cell-intrinsic pathogenicity. In contrast, introduction of canonical APDS2-associated PIK3R1 splice mutations into the same genetic background did not produce these abnormalities, establishing a variant-class-specific mechanism of PI3K dysfunction. Together, these findings define PIK3R1 c.1710dup as a distinct pathogenic variant that links PI3K-pathway dysregulation to human motor-neuron degeneration and expands the mechanistic spectrum of PIK3R1-associated disease.

top10_weekly.title: Galectin-3 links microglial neuroinflammation to Aβ aggregation and lysosomal processing.
top10_weekly.abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the molecular mechanisms linking microglial dysfunction to amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify galectin-3 (Gal3) as a regulator of plaque-associated microglial responses, linking Aβ aggregation, lysosomal function, and neuritic pathology. Using postmortem brain tissue from AD patients, we found that Gal3+ microglia preferentially associate with cored plaques and correlate with increased LAMP1+ dystrophic neurites. Gal3 was also detected in microglial lysosomal compartments, extramicroglial dystrophic structures, and in association with extracellular amyloid fibrils, suggesting roles in both intracellular and extracellular Aβ processing. In APP mice, Gal3 deficiency reduced plaque burden and neuritic dystrophy, increased plaque compaction, and enhanced TREM2 coverage around amyloid plaques. Mechanistically, in vitro microglial experiments showed that Gal3 modulates Aβ uptake and lysosomal processing, whereas lysosomal dysfunction promoted the accumulation of fibrillar Aβ from initially monomeric species, particularly in Gal3-deficient cells. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Gal3 preferentially binds fibrillar Aβ, inhibits secondary nucleation, and alters fibril morphology, while Gal3-modified fibrillar Aβ reduces N2a neuronal cell number. Finally, in silico structural analyses identified candidate Gal3 interactors enriched in leucine-rich-repeat and immunoglobulin-like proteins, supporting a role for this lectin in immune receptor regulation. Complementary in vivo transcriptomic profiling showed that Gal3 deletion suppresses type I interferon and microglial neurodegenerative transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings position Gal3 at the interface between Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and plaque-associated microglial responses in AD.

top10_weekly.title: Thalamocortical vulnerability in autism spectrum disorder: a computational model of CPEB4 mis-splicing.
top10_weekly.abstract: Skipping of a neuronal microexon in cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein 4 (CPEB4) transcripts has been linked to idiopathic autism spectrum disorder, but the most susceptible brain regions and cell types are unknown. We asked whether the balance between the splicing activator serine/arginine repetitive matrix 4 (SRRM4) and the RNA-binding repressors polypyrimidine tract-binding proteins 1 and 2 (PTBP1 and PTBP2) is sufficient to predict regional differences in microexon inclusion, and which predictions withstand uncertainty in unmeasured parameters. We modeled their competitive binding to the intronic motifs flanking the microexon, including destabilization of SRRM4 expression by sustained histone deacetylase inhibition, and applied the model to human brain transcriptomic data from tissue samples, single cells and developmental stages. The thalamus expressed markedly less SRRM4 mRNA than the anterior cingulate cortex, and the model predicted lower microexon inclusion in the thalamus in every draw of the sensitivity analysis, although the size of the difference varied widely and absolute inclusion values were poorly constrained. A larger thalamic effect of histone deacetylase inhibition was not robust: it followed from the assumed regional difference in super-enhancer susceptibility, and the cingulate cortex lost more inclusion when this susceptibility was equal in both regions. The model is not experimentally validated, and microexon inclusion has not been measured in the human thalamus. These results propose regional SRRM4 supply as a testable determinant of CPEB4 microexon splicing and identify the measurements needed to test it: microexon inclusion and SRRM4, PTBP1 and PTBP2 protein in thalamic nuclei and cingulate cortex.

top10_weekly.title: Functional transcriptomic profile of mouse controlled cortical impact model of post-traumatic epilepsy with robust spontaneous recurrent seizures.
top10_weekly.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of acquired epilepsy, yet the molecular changes linking the initial injury to post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) remain incompletely understood. Here, we used a severe controlled cortical impact mouse model that develops robust spontaneous recurrent seizures to characterize the temporal and regional progression of post-traumatic transcriptional responses. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on the contralateral cortex and hippocampus collected from TBI and time-matched sham mice at 7, 21, and 60 days after injury, corresponding to the acute injury, latent period, and chronic epilepsy phases, respectively. Transcriptomic changes were characterized using differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis, Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes gene-set enrichment analyses, and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. Transcriptomic responses were strongly dependent on brain region and disease phase. At 7 days, the cortex showed enhanced neuronal and structural signaling alongside suppression of immune, metabolic, and cell-cycle processes, whereas the hippocampus showed prominent neuroimmune activation and metabolic stress. By 21 days, before the emergence of spontaneous seizures, the hippocampus shifted toward partial normalization of metabolic pathway enrichment, accompanied by suppression of neurotransmission, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal organization. In contrast, the cortex showed increased enrichment of immune and tissue-remodeling processes. Although relatively few DEGs were detected at 60 days, a selective hippocampal signature persisted after PTE was established. Pathway analyses converged on coordinated changes in neuroimmune, metabolic, lipid-regulatory, and synaptic processes. Upstream Regulator Analysis further identified a temporal reversal in APOE-associated regulatory activity, linking inflammatory and lipid-metabolic responses with later synaptic remodeling. The 21-day post-injury hippocampus represents a critical disease-modification window. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PTE progression involves phase-specific molecular remodeling that shifts from an early cortical response to sustained hippocampal dysregulation. The latent hippocampal signature identifies a potentially actionable molecular window before recurrent seizure onset.

top10_weekly.title: Ribosome-associated vesicles promote activity-dependent local translation in neurons.
top10_weekly.abstract: Local protein synthesis in axons and dendrites underpins synaptic plasticity. However, the composition of the protein synthesis machinery in distal neuronal processes and the mechanisms for its deployment to local translation sites remain unclear. Here, we employed multi-scale imaging that combines cryo-electron tomography, volume electron microscopy, and live-cell imaging to identify endoplasmic reticulum-derived KDEL-positive vesicles, a subset of which are decorated with ribosomes (Ribosome-Associated Vesicles, RAVs) in neurites. We demonstrate that neuronal stimulation triggers compartment-specific responses: dendrites accumulate stationary KDEL-positive vesicles at sites of enhanced translation, while axons accelerate vesicle transport. cLTP stimulation additionally increases the proportion of KDEL-positive vesicles that carry ribosomes, expanding the local RAV pool. Real-time imaging of translation at single mRNA resolution reveals that RAV-associated translation sites exhibit ∼30% greater nascent-peptide signal amplitude compared to periods without RAV association, indicating that RAVs boost local translation output. These findings establish RAVs as specialized platforms that integrate activity-dependent signals with local protein synthesis, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how neurons achieve precise spatiotemporal control of translation.

top10_weekly.title: Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry for real-time serotonin dynamics in human iPSC-derived neural spheroids.
top10_weekly.abstract: Measuring neurotransmission in the human brain could advance our understanding of disorders, including depression. Although fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) has provided valuable insights into neurotransmission in animal models, its application to human systems remains challenging. Here, we present an FSCV-based framework for real-time serotonin measurements in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived three-dimensional (3D) neuronal cultures. We demonstrate reproducible detection of spontaneous and evoked serotonin release from 3D serotonergic spheroids and show that serotonin dynamics differ between serotonin reuptake inhibitors. We investigate how a molecular stress mediator influences serotonin signaling and antidepressant effectiveness. Finally, we extend the platform to co-cultures containing microglia-like cells to examine serotonin dynamics under inflammatory conditions. We present a translational, label-free technology to measure serotonin dynamics in real-time in human stem cell-derived models. This method studies serotonin regulation, with potential applications to drug development and the mechanistic dissection of psychiatric disorders, such as depression.

primary.title: Insights into how JIP3 and JIP4 adaptor proteins relieve the auto-inhibited form of the kinesin-1 motor.
primary.abstract: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear. JIP3 and JIP4 are adaptors that activate kinesin-1 and dynein-dynactin motors, enabling bidirectional transport along microtubules. Here, we characterized the interaction between the kinesin-1 heavy chain, KIF5B, and both JIP3 and JIP4 (JIP3/4), using mutagenesis and binding experiments associated with modelling. We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction. JIP3/4 binds to the CC4 coiled-coil domain of KIF5B, with no significant interaction detected with the distal tail. Conversely, KIF5B-CC4 binds to the RH1 domain of JIP3/4, with the preceding disordered N-terminus modulating the force of the binding. Notably, JIP3 and JIP4 exhibit ∼40-fold differences in affinity for KIF5B. We performed extensive site-directed mutagenesis on KIF5B-binding regions of JIP3/JIP4 targeting accessible charged residues and sequence differences between JIP3 and JIP4. This revealed multiple weak-affinity binding sites that collectively define an extensive KIF5B-binding surface on the RH1 domain of JIP3. Importantly, the KIF5B-binding surface on JIP3 differs from that of the DLIC (dynein light intermediate chain), confirming no competition between the two motors. Altogether, the fragment and mutant mapping of KIF5B binding to JIP3 and JIP4 presented here provides insights into how the auto-inhibited form of kinesin-1 might be relieved, with the CC4 region playing a central role.

primary.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
primary.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

primary.title: JIP4 and RILPL1 utilize opposing motor force to dynamically regulate lysosomal tubulation.
primary.abstract: Lysosomes are dynamic organelles that remodel their membrane in response to stimuli. We previously uncovered a process we term LYsosomal Tubulation/sorting driven by LRRK2 (LYTL), wherein damaged lysosomes generate tubules sorted into vesicles. LYTL is orchestrated by the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 that recruits the motor adaptor protein and RHD family member JIP4 to lysosomes. JIP4 enhances LYTL tubule extension toward the plus-end of microtubules. To identify new players involved in LYTL, we mapped the lysosomal proteome after LRRK2 kinase inhibition. We found that RILPL1 is recruited to dysfunctional lysosomes in an LRRK2 kinase activity-dependent manner, facilitated by pRAB proteins. Unlike JIP4, RILPL1 induces retraction of LYTL tubules by binding to p150Glued, thereby moving lysosomal tubules toward the minus-end of microtubules. Our findings emphasize the dynamic regulation of LYTL tubules by two distinct RHD proteins and pRAB effectors, acting as opposing motor adaptor proteins. These opposing forces create a metastable lysosomal membrane deformation, enabling dynamic tubulation events.

primary.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
primary.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

secondary.title: Characterization of a novel inherited splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3 expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: The MAPK8IP3 gene encodes JIP3, a kinesin-1 adapter protein crucial for axonal transport and JNK signaling pathway regulation. This gene exhibits extreme intolerance to loss-of-function variants. Heterozygous pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants are linked to a neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable brain abnormalities (NEDBA). This study characterizes a novel inherited canonical splice-site variant identified in a three-generation family. METHODS: Exome sequencing was performed on three affected individuals from a single non-consanguineous family with presenting neurological abnormalities. The molecular consequences of the identified variant were evaluated by RNA analysis. Clinical features of the variant carriers were evaluated in detail. RESULTS: We identified a heterozygous dinucleotide deletion (c.2630-2_2630-1del) at the canonical acceptor splice site of MAPK8IP3. This variant co-segregated with the neurological phenotype in an affected mother and her two children. RNA analysis demonstrated that this variant leads to a partial deletion of exon 22 (r.2630_2673del), which is predicted to cause a frameshift and introduce a premature termination codon (p.Gly877Valfs∗36). Notably, despite carrying an identical genotype, the three affected individuals exhibited marked interindividual variability in clinical severity, ranging from mild specific learning difficulties to global developmental delay with severe intellectual disability and autism. best.title: Insights into how JIP3 and JIP4 adaptor proteins relieve the auto-inhibited form of the kinesin-1 motor.
best.abstract: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear. JIP3 and JIP4 are adaptors that activate kinesin-1 and dynein-dynactin motors, enabling bidirectional transport along microtubules. Here, we characterized the interaction between the kinesin-1 heavy chain, KIF5B, and both JIP3 and JIP4 (JIP3/4), using mutagenesis and binding experiments associated with modelling. We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction. JIP3/4 binds to the CC4 coiled-coil domain of KIF5B, with no significant interaction detected with the distal tail. Conversely, KIF5B-CC4 binds to the RH1 domain of JIP3/4, with the preceding disordered N-terminus modulating the force of the binding. Notably, JIP3 and JIP4 exhibit ∼40-fold differences in affinity for KIF5B. We performed extensive site-directed mutagenesis on KIF5B-binding regions of JIP3/JIP4 targeting accessible charged residues and sequence differences between JIP3 and JIP4. This revealed multiple weak-affinity binding sites that collectively define an extensive KIF5B-binding surface on the RH1 domain of JIP3. Importantly, the KIF5B-binding surface on JIP3 differs from that of the DLIC (dynein light intermediate chain), confirming no competition between the two motors. Altogether, the fragment and mutant mapping of KIF5B binding to JIP3 and JIP4 presented here provides insights into how the auto-inhibited form of kinesin-1 might be relieved, with the CC4 region playing a central role.

best.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
best.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

best.abstract: BACKGROUND: The MAPK8IP3 gene encodes JIP3, a kinesin-1 adapter protein crucial for axonal transport and JNK signaling pathway regulation. This variant co-segregated with the neurological phenotype in an affected mother and her two children. RNA analysis demonstrated that this variant leads to a partial deletion of exon 22 (r.2630_2673del), which is predicted to cause a frameshift and introduce a premature termination codon (p.Gly877Valfs∗36). best.title: JIP4 and RILPL1 utilize opposing motor force to dynamically regulate lysosomal tubulation.
best.abstract: Lysosomes are dynamic organelles that remodel their membrane in response to stimuli. We previously uncovered a process we term LYsosomal Tubulation/sorting driven by LRRK2 (LYTL), wherein damaged lysosomes generate tubules sorted into vesicles. LYTL is orchestrated by the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 that recruits the motor adaptor protein and RHD family member JIP4 to lysosomes. JIP4 enhances LYTL tubule extension toward the plus-end of microtubules. To identify new players involved in LYTL, we mapped the lysosomal proteome after LRRK2 kinase inhibition. We found that RILPL1 is recruited to dysfunctional lysosomes in an LRRK2 kinase activity-dependent manner, facilitated by pRAB proteins. Unlike JIP4, RILPL1 induces retraction of LYTL tubules by binding to p150Glued, thereby moving lysosomal tubules toward the minus-end of microtubules. Our findings emphasize the dynamic regulation of LYTL tubules by two distinct RHD proteins and pRAB effectors, acting as opposing motor adaptor proteins. These opposing forces create a metastable lysosomal membrane deformation, enabling dynamic tubulation events.

best.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
best.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

primary.title: Thalamocortical vulnerability in autism spectrum disorder: a computational model of CPEB4 mis-splicing.
primary.abstract: Skipping of a neuronal microexon in cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein 4 (CPEB4) transcripts has been linked to idiopathic autism spectrum disorder, but the most susceptible brain regions and cell types are unknown. We asked whether the balance between the splicing activator serine/arginine repetitive matrix 4 (SRRM4) and the RNA-binding repressors polypyrimidine tract-binding proteins 1 and 2 (PTBP1 and PTBP2) is sufficient to predict regional differences in microexon inclusion, and which predictions withstand uncertainty in unmeasured parameters. We modeled their competitive binding to the intronic motifs flanking the microexon, including destabilization of SRRM4 expression by sustained histone deacetylase inhibition, and applied the model to human brain transcriptomic data from tissue samples, single cells and developmental stages. The thalamus expressed markedly less SRRM4 mRNA than the anterior cingulate cortex, and the model predicted lower microexon inclusion in the thalamus in every draw of the sensitivity analysis, although the size of the difference varied widely and absolute inclusion values were poorly constrained. A larger thalamic effect of histone deacetylase inhibition was not robust: it followed from the assumed regional difference in super-enhancer susceptibility, and the cingulate cortex lost more inclusion when this susceptibility was equal in both regions. The model is not experimentally validated, and microexon inclusion has not been measured in the human thalamus. These results propose regional SRRM4 supply as a testable determinant of CPEB4 microexon splicing and identify the measurements needed to test it: microexon inclusion and SRRM4, PTBP1 and PTBP2 protein in thalamic nuclei and cingulate cortex.

primary.title: The Cxcl14 chemokine defines pioneer axon guidance and early circuit assembly in the inner ear.
primary.abstract: The nervous system wiring requires the precise coordination of axon guidance, neuronal migration, and target cell recognition. Here, we show that inner ear circuit formation relies on pioneer cells extending an axonal scaffold that selectively targets early-born hair cells. High spatiotemporal imaging of pioneer axons reveals how they navigate through the cranial environment, establishing dynamic cell-cell contacts with other axons to finally stabilize in target cells. These pioneer axons are required not only for follower axon growth but also for coordinated migration of follower neurons, revealing a cellular hierarchy underlying circuit assembly. We identify the chemokine Cxcl14 as a novel instructive guidance cue regulating pioneer axon extension, turning, and fasciculation at discrete cellular decision points. Loss of Cxcl14 disrupts axonal navigation, compromises synaptic organization in hair cells, and impairs mechanosensory-based behavior. Together, our findings establish a new chemokine-based mechanism linking pioneer axon guidance to early sensory circuit assembly necessary for building mechanosensory networks.

primary.title: RBM42 couples alternative splicing to cytoskeletal organization to direct cortical development.
primary.abstract: Alternative splicing coordinates gene expression programs that shape the developing cerebral cortex. Here, we used nervous system-specific Rbm42 conditional knockout mice, RBM42-depleted human SH-SY5Y cells, RNA sequencing, RIP-seq, proteomics, and splice-switching rescue to define how the spliceosomal RNA-binding protein RBM42 supports cortical development. Rbm42 loss caused perinatal lethality, cortical thinning, defective lamination, reduced progenitor proliferation, increased apoptosis, and disrupted neuronal cytoskeletal organization. RBM42 bound and regulated cytoskeleton-associated transcripts, including NIN/Nin and NUMA1/Numa1, and its loss altered their splicing in human cells and mouse cortex. Restoring RBM42 corrected these splicing defects and improved proliferation and neurite growth. Selective correction of NIN exon 18 mis-splicing partially restored βIII-tubulin organization and proliferation but did not rescue apoptosis. These findings connect spliceosome-dependent isoform control with cytoskeletal remodeling during cortical development and provide a mechanistic framework for RBM42-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

primary.title: Astrocytes contribute to long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism affecting microglia in fragile X syndrome.
primary.abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) influence membrane structure and function, energy metabolism, inflammation, and the ability to regulate microglial activity. We show involvement of astrocytes in long-chain PUFA metabolism in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived astrocytes with fragile X syndrome (FXS). FXS astrocytes secreted more n-6 docosapentaenoic acid (n-6 DPA) and displayed a higher n-3 DPA to docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) ratio in medium than controls, consistent with an altered n-6 to n-3 PUFA balance in plasma from the FXS mouse. The FXS-specific increase in n-6 DPA secretion was abolished by treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), which affected gene expression in astrocyte subpopulations and modulated secreted triacylglycerol species. Microglial exposure to n-6 DPA stimulated expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which also tended to increase in microglia with reduced inflammatory marker expression when cultured in medium from ATRA-treated astrocytes. The results indicate that astrocyte-mediated n-6 DPA regulates the trophic functions of microglia in FXS.

primary.title: WFS1 deficiency impacts GnRH neuron development through mechanisms involving ER stress dysregulation.
primary.abstract: Wolfram Syndrome, a rare neurodegenerative disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the WFS1 gene, presents with endocrine and neurological features. Although hypogonadism has been described in Wolfram Syndrome, the role of WFS1 in reproductive development is not well understood. Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by deficient development or function of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons. Through whole-exome sequencing in familial CHH cases, we identified two rare heterozygous missense variants in WFS1. Functional in vitro assays revealed reduced protein levels, activation of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and unfolded protein response (UPR). Zebrafish and mouse embryos studies showed WFS1 expression in regions critical for GnRH neuron development. Knockdown of wfs1b in Tg(GnRH3:EGFP) zebrafish embryos disrupted GnRH3 neuronal architecture and downregulated isl1a, a key transcription factor for axon guidance. Our findings support a mechanistic model linking WFS1-mediated ER homeostasis, isl1a expression, and GnRH neuron development. We propose WFS1 as a novel candidate modifier in CHH pathogenesis and provide in vivo evidence that ER stress and isl1a dysregulation impair the formation of GnRH neuronal network.

primary.title: Genomic landscape of rare variants in a Chinese autism cohort and discovery of novel risk genes.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a genetically complex neurodevelopmental condition with a high heritability. However, genomic studies of ASD have been underrepresented in East Asian populations, and the molecular yield in ASD cohorts remains modest. Here, we present a whole-genome sequencing analysis of 3109 samples across 1033 Chinese ASD families. By examining a wide spectrum of genetic variation, we identified rare ASD-associated variants in 19.2% of affected individuals, providing a population-specific view of the genetic architecture of ASD. We identify significant enrichment of de novo variants in probands, nominate or strengthen candidate risk genes (e.g., NCL, SPPL3, ADGRB1, SLC9A3, KIF1B) through mutational burden, evolutionary constraint, recurrent missense site, and functional assays, and implicate convergent pathways including protein palmitoylation. By integrating over 40,000 ASD cases across unpublished and published global cohorts, we identify 245 ASD risk genes, including 45 with limited prior evidence and 32 with no prior association. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the developing human cortex reveals that ASD risk genes exhibit widespread yet heterogeneous expression across all major cell types, with peak expression in excitatory neurons, particularly intratelencephalic neurons, and enriched expression in microglia (e.g., C1QC, CARD11, SNX13, MEF2C, FOXP2, TCF12, MED13L), suggesting convergent involvement of both synaptic and neuroimmune mechanisms. Together, our findings expand the ASD genetic landscape and suggest convergent pathogenic axes involving transcriptional regulation, synaptic signaling and plasticity, and neuroimmune interactions. This work supports the development of inclusive diagnostic strategies and provides a foundation for mechanistic and intervention exploration in ASD.

Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

primary.title: Overexpression of endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1 alters neuronal metabolism, growth, and synaptic activity.
primary.abstract: Acetyl-CoA is a molecule central to cellular metabolic homeostasis. As part of the secretory pathway, acetyl-CoA is imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound transporter AT-1 (SLC33A1). AT-1 mutations have been linked to peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay with premature death, and intellectual disability with progeria. Here, we show that AT-1 overexpression impacts diverse phenotypes related to neuronal function and plasticity. Differences in ribosomal, synaptic processing, and metabolic pathways were identified at transcriptomic and proteomic levels. Metabolic adaptations included changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, architecture, and respiration, and tracing experiments revealed changes in the fate of glucose favoring glycogen storage over the pentose phosphate pathway. Altered redox was linked to NAD-dependent proteins SIRT1 and CtBP2. Depletion of lipid stores was associated with greater plasticity in fuel substrate utilization. Metabolic adaptation was coincident with decreased synaptic activity, indicating that neuronal communication is coordinated, in part, through acetyl-CoA metabolism.

secondary.title: Phenotypic expansion of TUBGCP6 primary microcephaly: severe cortical malformations without chorioretinopathy and insights into variant interpretation.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Biallelic variants of TUBGCP6 are associated with primary microcephaly, chorioretinopathy, short stature, and intellectual disability (ID). Most reported cases had at least one loss-of-function variant. PURPOSE: : We aimed to refine the phenotypic spectrum associated with novel TUBGCP6 variants in 3 patients, including 2 with biallelic missense variants, and compare them with 13 previously reported cases. METHODS: : Neurological, cognitive, and neuroimaging data were assessed in 3 patients carrying TUBGCP6 variants identified using next-generation sequencing. These 3 patients were recruited through the Microfanc project (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01565005) or a call for collaboration with the ITHACA European Reference Network. Functional analyses of the fibroblasts from 1 patient included Western blotting, immunofluorescence, and proximity ligation assays. Variants were further characterized using complementary sequence- and structure-based in silico analyses, including structural modeling, stability, conservation, and protein language model-based predictions. RESULTS: : None of the patients had chorioretinopathy or short stature at the last follow-up (age: 7.8, 15, and 17.6 years). Two patients presented with malformations of cortical development, microcephaly, gyral simplification, and focal epilepsy. Cognitive impairment ranged from borderline intelligence quotient to severe ID. Patient 1 carried compound heterozygous missense variants, p.(Val359Ile) and p.(Gly990Arg). TUBGCP6 failed to localize to the centrosome and to interact with γ-tubulin. Patient 2 carried the homozygous missense variant p.(Leu448Pro) predicted to destabilize TUBGCP6. Patient 3 harbored 2 compound heterozygous frameshift variants, p.(Gln1389GlyfsTer13), which was predicted to under gononsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), and p.(Pro1759AlafsTer68), which may produce an aberrant C-terminal extension, although NMD remains possible. CONCLUSION: : This study expands the phenotypic spectrum of TUBGCP6-related diseases to include malformations of cortical development, microcephaly with or without ID, and the absence of chorioretinopathy. Our combined in vitro and in silico findings suggest that stable but dysfunctional TUBGCP6 may produce a more severe brain phenotype than a complete loss of function, while sparing the retina. However, these mechanistic insights remain preliminary.

secondary.title: Gut microbiota profiles and neurodevelopmental symptoms in children from a prenatal-risk enriched birth cohort: findings from the PREDO study.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) are common neurodevelopmental conditions whose early-life biological correlates remain incompletely understood. Children's gut microbiota may represent a biological pathway through which immune-metabolic and gut-brain signalling links early-life adversity with neurodevelopment. We examined gut microbiota profiles associated with ADHD and ASD symptoms in children from the Prediction and Prevention of Preeclampsia and Intrauterine Growth Restriction (PREDO) birth cohort. METHODS: We analysed data from 323 Finnish children assessed at a mean age of 8.6 years. Stool microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA sequencing and differential taxonomic abundance was assessed using MaAsLin2. ADHD and ASD symptoms were mother-rated using the Conners' Parent Rating Scale-Revised and Autism Spectrum Screening Questionnaire. RESULTS: Clinically relevant ADHD and ASD symptoms were associated with metric-specific reductions in alpha diversity, whereas beta diversity did not differ between groups. Male children with clinically relevant ADHD symptoms showed lower abundance of Lachnospiraceae_FCS020_group, Subdoligranulum, Fusicatenibacter, and Anaerostipes (ps ≤ 0.049). Female children with clinically relevant ADHD symptoms showed a distinct profile, including higher Negativibacillus and Faecalibacterium (p ≤ 0.018). Children with clinically relevant ASD symptoms showed lower abundance of six genera, including Anaerostipes and Lachnospiraceae_ND3007_group (p ≤ 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In this prenatal-risk enriched cohort, ADHD and ASD symptoms were associated with distinct gut microbiota profiles, including alterations in taxa implicated in short-chain fatty acid metabolism, immune regulation, and gut-brain signalling. These findings support microbiota-immune-brain pathways as a hypothesis-generating framework for future longitudinal and multi-omics research.

secondary.title: Proteomic Analysis of Plasma Small Extracellular Vesicles and Targeted Metabolomic Analysis of Plasma From Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder.
secondary.abstract: Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder with deficits in social communication and interaction, restricted and repetitive behaviors, and unusual stereotyped interests or activities. With a lack of molecular information on the etiology of ASD, early diagnosis of this disease remains a challenge. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), as extracellular vesicles containing various important biomolecules, have been demonstrated to have a functional impact on physiological processes in the central nervous system. Herein, we profiled the proteome of plasma sEVs collected from preschool children with autism and performed targeted metabolic analysis on their plasma samples. Screening of the differentiated proteins between autistic and healthy children revealed potential biomarkers, including those involved in calcium ion binding, such as MACF1 and CALM3. Bioinformatic investigation further identified 10 outlier proteins, such as EHD1 and ERF3A, strongly associated with autism. Targeted metabolic analysis and IPA prediction suggested the potential involvement of the PI3K-AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. The sEV proteomic and plasma metabolomic analyses were performed in parallel, and pathway-level findings from each dataset were compared descriptively. These results provide insight into the biological mechanism of autism and promise in determining biomarkers for the early diagnosis of ASD. secondary.title: Decolonising Autistic Phenomenology: Towards a Critical-Enactive Account of Cognitive Diversity.
secondary.abstract: Recent years have seen a turn toward phenomenological, ecological, and enactive approaches to autism and neurodiversity, within the philosophy of psychiatry and cognitive science. These approaches challenge dominant neuro-reductionist and computational biomedical paradigms, centring embodiment, relationality, affectivity, and the constitutive role of sociomaterial environments in cognition. However, both phenomenological and ecological-enactive approaches are heterogeneous; not all escape the Eurocentric neuronormative assumptions underlying colonial modernity. This paper argues that, where classical phenomenology positions autism as a deviation from implicitly Western standards of 'neurotypical' embodiment and intersubjectivity, critical phenomenology and enactivism supply promising resources to reconceive autistic traits as intrinsically meaningful forms of sense-making - whilst interrogating the universality of categories such as 'autism' and 'neurotypicality.' Critical phenomenology draws attention to how power shapes embodiment, stretching the phenomenological method to confront its own complicity in Eurocentric neuronormativity. Enactivism goes further, providing an inclusive relational ontology of cognitive diversity that can facilitate dialogue with non-Western and Indigenous ways of knowing. Yet it risks becoming politically neutralised when inattentive to coloniality and intersectional oppression. Drawing insight from South Asian autistic experiences, I sketch out a critical-enactive framework oriented toward dismantling both neuronormative and Eurocentric (including logocentric and anthropocentric) assumptions in phenomenology and cognitive science. This decolonial approach paves the way for a pluralistic, intercultural understanding of autism - and embodied cognitive diversity, more broadly - doing justice to culturally and ecologically situated styles of sense-making, without essentialising neurological or cognitive differences.

secondary.title: Subfield-specific hippocampal enlargement in high-functioning autism spectrum disorder.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although previous studies have reported abnormal hippocampal volumes in children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), the specific alterations in hippocampal subfields and their relationships with clinical symptoms in high-functioning ASD (HF-ASD) remain unclear. METHODS: In this study, we analyzed T1-weighted structural MRI data from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I (ABIDE-I), including 182 children and adolescents with HF-ASD and 213 age- and sex-matched typically developing controls (TDC). Using a linear mixed-effects model, we compared hippocampal volumes between groups, and examined associations between volumes and clinical measurements. RESULTS: Compared to TDC, the children and adolescents with HF-ASD exhibited significantly increased volumes in the right entire hippocampus, presubiculum, subiculum, and granule cell layer of the dentate gyrus (GC-DG). No significant volumetric differences were observed within the child or adolescent subgroups, nor between these age groups. Notably, presubiculum volume showed a positive correlation with verbal scores and a negative correlation with social scores in the HF-ASD group. CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate subfield-specific hippocampal overgrowth in children and adolescents with HF-ASD and presubiculum volume alteration may be a potential neuroanatomical correlate underlying verbal and social dysfunctions.

secondary.title: Association of Pubertal Timing and Progression with Variation in the Dual Systems Imbalance Gap: The Moderating Role of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
secondary.abstract: This study sought to examine the direct effects of puberty on dual systems imbalance for male and female youth and test for a moderating effect of autism spectrum disorder. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development data were analyzed. Ordinary least squares regression was used to test for direct and moderated effects of interest. Earlier pubertal development was associated only marginally significantly associated with greater dual systems imbalance characterized by greater sensation-seeking and lower impulse control for male youth. Autism spectrum disorder was significantly and negatively associated with dual systems imbalance, meaning lower sensation-seeking and greater impulse control. No significant direct effects were observed for female youth. No significant moderation effects were observed for either sex. Findings suggest the importance of autism and potentially pubertal developmental rate for understanding dual systems development for male youth, but not female youth.

secondary.title: Associations of Blood Metal(loid) Mixture with Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: A Case-Control Study.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder influenced by both genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures. Heavy metals and metalloids can cross the blood-brain barrier and disturb neurodevelopment; however, most previous studies focused on single-metal effects rather than real-world mixed co-exposure. This case-control study aimed to evaluate associations between blood metal(loid) mixtures and childhood ASD risk. 30 children with ASD and 30 typically-developing controls aged 2-7 years were enrolled in Guangxi, China. Whole-blood concentrations of lead, mercury, arsenic, cadmium, chromium, and manganese were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Univariate analyses, multivariable logistic regression, and quantile-based g-computation (qgcomp) were applied to assess individual and joint effects. Univariate results showed higher blood lead and cadmium concentrations in ASD children. After adjusting for covariates, each doubling of blood cadmium concentration was associated with higher odds of ASD (Firth-penalized OR = 18.64, 95% CI: 1.75-315.18; P = 0.014); the maximum-likelihood estimate was similar in direction but wider (OR = 27.96, 95% CI: 2.20-577.77; P = 0.017). Because of the small number of events this estimate is interpreted with caution. In the qgcomp model, a simultaneous one-quartile increase in all six metal(loid)s was associated with higher odds of ASD, although the joint effect was not statistically significant (OR = 1.28, 95% CI: 0.70-2.35; P = 0.422). Cadmium carried the largest positive weight within the mixture (0.43), and manganese the largest negative weight (- 0.31); because the weights are constrained to sum to unity in absolute value and the joint effect was not significant, they are interpreted as descriptive summaries of relative contribution rather than as tests of the effect of each metal(loid). Our findings suggest that blood cadmium concentration may be associated with ASD, but the evidence is limited: the joint effect of the mixture was not statistically significant, the component weights are descriptive rather than tests of individual effects, and the single-metal estimate for cadmium was imprecise. These observations highlight the necessity of mixture-exposure assessment in ASD-related environmental epidemiological research, and require replication in larger samples.

secondary.title: Perspectives of parents of children with monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders on research involving patient-derived neuronal models.
secondary.abstract: Patient-derived stem cell-based neuronal models hold great promise for advancing research into monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders (mNDDs). These neuronal models are generated using induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) technologies, and are perceived as "ethically sensitive". To date, ethical discussions on the use of neuronal models have predominantly focused on three-dimensional (3D) neuronal models, such as brain organoids, while two-dimensional (2D) neuronal models - which are widely used in current research settings - remain underexplored. A better understanding of the perspectives of parents of children with mNDDs on ethical issues - including the moral status of 2D models, informed consent, autonomy, privacy and misuse - is needed. We report the results of a semi-structured interview study among parents of children with mNDDs (n = 28) investigating their perspectives on the ethically responsible use of 2D patient-derived neuronal models in research. Respondents ascribed limited intrinsic value to neuronal models, often viewing them as ethically comparable to other somatic cells. They were highly motivated to enroll their child in iPSC research, but suggested that researchers: (1) restrict the use of their child's donated material to purposes benefiting the mNDD community, (2) protect their child's privacy, (3) communicate about research findings and reuse of donated material, and (4) minimize risks and burdens of research procedures for their (vulnerable) child. Based on these findings, we provide recommendations to research groups for informed consent and engagement processes to support responsible inclusion of children with mNDDs and their families in research using iPSC-based neuronal models.

secondary.title: International Multicenter Retrospective Study on UBTF-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: UBTF encodes the upstream binding transcription factor (UBTF), a protein essential for rRNA synthesis. Dominantly acting pathogenic variants, either de novo or inherited, have been associated with a broad clinical childhood-onset neurodegenerative/neurodevelopmental spectrum whose genotype-phenotype correlation has not been accurately defined yet. This multicenter study aims to conduct a retrospective analysis of a large cohort of patients with pathogenic variants in the UBTF gene to refine diagnostic criteria and identify clinically relevant outcome measures for future trials. METHODS: Clinical centers provided clinical, molecular, and neuroimaging data on patients carrying pathogenic or predicted pathogenic UBTF variants, consistent with the clinical phenotype. Data were collected using an human phenotype ontology-based standardized electronic case report form and included unreported cases or updated information on patients reported in the literature from January 2017 to December 2024. RESULTS: A cohort of 49 patients (23 previously unreported) was included in the study. The disease typically presented at ≤3 years (89.6%) with neuroregression in 71.4% of cases, either in a child with preexisting neurodevelopmental delay (42.9%) or after previously normal psychomotor development (28.6%). Less frequently, neurodevelopmental delay occurred in isolation (26.5%). During disease progression, patients developed behavioral abnormalities (81.6%), movement disorders (78.3%), autonomic manifestations (50.0%), and epilepsy (34.7%). At the last follow-up (mean age 13 years and 6 months), only 2 patients were deceased (4.1%). The main neuroimaging findings included white matter hyperintensity (68.1%), cerebral (66.0%) and cerebellar (51.1%) atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum (38.3%). However, brain MRI findings were reported as normal in 21.3% of cases. We identified 7 novel UBTF variants (c.271G>C; c.349A>T; c.495C>A; c.517G>A; c.761A>G; c.1048-2A>G; and c.1625_1626+15del). Genotype-phenotype analysis led to the distinction of 2 allelic, clinically distinct disorders: a childhood-onset neurodegenerative disease due to gain-of-function variants, characterized by the triad of neuroregression, movement, and behavioral disorders, and a neurodevelopmental disorder with a milder clinical course associated with loss-of-function/hypomorphic variants. DISCUSSION: The results from our deep-phenotyping analysis suggest the classification of UBTF-related disease into 2 main clinical syndromes impacting the natural history of the disease with a different degree of severity and complexity. This novel observation should be considered in the management and prognosis of patients and will be fundamental in the design of targeted therapies.

secondary.title: Cross-tissue transcriptome-wide association analyses prioritize the 17q21.31 locus in autism spectrum disorder.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has a complex genetic architecture, and the regulatory transcripts underlying common-variant associations with ASD risks remain incompletely resolved. We integrated ASD genome-wide association summary statistics with genetically predicted expression across 29 GTEx v8 tissues using Joint-Tissue Imputation (JTI) and FUSION, followed by summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), regional conditional/joint analysis, colocalization and comparison with external ASD molecular evidence. All-tissue false-discovery-rate correction identified 264 significant JTI gene-tissue associations representing 64 genes and 561 FUSION associations representing 128 genes, with an overlap of 40 genes between JTI and FUSION and 152 unique genes in the union set. Brain eQTL and mQTL SMR identified 22 and 21 significant probes, respectively, while analyses across 16 non-brain tissues identified 59 significant probe-tissue associations. TWAS signals converged at 17q21.31. Conditional/joint FUSION retained only the Brain Cerebellar Hemisphere MAPT-AS1 model among 353 significant associations in the primary regional analysis, with the same model retained in an extended-window sensitivity analysis. BrainMeta-ASD colocalization was completed for 23 probes; none met the prespecified criterion for strong colocalization, and MAPT showed the highest PP·H4 (0.5052). Among the 152 union genes, 82 were supported by at least one of the Huang, Matoba or Gandal studies and 15 by at least two; MAPT and XRN2 were the only genes supported by all three data sets. MAPT-AS1 was supported by Matoba et al. in H-MAGMA analysis and is classified as a Category 2 gene in SFARI Gene, while Walker et al. provided additional developmental-brain context through prenatal-brain TWAS. These findings prioritize 17q21.31 as an ASD-associated locus supported across multiple genetic and regulatory evidence layers.

secondary.title: Disruption of GAD1 protein architecture by a novel missense variant in a consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intellectual disability represents a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental disorders marked by significant impairments in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior. Among the various causes, genetic factors play a major role, with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID) constituting a genetically diverse subgroup. ARID is prevalent in consanguineous families and arises from homozygous mutations that disrupt critical genes involved in brain development and function. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to identify disease-causing genetic variants responsible for ARID in a consanguineous Pakistani family and to evaluate the structural and functional impact of a novel variant identified in GAD1 through protein modeling. METHODS: A consanguineous family affected with intellectual disability was enrolled. Whole-exome sequencing was performed on an affected individual, followed by bioinformatics analysis including alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome, variant calling, and annotation. Variants were filtered based on rarity, predicted functional impact, and autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Candidate variants were validated and assessed by Sanger sequencing and segregation analysis. Protein modeling was performed to evaluate the structural impact of the identified variant. RESULTS: A novel homozygous missense variant NM_000817:c.1700G>A;p.Arg567Gln in GAD1 was identified. Segregation analysis confirmed co-segregation of the variant with the affected phenotype. Protein modeling suggested that the variant may disrupt GAD1 enzymatic function involved in gamma-aminobutyric acid synthesis. CONCLUSION: This study emphasizes the significance of genetic investigation in familial cases and the crucial role that GAD1 mutations play in neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability. The results advance the knowledge of molecular causes of ARID and broaden the mutational range.

secondary.title: Stress-induced alterations in neurodevelopment in iPSC-Derived i n vitro model systems.
secondary.abstract: Psychological stress is common in women during pregnancy and after childbirth, showing a prevalence of up to 15.6% in pregnant women in developing countries. Clinical and pre-clinical studies have implicated their role in negatively affecting pregnancy outcomes and have been linked to adverse child outcomes. Yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, specifically the signatures associated with their effect on human fetal development. Thereby, impairing our further understanding of the effects of therapeutics used to treat these disorders in expecting mothers. This study proposes the use of human iPSC-derived embryoid bodies (EBs) and forebrain-specific organoids as complementary human developmental models to investigate the effects of exposure to prenatal stress (mediated by glucocorticoids) across distinct stages, in vitro. Our findings suggested that excessive glucocorticoids altered early lineage specification in an exposure-dependent manner. This was evidenced by a brief increase in pluripotent and neural progenitor populations, with mild alterations in proliferative dynamics without a net change in proliferative capacity. Changes in lineage-associated markers were observed in ectodermal and meso-endodermal layers of EBs. Particularly, focusing on neurogenesis (forebrain-specific organoids) to understand the impact of stress on neurodevelopment, we saw concentration-dependent changes in progenitor maintenance and neuronal- glial differentiation. Furthermore, the activation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses can be implicated as signalling mechanisms responsible for the differences observed. Together, these results suggest that glucocorticoid signalling linked to prenatal stress can alter developmental trajectories by modifying cellular states rather than directly altering proliferation or survival during early development.

secondary.title: Persistent autism-like behaviors and multilevel neurobiological abnormalities following prenatal valproic acid exposure in rats.
secondary.abstract: Prenatal valproic acid (VPA) exposure is widely used to model autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the persistence of its behavioral effects and the accompanying multilevel neurobiological abnormalities remain incompletely understood. Here, we integrated behavioral, histological, morphological, electrophysiological, molecular, metabolomic, and epigenomic analyses to characterize the long-term effects of prenatal VPA exposure in rats from early postnatal life through adulthood. Prenatal VPA exposure caused delayed early development and persistent ASD-like phenotypes, including repetitive behaviors, impaired social interaction, anxiety-like behavior, reduced exploration, and cognitive deficits. These behavioral abnormalities were accompanied by neuronal and glial alterations and reduced dendritic complexity and spine density in the medial prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, as well as reduced excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs and decreased expression of key synaptic proteins in the medial prefrontal cortex. Multi-omics profiling further identified candidate metabolic alterations involving membrane lipid remodeling, neuromodulatory metabolism, and inflammatory lipid signaling, alongside bidirectional, locus-specific DNA methylation changes enriched in neurodevelopmental and synaptic pathways. Together, these findings show that prenatal VPA exposure produces persistent ASD-like phenotypes accompanied by multilevel cellular, structural, synaptic, metabolic, and epigenetic abnormalities. This work provides an integrated framework for understanding the long-term consequences of prenatal VPA exposure and supports the VPA model as a valuable platform for investigating mechanisms underlying ASD.

secondary.title: Deep Brain Stimulation of the Nucleus Accumbens and Anterior Limb of the Internal Capsule in Severe Autism Spectrum Disorder: Clinical Outcomes and Infralimbic-Accumbens Circuit Involvement.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder with limited effective treatments. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) has emerged as a potential intervention, yet its efficacy and mechanisms remain poorly understood. We conducted a prospective, single-arm cohort study of nucleus accumbens-anterior limb of the internal capsule (NAc-ALIC) DBS in patients with severe ASD, observing preliminary safety and longitudinal reductions in repetitive-behaviour and social-domain symptom severity during follow-up. Exploratory sweet-spot analysis suggested a candidate medial-ventral NAc region associated with social-domain score reductions. In a maternal immune activation mouse model, NAc-DBS enhanced social novelty preference and reduced repetitive behaviours. NAc-DBS partially normalized aberrant oscillatory activity in the NAc and infralimbic cortex (IL), increased IL neuronal activity, and enhanced cross-frequency coupling. Chemogenetic activation of the IL→NAc projection enhanced social novelty preference, whereas inhibition of IL neurons projecting to the NAc attenuated the DBS-associated social novelty improvement without affecting marble-burying behaviour. NAc-DBS also increased glutamate, AMPA receptor, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor levels, consistent with enhanced synaptic plasticity. Together, these findings provide exploratory clinical evidence of longitudinal reductions in symptom severity during follow-up after NAc-ALIC DBS and suggest that NAc stimulation modulates IL and NAc neural activity, implicates the IL→NAc pathway, and engages plasticity-related processes.

secondary.title: Maternal gluten diet exacerbates offspring autistic-like behaviors through the gut-brain axis mediated by gut microbial metabolite elaidic acid.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental conditions characterized by social deficits and stereotyped behaviors, for which effective treatments remain lacking. Here we investigated whether early-life gluten exposure exacerbates autism-like behaviors in BTBR mice and explored the underlying microbiota-metabolite-brain mechanism. Early-life gluten exposure aggravated social avoidance, anxiety, and repetitive behaviors in BTBR offspring, accompanied by reduced mushroom dendritic spine density and diminished microglial branch complexity in the hippocampus. Microbiota sequencing revealed gut microbial dysbiosis, with increased abundance of Hungatella hathewayi and Eubacterium sp. Marseille-P4003. Consistent with their capacity for lipid transformation, untargeted metabolomics showed enrichment of unsaturated fatty acid metabolism and elevated fecal elaidic acid levels. Clinically, targeted quantification confirmed that fecal elaidic acid was significantly higher in children with ASD than in their healthy siblings. Supporting a causal role, exogenous elaidic acid administration dose-dependently worsened behavioral deficits and induced hippocampal spine loss and amoeboid microglial activation. Mechanistically, intestinal transcriptomics revealed activation of antigen processing and presentation and cytokine signaling pathways, whereas hippocampal transcriptomics showed downregulation of immune negative regulators (Egr2, Egr4) alongside enrichment of MHC-I and TNF pathways, indicating impaired central immune restraint. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that early-life gluten exposure induces gut microbiota dysbiosis that drives elaidic acid accumulation, which in turn activates intestinal immunity and suppresses hippocampal immune negative regulation via the gut-brain axis, ultimately aggravating neuroinflammation and autism-like behaviors.

secondary.title: Differential frontostriatal ΔFosB dynamics and behavioral flexibility in autism like VPA-exposed mice.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) involves social impairments, repetitive behaviors, and behavioral inflexibility, defined as an inability to adapt behavior to changing contingencies, and is linked to frontostriatal dysfunction. How behavioral training modulates these circuits is unclear, but ΔFosB, a marker of sustained neural activity, may be useful to establish their relationship. The aim was to evaluate frontostriatal ΔFosB expression following prenatal exposure to valproic acid (VPA) and to determine how experience in the midsession reversal (MSR) task modulates posterior ΔFosB expression. CD-1 mice were prenatally exposed to VPA (500 mg/kg) or vehicle. Brains from postnatal day (PND) 30 mice were analyzed to quantify baseline ΔFosB + cells in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), dorsal striatum (DS), and ventral striatum (VS). In the second experiment, mice performed the MSR task for 13 days. Then, ΔFosB was re-evaluated at PND43 to assess experience-dependent changes. At PND30, VPA-exposed mice showed a significant increase in ΔFosB + cells in mPFC, OFC, DS, and VS, suggesting sustained activity-dependent engagement of the frontostriatal circuit. In the MSR task, mice adapted to contingency shifts using mixed strategies, including win-stay/lose-shift behavior and temporal estimation, whereas VPA mice showed less consistent strategy selection after reversal. After MSR, ΔFosB expression in the OFC and striatum of VPA mice normalized to control levels and remained persistently elevated in the mPFC at PND43. Thus, prenatal VPA induces long-term increases in neuronal transcriptional changes, suggesting activity-dependent plasticity in the frontostriatal circuit. Despite these neural alterations, behavioral flexibility was preserved, suggesting circuit-level adaptations underlying ASD-related strategies. Future studies could broaden these results by examining sex differences and characterizing the cellular and molecular changes dependent on frontostriatal ΔFosB dynamics.

best.title: Thalamocortical vulnerability in autism spectrum disorder: a computational model of CPEB4 mis-splicing.
best.abstract: Skipping of a neuronal microexon in cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein 4 (CPEB4) transcripts has been linked to idiopathic autism spectrum disorder, but the most susceptible brain regions and cell types are unknown. We asked whether the balance between the splicing activator serine/arginine repetitive matrix 4 (SRRM4) and the RNA-binding repressors polypyrimidine tract-binding proteins 1 and 2 (PTBP1 and PTBP2) is sufficient to predict regional differences in microexon inclusion, and which predictions withstand uncertainty in unmeasured parameters. We modeled their competitive binding to the intronic motifs flanking the microexon, including destabilization of SRRM4 expression by sustained histone deacetylase inhibition, and applied the model to human brain transcriptomic data from tissue samples, single cells and developmental stages. The thalamus expressed markedly less SRRM4 mRNA than the anterior cingulate cortex, and the model predicted lower microexon inclusion in the thalamus in every draw of the sensitivity analysis, although the size of the difference varied widely and absolute inclusion values were poorly constrained. A larger thalamic effect of histone deacetylase inhibition was not robust: it followed from the assumed regional difference in super-enhancer susceptibility, and the cingulate cortex lost more inclusion when this susceptibility was equal in both regions. The model is not experimentally validated, and microexon inclusion has not been measured in the human thalamus. These results propose regional SRRM4 supply as a testable determinant of CPEB4 microexon splicing and identify the measurements needed to test it: microexon inclusion and SRRM4, PTBP1 and PTBP2 protein in thalamic nuclei and cingulate cortex.

best.title: The Cxcl14 chemokine defines pioneer axon guidance and early circuit assembly in the inner ear.
best.abstract: The nervous system wiring requires the precise coordination of axon guidance, neuronal migration, and target cell recognition. Here, we show that inner ear circuit formation relies on pioneer cells extending an axonal scaffold that selectively targets early-born hair cells. High spatiotemporal imaging of pioneer axons reveals how they navigate through the cranial environment, establishing dynamic cell-cell contacts with other axons to finally stabilize in target cells. These pioneer axons are required not only for follower axon growth but also for coordinated migration of follower neurons, revealing a cellular hierarchy underlying circuit assembly. We identify the chemokine Cxcl14 as a novel instructive guidance cue regulating pioneer axon extension, turning, and fasciculation at discrete cellular decision points. Loss of Cxcl14 disrupts axonal navigation, compromises synaptic organization in hair cells, and impairs mechanosensory-based behavior. Together, our findings establish a new chemokine-based mechanism linking pioneer axon guidance to early sensory circuit assembly necessary for building mechanosensory networks.

best.title: RBM42 couples alternative splicing to cytoskeletal organization to direct cortical development.
best.abstract: Alternative splicing coordinates gene expression programs that shape the developing cerebral cortex. Here, we used nervous system-specific Rbm42 conditional knockout mice, RBM42-depleted human SH-SY5Y cells, RNA sequencing, RIP-seq, proteomics, and splice-switching rescue to define how the spliceosomal RNA-binding protein RBM42 supports cortical development. Rbm42 loss caused perinatal lethality, cortical thinning, defective lamination, reduced progenitor proliferation, increased apoptosis, and disrupted neuronal cytoskeletal organization. RBM42 bound and regulated cytoskeleton-associated transcripts, including NIN/Nin and NUMA1/Numa1, and its loss altered their splicing in human cells and mouse cortex. Restoring RBM42 corrected these splicing defects and improved proliferation and neurite growth. Selective correction of NIN exon 18 mis-splicing partially restored βIII-tubulin organization and proliferation but did not rescue apoptosis. These findings connect spliceosome-dependent isoform control with cytoskeletal remodeling during cortical development and provide a mechanistic framework for RBM42-associated neurodevelopmental disease.
