best.title: Kinesin-3 KIF1A functions as a diligent worker and its functionality is regulated by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
best.abstract: Long-distance intracellular transport is driven by motor proteins that walk along microtubule tracks. The fate of the motor protein after transport is unclear. Classically, motor proteins have been thought to function as Diligent Workers (DW) that remain attached to cargo during the entire transport event and are degraded at the end of the journey. In contrast, previous work suggests that kinesin-1 transport can be described by a Loose Bucket Brigade (LBB) model in which individual motor proteins participate in multiple rounds of transport. Here, we used live-cell imaging in iNeurons to test whether the kinesin-3 KIF1A functions as a DW during axonal transport. We demonstrate that the fluorescence intensity of KIF1A on particles undergoing axonal transport does not change over time, suggesting that KIF1A remains attached to its cargo for the entire transport event. We determined that KIF1A has a relatively short protein half-life, consistent with KIF1A being degraded at the end of the journey. Moreover, protein turnover appears to be tightly controlled in iNeurons, as treating cells with inhibitors of the ubiquitin/proteasome system results in a cessation of KIF1A-driven transport, the appearance of KIF1A aggregates in the cell body, and their subsequent degradation through aggrephagy. These results suggest that KIF1A transport fits the DW model and that KIF1A protein levels may play a role in signaling proteostatic stress in neuronal cells.

best.title: HDAC6 inhibition promotes peripheral nerve development and regeneration via neurofilament acetylation.
best.abstract: Peripheral nerve injury remains challenging due to limited neuronal regeneration. Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) regulates microtubule dynamics, but its role in peripheral nervous system (PNS) development and repair is incompletely understood. This study investigates the expression, function, and mechanism of HDAC6 in PNS maturation and regeneration. HDAC6 was abundantly expressed in dorsal root ganglia and sciatic nerves. During postnatal development (P1-P28), HDAC6 expression progressively declined, inversely correlating with increased α-tubulin K40 and global acetylation. Pharmacological HDAC6 inhibition with Tubastatin A (Tub A) or suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA) accelerated nerve maturation, evidenced by enhanced conduction velocity, myelination, and cytoskeletal integrity. In a sciatic nerve crush model, HDAC6 inhibition promoted functional recovery, axonal regeneration, and remyelination. In vitro, HDAC6 inhibition or siRNA knockdown enhanced neurite outgrowth and growth cone expansion in both motor and sensory neurons. Mechanistically, acetylome identified neurofilament light chain (NEFL) as a novel HDAC6 substrate. Among several hypoacetylated lysine residues post-injury, K316 showed the greatest decrease. Direct HDAC6-NEFL interaction was confirmed by molecular docking and co-immunoprecipitation. Expression of an acetylation-mimetic NEFL (K316Q) mutant promoted neurite outgrowth and growth cone maturation compared with wild-type or acetylation-deficient (K316R) mutants. Collectively, HDAC6 acts as a key negative regulator of PNS development and regeneration, and NEFL K316 acetylation serves as a critical molecular switch for axonal growth. Targeting HDAC6 represents a promising strategy for peripheral nerve repair.

best.title: APC regulates NSLIT2-induced internalization and signaling of the chemorepellent receptor, ROBO1.
best.abstract: The SLIT-Roundabout signaling pathway regulates axon guidance and cell migration, and ROBO1 is a receptor for SLIT ligands. ROBO1 undergoes constitutive endocytosis, which is enhanced upon NSLIT2 binding, but the molecular mechanisms and functional consequences of this process are not well understood. Using pharmacologic inhibitors and molecular techniques, we found that clathrin-mediated endocytosis is necessary for NSLIT2-induced inhibition of cell spreading. To explore the underlying mechanisms, we performed proximity-dependent biotin identification to identify ROBO1-interacting proteins whose association with the cytoplasmic domain of ROBO1 is differentially regulated by NSLIT2. We discovered that adenomatous polyposis coli, a multifunctional tumor suppressor, is in close proximity to ROBO1 but dissociates upon binding of NSLIT2 and that this dissociation is necessary for clathrin-mediated endocytosis of ROBO1 and subsequent effects on cell morphology. These findings provide new insights into the functional mechanisms by which NSLIT2 binding to ROBO1 affects changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture.

best.title: Proximity-Induced Targeted Degradation of Microtubule-Associated Protein Tau Pre-mRNA Using Small Bifunctional Molecules.
best.abstract: Dysregulation of RNA processing caused by single-nucleotide mutations can profoundly alter cellular homeostasis and drive disease. A prominent example is the aberrant alternative splicing of the microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) gene, which leads to imbalances in 3R and 4R tau isoforms and is associated with multiple tauopathies. In particular, mutations such as the disinhibition-dementia-parkinsonism-amyotrophy complex (DDPAC) variant promote exon 10 inclusion, increasing the 4R/3R ratio and contributing to tau aggregation and neurodegeneration. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) can reduce MAPT mRNA levels, while small molecules have been developed to modulate MAPT pre-mRNA splicing by targeting regulatory RNA structures. Here, we investigated an alternative approach based on Proximity-Induced Nucleic Acid Degradation (PINAD), in which an RNA-binding ligand is conjugated to an RNA-cleaving warhead. We designed and synthesized a library of 24 bifunctional small molecules derived from a previously reported MAPT pre-mRNA SRE-binding ligand. Screening in SH-SY5Y cells identified PINAD-23, which reduced MAPT mRNA levels in a dose-dependent manner and decreased the expression of both 3R and 4R tau isoforms. Biochemical studies using a model MAPT RNA showed that PINAD-23 binds the target RNA and promotes RNA cleavage. Defined cleavage products detected under metal-free conditions supported a contribution from a base-mediated pathway, while Cu(II) binding by the diimidazole warhead and Cu(II)-dependent RNA cleavage supported the involvement of a copper-dependent pathway. These findings provide a proof of concept for converting a previously characterized MAPT RNA-binding ligand into a bifunctional small molecule capable of inducing target RNA cleavage and reducing downstream tau expression.

best.title: Elevation of the mechanically-sensitive e protein emerin links nuclear mechanotransduction to tau-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in neurons.
best.abstract: Neurodegenerative tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease, are neuropathologically defined by pathological tau deposition. While tau drives neurotoxicity by disrupting cytoskeletal, nucleoskeletal, and genomic architecture, cellular mechanisms mediating tau-induced dysfunction of the cytoskeleton and nucleoskeleton are incompletely understood. Here, we identify proteins with differing abundance in a cellular tauopathy model, iTau. Building upon previous findings that pathogenic tau reduces nuclear tension, we find elevated levels of emerin, a central regulator of nuclear mechanotransduction, in iTau neurons and tau mutant iPSC-derived neurons. Neuronal emerin overexpression drives neurotoxicity, increases filamentous actin (F-actin), and induces nuclear invagination, mimicking cellular phenotypes of tauopathy. Alterations in emerin binding partners reflect its cytosolic relocalization in iTau neurons, suggesting that pathogenic tau may impact nuclear mechanotransduction by altering emerin levels and localization. Overall, we identify emerin as a potential mediator of cytoskeletal and nucleoskeletal remodeling in tauopathy and provide a foundation for future studies of emerin function in neurons.

primary.title: Motor neuron disease due to a novel PIK3R1 mutation.
primary.abstract: Mutations in PIK3R1, which encodes the regulatory subunit (p85α) of class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), are associated with immunologic and developmental disorders, but their effects on the nervous system have not been studied. We identified a novel heterozygous frameshift mutation (PIK3R1 c.1710dup) in a patient with common variable immunodeficiency who developed adult-onset, slowly progressive ALS-like motor-neuron disease. Studies of patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) demonstrated PIK3R1 haploinsufficiency with selective AKT activation. Investigation of patient's iPSC-derived motor neurons (iMNs) showed reduced neuronal electrical activity, and markedly increased apoptosis. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed coordinated up-regulation of differentiation and apoptosis programs across neuronal and glial clusters. Engineering the PIK3R1 c.1710dup mutation into healthy-control iPSCs reproduced the impaired electrical activity, increased apoptosis, and transcriptional vulnerability, confirming the variant's cell-intrinsic pathogenicity. In contrast, introduction of canonical APDS2-associated PIK3R1 splice mutations into the same genetic background did not produce these abnormalities, establishing a variant-class-specific mechanism of PI3K dysfunction. Together, these findings define PIK3R1 c.1710dup as a distinct pathogenic variant that links PI3K-pathway dysregulation to human motor-neuron degeneration and expands the mechanistic spectrum of PIK3R1-associated disease.

primary.title: Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry for real-time serotonin dynamics in human iPSC-derived neural spheroids.
primary.abstract: Measuring neurotransmission in the human brain could advance our understanding of disorders, including depression. Although fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) has provided valuable insights into neurotransmission in animal models, its application to human systems remains challenging. Here, we present an FSCV-based framework for real-time serotonin measurements in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived three-dimensional (3D) neuronal cultures. We demonstrate reproducible detection of spontaneous and evoked serotonin release from 3D serotonergic spheroids and show that serotonin dynamics differ between serotonin reuptake inhibitors. We investigate how a molecular stress mediator influences serotonin signaling and antidepressant effectiveness. Finally, we extend the platform to co-cultures containing microglia-like cells to examine serotonin dynamics under inflammatory conditions. We present a translational, label-free technology to measure serotonin dynamics in real-time in human stem cell-derived models. This method studies serotonin regulation, with potential applications to drug development and the mechanistic dissection of psychiatric disorders, such as depression.

primary.title: Differential impact of dynein pathogenic variants on mitotic spindle organization and cortical organoid growth.
primary.abstract: Mutations in the dynein heavy chain gene (DYNC1H1) cause a spectrum of neurological disorders, including malformations of cortical development (MCD) and spinal muscular atrophy with lower extremity predominance (SMALED). How these mutations differentially affect dynein functions in the nervous system, leading to distinct pathologies, remains unknown. Using patient-derived cortical organoids, we address how MCD- and SMALED-causing dynein mutations alter human cortical development. We show that MCD-associated mutations alter the growth of organoids, but that SMALED organoids are unaffected, consistent with the microcephaly phenotypes of individuals with MCD. These defects are mirrored by a large increase in apoptotic cell death in MCD organoids. MCD mutations - but not SMALED mutations - strongly affect radial glial progenitor divisions, by inducing severe mitotic spindle defects and leading to prolonged mitotic duration. Mitotic checkpoint inhibition alleviates mitotic delay but fails to prevent apoptosis, indicating that mitotic arrest is not the cause of cell death in MCD. These findings reveal how specific dynein mutations can distinctly disrupt cortical development, establishing mitotic spindle dysfunction and apoptosis as central mechanisms underlying dynein-related microcephaly.

primary.title: Heparan sulfate sulfatases are essential for the patterning of human stem cell-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
primary.abstract: Midbrain dopaminergic neurons (mDA) are selectively lost in Parkinson's disease, driving sustained efforts to generate bona fide mDA neurons from human-induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) for replacement therapy. While morphogen gradients and transcription factors have been extensively studied, extracellular regulators remain largely overlooked. Here, we identify the heparan sulfate-modifying enzymes SULF1 and SULF2 as essential for establishing mDA neuron identity in vitro. Using CRISPR/Cas9-engineered iPSCs, we show that loss of SULF1/2 increases 6-O-sulfated heparan sulfate species and disrupts patterning both at the anteroposterior and dorsoventral axes in human iPSC-derived mDA cultures. Double-knockout cells thus fail to acquire ventral midbrain fates and instead adopt hindbrain, spinal cord and neural crest-like identities as revealed by single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Mechanistically, we partially explain the changed patterning to aberrant FGF signaling and demonstrate that FGF inhibition redirects cells toward midbrain fates, however without restoring ventral identity. These findings establish a critical role for SULF1/2 in mDA neuron in vitro differentiation and uncover a previously unrecognized layer of extracellular control over neural patterning.

primary.title: High-throughput screening of patient iPSC-derived neurons identifies the gut microbial metabolites that attenuate Alzheimer's disease pathology.
primary.abstract: Gut microbiota-derived metabolites influence the gut-brain axis and may impact Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology. However, the microbial metabolites involved in this process and their functional roles are largely unknown. We screened 352 gut metabolites in induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)-derived neurons from individuals with AD to identify compounds that reduce tau hyperphosphorylation. We identified agmatine as a lead candidate, which decreased hyperphosphorylated tau in neurons and cerebral organoids. In 5xFAD mice, agmatine (100 mg/kg/day) improved cognition, reduced amyloid plaques, lowered neuroinflammation, and increased beneficial gut bacteria, including Agathobacter and Bacteroides. Transcriptomic analysis showed that agmatine downregulated complement and inflammatory genes (C1QB, C2, C3AR1, CCL3, CXCL8, and CXCL6) in patient iPSC-derived cerebral organoids. Agmatine also decreased C3aR and pSTAT3 levels in vivo, mechanistically supporting the reduced tau phosphorylation in iPSC-derived neurons. Altogether, these findings identified the therapeutic potential of gut-derived metabolites and identified agmatine as potential treatment for AD.

primary.title: iPSC-derived RPE and retinal organoids from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients show differences in ABCA4 function.
primary.abstract: Stargardt disease is a phenotypically heterogeneous disease caused by bi-allelic mutations in the ABCA4 gene. We generated retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, photoreceptor precursors (PhRPs), and retinal organoids (ROs) from two induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell lines derived from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients. We observed that RPE cells from the patient with peripheral affectation showed reduced ABCA4 expression, reduced phagocytosis and digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POSs), and accumulation of lipid byproducts. ROs from both patients show stunted segments, more rods, caspase-3 activation, and lipofuscin accumulation at week 45 of maturation. Phenotypical differences seen in Stargardt disease patients are caused by their specific ABCA4 variants, but cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the process of photoreceptor degeneration are still poorly understood. Here, we suggest that peripheral phenotypes associated with these macular dystrophies can be linked to poor clearance of POSs by RPE cells, giving these cells a higher role in the pathogenesis of the disease.

primary.title: Astrocytes contribute to long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism affecting microglia in fragile X syndrome.
primary.abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) influence membrane structure and function, energy metabolism, inflammation, and the ability to regulate microglial activity. We show involvement of astrocytes in long-chain PUFA metabolism in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived astrocytes with fragile X syndrome (FXS). FXS astrocytes secreted more n-6 docosapentaenoic acid (n-6 DPA) and displayed a higher n-3 DPA to docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) ratio in medium than controls, consistent with an altered n-6 to n-3 PUFA balance in plasma from the FXS mouse. The FXS-specific increase in n-6 DPA secretion was abolished by treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), which affected gene expression in astrocyte subpopulations and modulated secreted triacylglycerol species. Microglial exposure to n-6 DPA stimulated expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which also tended to increase in microglia with reduced inflammatory marker expression when cultured in medium from ATRA-treated astrocytes. The results indicate that astrocyte-mediated n-6 DPA regulates the trophic functions of microglia in FXS.

primary.title: KIF1A-Mediated Axonal Transport of Netrin-1 in iPSC-Derived Human Forebrain Neurons.
primary.abstract: Netrin-1 is a secreted laminin-like protein that functions as a guidance cue for axon pathfinding in development. Netrin-1 also modulates synapse formation in developing neurons and long-term potentiation in mature neurons. Netrin-1 is expressed in human neurons; however, its intracellular distribution and trafficking have not been assessed. Moreover, there is a genetic association in Caenorhabditis elegans between UNC-6/netrin-1 and UNC-104/KIF1A, a kinesin-3 motor protein required for axonal transport. We characterized the endogenous expression of netrin-1 via immunocytochemistry and demonstrated it is localized to both the axon and dendrites of induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived human forebrain neurons. Next, live-cell imaging of netrin-1-mRFP revealed rapid, bidirectional axonal transport, comparable to that of other cargos undergoing microtubule-based trafficking in vertebrate neurons. To identify the netrin-1 vesicle population, co-localization analyses demonstrated that netrin-1 puncta overlap with the dense-core vesicle marker Chromogranin A. Netrin-1-mRFP and Chromogranin A-eGFP also undergo co-transport within the axon. Finally, we demonstrated a role for the kinesin-3 motor protein, KIF1A, in Netrin-1 transport by demonstrating that KIF1A-associated neurological disease (KAND) patient variants significantly reduce netrin-1 axonal transport.

primary.title: OGT regulates RNA-binding protein nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, but this fails in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
primary.abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

primary.title: Time-dependent effects of rapid-acting antidepressants in iPSC-derived neurons from treatment-resistant depression and healthy volunteers.
primary.abstract: Rapid-acting antidepressants like ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics show promise for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), but the molecular mechanisms that contribute to their therapeutic effects remain unclear. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offer a platform to model human cortical neurons and investigate drug effects in a human-relevant system. Here, iPSCs from individuals with TRD and healthy volunteers (HVs) were differentiated into mature cortical-like neurons and treated for six and 24 h with agents being investigated as rapid-acting antidepressants, including (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine (HNK), psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI). Bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing assessed global and cell-type-specific transcriptomic responses. Synaptic proteins were evaluated via Western blotting and immunocytochemistry. To validate translational relevance, transcriptomic results were compared to CSF proteomics from ketamine-treated HVs. Despite differing initial pharmacological targets, overall gene expression across all compounds was highly correlated at matched timepoints compared to vehicle control, suggesting shared downstream effects. Both glutamatergic and serotonergic drugs converged on pathways involving inflammation, mTORC1 signaling, and cellular growth. At the single-cell level, (2 R,6 R)-HNK showed distinct cell-type specific alterations: upregulation in excitatory neurons and concomitant downregulation of inhibitory neuron populations. Differentially expressed genes from (2 R,6 R)-HNK-treated neurons also overlapped with CSF proteomic signatures from ketamine-treated individuals, supporting the model's translational relevance. This study is the first to assess multiple putative rapid-acting antidepressants in parallel using an iPSC-derived neuron model. Both convergent and drug-specific changes in gene expression and pathway enrichment were observed across diverse compounds, supporting the use of human iPSC-derived neurons in antidepressant drug discovery. primary.title: Convergent neuroimmune signaling underlying rapid antidepressant response to ketamine and psychedelics.
primary.abstract: Despite distinct receptor targets, both ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics produce a rapid clinical response and share biological signatures that suggest convergence on common downstream molecular mediators. To identify shared biomarkers of rapid antidepressant response, this study integrated CSF proteomics from healthy volunteers (HVs) who received intravenous ketamine with transcriptomic analyses from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from participants with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and HVs; iPSCs were treated with ketamine, its metabolite (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), or psilocybin. Multimodal clinical characterization (transcriptomics (n = 16 TRD; 11 HV), magnetoencephalography (MEG) (n = 30 TRD; 25 HV), and plasma cytokines (n = 39 TRD; 25 HV) were also performed on TRD and HV participants who received a single dose of intravenous ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) or placebo. Conserved immune pathways were identified across CSF and iPSC neurons with interleukin-15 (IL)-15 and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) emerging as key regulatory hubs. Transcriptomically, in whole blood, ketamine responders exhibited decreased IL-15 and elevated B-cell signaling pathways at baseline that were reversed post-treatment. At the protein level, plasma IL-7 levels (primary B-cell driver) correlated with baseline MEG gamma power, reaching brain-wide significance across all participants (main effect pFDR < 0.05). The association was most pronounced in the TRD participants across subcortical regions (diagnosis x IL-7 pFDR < 10-14). Post-ketamine, the TRD IL-7-gamma relationship inverted, paralleling widespread gamma power reductions throughout default-mode network regions (session x IL-7 pclc < 0.05). In mixed-effects models, cytokine ratios linked to IL-7/IL-15 signaling predicted antidepressant response (IL-4/interferon gamma (IFN-γ) pFDR < 0.041) and non-response (MCP-1/IL-7 pFDR < 0.009), suggesting that rebalancing within the IL-7/IL-15 axis may contribute to therapeutic efficacy. secondary.title: Perspectives of parents of children with monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders on research involving patient-derived neuronal models.
secondary.abstract: Patient-derived stem cell-based neuronal models hold great promise for advancing research into monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders (mNDDs). These neuronal models are generated using induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) technologies, and are perceived as "ethically sensitive". To date, ethical discussions on the use of neuronal models have predominantly focused on three-dimensional (3D) neuronal models, such as brain organoids, while two-dimensional (2D) neuronal models - which are widely used in current research settings - remain underexplored. A better understanding of the perspectives of parents of children with mNDDs on ethical issues - including the moral status of 2D models, informed consent, autonomy, privacy and misuse - is needed. We report the results of a semi-structured interview study among parents of children with mNDDs (n = 28) investigating their perspectives on the ethically responsible use of 2D patient-derived neuronal models in research. Respondents ascribed limited intrinsic value to neuronal models, often viewing them as ethically comparable to other somatic cells. They were highly motivated to enroll their child in iPSC research, but suggested that researchers: (1) restrict the use of their child's donated material to purposes benefiting the mNDD community, (2) protect their child's privacy, (3) communicate about research findings and reuse of donated material, and (4) minimize risks and burdens of research procedures for their (vulnerable) child. Based on these findings, we provide recommendations to research groups for informed consent and engagement processes to support responsible inclusion of children with mNDDs and their families in research using iPSC-based neuronal models.

secondary.title: A Deep Quantitative Proteome Turnover Platform for Human iPSC-Derived Neurons.
secondary.abstract: Quantitative evaluation of protein turnover in human neurons is crucial for understanding neuron homeostasis and guiding drug development for neurological diseases. However, measuring protein turnover in postmitotic neurons remains challenging because of the broad dynamic range of neuronal protein half-lives and limited proteome coverage in SILAC (stable isotope labeling by amino acids in cell culture) experiments. Here, we established a comprehensive analytical platform for protein turnover measurements in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons by integrating optimized dynamic SILAC labeling, extensive offline peptide fractionation, data-independent acquisition (DIA) LC-MS/MS, and a streamlined computational workflow with stringent kinetic modeling and filtering criteria. As a result, this platform enabled the quantification of 10,792 apparent protein half-lives from 162,854 unique peptides, substantially expanding the coverage of low-abundance regulatory proteins and therapeutically relevant targets, including 72% of the human kinome, 45% of FDA-approved drug targets, and 72% of potential drug targets. Comparative analyses of glutamatergic cortical neurons and spinal motor neurons revealed globally conserved proteome dynamics alongside subtype-specific differences in protein turnover and abundance. To maximize the accessibility and utility of these datasets, we developed NeuronProfile (https://www.neuronprofile.com/), an interactive resource for exploring protein turnover, abundance, protein copy number, peptide-level kinetics, subcellular localization, and therapeutically relevant proteins in human neurons. Together, this work establishes a robust analytical platform and community resource for quantitative studies of neuronal proteostasis, therapeutic target prioritization, and neurological disease research.

secondary.title: Impaired cellular stress adaptability in Alzheimer's disease patient-derived fibroblasts: a PFKFB3-linked transcriptomic response to oxidative stress.
secondary.abstract: Aging-related impairment in cellular stress adaptability may contribute to vulnerability to Alzheimer's disease (AD), but patient-derived experimental models that preserve agingassociated molecular features remain underused. Here, we investigated transcriptomic responses to oxidative stress in ex vivo dermal fibroblasts derived from patients with AD and control participants matched for age and sex. Fibroblasts were exposed to hydrogen peroxide to induce reactive oxygen species-mediated stress, followed by RNA sequencing to identify disease-associated differences in stress-responsive gene regulation. AD-derived fibroblasts exhibited distinct oxidative stress response patterns, with altered regulation of pathways related to endoplasmic reticulum stress, immune activation, autophagy, protein synthesis, and cell cycle control. Systematic candidate gene prioritization identified PFKFB3 as a key stress-responsive gene showing reduced induction in AD fibroblasts. Lower PFKFB3 responsiveness was associated with poorer cognitive performance and higher levels of neurodegeneration-related blood biomarkers, including plasma pTau217, neurofilament light chain, and glial fibrillary acidic protein. In immortalized human astrocytes, PFKFB3 knockdown reduced cell viability under oxidative stress and altered transcriptional programs related to proteostasis, metabolic regulation, and immune activation. These findings suggest that AD is associated with impaired cellular stress adaptability in patient-derived fibroblasts and highlight PFKFB3 as a candidate node linking oxidative stress responsiveness, glial vulnerability, and AD-related pathological burden.

secondary.title: Establishment of polyclonal human induced pluripotent stem cell lines from peripheral blood using a semi-automated processing system.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The generation of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) with homogeneous and stable quality at an affordable cost is key to industrialize hiPSC-based cell therapies and drug development; however, conventional manual production is labor-intensive and difficult to standardize. Automated closed-system approaches can improve reproducibility, reduce contamination risk, and enable scale-out manufacturing, yet concerns remain regarding the quality of hiPSCs produced using this approach specialized in hiPSC generation from peripheral blood cells. METHODS: Here we developed a prototype semi-automated hiPSC production system to generate polyclonal hiPSC lines from peripheral blood cells. The semi-automated device consists of a spiral microfluidic module for leukocyte separation, followed by modules for leukocyte expansion culture and the transduction of a Sendai virus (SeV) vector carrying reprogramming factors. Subsequently, the transduced leukocytes were manually cultured and expanded to generate polyclonal hiPSC lines. RESULTS: The generated polyclonal hiPSC populations maintained a normal karyotype and carried minimal residual SeV vector. Importantly, they exhibited self-renewing capacity and pluripotency comparable to those of established clonal hiPSC lines. Furthermore, when subjected to directed differentiation towards cartilage and kidney organoids, the polyclonal hiPSC lines efficiently differentiated into these lineages. CONCLUSIONS: The semi-automated system enabled the generation of high-quality polyclonal hiPSC lines, which will hold promise for future applications in cell therapy and drug development.

secondary.title: Stress-induced alterations in neurodevelopment in iPSC-Derived i n vitro model systems.
secondary.abstract: Psychological stress is common in women during pregnancy and after childbirth, showing a prevalence of up to 15.6% in pregnant women in developing countries. Clinical and pre-clinical studies have implicated their role in negatively affecting pregnancy outcomes and have been linked to adverse child outcomes. Yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, specifically the signatures associated with their effect on human fetal development. Thereby, impairing our further understanding of the effects of therapeutics used to treat these disorders in expecting mothers. This study proposes the use of human iPSC-derived embryoid bodies (EBs) and forebrain-specific organoids as complementary human developmental models to investigate the effects of exposure to prenatal stress (mediated by glucocorticoids) across distinct stages, in vitro. Our findings suggested that excessive glucocorticoids altered early lineage specification in an exposure-dependent manner. This was evidenced by a brief increase in pluripotent and neural progenitor populations, with mild alterations in proliferative dynamics without a net change in proliferative capacity. Changes in lineage-associated markers were observed in ectodermal and meso-endodermal layers of EBs. Particularly, focusing on neurogenesis (forebrain-specific organoids) to understand the impact of stress on neurodevelopment, we saw concentration-dependent changes in progenitor maintenance and neuronal- glial differentiation. Furthermore, the activation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses can be implicated as signalling mechanisms responsible for the differences observed. Together, these results suggest that glucocorticoid signalling linked to prenatal stress can alter developmental trajectories by modifying cellular states rather than directly altering proliferation or survival during early development.

secondary.title: Restoration of BDNF/TrkB signaling rescues presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis iPSC-derived neurons.
secondary.abstract: GM1 gangliosidosis is a lysosomal storage disease characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and severe central nervous system (CNS) dysfunction. Although the abnormal intracellular accumulation of GM1 ganglioside is recognized as a major pathological feature, the molecular mechanisms underlying neuronal dysfunction remain unclear. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays essential roles in CNS development and the maintenance of synaptic function and plasticity; however, its contribution to the pathology of lysosomal storage diseases remains unclear. We previously identified a marked impairment of neurotransmitter release in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by reduced expression of synapse-related molecules. In this study, we investigated the potential involvement of endogenous BDNF signaling in synaptic dysfunction using human iPSC-derived neurons. We found that endogenous BDNF expression was significantly reduced in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by a marked decrease in full-length tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a key mediator of BDNF signaling. Further, the gene expression of synapse-related molecules involved in neurotransmitter release, including SNAP25 and VAMP2, was reduced. Importantly, exogenous BDNF supplementation ameliorated presynaptic dysfunction and substantially restored the expression of synapse-related molecules, which were reduced in disease neurons. Furthermore, 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (7,8-DHF), a selective TrkB agonist, markedly reversed presynaptic dysfunction. These findings suggest that impaired BDNF/TrkB signaling contributes to presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis and identify the enhancement of this pathway as a potential therapeutic strategy.

secondary.title: Base editing rescues a hereditary motor neuron disease in mouse and patient-derived iPSC organoid models.
secondary.abstract: In hereditary motor neuron diseases (MNDs), including forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) caused by single-nucleotide variants, effective therapeutic strategies need to address both gain- and loss-of-function mechanisms. Genome editing-based gene therapy represents a promising approach for simultaneously targeting these mechanisms. To establish proof-of-concept for base editing in a hereditary MND, we targeted the P285L variant in the TRK-fused gene (TFG), which causes hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with proximal dominant involvement (HMSN-P), a disorder that shares clinical and histopathological features with ALS. We identified the optimal adenine base editor by comparing candidate editors in HMSN-P patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We then generated a transgenic mouse model expressing human TFG P285L and evaluated the selected editor by subpial delivery of adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors to the spinal cord. AAV-mediated base editing prolonged survival, preserved motor neurons, and attenuated axon loss in ventral nerve roots. Treatment with the selected base editing vector reduced TFG aggregation and suppressed neuronal death in HMSN-P iPSC-derived neuromuscular organoids. Collectively, these findings support the therapeutic potential of base editing for hereditary MNDs.

best.title: Motor neuron disease due to a novel PIK3R1 mutation.
best.abstract: Mutations in PIK3R1, which encodes the regulatory subunit (p85α) of class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), are associated with immunologic and developmental disorders, but their effects on the nervous system have not been studied. We identified a novel heterozygous frameshift mutation (PIK3R1 c.1710dup) in a patient with common variable immunodeficiency who developed adult-onset, slowly progressive ALS-like motor-neuron disease. Studies of patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) demonstrated PIK3R1 haploinsufficiency with selective AKT activation. Investigation of patient's iPSC-derived motor neurons (iMNs) showed reduced neuronal electrical activity, and markedly increased apoptosis. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed coordinated up-regulation of differentiation and apoptosis programs across neuronal and glial clusters. Engineering the PIK3R1 c.1710dup mutation into healthy-control iPSCs reproduced the impaired electrical activity, increased apoptosis, and transcriptional vulnerability, confirming the variant's cell-intrinsic pathogenicity. In contrast, introduction of canonical APDS2-associated PIK3R1 splice mutations into the same genetic background did not produce these abnormalities, establishing a variant-class-specific mechanism of PI3K dysfunction. Together, these findings define PIK3R1 c.1710dup as a distinct pathogenic variant that links PI3K-pathway dysregulation to human motor-neuron degeneration and expands the mechanistic spectrum of PIK3R1-associated disease.

best.title: Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry for real-time serotonin dynamics in human iPSC-derived neural spheroids.
best.abstract: Measuring neurotransmission in the human brain could advance our understanding of disorders, including depression. Although fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) has provided valuable insights into neurotransmission in animal models, its application to human systems remains challenging. Here, we present an FSCV-based framework for real-time serotonin measurements in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived three-dimensional (3D) neuronal cultures. We demonstrate reproducible detection of spontaneous and evoked serotonin release from 3D serotonergic spheroids and show that serotonin dynamics differ between serotonin reuptake inhibitors. We investigate how a molecular stress mediator influences serotonin signaling and antidepressant effectiveness. Finally, we extend the platform to co-cultures containing microglia-like cells to examine serotonin dynamics under inflammatory conditions. We present a translational, label-free technology to measure serotonin dynamics in real-time in human stem cell-derived models. This method studies serotonin regulation, with potential applications to drug development and the mechanistic dissection of psychiatric disorders, such as depression.

best.title: Differential impact of dynein pathogenic variants on mitotic spindle organization and cortical organoid growth.
best.abstract: Mutations in the dynein heavy chain gene (DYNC1H1) cause a spectrum of neurological disorders, including malformations of cortical development (MCD) and spinal muscular atrophy with lower extremity predominance (SMALED). How these mutations differentially affect dynein functions in the nervous system, leading to distinct pathologies, remains unknown. Using patient-derived cortical organoids, we address how MCD- and SMALED-causing dynein mutations alter human cortical development. We show that MCD-associated mutations alter the growth of organoids, but that SMALED organoids are unaffected, consistent with the microcephaly phenotypes of individuals with MCD. These defects are mirrored by a large increase in apoptotic cell death in MCD organoids. MCD mutations - but not SMALED mutations - strongly affect radial glial progenitor divisions, by inducing severe mitotic spindle defects and leading to prolonged mitotic duration. Mitotic checkpoint inhibition alleviates mitotic delay but fails to prevent apoptosis, indicating that mitotic arrest is not the cause of cell death in MCD. These findings reveal how specific dynein mutations can distinctly disrupt cortical development, establishing mitotic spindle dysfunction and apoptosis as central mechanisms underlying dynein-related microcephaly.

best.title: Heparan sulfate sulfatases are essential for the patterning of human stem cell-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
best.abstract: Midbrain dopaminergic neurons (mDA) are selectively lost in Parkinson's disease, driving sustained efforts to generate bona fide mDA neurons from human-induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) for replacement therapy. While morphogen gradients and transcription factors have been extensively studied, extracellular regulators remain largely overlooked. Here, we identify the heparan sulfate-modifying enzymes SULF1 and SULF2 as essential for establishing mDA neuron identity in vitro. Using CRISPR/Cas9-engineered iPSCs, we show that loss of SULF1/2 increases 6-O-sulfated heparan sulfate species and disrupts patterning both at the anteroposterior and dorsoventral axes in human iPSC-derived mDA cultures. Double-knockout cells thus fail to acquire ventral midbrain fates and instead adopt hindbrain, spinal cord and neural crest-like identities as revealed by single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Mechanistically, we partially explain the changed patterning to aberrant FGF signaling and demonstrate that FGF inhibition redirects cells toward midbrain fates, however without restoring ventral identity. These findings establish a critical role for SULF1/2 in mDA neuron in vitro differentiation and uncover a previously unrecognized layer of extracellular control over neural patterning.

best.title: High-throughput screening of patient iPSC-derived neurons identifies the gut microbial metabolites that attenuate Alzheimer's disease pathology.
best.abstract: Gut microbiota-derived metabolites influence the gut-brain axis and may impact Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology. However, the microbial metabolites involved in this process and their functional roles are largely unknown. We screened 352 gut metabolites in induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)-derived neurons from individuals with AD to identify compounds that reduce tau hyperphosphorylation. We identified agmatine as a lead candidate, which decreased hyperphosphorylated tau in neurons and cerebral organoids. In 5xFAD mice, agmatine (100 mg/kg/day) improved cognition, reduced amyloid plaques, lowered neuroinflammation, and increased beneficial gut bacteria, including Agathobacter and Bacteroides. Transcriptomic analysis showed that agmatine downregulated complement and inflammatory genes (C1QB, C2, C3AR1, CCL3, CXCL8, and CXCL6) in patient iPSC-derived cerebral organoids. Agmatine also decreased C3aR and pSTAT3 levels in vivo, mechanistically supporting the reduced tau phosphorylation in iPSC-derived neurons. Altogether, these findings identified the therapeutic potential of gut-derived metabolites and identified agmatine as potential treatment for AD.

best.title: Perspectives of parents of children with monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders on research involving patient-derived neuronal models.
best.abstract: Patient-derived stem cell-based neuronal models hold great promise for advancing research into monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders (mNDDs). These neuronal models are generated using induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) technologies, and are perceived as "ethically sensitive". To date, ethical discussions on the use of neuronal models have predominantly focused on three-dimensional (3D) neuronal models, such as brain organoids, while two-dimensional (2D) neuronal models - which are widely used in current research settings - remain underexplored. A better understanding of the perspectives of parents of children with mNDDs on ethical issues - including the moral status of 2D models, informed consent, autonomy, privacy and misuse - is needed. We report the results of a semi-structured interview study among parents of children with mNDDs (n = 28) investigating their perspectives on the ethically responsible use of 2D patient-derived neuronal models in research. Respondents ascribed limited intrinsic value to neuronal models, often viewing them as ethically comparable to other somatic cells. They were highly motivated to enroll their child in iPSC research, but suggested that researchers: (1) restrict the use of their child's donated material to purposes benefiting the mNDD community, (2) protect their child's privacy, (3) communicate about research findings and reuse of donated material, and (4) minimize risks and burdens of research procedures for their (vulnerable) child. Based on these findings, we provide recommendations to research groups for informed consent and engagement processes to support responsible inclusion of children with mNDDs and their families in research using iPSC-based neuronal models.

best.title: iPSC-derived RPE and retinal organoids from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients show differences in ABCA4 function.
best.abstract: Stargardt disease is a phenotypically heterogeneous disease caused by bi-allelic mutations in the ABCA4 gene. We generated retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, photoreceptor precursors (PhRPs), and retinal organoids (ROs) from two induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell lines derived from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients. We observed that RPE cells from the patient with peripheral affectation showed reduced ABCA4 expression, reduced phagocytosis and digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POSs), and accumulation of lipid byproducts. ROs from both patients show stunted segments, more rods, caspase-3 activation, and lipofuscin accumulation at week 45 of maturation. Phenotypical differences seen in Stargardt disease patients are caused by their specific ABCA4 variants, but cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the process of photoreceptor degeneration are still poorly understood. Here, we suggest that peripheral phenotypes associated with these macular dystrophies can be linked to poor clearance of POSs by RPE cells, giving these cells a higher role in the pathogenesis of the disease.

best.title: A Deep Quantitative Proteome Turnover Platform for Human iPSC-Derived Neurons.
best.abstract: Quantitative evaluation of protein turnover in human neurons is crucial for understanding neuron homeostasis and guiding drug development for neurological diseases. However, measuring protein turnover in postmitotic neurons remains challenging because of the broad dynamic range of neuronal protein half-lives and limited proteome coverage in SILAC (stable isotope labeling by amino acids in cell culture) experiments. Here, we established a comprehensive analytical platform for protein turnover measurements in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons by integrating optimized dynamic SILAC labeling, extensive offline peptide fractionation, data-independent acquisition (DIA) LC-MS/MS, and a streamlined computational workflow with stringent kinetic modeling and filtering criteria. As a result, this platform enabled the quantification of 10,792 apparent protein half-lives from 162,854 unique peptides, substantially expanding the coverage of low-abundance regulatory proteins and therapeutically relevant targets, including 72% of the human kinome, 45% of FDA-approved drug targets, and 72% of potential drug targets. Comparative analyses of glutamatergic cortical neurons and spinal motor neurons revealed globally conserved proteome dynamics alongside subtype-specific differences in protein turnover and abundance. To maximize the accessibility and utility of these datasets, we developed NeuronProfile (https://www.neuronprofile.com/), an interactive resource for exploring protein turnover, abundance, protein copy number, peptide-level kinetics, subcellular localization, and therapeutically relevant proteins in human neurons. Together, this work establishes a robust analytical platform and community resource for quantitative studies of neuronal proteostasis, therapeutic target prioritization, and neurological disease research.

best.title: Astrocytes contribute to long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism affecting microglia in fragile X syndrome.
best.abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) influence membrane structure and function, energy metabolism, inflammation, and the ability to regulate microglial activity. We show involvement of astrocytes in long-chain PUFA metabolism in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived astrocytes with fragile X syndrome (FXS). FXS astrocytes secreted more n-6 docosapentaenoic acid (n-6 DPA) and displayed a higher n-3 DPA to docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) ratio in medium than controls, consistent with an altered n-6 to n-3 PUFA balance in plasma from the FXS mouse. The FXS-specific increase in n-6 DPA secretion was abolished by treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), which affected gene expression in astrocyte subpopulations and modulated secreted triacylglycerol species. Microglial exposure to n-6 DPA stimulated expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which also tended to increase in microglia with reduced inflammatory marker expression when cultured in medium from ATRA-treated astrocytes. The results indicate that astrocyte-mediated n-6 DPA regulates the trophic functions of microglia in FXS.

best.title: KIF1A-Mediated Axonal Transport of Netrin-1 in iPSC-Derived Human Forebrain Neurons.
best.abstract: Netrin-1 is a secreted laminin-like protein that functions as a guidance cue for axon pathfinding in development. Netrin-1 also modulates synapse formation in developing neurons and long-term potentiation in mature neurons. Netrin-1 is expressed in human neurons; however, its intracellular distribution and trafficking have not been assessed. Moreover, there is a genetic association in Caenorhabditis elegans between UNC-6/netrin-1 and UNC-104/KIF1A, a kinesin-3 motor protein required for axonal transport. We characterized the endogenous expression of netrin-1 via immunocytochemistry and demonstrated it is localized to both the axon and dendrites of induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived human forebrain neurons. Next, live-cell imaging of netrin-1-mRFP revealed rapid, bidirectional axonal transport, comparable to that of other cargos undergoing microtubule-based trafficking in vertebrate neurons. To identify the netrin-1 vesicle population, co-localization analyses demonstrated that netrin-1 puncta overlap with the dense-core vesicle marker Chromogranin A. Netrin-1-mRFP and Chromogranin A-eGFP also undergo co-transport within the axon. Finally, we demonstrated a role for the kinesin-3 motor protein, KIF1A, in Netrin-1 transport by demonstrating that KIF1A-associated neurological disease (KAND) patient variants significantly reduce netrin-1 axonal transport.

best.title: Impaired cellular stress adaptability in Alzheimer's disease patient-derived fibroblasts: a PFKFB3-linked transcriptomic response to oxidative stress.
best.abstract: Aging-related impairment in cellular stress adaptability may contribute to vulnerability to Alzheimer's disease (AD), but patient-derived experimental models that preserve agingassociated molecular features remain underused. Here, we investigated transcriptomic responses to oxidative stress in ex vivo dermal fibroblasts derived from patients with AD and control participants matched for age and sex. Fibroblasts were exposed to hydrogen peroxide to induce reactive oxygen species-mediated stress, followed by RNA sequencing to identify disease-associated differences in stress-responsive gene regulation. AD-derived fibroblasts exhibited distinct oxidative stress response patterns, with altered regulation of pathways related to endoplasmic reticulum stress, immune activation, autophagy, protein synthesis, and cell cycle control. Systematic candidate gene prioritization identified PFKFB3 as a key stress-responsive gene showing reduced induction in AD fibroblasts. Lower PFKFB3 responsiveness was associated with poorer cognitive performance and higher levels of neurodegeneration-related blood biomarkers, including plasma pTau217, neurofilament light chain, and glial fibrillary acidic protein. In immortalized human astrocytes, PFKFB3 knockdown reduced cell viability under oxidative stress and altered transcriptional programs related to proteostasis, metabolic regulation, and immune activation. These findings suggest that AD is associated with impaired cellular stress adaptability in patient-derived fibroblasts and highlight PFKFB3 as a candidate node linking oxidative stress responsiveness, glial vulnerability, and AD-related pathological burden.

best.title: OGT regulates RNA-binding protein nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, but this fails in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
best.abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

best.title: Establishment of polyclonal human induced pluripotent stem cell lines from peripheral blood using a semi-automated processing system.
best.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The generation of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) with homogeneous and stable quality at an affordable cost is key to industrialize hiPSC-based cell therapies and drug development; however, conventional manual production is labor-intensive and difficult to standardize. Automated closed-system approaches can improve reproducibility, reduce contamination risk, and enable scale-out manufacturing, yet concerns remain regarding the quality of hiPSCs produced using this approach specialized in hiPSC generation from peripheral blood cells. METHODS: Here we developed a prototype semi-automated hiPSC production system to generate polyclonal hiPSC lines from peripheral blood cells. The semi-automated device consists of a spiral microfluidic module for leukocyte separation, followed by modules for leukocyte expansion culture and the transduction of a Sendai virus (SeV) vector carrying reprogramming factors. Subsequently, the transduced leukocytes were manually cultured and expanded to generate polyclonal hiPSC lines. RESULTS: The generated polyclonal hiPSC populations maintained a normal karyotype and carried minimal residual SeV vector. Importantly, they exhibited self-renewing capacity and pluripotency comparable to those of established clonal hiPSC lines. Furthermore, when subjected to directed differentiation towards cartilage and kidney organoids, the polyclonal hiPSC lines efficiently differentiated into these lineages. CONCLUSIONS: The semi-automated system enabled the generation of high-quality polyclonal hiPSC lines, which will hold promise for future applications in cell therapy and drug development.

best.title: Stress-induced alterations in neurodevelopment in iPSC-Derived i n vitro model systems.
best.abstract: Psychological stress is common in women during pregnancy and after childbirth, showing a prevalence of up to 15.6% in pregnant women in developing countries. Clinical and pre-clinical studies have implicated their role in negatively affecting pregnancy outcomes and have been linked to adverse child outcomes. Yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, specifically the signatures associated with their effect on human fetal development. Thereby, impairing our further understanding of the effects of therapeutics used to treat these disorders in expecting mothers. This study proposes the use of human iPSC-derived embryoid bodies (EBs) and forebrain-specific organoids as complementary human developmental models to investigate the effects of exposure to prenatal stress (mediated by glucocorticoids) across distinct stages, in vitro. Our findings suggested that excessive glucocorticoids altered early lineage specification in an exposure-dependent manner. This was evidenced by a brief increase in pluripotent and neural progenitor populations, with mild alterations in proliferative dynamics without a net change in proliferative capacity. Changes in lineage-associated markers were observed in ectodermal and meso-endodermal layers of EBs. Particularly, focusing on neurogenesis (forebrain-specific organoids) to understand the impact of stress on neurodevelopment, we saw concentration-dependent changes in progenitor maintenance and neuronal- glial differentiation. Furthermore, the activation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses can be implicated as signalling mechanisms responsible for the differences observed. Together, these results suggest that glucocorticoid signalling linked to prenatal stress can alter developmental trajectories by modifying cellular states rather than directly altering proliferation or survival during early development.

best.title: Restoration of BDNF/TrkB signaling rescues presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis iPSC-derived neurons.
best.abstract: GM1 gangliosidosis is a lysosomal storage disease characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and severe central nervous system (CNS) dysfunction. Although the abnormal intracellular accumulation of GM1 ganglioside is recognized as a major pathological feature, the molecular mechanisms underlying neuronal dysfunction remain unclear. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays essential roles in CNS development and the maintenance of synaptic function and plasticity; however, its contribution to the pathology of lysosomal storage diseases remains unclear. We previously identified a marked impairment of neurotransmitter release in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by reduced expression of synapse-related molecules. In this study, we investigated the potential involvement of endogenous BDNF signaling in synaptic dysfunction using human iPSC-derived neurons. We found that endogenous BDNF expression was significantly reduced in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by a marked decrease in full-length tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a key mediator of BDNF signaling. Further, the gene expression of synapse-related molecules involved in neurotransmitter release, including SNAP25 and VAMP2, was reduced. Importantly, exogenous BDNF supplementation ameliorated presynaptic dysfunction and substantially restored the expression of synapse-related molecules, which were reduced in disease neurons. Furthermore, 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (7,8-DHF), a selective TrkB agonist, markedly reversed presynaptic dysfunction. These findings suggest that impaired BDNF/TrkB signaling contributes to presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis and identify the enhancement of this pathway as a potential therapeutic strategy.

best.abstract: In hereditary motor neuron diseases (MNDs), including forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) caused by single-nucleotide variants, effective therapeutic strategies need to address both gain- and loss-of-function mechanisms. Genome editing-based gene therapy represents a promising approach for simultaneously targeting these mechanisms. To establish proof-of-concept for base editing in a hereditary MND, we targeted the P285L variant in the TRK-fused gene (TFG), which causes hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with proximal dominant involvement (HMSN-P), a disorder that shares clinical and histopathological features with ALS. We identified the optimal adenine base editor by comparing candidate editors in HMSN-P patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We then generated a transgenic mouse model expressing human TFG P285L and evaluated the selected editor by subpial delivery of adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors to the spinal cord. AAV-mediated base editing prolonged survival, preserved motor neurons, and attenuated axon loss in ventral nerve roots. Treatment with the selected base editing vector reduced TFG aggregation and suppressed neuronal death in HMSN-P iPSC-derived neuromuscular organoids. Collectively, these findings support the therapeutic potential of base editing for hereditary MNDs.

best.title: Time-dependent effects of rapid-acting antidepressants in iPSC-derived neurons from treatment-resistant depression and healthy volunteers.
best.abstract: Rapid-acting antidepressants like ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics show promise for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), but the molecular mechanisms that contribute to their therapeutic effects remain unclear. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offer a platform to model human cortical neurons and investigate drug effects in a human-relevant system. Here, iPSCs from individuals with TRD and healthy volunteers (HVs) were differentiated into mature cortical-like neurons and treated for six and 24 h with agents being investigated as rapid-acting antidepressants, including (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine (HNK), psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI). Bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing assessed global and cell-type-specific transcriptomic responses. Synaptic proteins were evaluated via Western blotting and immunocytochemistry. To validate translational relevance, transcriptomic results were compared to CSF proteomics from ketamine-treated HVs. Despite differing initial pharmacological targets, overall gene expression across all compounds was highly correlated at matched timepoints compared to vehicle control, suggesting shared downstream effects. Both glutamatergic and serotonergic drugs converged on pathways involving inflammation, mTORC1 signaling, and cellular growth. At the single-cell level, (2 R,6 R)-HNK showed distinct cell-type specific alterations: upregulation in excitatory neurons and concomitant downregulation of inhibitory neuron populations. Differentially expressed genes from (2 R,6 R)-HNK-treated neurons also overlapped with CSF proteomic signatures from ketamine-treated individuals, supporting the model's translational relevance. This study is the first to assess multiple putative rapid-acting antidepressants in parallel using an iPSC-derived neuron model. Both convergent and drug-specific changes in gene expression and pathway enrichment were observed across diverse compounds, supporting the use of human iPSC-derived neurons in antidepressant drug discovery. best.title: Convergent neuroimmune signaling underlying rapid antidepressant response to ketamine and psychedelics.
best.abstract: Despite distinct receptor targets, both ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics produce a rapid clinical response and share biological signatures that suggest convergence on common downstream molecular mediators. To identify shared biomarkers of rapid antidepressant response, this study integrated CSF proteomics from healthy volunteers (HVs) who received intravenous ketamine with transcriptomic analyses from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from participants with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and HVs; iPSCs were treated with ketamine, its metabolite (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), or psilocybin. Multimodal clinical characterization (transcriptomics (n = 16 TRD; 11 HV), magnetoencephalography (MEG) (n = 30 TRD; 25 HV), and plasma cytokines (n = 39 TRD; 25 HV) were also performed on TRD and HV participants who received a single dose of intravenous ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) or placebo. Conserved immune pathways were identified across CSF and iPSC neurons with interleukin-15 (IL)-15 and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) emerging as key regulatory hubs. Transcriptomically, in whole blood, ketamine responders exhibited decreased IL-15 and elevated B-cell signaling pathways at baseline that were reversed post-treatment. At the protein level, plasma IL-7 levels (primary B-cell driver) correlated with baseline MEG gamma power, reaching brain-wide significance across all participants (main effect pFDR < 0.05). The association was most pronounced in the TRD participants across subcortical regions (diagnosis x IL-7 pFDR < 10-14). Post-ketamine, the TRD IL-7-gamma relationship inverted, paralleling widespread gamma power reductions throughout default-mode network regions (session x IL-7 pclc < 0.05). In mixed-effects models, cytokine ratios linked to IL-7/IL-15 signaling predicted antidepressant response (IL-4/interferon gamma (IFN-γ) pFDR < 0.041) and non-response (MCP-1/IL-7 pFDR < 0.009), suggesting that rebalancing within the IL-7/IL-15 axis may contribute to therapeutic efficacy. primary.title: Functional transcriptomic profile of mouse controlled cortical impact model of post-traumatic epilepsy with robust spontaneous recurrent seizures.
primary.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of acquired epilepsy, yet the molecular changes linking the initial injury to post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) remain incompletely understood. Here, we used a severe controlled cortical impact mouse model that develops robust spontaneous recurrent seizures to characterize the temporal and regional progression of post-traumatic transcriptional responses. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on the contralateral cortex and hippocampus collected from TBI and time-matched sham mice at 7, 21, and 60 days after injury, corresponding to the acute injury, latent period, and chronic epilepsy phases, respectively. Transcriptomic changes were characterized using differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis, Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes gene-set enrichment analyses, and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. Transcriptomic responses were strongly dependent on brain region and disease phase. At 7 days, the cortex showed enhanced neuronal and structural signaling alongside suppression of immune, metabolic, and cell-cycle processes, whereas the hippocampus showed prominent neuroimmune activation and metabolic stress. By 21 days, before the emergence of spontaneous seizures, the hippocampus shifted toward partial normalization of metabolic pathway enrichment, accompanied by suppression of neurotransmission, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal organization. In contrast, the cortex showed increased enrichment of immune and tissue-remodeling processes. Although relatively few DEGs were detected at 60 days, a selective hippocampal signature persisted after PTE was established. Pathway analyses converged on coordinated changes in neuroimmune, metabolic, lipid-regulatory, and synaptic processes. Upstream Regulator Analysis further identified a temporal reversal in APOE-associated regulatory activity, linking inflammatory and lipid-metabolic responses with later synaptic remodeling. The 21-day post-injury hippocampus represents a critical disease-modification window. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PTE progression involves phase-specific molecular remodeling that shifts from an early cortical response to sustained hippocampal dysregulation. The latent hippocampal signature identifies a potentially actionable molecular window before recurrent seizure onset.

primary.title: Parkinson's disease-linked D620N mutation selectively alters the brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35.
primary.abstract: Mutations in several genes are known to cause familial forms of Parkinson's disease (PD), including mutations in the vacuolar protein sorting 35 ortholog (VPS35) gene linked to late-onset, autosomal dominant PD. VPS35 encodes a core subunit of the retromer complex which functions in endosomal sorting and recycling. It remains unclear how the pathogenic D620N mutation in VPS35 disrupts retromer function to induce neurodegeneration in PD. Using cell- and rodent-based models expressing D620N VPS35, we performed interactome proteomics to identify alterations underlying the pathogenic effects of D620N VPS35 in PD. Using overexpression of VPS35 variants in HEK-293 T cells, we conducted tandem affinity purification (TAP) or co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) with protein chemical crosslinking to determine the native and non-native protein interactomes of wild-type (WT) and D620N VPS35, respectively. Notably, we can confirm the reduced interaction of D620N VPS35 with components of the WASH complex. Additionally, using a viral-mediated gene transfer model of human D620N VPS35 overexpression in adult rat brain, we identify the first brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35. These overexpression models reveal remarkably similar interaction profiles of WT and D620N VPS35, suggesting that the D620N mutation has a subtle effect on the overall VPS35 protein interactome. We also conducted proteomic analysis of brain tissue from a D620N VPS35 knockin (KI) mouse model that expresses VPS35 at endogenous levels. Using co-IP from hemibrain or striatal extracts of WT and D620N VPS35 KI mice, we reveal a high degree of similarity between the brain interactomes of WT and D620N VPS35, further suggesting a subtle effect of the D620N mutation on VPS35 protein interactions. Notably, in both hemibrain and striatum, we find a selective decrease in the interaction of two known interactors, TBC1D5 and VPS29, with D620N VPS35. We also performed global proteomic analysis of striatal tissue from D620N VPS35 KI mice and reveal a high degree of similarity between WT and D620N, further suggesting a subtle effect of this mutation. Together, our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the VPS35 protein interactome and reveals a selective effect of the PD-linked D620N mutation in mammalian cells and brain. Our study provides key insight into the mechanisms of retromer dysfunction in VPS35-linked PD.

primary.title: Cellular morphology emerges from polygenic, distributed transcriptional variation.
primary.abstract: Height and disease risk are canonical polygenic traits, but whether an analogous architecture governs cellular phenotypes remains unclear. Here, we show that cellular morphology behaves as a polygenic systems phenotype by integrating cross-modal modeling, perturbation profiling, and human genetic variation. An adversarially aligned autoencoder trained on four perturbation datasets predicted morphology from gene expression and generalized without retraining to matched RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and cell painting profiles from 100 genetically diverse induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) donors. Seventeen morphological features were strongly predicted, particularly those capturing organelle distribution and cytoskeletal architecture. Predictive signal was broadly distributed across genes, with weak individual gene-morphology correlations. Independent CRISPR perturbations supported model-prioritized genes including TIAM1, RAB31, and ABCC5, while genetic analyses identified variant-gene-morphology associations involving PDHX, SLC11A2, and MAPKAPK5. These findings extend polygenic models of complex traits to cellular architecture and provide a framework for interpreting cross-modal prediction in functional genomics.

secondary.title: Integrated serum metabolomics and hippocampal transcriptomics reveal metabolic reprogramming associated with BBB impairment and hippocampal injury in HFD-fed mice.
secondary.abstract: AIMS: Increasing evidence suggests that high-fat diet (HFD) consumption induces systemic metabolic disturbances and is associated with blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction and hippocampal injury. This study aimed to explore the potential mechanisms linking HFD-induced metabolic disturbances to BBB and hippocampal abnormalities. METHODS: Male C57BL/6J mice were fed an HFD or a normal diet (ND) for 12 weeks. Systemic metabolic and inflammatory status, hepatic lipid accumulation, neurobehavioral performance, hippocampal injury, BBB integrity, and hippocampal inflammatory alterations were systematically assessed. Integrated serum untargeted metabolomics and hippocampal transcriptomics were performed to identify key molecular pathways. RESULTS: HFD-fed mice exhibited systemic metabolic disturbances, increased BBB permeability, hippocampal neuronal injury and inflammation, and impaired motor coordination. Integrated serum metabolomic and hippocampal transcriptomic analyses identified alterations in histidine and glycerophospholipid metabolism. Hippocampal transcriptomic analysis revealed upregulation of carnosine dipeptidase 1 (Cndp1) and phospholipase A2 group IVE (Pla2g4e) and downregulation of diacylglycerol kinase kappa (Dgkk) and ethanolamine-phosphate phospho-lyase (Etnppl), which were further validated by RT-qPCR. Serum metabolomic analysis further revealed decreased serum carnosine levels. Given the reported neuroprotective properties of carnosine, we further investigated its effects in palmitic acid-treated HT22 cells. Carnosine improved cell viability, attenuated oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, and modulated the expression of Cndp1, Pla2g4e, Etnppl, and Dgkk. CONCLUSION: HFD was associated with BBB impairment, hippocampal inflammatory activation, neuronal injury, and behavioral alterations. Integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses implicated histidine and glycerophospholipid metabolism associated with HFD-induced metabolic disturbances and hippocampal injury.

secondary.title: Proteomic Analysis of Plasma Small Extracellular Vesicles and Targeted Metabolomic Analysis of Plasma From Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder.
secondary.abstract: Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder with deficits in social communication and interaction, restricted and repetitive behaviors, and unusual stereotyped interests or activities. With a lack of molecular information on the etiology of ASD, early diagnosis of this disease remains a challenge. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), as extracellular vesicles containing various important biomolecules, have been demonstrated to have a functional impact on physiological processes in the central nervous system. Herein, we profiled the proteome of plasma sEVs collected from preschool children with autism and performed targeted metabolic analysis on their plasma samples. Screening of the differentiated proteins between autistic and healthy children revealed potential biomarkers, including those involved in calcium ion binding, such as MACF1 and CALM3. Bioinformatic investigation further identified 10 outlier proteins, such as EHD1 and ERF3A, strongly associated with autism. Targeted metabolic analysis and IPA prediction suggested the potential involvement of the PI3K-AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. The sEV proteomic and plasma metabolomic analyses were performed in parallel, and pathway-level findings from each dataset were compared descriptively. These results provide insight into the biological mechanism of autism and promise in determining biomarkers for the early diagnosis of ASD. secondary.title: A unified framework for scalable differential testing for spatial omics.
secondary.abstract: A key challenge in spatial omics is identifying features whose values vary depending on both cell type and the surrounding cellular niche. Existing methods designed for spatial transcriptomic data do not generalize well to modalities beyond count-based data and do not scale efficiently to current data volumes. Here we introduce spotGLM, a mixture-aware generalized linear modeling framework for cell-type-specific differential testing across spatial modalities, and SPARROW, a power-preserving data distillation strategy for scalable inference. SpotGLM accommodates diverse data types including count-based gene expression, binomial isoform proportions and continuous chromatin accessibility scores within a unified statistical framework. We demonstrate the framework across spatial omics applications. On Visium HD data of colorectal cancer and mouse kidney, we recover cell-type-specific niche effects with serial-slice cross-platform validation. On long-read spatial RNA-seq data, we resolve cell-type-specific isoform switching in the mouse olfactory bulb. On spatial ATAC-seq data from mouse brain, we recover cell-type-specific spatial variation in regulatory motif accessibility.
