primary.title: Label-free, real-time optical biopsy with a handheld quantitative phase microscope.
primary.abstract: We present a compact, handheld quantitative phase imaging microscope that enables label-free, real-time optical imaging of bulk tissues with clear cellular and subcellular histological detail, effectively providing an "optical biopsy." The approach uses quantitative oblique back-illumination microscopy (qOBM) to obtain quantitative phase information of opaque samples using epi-illumination. The probe has a wide-field, non-scanning architecture that achieves 0.8 µm lateral and 5 µm axial resolution across a 300 µm × 300 µm field of view at 25 frames per second. The probe is also low-cost, contains no moving components, is easy to use and can operate through a sterile sheath, addressing key barriers to clinical implementation. To demonstrate its utility, we image (1) human skin in vivo, (2) murine and human brain tumors ex vivo, and (3) swine brain in vivo under typical neurosurgical conditions. By providing real-time, label-free histological information in a robust and accessible handheld format, this technology creates broad opportunities for future clinical translation, including intraoperative and point-of-care histological tissue assessment.

primary.title: Redox-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial nucleoids contributes to bioenergetic decline during neuronal aging.
primary.abstract: Why mitochondria progressively fail in aging neurons remains a fundamental question in neurobiology. Although bioenergetic decline and oxidative stress are hallmarks of aging, whether redox signaling remodels mitochondrial nucleoids (mt-nucleoids) to impair neuronal bioenergetics remains unclear. Using aged mouse neurons and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons, we demonstrate that redox-driven mt-nucleoid remodeling underlies reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and bioenergetic decline. Combining minimal photon fluxes (MINFLUX) nanoscopy with single-molecule transcription mapping, we identify distinct mt-nucleoid architectures governed by mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM)-mediated mtDNA compaction. Aging-associated oxidative stress drives mt-nucleoid remodeling from compact, transcriptionally active structures toward decompacted forms with reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and impaired mitochondrial ATP production. This remodeling involves species-specific TFAM redox mechanisms: cysteine oxidation promotes human TFAM polymerization, whereas methionine oxidation weakens mouse TFAM-mtDNA interactions. Notably, expressing an oxidation-resistant TFAM variant restores mt-nucleoid organization, mtDNA transcript abundance, and ATP production in aged neurons, identifying mt-nucleoid architecture as a potential target for preserving neuronal bioenergetics during aging.

secondary.title: A Correlative Light and Electron Microscopy Workflow for Nanoscale Three-Dimensional Reconstruction of Synaptic Projections From the Thalamic Reticular Nucleus.
secondary.abstract: Correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM) combines molecular specificity with nanoscale ultrastructural resolution and has become an important approach for investigating neural circuit organization. secondary.title: Protocol for imaging and analyzing the synaptic coverage of astrocytes with super-resolution STED microscopy in mouse brain slices.
secondary.abstract: Super-resolution has allowed us to image areas previously inaccessible due to the limits of standard microscopy techniques. Here, we present a protocol to determine the astroglial coverage of synapses. We detail the steps to obtain and label mouse brain slices followed by imaging using 3D stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy and analysis using a custom-made Fiji plug-in, with imaging at a lateral resolution of 80 nm. This technique ascertains the interaction between astrocytes and the glial cell's role in signaling and brain region function.

secondary.title: Cryo-electron tomography of functionally validated synapses in human induced neurons.
secondary.abstract: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) has provided unparalleled insights into synaptic architecture, yet its application to human neurons has been limited by sample preparation challenges. Here, we establish an integrated platform that combines human induced neurons (iNs) cultured directly on electron microscopy (EM) grids with functional electrophysiological validation and cryo-ET imaging. Human iNs formed extensive neuronal networks on EM grids, exhibited reliable synaptic transmission and intrinsic excitability, and maintained short-term synaptic plasticity. While iNs exhibited intact synaptic transmission on EM grids, we found that EM grids acted as a current sink for extracellular electrical stimulation. Following vitrification, cryo-ET enabled direct visualization of ultrastructural features of excitatory synapses, including synaptic vesicle pools, active zone proximal vesicles, postsynaptic densities, and associated organelles. Together, our results establish a foundation for structurally and functionally dissecting synaptic organization between human iNs and provide initial insight into cryo-ET imaging of synapses from stem cell-derived human neurons.

secondary.title: Corpora amylacea and synaptic organization in the human brain analyzed by volume electron microscopy.
secondary.abstract: The presence of corpora amylacea in the brain is a frequent finding in normal aging and in a broad spectrum of neurological disorders, yet the significance of these deposits for the organization of human cortical circuits remains unclear. Here, we combined complementary light and electron microscopy approaches to analyze temporal lobe epilepsy biopsy specimens with and without corpora amylacea. Samples containing corpora amylacea showed marked alterations in synaptic circuit microorganization, which were not restricted to areas of corpora amylacea accumulation but extended throughout the cortical tissue. These changes were characterized by neuronal loss, gliosis, reduced synaptic density, an increased proportion of inhibitory synapses, and larger synapses. Integration of these structural findings with clinical data from the same patients further supports the view that corpora amylacea are associated with disease-related pathological processes. Together, these findings provide a basis for understanding the potential significance of corpora amylacea in human brain circuit dysfunction and may help to inform future research studies focusing on disease mechanisms.

secondary.title: An Orthogonal Quantitative NMR-FRET Approach for Integrity-Resolved Analysis of Lipid Vesicle Dynamics.
secondary.abstract: While lipid-based vesicles gain increasing attention as biomembrane models, artificial cells, and drug carriers, analytical investigation of their composition and integrity remains a major challenge, particularly for monitoring changes during processing and membrane transport. To address this challenge, we present an orthogonal analytical platform that combines 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) spectroscopy to enable integrity-resolved quantification of lipid vesicles. While 1H NMR provides chemically selective calibration-based quantification of individual lipid species, FRET-based assays enable direct monitoring of intact vesicle translocation across membranes, allowing for discrimination between free lipids and vesicle-associated lipids. We investigated vesicles composed of different phospholipid mixtures, including their formation and integrity as well as their membrane transport, and revealed remarkable composition-dependent differences. While vesicles composed of phosphatidylcholine and cholesterol exhibit instability, compositional loss, and limited membrane transport, inclusion of anionic lipids, such as phosphatidylglycerol and phosphatidylserine, significantly improves structural integrity and increases the fraction of lipids transported in vesicular form. These results demonstrate that orthogonal quantification of free and vesicle-associated lipids provides mechanistic insights into vesicle dynamics during processing and membrane transport, supporting the rational design of vesicular systems for applications in artificial cell research and lipid-based nanomedicines, where vesicle composition directly governs mechanical stability as well as biological interactions.

best.title: Ribosome-associated vesicles promote activity-dependent local translation in neurons.
best.abstract: Local protein synthesis in axons and dendrites underpins synaptic plasticity. However, the composition of the protein synthesis machinery in distal neuronal processes and the mechanisms for its deployment to local translation sites remain unclear. Here, we employed multi-scale imaging that combines cryo-electron tomography, volume electron microscopy, and live-cell imaging to identify endoplasmic reticulum-derived KDEL-positive vesicles, a subset of which are decorated with ribosomes (Ribosome-Associated Vesicles, RAVs) in neurites. We demonstrate that neuronal stimulation triggers compartment-specific responses: dendrites accumulate stationary KDEL-positive vesicles at sites of enhanced translation, while axons accelerate vesicle transport. cLTP stimulation additionally increases the proportion of KDEL-positive vesicles that carry ribosomes, expanding the local RAV pool. Real-time imaging of translation at single mRNA resolution reveals that RAV-associated translation sites exhibit ∼30% greater nascent-peptide signal amplitude compared to periods without RAV association, indicating that RAVs boost local translation output. These findings establish RAVs as specialized platforms that integrate activity-dependent signals with local protein synthesis, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how neurons achieve precise spatiotemporal control of translation.

best.title: Depth-enhanced molecular imaging with two-photon oblique plane microscopy.
best.abstract: High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves ~ 300 nm lateral and ~ 650 nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and < 60 nm localization precision in vivo. Compared with two-photon point scanning, the lower illumination NA delivers order-of-magnitude lower peak intensity, enabling > 5 × faster volumetric acquisition (up to 3.25 × 106 voxels s-1). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by ~ 2 × and restores volumetric resolving power by > 2 × relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

best.title: Live-cell imaging of inter-organelle contacts using an integrated dimerization-dependent fluorescent protein reporter.
best.abstract: Organelles communicate with each other by building membrane contact sites (MCSs) via specialized protein-protein and/or protein-membrane interactions. Conventional light microscopy cannot distinguish organelles connected by MCSs from those merely juxtaposed. In addition, organelle contacts are dynamic, yet only a limited number of tools are available to monitor MCSs in living cells. In this study, we developed a series of reporters based on dimerization-dependent fluorescent proteins (ddFP) to visualize, quantify and follow inter-organelle contacts. We first generated an integrated system specifically designed to study contacts between late endocytic compartments (late endosomes and lysosomes) and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). This system utilizes a single plasmid coding for the two complementary ddFP components: green A (GA) and green B (GB) targeted to the ER and late endosomes and lysosomes (LE/Lys), respectively. This construct enabled the generation of a stable reporter cell line suitable for semi-quantitative imaging. The ddFP reporter, which we called ddFP LELYS-ER, did not perturb endogenous LE/Lys-ER contacts in stable cells, and detected changes in the number of LE/Lys-ER contacts, for example, upon downregulation of the ER-resident VAP tether protein family, or under conditions of lysosomal damage. Moreover, live-cell imaging revealed that LE/Lys-ER contacts have distinct shapes, mobilities and lifetimes. Finally, using the same vector design, we generated two additional integrated reporter systems adapted to the study of contacts between the ER and the plasma membrane, and between the ER and mitochondria.

best.title: Assessing cellular metabolic dynamics with two-photon NAD(P)H fluorescence polarization microscopy.
best.abstract: Altered metabolism enables adaptive advantages for cancer cells, driving the need for improved methods for noninvasive long-term monitoring of cellular metabolism. Here, we present a fast live-cell NADH imaging method that provides a real-time measurement of the fractional level of unbound NADH and show that it is a robust indicator of a cell's metabolic status. The method, two-photon fluorescence polarization ratiometric microscopy (FPRM), is easy and inexpensive to implement and more than an order of magnitude faster than fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM), a common means of assessing bound and unbound NADH levels. We show that FPRM returns instrument-independent ratiometric parameters that correlate with the expected metabolic changes arising from pharmaceutical and environmental perturbations. By correlating FPRM-returned parameters with cell morphology and migration in two- and three-dimensional collagen matrices, we demonstrate the technique's versatility in typical bioengineered platforms used in cancer metabolism research.

best.title: Lipid-induced Caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking is associated with lipid droplet growth.
best.abstract: Caveolae are 50 to 100 nm sized plasma membrane invaginations involved in cellular lipid uptake and lipid accumulation. Several caveolin1 and cavin1 mutations are associated with human lipodystrophy. Previous research identified caveolae proteins at lipid droplets, although their specific cellular function at lipid droplets is not understood. Here, we show that extracellular dietary lipids like oleic acid and cholesterol shift caveolae at the plasma membrane to highly spherical invaginations and induce the internalization of caveolin1. Within 3 h of lipid treatment, caveolin1 accumulates specifically to lipid droplets. Correlative fluorescence Focused Ion Beam - Scanning Electron Microscopy and split-APEX proteomics revealed that this localization occurs in the absence of intact caveolar vesicles but caveolin1 alone. Mechanistically, caveolin1 trafficking to lipid droplets is regulated by EHD2 at the plasma membrane, is dynamin independent, and proceeds via EEA1- and Rab5-positive endosomes within 1 h of oleic acid treatment. Lipid droplet accumulation of caveolin1 is independent of lysosomal activity. Functionally, caveolin1-enriched lipid droplets exhibit a significant increase in size, demonstrating that caveolin1 is critical for lipid droplet growth. Notably, the deletion of the central caveolin1 β-barrel (Cav1-F160X), a mutation identified in lipodystrophy patients, abolished caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking and lipid droplet growth. Taken together, our results show that dietary lipids trigger caveolin1 internalization and accumulation at lipid droplets and a caveolin1-dependent lipid droplet growth, thereby providing an initial mechanistic basis for the lipodystrophic phenotype associated with caveolin1 mutations.

best.title: Analysis of motor-based transport in primary cilia by dynamic mode decomposition of live-cell imaging data.
best.abstract: Kinesin-3 motor proteins are increasingly recognized for their important roles in cilia. The mammalian kinesin-3 motor KIF13B moves bidirectionally in primary cilia and regulates ciliary content, but its relationship to the intraflagellar transport (IFT) machinery is unclear. Here, we combine quantitative live-cell imaging with a new kymograph analysis based on dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to separate mobile from immobile protein populations in primary cilia. This approach simplifies extraction of molecular velocities from kymographs and improves directional analysis of molecular tracks using the Fourier and Radon transforms. Our novel analysis reveals that a KIF13B deletion mutant only retaining the motor domain and part of the forkhead-associated domain does not alter steady-state IFT velocity or frequency. However, when retrograde dynein-2 function is inhibited by ciliobrevin D or tanespimycin, both anterograde and retrograde IFT velocities decrease in parental cells, as expected, but remain unchanged in KIF13B mutant cells. Structured illumination, confocal and stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy further show that KIF13B localizes to the ciliary membrane and concentrates at the periciliary membrane region and the centriolar subdistal appendages, below the distal appendage marker FBF1. Our improved kymograph approach provides new insight into KIF13B ciliary function and simplifies the quantitative analysis of ciliary protein transport.

best.title: SPIFFI enables single-shot super-resolution and multidimensional imaging.
best.abstract: Fluorescence super-resolution microscopy has advanced optical imaging into the nanoscale regime, transforming biological and interdisciplinary research. However, wide-field super-resolution techniques often compromise temporal resolution, thereby limiting the capture of rapid and transient biological events in living systems. Here we introduce spatial polarization-induced fluorescence fluctuation imaging (SPIFFI), a multichannel polarimetric method for single-shot super-resolution imaging and six-dimensional information extraction. By leveraging the inherently smaller point spread function under polarized detection and capturing polarization-dependent spatial fluctuations across multiplexed channels, SPIFFI achieves instant resolution enhancement from a single exposure. This capability substantially enhances the feasibility of volumetric live-cell super-resolution imaging. Moreover, SPIFFI images can integrate seamlessly with existing fluctuation-based methods for further postprocessing and resolution improvement. We demonstrate the versatility of SPIFFI through experiments on both fixed and live cells, capturing rapid subcellular dynamics and enabling high-throughput, multidimensional imaging beyond the diffraction limit. SPIFFI thus offers a practical and robust platform for real-time super-resolution imaging in biological research.

best.title: Broadband backscattering confocal microscopy enables label-free 3D live cell nanoscale sensitive imaging.
best.abstract: Fluorescence microscopy is a cornerstone of biological research. However, fluorescent labeling is challenging in live cells and is constrained by photobleaching and phototoxicity. Label-free methods allow cells to be studied in their native state, but most techniques have poor contrast, lack 3D capability, rely on complex optics, or fail to provide structural information. We present here broadband backscattering confocal microscopy (BBCM), which employs a broadband supercontinuum laser and collects backscattered light in a confocal geometry using a photomultiplier tube. Broadband illumination averages out size-dependent oscillations that confound monochromatic backscattering. This eliminates blind spots and intensity ambiguities, allowing all scatterers to be visible, with the signal increasing approximately linearly with scatterer size. BBCM is easy to retrofit to standard confocal microscopes, requires no specialized optics, and is straightforward for nonspecialists. It enables high-contrast, label-free 3D imaging of live cells with size sensitivity to subcellular structures without employing custom optics or complex data processing.

best.title: CelFDrive - multimodal deep learning-assisted microscopy for automated detection of rare events.
best.abstract: The emergence of automated microscopy has enabled the collection of large datasets of rare biological events, accelerating discovery in biology. However, most existing methods cannot be readily integrated into microscopy setups or are limited to a single microscope type. We present CelFDrive, a software package that automatically detects rare events of interest and automates high-resolution three-dimensional imaging of target cells by integrating deep learning-assisted cell classification of auxiliary low-magnification fluorescence images. We show that CelFDrive reduced the mean time required to nominate a mitotic prophase candidate for high-resolution light-sheet imaging by over 30-fold relative to manual expert selection. This approach can be used to define the order of kinetochore assembly upon nuclear envelope breakdown. The trained CelFDrive detector demonstrated transferability by retaining mitotic cell detection capability in an independently generated dataset using a different cell line, DNA marker and imaging setup. As datasets grow and models improve, CelFDrive offers a clear path toward intelligent imaging systems that not only accelerate data collection, but also fundamentally enhance how biological questions are explored.

best.title: Dual-modality photoacoustic and optical coherence tomography imaging simultaneously tracks transplanted stem cells and their viability.
best.abstract: Monitoring transplanted cell viability in vivo, noninvasively remains a considerable challenge. By using multiwavelength photoacoustic microscopy powered by a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive contrast agent, we can relatively and semiquantitatively assess and longitudinally monitor the viability of human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived retinal pigment epithelium (hiPSC-RPE) cells in vivo. The contrast agent comprises colloidal chain-like gold nanoparticle (CGNP) clusters conjugated with IR775c, a heptamethine cyanine dye that undergoes selective oxidative quenching under elevated ROS conditions associated with cellular death (CGNP-IR775c). Dual-wavelength photoacoustic microscopy at 620 and 775 nanometers provides self-calibrated ratiometric measurements that enable relative viability assessment, distinguishing healthy from nonviable cell populations. In vitro studies demonstrated that CGNP-IR775c exhibited biocompatibility and showed dose-dependent ROS sensitivity across physiologically relevant H2O2 concentrations. hiPSC-RPE cells labeled by CGNP-IR775c were subretinally transplanted into living rabbit eyes and longitudinally monitored for 2 weeks, showing that laser-induced oxidative stress produced measurable photoacoustic signal changes that were consistent with the viability status of the transplanted cells. The imaging technology developed here provides a practical solution for noninvasive, longitudinal, and semiquantitative assessment of the transplanted cell viability in vivo, and may contribute to ophthalmology cell-based therapy in both preclinical and clinical settings.

best.title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain.
best.abstract: Extending the depth reach of multiphoton microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an 'exponentially hard' problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain; however, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal. Here we demonstrate a three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and nonlinear limits for safe laser exposure while satisfying the spatiotemporal requirements of single-cell resolution calcium (Ca2+) imaging. TrUDI achieves a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photon yield at the same laser power as in previous approaches thereby enabling in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 × 230 µm2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

best.title: Quantum-sensing-based super-resolution live cell microenvironment imaging.
best.abstract: Direct monitoring the multifaceted intracellular microenvironment is fundamental for deciphering localized cellular behavior and function. However, performing nanoscale spatiotemporal sensing of the dynamic physiochemical environment within a live cell has remained challenging, mainly limited by the lack of robust, biocompatible method which satisfies the requirements for spatiotemporal resolution, sensitivity, multi-physical sensing capability and long-term viability. Here we present a super-resolution-based quantum biosensing approach, namely Super-resolution Multi-physical field Imaging with Deconvolution, implemented in our custom-built setup which integrates nitrogen vacancy center-based quantum sensing with structured illumination microscopy. This enables quantitative, super-resolved, and long-term tracking of intracellular physical fields, featuring spatial resolution of 136 nm, temporal resolution of 150 ms, and field of view of 180×180 μm2. We further perform super-resolution multimodal imaging in a live cell, revealing the spatially heterogeneous reactive oxygen species dynamics under external stimulation. Our work enables the dynamic assessment of localized physiochemical dynamics under super-resolution quantum biosensing.

best.title: Space-time light-sheet microscopy.
best.abstract: Light-sheet microscopy (LSM) has revolutionized bioimaging by delivering high-contrast volumetric resolution with minimal photodamage. Spatial wavefront shaping, used to generate lattice and Airy light-sheets, has been particularly effective in advancing LSM beyond the Rayleigh limit. Despite its broad adoption, most LSM implementations rely on rigid dual-objective geometries that complicate sample handling and impose a trade-off between imaging field of view (FoV) and axial resolution. Here, we introduce space-time light-sheet microscopy (ST-LSM), a single-objective strategy that exploits space-time (ST) correlations for the first time. ST-LSM goes beyond separate spatial or temporal modulation to jointly modulate the spatiotemporal spectral structure of a pulse. This enabled light-sheets with wavelength-scale thickness over millimeter-scale distances. When compared to state-of-the-art approaches, ST-LSM eliminates the dual-objective constraint, expands the sample-accessible volume by 25×, and increases the FoV by 10× without sacrificing sectioning resolution. We demonstrate the versatility of ST-LSM by using a single setup to image specimens across four orders of magnitude in size, from whole roots and developing embryos, down to mammalian cells with sub-cellular axial resolution. These results position ST-LSM as an accessible practical optical microscopy platform at a variety of biological scales, by translating space-time wavepacket physics into a practical imaging modality.

best.title: Novel NaV1.6-Mitochondrial Complexes in Retinal Astrocyte Pockets Sequester GABA.
best.abstract: Voltage-gated sodium channels are best known for their capacity to generate and propagate electrical currents in neurons and muscle. Their expression in glial cells may also be of great importance given these cells' involvement in various disease processes. Here we identify a previously unrecognized voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.6-enriched microdomain in mouse retinal astrocytes. Using super-resolution confocal microscopy, electrophysiology, and transcriptomic analyses, we show that NaV1.6 forms high-density clusters within intracellular compartments devoid of the calcium-binding protein, S100β, typically understood to distribute throughout the entire astrocyte. These NaV1.6 pockets are polarized, clustering only on the bilayer facing retinal ganglion cell neurons, and are packed with unusually large, anaplerotic, and relatively depolarized mitochondria that closely appose NaV1.6 puncta. These metabolic compartments also accumulate high levels of GABA. Together, our findings reveal a specialized NaV1.6-mitochondrial complex in retinal astrocytes that expands the functional repertoire of voltage-gated sodium channels beyond direct neuronal electrical excitability.

best.title: Integrated two-photon and photoacoustic microscopy for single-cell neurometabolic imaging.
best.abstract: Understanding how neuronal activity couples with local energy metabolism is fundamental to brain function. Oxygen exchange between individual neurons and red blood cells (RBCs) is central to this process, yet no existing method can simultaneously capture their dynamics at single-cell resolution in vivo. Here, we introduce integrated two-photon and photoacoustic microscopy (TPM-PAM), which enables real-time imaging of single-neuron calcium activity alongside oxygen release from individual RBCs in awake mice. In TPM-PAM, a transparent micro-ring resonator-based ultrasound sensor breaks the long-standing tradeoff between optical access and acoustic sensitivity, while dual-wavelength kymography simultaneously quantifies single-RBC oxygenation and flow to derive the oxygen release rate. Incorporating nonlinear optical manipulation of the neurovascular unit with cellular precision, TPM-PAM reveals distinct neurometabolic responses to whisker stimulation, single-capillary occlusion, and single-neuron stimulation. This work establishes a powerful platform for dissecting neurometabolic coupling at the cellular scale and understanding oxygen-metabolic regulation in brain health and disease.

best.title: Submicromolar imaging of intrinsic chromophores by two-photon photothermal microscopy captures mitochondrial response to chemotherapy.
best.abstract: Intracellular chromophores {e.g., NADH [reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (oxidized form)] and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide)} play a central role in regulation of cellular metabolism. Although autofluorescence has been extensively used for label-free mapping of chromophores inside a cell, its sensitivity and molecular specificity are constrained by the low quantum yield and the fluorescence spectral overlap. Here, we address these challenges by using a photothermal approach to measure the optical absorption of chromophores rather than its autofluorescence. Our two-photon photothermal (2PPT) microscope exploits localized thermal transients generated through two-photon absorption, enabling detection of chromophore-specific signatures beyond the reach of autofluorescence. We demonstrate submicromolar limits of detection for the metabolic coenzymes NADH and FAD of 0.87 and 0.99 μM, respectively. Such high sensitivity enables differentiating the influence of mitochondrial shapes on metabolism. 2PPT can identify the biomolecular source of contrast from cellular mitochondria in a label-free manner on the basis of spectroscopy. 2PPT microscopy is used to study metabolic alterations of mitochondria in cancer under chemotherapy at the single-organelle level.

best.title: Time-lapse RESOLFT nanoscopy empowered by deep learning.
best.abstract: Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Reversible Saturable OpticaL Fluorescent Transition (RESOLFT) demonstrated great potential for live cell nanoscopy by using patterned light and reversibly switching fluorescent probes. Despite the latest improvement in both switching probes and optical schemes, the duration and frame rate of the time-lapse are still limited by photobleaching and spatial sampling steps. Here, we present two distinct strategies based on deep learning to restore low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) or under-sampled images pushing the experimental boundaries of RESOLFT. We demonstrate the capability of Hierarchical DivNoising (HDN) to restore low-SNR RESOLFT data while maintaining full spatial resolution, both in supervised and unsupervised settings. This allows a 10-fold reduction of light dose per frame, and up to 5 times longer imaging. Then, we present Fast-MoNaLISA, a method that reduces the acquisition time of any point-scanning systems. This allows a 4-fold increase in frame rate, and a reduction of scanning artefacts. Overall, our methods open up possibilities for dynamic data acquisition at the sub-organelle level, such as vesicles budding in and out from intact mitochondria, or the actin meshwork formation and dissociation.

best.title: Coincidence detection in aspiny interneuron dendrites.
best.abstract: Recent evidence for long-term potentiation (LTP) at glutamatergic synapses on GABAergic interneurons calls for close attention to the sub-cellular phenomena that underlie the induction of plasticity in aspiny dendrites. Neurogliaform interneurons exhibit large NMDA receptor-mediated currents, Hebbian LTP and supralinear summation of glutamatergic signals converging on dendritic compartments. Dendritic supralinearity in interneurons does not require sodium channels. Here we investigate the principles governing supralinear synaptic integration and its interaction with backpropagating action potentials in the synaptic plasticity context. We developed a biophysically realistic, multi-compartmental model of a murine (Mus musculus, male and female) hippocampal neurogliaform interneuron, with dendritic architecture and ion channel densities tuned to match ex vivo recordings. The interaction between synaptic inputs and action potentials was tested with patch-clamp electrophysiology and two-photon imaging of dendritic calcium-dependent fluorescence transients. Whether simulated glutamatergic excitatory postsynaptic potentials are clustered on a dendritic fragment or dispersed across the entire arbor, they summate supralinearly as assessed from the calculated somatic voltage response. Clustered inputs induce more pronounced local depolarizations and calcium transients than dispersed inputs. Action potentials generated at the soma backpropagate throughout the dendritic arbor but are attenuated at branch points. Coincident synaptic input and backpropagating action potentials relieve this attenuation, further enhance dendritic depolarizations, and greatly potentiate calcium influx via NMDA receptors. Despite differences in dendritic anatomy and in the roles of sodium channels, the interplay of orthodromic and antidromic voltage propagation and resultant calcium signal amplification exhibits remarkable similarities between neurogliaform interneurons and principal cells.Significance Statement Neurogliaform interneurons are key regulators of brain circuit activity, yet the dendritic mechanisms that enable these inhibitory cells to undergo synaptic plasticity remain poorly understood. Combining biophysically realistic computer modeling with electrophysiology and two-photon calcium imaging, we show that coincident synaptic input and backpropagating action potentials strongly amplify dendritic depolarization and calcium influx in these interneurons. Although their dendrites lack spines and do not rely on sodium-channel-dependent dendritic spikes, neurogliaform interneurons nonetheless use computational principles remarkably similar to those of excitatory principal neurons. These findings advance the understanding of how inhibitory circuits support learning-related plasticity and may provide foundational insight into disorders such as epilepsy and schizophrenia, in which abnormal dendritic signalling and inhibitory dysfunction are implicated.

best.title: Incomplete synaptic vesicle priming functionally disconnects CA1 pyramidal cells.
best.abstract: The hippocampal CA1 area is perceived as a nonrecurrent neuronal network, i.e., CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) within the CA1 area innervate mainly γ-aminobutyric acid-releasing interneurons but not each other. Here, we performed an unbiased examination of the functional properties of local CA1PC output synapses using in vitro two-photon glutamate imaging. Fluorescent transients measured with iGluSnFR3 in individual boutons displayed extraordinary heterogeneity in their amplitudes and short-term plasticity patterns upon a complex train of presynaptic action potential firing. Post hoc electron microscopy of the imaged boutons demonstrated that distinct postsynaptic structure-innervating boutons display different functional properties. Approximately 25% of the boutons innervate CA1PC spines, which either release glutamate with very low release probability or completely fail to release. Phorbol 12,13-dibutyrate and elevated calcium (2+) concentration, manipulations that enhance synaptic vesicle priming and fusion, convert these silent into properly functioning synapses. Our results provide evidence that CA1PCs are interconnected with structurally and molecularly intact glutamatergic synapses, but incomplete synaptic vesicle (SV) priming precludes SV release.

best.title: 53BP1 as a cofactor in the activation of the p53-family transcriptional program: A correlative multimodal microscopy approach.
best.abstract: Understanding how molecular mechanisms regulate cell function in tissues requires approaches that link phenotypes to mechanisms across different spatial scales. Here, we present automated multimodal multiplexed microscopy for image cytometry (A.M3.I.CO), a correlative imaging platform that combines multiscale resolution, from millimeters to nanometers, with automated workflows for high-throughput phenotypic profiling and targeted single-molecule analysis in situ. Applying A.M3.I.CO, we observed that 53BP1 is recruited at transcribed p53 target genes independently of the activating stimulus, providing evidence for the formation of a putative complex between 53BP1, p53, and the basal transcription machinery in single cells, as also supported by in vivo observations in tumor models. Extending our measurements to p63 and p73, we found that 53BP1 localized at p63- and p73-targeted transcription sites, suggesting a broader role in participating in p53 family-dependent transcription. These findings indicate an additional genome-surveillance pathway in transcriptional control regulating diverse cellular functions while establishing A.M3.I.CO as a platform for spatially resolved functional analysis.

best.title: Extended field-of-view two-photon imaging in the deep brain of freely behaving mice using lightweight microfabricated corrective optics.
best.abstract: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions. Miniaturized two-photon microscopes (MINI2Ps) enable deep brain imaging in freely moving animals when coupled with gradient index (GRIN)-based microendoscopes. However, intrinsic optical aberrations in GRIN-based microendoscopes degrade spatial resolution and limit the effective field-of-view (FOV). Here, we address these limitations using lightweight microfabricated optics to correct GRIN aberrations during deep brain MINI2P imaging. The aberration corrected system demonstrated improved and more homogeneous axial resolution across the FOV, resulting in more than fourfold increase in effective FOV. We applied the corrected system to the ventral posteromedial thalamus in freely moving mice and performed optical mapping of head direction (HD) tuned cells. These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus. Combining the MINI2P with aberration corrected GRIN-based microendoscopes is a powerful approach for large-scale and high-resolution functional imaging of deep brain circuits during naturalistic behavior.

best.title: Volume electron microscopy reveals oligodendrocyte axon selection patterns and spatial assembly of myelin and nodes.
best.abstract: Oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple axons, requiring single cells to coordinate target selection, sheath growth, and node formation across complex cortical geometry. We combined serial block-face electron microscopy, complete segmentation, and three-dimensional reconstruction to analyze early-myelinating oligodendrocytes in the somatosensory cortex of a postnatal day 14 rat at single-cell and nanoscale resolution. Individual oligodendrocytes initiated myelination across all contacted axons, while early ensheathment decreased with increasing process distance from the soma. Each oligodendrocyte also contacted axons within a restricted caliber range, independently of wrapping progression. At prospective nodes of Ranvier, transient cytoplasmic projections extended into axonal domains from adjacent oligodendrocytes and converged near presumptive paranodes. These observations support a structural model in which oligodendrocyte geometry, cell-specific axon selection, and intercellular interactions jointly organize early cortical myelination and nodal assembly, providing testable hypotheses for developmental myelination and repair after demyelination.

best.title: FLIM Playground: An interactive, end-to-end graphical user interface for analyzing single cells with fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy.
best.abstract: Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) is sensitive to molecular environments and enables high-resolution mapping of cellular heterogeneity. Yet, the journey from raw photon decays to biological insight remains fragmented by multi-step data extraction and siloed analyses, creating burdens for experts and non-experts alike. This work presents FLIM Playground, the first interactive graphical platform that unifies single-cell FLIM workflows. Modularly designed to encompass data extraction (if desired) and data analysis, FLIM Playground can check field-of-view metadata, calibrate and extract fluorescence lifetime features per region of interest along with morphology and texture features across channels, merge multiple datasets, and provide real-time visual analytic modules. Lifetime extraction was validated against commercial software and published results, and both data extraction and analysis were demonstrated on a FLIM dataset of cancer cell lines. By adopting best practices and offering interactivity, FLIM Playground promotes reproducibility, allows for expansion to new imaging modalities, and accelerates hypothesis-driven discovery.

best.title: Btbd11 regulates glutamatergic synapse organization in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons.
best.abstract: The mechanisms that underlie glutamatergic synapse organization and function in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) are not well described, despite evidence that impaired glutamatergic excitation of INs is implicated in psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and anxiety. Glutamatergic synapses received by INs have unique basal transmission properties and exhibit distinct synaptic plasticity compared to those received by excitatory neurons, likely due to cell-type specific differences in postsynaptic density (PSD) composition and maintenance mechanisms. In the present study, we show that the interneuron-specific protein Btbd11 regulates excitatory synapse transmission in mixed-sex primary cultured rat and mouse hippocampal interneurons through promotion of phase separation and support of postsynaptic nanoarchitecture. Btbd11 forms a phase separated protein complex with Psd-95 and TARPγ2 and impacts the stability of TARPγ2 and GluA1 within glutamatergic IN synapses in an expression- and phase separation-dependent manner. Using super resolution imaging, we show that Btbd11 displays nanoscale clustering properties within IN synapses that correlate with Psd-95 nanostructure. Furthermore, genetic deletion of Btbd11 decreases PSD protein expression, reduces synapse size, and disrupts Psd-95 nanocluster organization. These effects manifest as a drastic reduction in glutamatergic synaptic transmission onto INs when Btbd11 is deleted. Together, these data provide insights into a novel cell type-specific synaptic regulatory mechanism in an understudied synapse population.Significance Statement Although glutamatergic excitation of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) is essential for maintenance of balanced signaling in the brain and dysregulation has been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, the molecular mechanisms underlying IN-specific glutamatergic transmission are not well characterized. Using protein modeling, molecular biology, live-cell and super-resolution imaging, we describe a unique mechanism of glutamatergic synapse organization in INs by Btbd11, an IN-specific synaptic protein. Btbd11 promotes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and regulates PSD protein mobility, the abundance of key synaptic proteins, and nanoscale synaptic organization. Collectively, this is critical for glutamatergic synaptic transmission within INs. Understanding Btbd11's role at the synapse highlights the importance of synaptic LLPS, providing insight into the regulatory mechanisms in an understudied synapse with psychiatric disease relevance.

best.abstract: Rubicon is a negative regulator of autophagy and the endolysosomal network (ELN) and an antagonist of the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex II (PI3KC3-C2). Rubicon is specific for the UV radiation resistance-associated gene protein (UVRAG)-containing PI3KC3-C2 over the purely autophagic ATG14-containing PI3KC3-C1 complex. Here, we determined the high-resolution cryoelectron microscopy structure of PI3KC3-C2 in complex with the PI3KC3-binding domain of Rubicon and compared it to cryo-EM structures of unbound PI3KC3-C2 and PI3KC3-C1. Rubicon binds directly to PI3KC3-C2 only via the BARA domain of the BECN1 subunit, which is common to both C1 and C2. The selectivity of Rubicon for the PI3KC3-C2 complex over the PI3KC3-C1 complex is attributed to a conformation of the BECN1BARA domain induced by UVRAG, rather than to direct contact with UVRAG or direct antagonism by the ATG14 subunit of PI3KC3-C1. Targeted disruption of the Rubicon:PI3K3-C2 structural interface by site-directed mutations enhances mitophagic activity in human epithelial cells to levels comparable to those observed in Rubicon knockout cells. Similarly, disruption of the interaction in Rubicon-overexpressing hippocampal neurons restored lysosomal flux to wild-type levels. These data show that suppressing the function of PI3K3-C2 can fully account for the negative regulatory effects of Rubicon in the autophagy and ELN pathways.

best.title: Three-photon population imaging of subcortical brain regions.
best.abstract: Monitoring large-scale neuronal activity in deep brain circuits is crucial for understanding the principles of brain function. However, existing large-scale cellular-resolution imaging techniques are limited in imaging depth and cannot monitor activity in areas deeper than the cortex in the intact brain. LIFT combines high-numerical-aperture optimized sampling, using a custom scanning module, with deep learning-based denoising, to enable population imaging in subcortical brain regions of mice and deep cortical regions of rats. We demonstrate calcium imaging in the intact mouse brain from more than 1500 cells across CA1, the surrounding white matter, and adjacent deep layers of the cortex, and show population imaging with high SNR at a depth of 1.2 mm in the rat cortex. The LIFT microscope offers versatility in imaging scale and rate and was built entirely from off-the-shelf components.

best.title: MIMAS: An open-source microlens-array miniature microscope for accessible large-field cortical imaging in freely behaving mice.
best.abstract: Large-scale cortical dynamics during natural behavior are difficult to measure because head-mounted imaging systems must balance field of view, spatial resolution, weight, and optical complexity. Existing wide-field miniature microscopes often rely on compound or custom-corrected optical assemblies, which increase device complexity and limit accessibility for laboratories without specialized optics expertise. Here, we present the Miniature Integrated Microlens Array System (MIMAS), an open-source head-mounted fluorescence microscope that replaces conventional multi-element optics with a 4 × 5 microlens array as its sole imaging element. By combining modular subfield acquisition with computational registration and stitching, MIMAS achieves cellular-resolution imaging across an approximately 4 × 4.5 mm2 field of view while weighing only 2.31 g. In freely behaving mice with sparse labeling of layer 2/3 cortical neurons, MIMAS enabled simultaneous calcium imaging across multiple dorsal cortical regions, with signals extracted from thousands of neurons. This broad sampling captured distributed cortical activity related to locomotor state and sparse position-modulated responses during open-field exploration without detectable disruption of locomotion or loss of signal quality over 30 min of recording. Beyond neuronal imaging, MIMAS also supported wide-field vascular imaging and resolved vessel caliber-dependent hemodynamic responses to isoflurane. These results establish MIMAS as a lightweight, accessible, and versatile platform for large-scale fluorescence imaging in freely behaving mice and demonstrate an alternative strategy for wide-field cortical imaging that lowers the optical complexity barrier for individual laboratories.

best.title: Deep learning-enhanced single-shot triorganelle STED-FLIM imaging of lipid dynamics in living cells.
best.abstract: Lipid homeostasis is orchestrated by rapid exchange and remodeling across the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), lipid droplets (LDs), and mitochondria. However, live-cell visualization of this triorganelle network remains limited by subdiffraction structures, multiplexed labeling burden, and the ambiguity of intensity-only readouts. Here, we introduce a single-shot stimulated emission depletion-fluorescence lifetime imaging (STED-FLIM) workflow that combines Nile Red analogs with deep learning-based demultiplexing to generate compartment-resolved maps of lipid-organelle organization and dynamics. By combining the STED-resolved nanoscale ultrastructure with lifetime-encoded microenvironmental contrast, our approach separates ER, LDs, and mitochondria from a single acquisition and enables automated tricompartment quantification using a lightweight VGG16-UNet segmentation model. This platform captures coordinated remodeling across the ER-LD-mitochondria axis during lipid stress, including ferroptosis- and apoptosis-associated transitions, while simultaneously reporting nanoscale organization and microenvironmental shifts. Together, this strategy provides a practical route to high-spatiotemporal-resolution, lifetime-encoded multiorganelle lipid imaging in living cells.

primary.title: The people behind the papers - Pavel Tomancak and Jean-Yves Tinevez.
primary.abstract: Segmenting cells and tracking their internal structures remains a complex image-analysis challenge in cell and developmental biology. In their work, Johannes Girstmair, Tobias Pietzsch, Pavel Tomancak, Jean-Yves Tinevez and colleagues demonstrate how Mastodon, an existing Fiji/ImageJ plugin, can visualise and analyse cell lineages and track cells in 3D within large microscopy datasets. To learn more about their work, we talked to the two corresponding authors, Pavel Tomancak, Principal Investigator at the Max Planck Institute of Molecular Cell Biology and Genetics, Germany, and director of the Central European Institute of Technology, Czech Republic, as well as Jean-Yves Tinevez, founder and leader of the Image Analysis Facility, Institute Pasteur, France.

primary.title: Making smart microscopy deployable in imaging core facilities.
primary.abstract: Smart microscopy, in which real-time image analysis enables microscopes to adapt their acquisition dynamically, is becoming central to biological imaging. However, deploying such workflows in imaging facilities remains challenging. The computers that control microscopes in a facility are shared, governed by institutional policies, often offline and run vendor-specific software. As a result, installing custom software environments for the workflow of each user is both unsafe and unsustainable. We argue that smart microscopy requires a practical deployment strategy that links open-source bioimage analysis with commercial acquisition software without turning acquisition computers into development platforms. Using our recently developed tools, NucleiSky and LabConstrictor, as examples, we demonstrate how microscope control and external image analysis can be integrated while keeping the custom Python environment separate from the vendor-managed environment. The deployment strategy might vary - for instance, a USB drive, a facility workstation, a server or a network share - but the underlying principle remains the same: smart-microscopy workflows must be straightforward to approve, launch, reuse, audit and remove. Smart microscopy will become routine only when it is both powerful and deployable.

primary.title: Partaker: deep-learning-based single-cell-resolution analysis of multi-dimensional, long-term, microfluidic-based time-lapse microscopy data.
primary.abstract: MOTIVATION: Deep-learning segmentation models for microbial time-lapse fluorescence microscopy already exist, but they are often difficult to use consistently across experiments and are not packaged with unified workflows for combining models, quantifying multi-channel fluorescence, and scaling analyses to large microfluidic imaging datasets. RESULTS: To address these challenges, we developed Partaker, an easy-to-use Python-based graphical tool for deep-learning segmentation, multi-channel fluorescence quantification, and morphological analysis of microbial cells over time. Partaker supports extensible model integration, efficient handling of large imaging datasets, and interactive visualization, enabling time-resolved analysis of population fluorescence distributions from per-cell measurements. We demonstrate performance using a two-strain validation experiment (housekeeping and inducible) and show robust recovery of population-level fluorescence dynamics with single-cell resolution. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Partaker is implemented in Python and is available on GitHub (https://github.com/SamOliveiraLab/partaker). A versioned release of the software is archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18844425). Documentation, example datasets, and installation instructions are provided in the repository.

primary.title: SynapTrack: An automated tool for synapse quantification.
primary.abstract: Reliable synapse quantification remains challenging, particularly in high-throughput fluorescence imaging workflows. Here we present SynapTrack, a fully automated FIJI/ImageJ-based tool for quantifying synapses in cultured neurons and brain tissue sections with minimal user intervention. SynapTrack combines channel-specific preprocessing, background subtraction, and SynQuant-based detection of colocalised pre- and postsynaptic puncta. In cultured neurons, it additionally measures cell number and total dendritic length, enabling normalisation of synapse counts per cell and per 10 micrometer of dendrite. Using hippocampal cultures, SynapTrack reliably quantified excitatory and inhibitory synapses, captured the expected predominance of excitatory contacts, and reduced inter-sample variability through structural normalisation. Compared with SynBot, SynapTrack detected more synapses while better preserving biologically meaningful differences between synapse types. For tissue sections, in which cell counting and dendritic segmentation are impractical, we developed SynapTrack_Tissue, an adapted workflow based on presynaptic-postsynaptic colocalisation alone. Despite the lack of cellular normalisation, this approach produced stable measurements across heterogeneous neuropil regions. Because all spatial parameters are defined in micrometres, analysis settings are portable across imaging systems. SynapTrack therefore provides a standardised and scalable framework for synapse quantification in both cultured neurons and tissue sections.

secondary.title: Comparison of manual counting with two rule-based image analysis programs, ImageJ and CellProfiler, for quantitative analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemical positivity in rat brainstem sections.
secondary.abstract: Quantitative and semiquantitative assessment of biomarker expression using immunohistochemistry (IHC) can be performed using several analytical approaches. Manual counting remains widely used but is inherently subjective and susceptible to observer variability. Rule-based image-analysis platforms may provide accessible alternatives, highlighting the need for direct method-comparison and agreement studies. c-Fos is a well-established marker of neuronal activation commonly quantified by counting IHC-positive cells. This study compared manual counting, ImageJ, and CellProfiler for quantifying c-Fos-positive cells in rat brainstem sections. Of 125 images initially evaluated, one was excluded as an extreme outlier, leaving 124 images for final analysis. Each image was independently analyzed by two trained observers using all three methods. ImageJ and CellProfiler were applied through their standard graphical interfaces and built-in functions using predefined user-guided threshold ranges, without additional plugins, scripts, machine-learning models, or custom code. Agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and Bland-Altman analysis. No statistically significant difference in c-Fos-positive cell counts was observed among the three methods (Friedman test, P = 0.07). Median (IQR) counts were 6.75 (0.50-13.50) for manual counting, 6.25 (1.00-14.38) for ImageJ, and 6.00 (0.63-14.50) for CellProfiler. Inter-observer agreement was excellent for manual counting (ICC = 0.983), ImageJ (ICC = 0.964), and CellProfiler (ICC = 0.962). Inter-method agreement was also excellent (single-measures ICC = 0.971; 95% CI = 0.961-0.979). Bland-Altman analysis showed small mean biases of 0.33, 0.27, and -0.07 cells, with no significant proportional bias. Manual counting, ImageJ, and CellProfiler produced statistically comparable c-Fos-positive cell counts with excellent agreement. Under the predefined user-guided threshold ranges used, both software platforms closely matched manual counting; however, image-dependent threshold adjustment remains a potential source of observer variability.

secondary.title: DINOSim: Training-Free Semantic Segmentation on Microscopy Images.
secondary.abstract: We present DINOSim, a training-free method for segmenting objects in microscopy images without the need for large annotated datasets or additional model training. DINOSim builds on the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder, which captures semantic information from images. By comparing the encoder's features of image patches to those of a user-selected reference, DINOSim generates pseudo-labels that guide semantic segmentation. Subsequently, a k-nearest neighbors framework is used to refine predictions across new images. Our experiments show that DINOSim can effectively segment previously unseen objects in diverse microscopy datasets, offering performance comparable to supervised approaches while avoiding the need for costly manual labeling. We also investigate how different choices of user prompt selection and model size affect accuracy and generalization. To make the method widely accessible, we provide an open-source napari plugin (github.com/AAitorG/napari-DINOSim), enabling researchers to apply DINOSim to their own data easily. Overall, DINOSim offers a fast, flexible and practical solution for bioimage analysis, particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings.

secondary.title: Benchmarking cell segmentation in two Spatialomics platforms with open-source software.
secondary.abstract: UNLABELLED: The in situ tissue microenvironment is a complex mixture of different cell types, microanatomic structures, and acellular matrix material. Further, disease perturbs the morphologies of these features significantly. Spatial proteomics utilizing optical or mass spectrometer imaging simultaneously detects expression and subcellular localization of many proteins. Accurate identification of heterogeneous, irregular, and tightly interdigitating cell boundaries is a crucial step for all downstream analyses, including cell phenotyping and cell-cell interaction networks. We describe a benchmarking approach for rapid assessment of segmentation algorithm performance in melanoma and breast cancer contexts using mass spectrometer and optical spatial omics imaging platforms. Comparison of cell segmentation by fourteen methods to pathologist ground-truth annotation with Jaccard pixel index and F1 object measurement identified Cellpose models that performed well across different tumor samples and data sources with minimal fine-tuning. Algorithms utilizing cell membrane and nuclear features demonstrated better performance in both tumor samples. This benchmarking approach is a rapid and effective method to assess performance of cell segmentation methods in different contexts for efficient algorithm selection and iterative model training. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70919-2.

secondary.title: NucGen3D: A synthetic framework for large-scale 3D nuclear segmentation with open-source training data and models.
secondary.abstract: Robust nuclear segmentation in 3D microscopy images is a critical yet unsolved challenge in quantitative cell biology. The main challenges are the scarcity and variability of annotated volumetric datasets. Since these data are difficult to obtain, most state-of-the-art approaches, including Cellpose, segment individual 2D slices and then heuristically reconstruct 3D volumes, thereby losing critical spatial context. Our analysis of expert annotator performance confirms that ignoring 3D context introduces substantial variability in nuclear detection and annotation. While a few 3D models are trained on small or toy datasets, no large-scale, openly available resource currently exists to enable robust training of high-capacity 3D segmentation networks. To address this problem, we present NucGen3D, a customizable simulation framework that generates large-scale, annotated 3D microscopy datasets from limited 2D input, specifically the 2018 Data Science Bowl dataset. NucGen3D produces realistic 3D volumes across diverse biological and imaging scenarios, including variations in nuclear morphology, spatial arrangement, and imaging noise. Using this synthetic data, we trained two models from scratch: a 2D convolutional neural network under Cellpose-like conditions, and a fully 3D convolutional model that extends the 2D settings. We evaluated both on a challenging, independent real-world dataset with complex nuclear architectures. Both models, especially the 3D model, achieve competitive performance with respect to state-of-the-art methods, including those trained on larger annotated datasets or based on more complex architectures. These results demonstrate that synthetic data can effectively substitute for full 3D annotations when training models at scale. To promote reproducibility and further research, we release both the NucGen3D framework and the fully trained 3D segmentation model as open source, making this the first end-to-end open resource for large-scale 3D nuclear segmentation.

secondary.title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath.
secondary.abstract: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10-9 absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

secondary.title: CellColocDB: a disease-centred resource linking GWAS loci to genes, cell contexts, and fine-mapping evidence.
secondary.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified disease-associated loci, but linking these signals to molecular mechanisms remains difficult because of linkage disequilibrium and context-dependent genetic regulation. CellColocDB is a disease- and window-centred resource integrating GWAS-QTL colocalization across bulk, sorted-cell, and single-cell QTL datasets. The current release includes 2805 GWAS datasets covering 1201 diseases and traits and 40 516 GWAS windows, together with 23 QTL sources, 316 QTL contexts, and 89 842 molecular features. CellColocDB contains 3 572 118 coloc.abf results with PP.H4 > 0.5, including 1 609 418 with PP.H4 ≥ 0.8. Analyses are organized as GWAS dataset × GWAS window × QTL context × molecular feature tasks, allowing contexts and molecular features to be compared within the same GWAS region. coloc.abf is the primary colocalization analysis, with coloc-SuSiE and SMR/HEIDI providing complementary evidence where available. Task-specific ABF top SNPs are linked to CAUSALdb2 fine-mapping results from seven methods. Results are available through disease-, QTL context-, gene-, and locus-level views, with regional association tracks and matched variants, and can be queried by gene, genomic region, or GWAS window ID. CellColocDB is freely available at http://www.mulinlab.org/colocdb/.

secondary.title: CellScore: an open-source image-based pipeline for automated cell quantification in microalgae.
secondary.abstract: Accurate quantification of microalgal cell density is essential for both basic research and industrial applications, as it directly reflects culture growth, productivity, and physiological status. There are existing methods routinely used to measure cell counts, although many are limited by high cost, labor-intensive workflows, or steep technical barriers. To address these limitations, we developed CellScore, a rapid and accessible image-based pipeline for microalgal cell counting implemented in ImageJ, a widely adopted open-source platform in the biological sciences ( https://github.com/shijieh/imageJ-annotate ). By leveraging the broad user base and ease of installation of the software, CellScore enables researchers to obtain reliable cell counts from standard microscopy images with minimal specialized equipment. Although the workflow has only been tested with three microalgae species of similar morphologies, the pipeline balances automation with user control and includes practical troubleshooting strategies to facilitate adoption by new users. Thus, CellScore has the potential to be used broadly across other species, however, broader validation across diverse morphologies is required. Overall, CellScore provides a cost-effective, user-friendly, and reproducible solution for routine microalgal cell quantification in both laboratory and applied settings.

secondary.title: A seamless workflow for STXM-NEXAFS data analysis using napari: implementation of an ROI spectrum extraction function.
secondary.abstract: Scanning transmission soft X-ray microscopy (STXM), combined with near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS), enables the mapping of elemental distributions and chemical properties at a spatial resolution of tens of nanometers. A common approach for analyzing STXM data is to compare NEXAFS spectra obtained from regions of interest (ROIs). However, ROI-based spectral comparison typically requires frequent switching among multiple software applications. ROI spectrum extraction, spectrum normalization, and figure creation are often performed using separate applications, which increase analytical time and the likelihood of errors.•We developed a Python-based workflow for STXM-NEXAFS data analysis that implements functions for extracting mean ROI spectra in napari, an open-source multidimensional image viewer.•These napari-based functions provide a seamless workflow from ROI selection to figure preparation within Python, without switching between multiple software applications.•The seamless workflow improves analytical efficiency and facilitates broader use of STXM-NEXAFS analysis.

secondary.title: A Deep Learning Pipeline for Cell Segmentation and Viability Quantification in 3D Constructs From Fluorescence Microscopy Images.
secondary.abstract: With the increasing adoption of 3D cell cultures and bioprinting in biomedical research, there is a growing demand for reliable and accurate monitoring methods. While fluorescence microscopy is widely accepted for 2D cell cultures, when introducing the third dimension it often suffers from signal attenuation and out-of-focus interference, making automated image analysis challenging. In this study, a hybrid pipeline that integrates deep learning and traditional image processing techniques is presented with the aim of establishing an automated tool for cell segmentation and viability assessment in 3D from fluorescence microscopy images. A U 2-Net architecture was trained on 2D cell cultures for cell segmentation, while watershed-based separation and intensity-based classification were employed for viability detection. The model demonstrated accurate segmentation with minimal overfitting. Quantitative comparisons with manual counts and ImageJ-based results confirmed its accuracy. We then demonstrated the possibility of extending this model to 3D constructs by tracking cell density and viability during time in the case of human umbilical vein endothelial cells bioprinted in gelatin methacrylate at different seeding densities, taken as case study. Automated counts closely matched manual ones, highlighting the method reliability and minimal invasiveness avoiding the need for sacrificing the construct. Hence, this approach provides a scalable, reproducible, and efficient alternative to manual counting in 3D environments, enabling high-throughput analysis of complex fluorescence microscopy data.

secondary.title: BasNet: Attention U-Net-Based Automated Axon Segmentation in Bielschowsky Silver-Stained Histology.
secondary.abstract: Reliable automatic quantification of axon density in histologic sections is important for both research and clinical neuropathology applications - however, it remains a challenge for silver-impregnation stains, such as Bielschowsky. Classical color-deconvolution approaches perform poorly on silver stains, and manual annotation of densely packed axons is time-consuming and subject to inter-rater variability. We developed an automated axon segmentation pipeline in Bielschowsky silver-stained histological brain sections based on an attention U-Net architecture with attention-gated skip connections, trained using Focal Tversky Loss to handle class imbalance and thin structure recovery. Ground truth was manually annotated on 33 image tiles (covering over 25 million pixels) derived from 26 whole-slide images from varying brain regions of four multiple sclerosis patients. Slides were prepared by different laboratory technicians at different time points to capture realistic staining variability. Model performance was evaluated on a held-out test set of unseen tiles. On the test set (eight held-out tiles) the model achieved a mean pixel-wise F1/Dice of 0.717 and an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.584. A dedicated inter-rater experiment on two representative tiles yielded rater-to-rater F1 scores of 0.637 and 0.671, while model-to-rater agreement (F1: 0.681-0.736) met or exceeded that human ceiling. Generated whole-slide density and orientation visualizations accurately reflected regional axon distributions and provided quantitative readouts suitable for downstream analysis. Our attention U-Net provides an open-source solution for axon segmentation from Bielschowsky-stained sections, reducing manual effort and enabling reproducible, slide-level quantitative metrics. This tool can facilitate studies of axonal pathology across research and clinical settings.

best.title: Making smart microscopy deployable in imaging core facilities.
best.abstract: Smart microscopy, in which real-time image analysis enables microscopes to adapt their acquisition dynamically, is becoming central to biological imaging. However, deploying such workflows in imaging facilities remains challenging. The computers that control microscopes in a facility are shared, governed by institutional policies, often offline and run vendor-specific software. As a result, installing custom software environments for the workflow of each user is both unsafe and unsustainable. We argue that smart microscopy requires a practical deployment strategy that links open-source bioimage analysis with commercial acquisition software without turning acquisition computers into development platforms. Using our recently developed tools, NucleiSky and LabConstrictor, as examples, we demonstrate how microscope control and external image analysis can be integrated while keeping the custom Python environment separate from the vendor-managed environment. The deployment strategy might vary - for instance, a USB drive, a facility workstation, a server or a network share - but the underlying principle remains the same: smart-microscopy workflows must be straightforward to approve, launch, reuse, audit and remove. Smart microscopy will become routine only when it is both powerful and deployable.

best.title: Comparison of manual counting with two rule-based image analysis programs, ImageJ and CellProfiler, for quantitative analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemical positivity in rat brainstem sections.
best.abstract: Quantitative and semiquantitative assessment of biomarker expression using immunohistochemistry (IHC) can be performed using several analytical approaches. Manual counting remains widely used but is inherently subjective and susceptible to observer variability. Rule-based image-analysis platforms may provide accessible alternatives, highlighting the need for direct method-comparison and agreement studies. c-Fos is a well-established marker of neuronal activation commonly quantified by counting IHC-positive cells. This study compared manual counting, ImageJ, and CellProfiler for quantifying c-Fos-positive cells in rat brainstem sections. Of 125 images initially evaluated, one was excluded as an extreme outlier, leaving 124 images for final analysis. Each image was independently analyzed by two trained observers using all three methods. ImageJ and CellProfiler were applied through their standard graphical interfaces and built-in functions using predefined user-guided threshold ranges, without additional plugins, scripts, machine-learning models, or custom code. Agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and Bland-Altman analysis. No statistically significant difference in c-Fos-positive cell counts was observed among the three methods (Friedman test, P = 0.07). Median (IQR) counts were 6.75 (0.50-13.50) for manual counting, 6.25 (1.00-14.38) for ImageJ, and 6.00 (0.63-14.50) for CellProfiler. Inter-observer agreement was excellent for manual counting (ICC = 0.983), ImageJ (ICC = 0.964), and CellProfiler (ICC = 0.962). Inter-method agreement was also excellent (single-measures ICC = 0.971; 95% CI = 0.961-0.979). Bland-Altman analysis showed small mean biases of 0.33, 0.27, and -0.07 cells, with no significant proportional bias. Manual counting, ImageJ, and CellProfiler produced statistically comparable c-Fos-positive cell counts with excellent agreement. Under the predefined user-guided threshold ranges used, both software platforms closely matched manual counting; however, image-dependent threshold adjustment remains a potential source of observer variability.

best.title: DINOSim: Training-Free Semantic Segmentation on Microscopy Images.
best.abstract: We present DINOSim, a training-free method for segmenting objects in microscopy images without the need for large annotated datasets or additional model training. DINOSim builds on the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder, which captures semantic information from images. By comparing the encoder's features of image patches to those of a user-selected reference, DINOSim generates pseudo-labels that guide semantic segmentation. Subsequently, a k-nearest neighbors framework is used to refine predictions across new images. Our experiments show that DINOSim can effectively segment previously unseen objects in diverse microscopy datasets, offering performance comparable to supervised approaches while avoiding the need for costly manual labeling. We also investigate how different choices of user prompt selection and model size affect accuracy and generalization. To make the method widely accessible, we provide an open-source napari plugin (github.com/AAitorG/napari-DINOSim), enabling researchers to apply DINOSim to their own data easily. Overall, DINOSim offers a fast, flexible and practical solution for bioimage analysis, particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings.
