best.title: Partaker: deep-learning-based single-cell-resolution analysis of multi-dimensional, long-term, microfluidic-based time-lapse microscopy data.
best.abstract: MOTIVATION: Deep-learning segmentation models for microbial time-lapse fluorescence microscopy already exist, but they are often difficult to use consistently across experiments and are not packaged with unified workflows for combining models, quantifying multi-channel fluorescence, and scaling analyses to large microfluidic imaging datasets. RESULTS: To address these challenges, we developed Partaker, an easy-to-use Python-based graphical tool for deep-learning segmentation, multi-channel fluorescence quantification, and morphological analysis of microbial cells over time. Partaker supports extensible model integration, efficient handling of large imaging datasets, and interactive visualization, enabling time-resolved analysis of population fluorescence distributions from per-cell measurements. We demonstrate performance using a two-strain validation experiment (housekeeping and inducible) and show robust recovery of population-level fluorescence dynamics with single-cell resolution. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Partaker is implemented in Python and is available on GitHub (https://github.com/SamOliveiraLab/partaker). A versioned release of the software is archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18844425). Documentation, example datasets, and installation instructions are provided in the repository.

best.title: Benchmarking cell segmentation in two Spatialomics platforms with open-source software.
best.abstract: UNLABELLED: The in situ tissue microenvironment is a complex mixture of different cell types, microanatomic structures, and acellular matrix material. Further, disease perturbs the morphologies of these features significantly. Spatial proteomics utilizing optical or mass spectrometer imaging simultaneously detects expression and subcellular localization of many proteins. Accurate identification of heterogeneous, irregular, and tightly interdigitating cell boundaries is a crucial step for all downstream analyses, including cell phenotyping and cell-cell interaction networks. We describe a benchmarking approach for rapid assessment of segmentation algorithm performance in melanoma and breast cancer contexts using mass spectrometer and optical spatial omics imaging platforms. Comparison of cell segmentation by fourteen methods to pathologist ground-truth annotation with Jaccard pixel index and F1 object measurement identified Cellpose models that performed well across different tumor samples and data sources with minimal fine-tuning. Algorithms utilizing cell membrane and nuclear features demonstrated better performance in both tumor samples. This benchmarking approach is a rapid and effective method to assess performance of cell segmentation methods in different contexts for efficient algorithm selection and iterative model training. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70919-2.

best.title: NucGen3D: A synthetic framework for large-scale 3D nuclear segmentation with open-source training data and models.
best.abstract: Robust nuclear segmentation in 3D microscopy images is a critical yet unsolved challenge in quantitative cell biology. The main challenges are the scarcity and variability of annotated volumetric datasets. Since these data are difficult to obtain, most state-of-the-art approaches, including Cellpose, segment individual 2D slices and then heuristically reconstruct 3D volumes, thereby losing critical spatial context. Our analysis of expert annotator performance confirms that ignoring 3D context introduces substantial variability in nuclear detection and annotation. While a few 3D models are trained on small or toy datasets, no large-scale, openly available resource currently exists to enable robust training of high-capacity 3D segmentation networks. To address this problem, we present NucGen3D, a customizable simulation framework that generates large-scale, annotated 3D microscopy datasets from limited 2D input, specifically the 2018 Data Science Bowl dataset. NucGen3D produces realistic 3D volumes across diverse biological and imaging scenarios, including variations in nuclear morphology, spatial arrangement, and imaging noise. Using this synthetic data, we trained two models from scratch: a 2D convolutional neural network under Cellpose-like conditions, and a fully 3D convolutional model that extends the 2D settings. We evaluated both on a challenging, independent real-world dataset with complex nuclear architectures. Both models, especially the 3D model, achieve competitive performance with respect to state-of-the-art methods, including those trained on larger annotated datasets or based on more complex architectures. These results demonstrate that synthetic data can effectively substitute for full 3D annotations when training models at scale. To promote reproducibility and further research, we release both the NucGen3D framework and the fully trained 3D segmentation model as open source, making this the first end-to-end open resource for large-scale 3D nuclear segmentation.

best.title: SynapTrack: An automated tool for synapse quantification.
best.abstract: Reliable synapse quantification remains challenging, particularly in high-throughput fluorescence imaging workflows. Here we present SynapTrack, a fully automated FIJI/ImageJ-based tool for quantifying synapses in cultured neurons and brain tissue sections with minimal user intervention. SynapTrack combines channel-specific preprocessing, background subtraction, and SynQuant-based detection of colocalised pre- and postsynaptic puncta. In cultured neurons, it additionally measures cell number and total dendritic length, enabling normalisation of synapse counts per cell and per 10 micrometer of dendrite. Using hippocampal cultures, SynapTrack reliably quantified excitatory and inhibitory synapses, captured the expected predominance of excitatory contacts, and reduced inter-sample variability through structural normalisation. Compared with SynBot, SynapTrack detected more synapses while better preserving biologically meaningful differences between synapse types. For tissue sections, in which cell counting and dendritic segmentation are impractical, we developed SynapTrack_Tissue, an adapted workflow based on presynaptic-postsynaptic colocalisation alone. Despite the lack of cellular normalisation, this approach produced stable measurements across heterogeneous neuropil regions. Because all spatial parameters are defined in micrometres, analysis settings are portable across imaging systems. SynapTrack therefore provides a standardised and scalable framework for synapse quantification in both cultured neurons and tissue sections.

best.title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath.
best.abstract: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10-9 absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

best.title: CellColocDB: a disease-centred resource linking GWAS loci to genes, cell contexts, and fine-mapping evidence.
best.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified disease-associated loci, but linking these signals to molecular mechanisms remains difficult because of linkage disequilibrium and context-dependent genetic regulation. CellColocDB is a disease- and window-centred resource integrating GWAS-QTL colocalization across bulk, sorted-cell, and single-cell QTL datasets. The current release includes 2805 GWAS datasets covering 1201 diseases and traits and 40 516 GWAS windows, together with 23 QTL sources, 316 QTL contexts, and 89 842 molecular features. CellColocDB contains 3 572 118 coloc.abf results with PP.H4 > 0.5, including 1 609 418 with PP.H4 ≥ 0.8. Analyses are organized as GWAS dataset × GWAS window × QTL context × molecular feature tasks, allowing contexts and molecular features to be compared within the same GWAS region. coloc.abf is the primary colocalization analysis, with coloc-SuSiE and SMR/HEIDI providing complementary evidence where available. Task-specific ABF top SNPs are linked to CAUSALdb2 fine-mapping results from seven methods. Results are available through disease-, QTL context-, gene-, and locus-level views, with regional association tracks and matched variants, and can be queried by gene, genomic region, or GWAS window ID. CellColocDB is freely available at http://www.mulinlab.org/colocdb/.

best.title: CellScore: an open-source image-based pipeline for automated cell quantification in microalgae.
best.abstract: Accurate quantification of microalgal cell density is essential for both basic research and industrial applications, as it directly reflects culture growth, productivity, and physiological status. There are existing methods routinely used to measure cell counts, although many are limited by high cost, labor-intensive workflows, or steep technical barriers. To address these limitations, we developed CellScore, a rapid and accessible image-based pipeline for microalgal cell counting implemented in ImageJ, a widely adopted open-source platform in the biological sciences ( https://github.com/shijieh/imageJ-annotate ). By leveraging the broad user base and ease of installation of the software, CellScore enables researchers to obtain reliable cell counts from standard microscopy images with minimal specialized equipment. Although the workflow has only been tested with three microalgae species of similar morphologies, the pipeline balances automation with user control and includes practical troubleshooting strategies to facilitate adoption by new users. Thus, CellScore has the potential to be used broadly across other species, however, broader validation across diverse morphologies is required. Overall, CellScore provides a cost-effective, user-friendly, and reproducible solution for routine microalgal cell quantification in both laboratory and applied settings.

best.abstract: Scanning transmission soft X-ray microscopy (STXM), combined with near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS), enables the mapping of elemental distributions and chemical properties at a spatial resolution of tens of nanometers. best.title: A Deep Learning Pipeline for Cell Segmentation and Viability Quantification in 3D Constructs From Fluorescence Microscopy Images.
best.abstract: With the increasing adoption of 3D cell cultures and bioprinting in biomedical research, there is a growing demand for reliable and accurate monitoring methods. While fluorescence microscopy is widely accepted for 2D cell cultures, when introducing the third dimension it often suffers from signal attenuation and out-of-focus interference, making automated image analysis challenging. In this study, a hybrid pipeline that integrates deep learning and traditional image processing techniques is presented with the aim of establishing an automated tool for cell segmentation and viability assessment in 3D from fluorescence microscopy images. A U 2-Net architecture was trained on 2D cell cultures for cell segmentation, while watershed-based separation and intensity-based classification were employed for viability detection. The model demonstrated accurate segmentation with minimal overfitting. Quantitative comparisons with manual counts and ImageJ-based results confirmed its accuracy. We then demonstrated the possibility of extending this model to 3D constructs by tracking cell density and viability during time in the case of human umbilical vein endothelial cells bioprinted in gelatin methacrylate at different seeding densities, taken as case study. Automated counts closely matched manual ones, highlighting the method reliability and minimal invasiveness avoiding the need for sacrificing the construct. Hence, this approach provides a scalable, reproducible, and efficient alternative to manual counting in 3D environments, enabling high-throughput analysis of complex fluorescence microscopy data.

best.title: BasNet: Attention U-Net-Based Automated Axon Segmentation in Bielschowsky Silver-Stained Histology.
best.abstract: Reliable automatic quantification of axon density in histologic sections is important for both research and clinical neuropathology applications - however, it remains a challenge for silver-impregnation stains, such as Bielschowsky. Classical color-deconvolution approaches perform poorly on silver stains, and manual annotation of densely packed axons is time-consuming and subject to inter-rater variability. We developed an automated axon segmentation pipeline in Bielschowsky silver-stained histological brain sections based on an attention U-Net architecture with attention-gated skip connections, trained using Focal Tversky Loss to handle class imbalance and thin structure recovery. Ground truth was manually annotated on 33 image tiles (covering over 25 million pixels) derived from 26 whole-slide images from varying brain regions of four multiple sclerosis patients. Slides were prepared by different laboratory technicians at different time points to capture realistic staining variability. Model performance was evaluated on a held-out test set of unseen tiles. On the test set (eight held-out tiles) the model achieved a mean pixel-wise F1/Dice of 0.717 and an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.584. A dedicated inter-rater experiment on two representative tiles yielded rater-to-rater F1 scores of 0.637 and 0.671, while model-to-rater agreement (F1: 0.681-0.736) met or exceeded that human ceiling. Generated whole-slide density and orientation visualizations accurately reflected regional axon distributions and provided quantitative readouts suitable for downstream analysis. Our attention U-Net provides an open-source solution for axon segmentation from Bielschowsky-stained sections, reducing manual effort and enabling reproducible, slide-level quantitative metrics. This tool can facilitate studies of axonal pathology across research and clinical settings.

primary.title: Drp-1 Participates in LPS-Induced Neuroinflammation and Microglia-Neuron Interaction Through mtDNA-cGAS-STING Axis.
primary.abstract: To investigate the role of dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp-1) in the process of LPS-induced microglial injury and its initiated neuroinflammation. C57BL/6J mice or BV2 microglia were challenged with LPS, and the behavioral performance and the cell viability were tested, respectively. The expression of Drp-1, inflammatory factors, and key molecules of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway was measured in the mouse hippocampus or in microglia in vitro, together with the abundance of mtDNA. Moreover, the effect of Drp-1 was further explored by siRNA in vitro and its selective inhibitor Mdivi-1 in vivo. Furthermore, a co-culture system of microglia and neurons was used to observe the potential role of cell-free mtDNA in the microglia-neuron crosstalk. Meanwhile, the plasma levels of cell-free mitochondrial DNA (cf-mtDNA) were detected in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). In vivo, intraperitoneal injection of LPS could result in anxious-like and depression-like behaviors in mice, together with a significant microglial activation and its related neuroinflammation, mtDNA release, and the imbalanced expression of synaptic plasticity, Drp-1, cGAS, STING, p-STING, and IRF3 in the hippocampus. All these behavioral and neuropathological changes could be reversed by treatment with Mdivi-1. Moreover, LPS-induced behavioral dysfunction and neuropathological injuries were also observed in mice that received hippocampal stereotactic injection of mtDNA. In vitro, besides the detrimental effect of LPS on microglia, our results indicated a crucial role of microglia-derived mtDNA in linking Drp-1-associated mitochondrial dysfunction to LPS-induced microglial injury and neuroinflammation, and in the crosstalk between HT22 and BV2 cells. Additionally, the plasma concentration of cf-mtDNA was increased in MDD patients, with a significant positive correlation with plasma levels of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IFN-γ. As a key regulator of mitochondrial fission, the imbalanced expression of Drp-1 participates in LPS-induced microglial injury and neuroinflammation via the Drp-1-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis.

primary.title: Motor neuron disease due to a novel PIK3R1 mutation.
primary.abstract: Mutations in PIK3R1, which encodes the regulatory subunit (p85α) of class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), are associated with immunologic and developmental disorders, but their effects on the nervous system have not been studied. We identified a novel heterozygous frameshift mutation (PIK3R1 c.1710dup) in a patient with common variable immunodeficiency who developed adult-onset, slowly progressive ALS-like motor-neuron disease. Studies of patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) demonstrated PIK3R1 haploinsufficiency with selective AKT activation. Investigation of patient's iPSC-derived motor neurons (iMNs) showed reduced neuronal electrical activity, and markedly increased apoptosis. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed coordinated up-regulation of differentiation and apoptosis programs across neuronal and glial clusters. Engineering the PIK3R1 c.1710dup mutation into healthy-control iPSCs reproduced the impaired electrical activity, increased apoptosis, and transcriptional vulnerability, confirming the variant's cell-intrinsic pathogenicity. In contrast, introduction of canonical APDS2-associated PIK3R1 splice mutations into the same genetic background did not produce these abnormalities, establishing a variant-class-specific mechanism of PI3K dysfunction. Together, these findings define PIK3R1 c.1710dup as a distinct pathogenic variant that links PI3K-pathway dysregulation to human motor-neuron degeneration and expands the mechanistic spectrum of PIK3R1-associated disease.

primary.title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis CpsA interferes with the TBK1-p62 axis to inhibit xenophagy.
primary.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) survives in macrophages by interfering with host lysosomal trafficking. Previously, we demonstrated that the Mtb protein, CpsA, is critical for bacterial survival in macrophages and infection in mice and that it can inhibit a noncanonical autophagy pathway. primary.title: Strontium-90 Radiotherapy Suppresses Fibrosis by Attenuating the FAK-RhoA/ROCK-YAP/TAZ Mechanosignaling Axis in Hypertrophic Scars.
primary.abstract: Hypertrophic scar (HTS) fibrosis is sustained by abnormal mechanical signaling, but how strontium-90 (Sr-90) superficial radiotherapy counteracts this process is unclear. We combined primary HTS fibroblasts and a rabbit ear HTS model with atomic force microscopy, molecular and functional assays, histology, and RNA sequencing to examine cell mechanics and FAK-RhoA/ROCK-YAP/TAZ signaling. Sr-90 reduced fibroblast stiffness and stress-fiber organization, inhibited nuclear YAP/TAZ localization, TEAD activity, profibrotic gene expression, migration, adhesion, and collagen-gel contraction, while increasing LATS1/2 phosphorylation and suppressing FAK/Src-RhoA/ROCK-MLC2 signaling. YAP/TAZ overexpression partially reversed these effects, TEAD1/4 silencing diminished the reversal, and non-phosphorylatable YAP-5SA/TAZ-4SA mutants produced stronger rescue than the corresponding wild-type proteins under irradiation. In rabbits, Sr-90 reduced scar pathology, YAP/TAZ-TEAD interaction, and FAK-RhoA signaling and downregulated Hippo- and focal-adhesion-related transcriptional programs. These findings show that Sr-90 suppresses HTS fibrosis by weakening the mechanical-signaling network that converges on YAP/TAZ and by enhancing LATS1/2-dependent YAP/TAZ inactivation.

primary.title: VPS35 Regulates Microglial Lipid Droplet Accumulation in Parkinson's Disease via Rab7.
primary.abstract: Microglial dysfunction and aberrant lipid metabolism are emerging as key contributors to Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, the specific role and regulation of lipid droplets (LDs) within microglia remain poorly defined. In this study, we employed MPTP- and LPS-induced PD mouse models and an in vitro system utilizing astrocyte-conditioned medium to model disease-relevant lipid stress and found enhanced LD accumulation in microglia. VPS35 expression was decreased in microglia, correlating with elevated microglial LD levels in PD mouse models. We then performed genetic manipulations (knockdown and overexpression) of VPS35, including the PD-associated D620N mutant, in primary microglia and assessed LD accumulation, phagocytic function, inflammatory responses, and integrated stress pathways. We showed that VPS35 knockdown exacerbated the accumulation of LDs in microglia. Conversely, VPS35 overexpression ameliorated LD formation, improved phagocytic function, and reduced inflammatory and integrated stress responses in microglia. The PD-related VPS35[D620N] mutation abolished these protective effects. We further found that VPS35 interacts with Rab7 to maintain lysosomal function, and the D620N mutation disrupts this interaction, leading to defective LD clearance. Our findings reveal VPS35 dysfunction as a key pathogenic mechanism in PD, where the D620N mutation disrupts microglial lipid handling to promote disease progression, thereby nominating VPS35 restoration as a promising therapeutic strategy.

secondary.title: Spatial mTOR biology: From organelle localization to biomolecular condensates and metabolic control.
secondary.abstract: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) coordinates cell growth, metabolism, protein synthesis, autophagy, and survival by integrating nutrient availability, growth factors, energy status, mechanical cues, and cellular stress. Beyond classical biochemical cascades, mTOR signaling specificity is fundamentally governed by subcellular localization, temporal recruitment, and microenvironmental context. This review synthesizes current insights into the spatial architecture of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) across lysosomes, endosomes, plasma-membrane microdomains, organelle contact sites, neuronal processes, the nucleus, and biomolecular condensates. We examine how physical principles-including membrane composition and curvature, molecular confinement, macromolecular crowding, scaffold-mediated multivalent interactions, organelle positioning, mechanical tension, and localized translation-dictate signaling outcomes. Furthermore, we contrast membrane-anchored molecular assemblies with three-dimensional biomolecular condensates, detailing their interplay during stress adaptation. Spatial constraints in specialized cell geometries, such as neuronal compartments and developing tissues, illustrate how identical signaling machinery yields divergent functional outputs under altered diffusion environments. We also evaluate how advances in spatial multi-omics and super-resolution imaging extend these subcellular paradigms to tissue-scale heterogeneity. Finally, we highlight major translational hurdles, including the trade-off between spatial resolution and dynamic temporal tracking in current technologies, as well as the inability of conventional pharmacotherapies to selectively target discrete subcellular mTOR pools. Establishing spatial organization as a primary determinant of mTOR signaling clarifies context-dependent physiological outputs and provides a roadmap for developing next-generation spatially targeted therapeutics.

secondary.title: PDE2A is involved in negative emotional behaviors via the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway in the SPS&S model.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by negative affective symptoms, including anxiety, depression, anhedonia, and fear. The molecular mechanisms underlying these symptoms remain poorly understood. Phosphodiesterase 2A (PDE2A), a regulator of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling, has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the role of the PDE2A-cAMP-protein kinase A (PKA) signaling pathway in negative emotional behaviors induced by traumatic stress. METHODS: Transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes and enriched pathways. A rat PTSD model was established using single prolonged stress combined with foot shocks (SPS&S). Behavioral tests were performed, and PDE2A-cAMP-PKA signaling alterations in the amygdala were examined. The effects of PDE2A inhibitor Hcyb1 and the PKA inhibitor H89 were evaluated. RESULTS: Bioinformatics analysis identified PDE2A as a hub gene associated with PTSD, with significant enrichment of the cAMP signaling pathway. SPS&S rats exhibited anxiety-, depression-like behaviors, and anhedonia, accompanied by increased PDE2A expression and reduced cAMP and phosphorylated PKA (p-PKA) levels in the amygdala. Hcyb1 treatment alleviated behavioral deficits, decreased PDE2A expression, and restored cAMP and p-PKA signaling. H89 blocked p-PKA activation and partially reversed the behavioral benefits of Hcyb1. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that amygdala PDE2A-cAMP-PKA signaling is associated with negative emotional behaviors in the SPS&S model. PDE2A inhibition may ameliorate behavioral deficits through PKA-related signaling. However, the peripheral blood transcriptomic data, lack of direct PDE2A activity and cAMP/cGMP measurements, and limited biochemical validation constrain mechanistic interpretation. Further studies using brain-derived datasets and comprehensive biochemical approaches are warranted.

secondary.title: TRIB3 Knockdown Attenuates Post-cardiac Arrest Brain Injury with Suppression of Mitophagy: Involvement of AKT-FOXO3a-BNIP3 Signaling.
secondary.abstract: Brain injury after cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CA-CPR) is a major cause of poor neurological outcomes among survivors, yet effective mechanism-based interventions remain lacking. Mitophagy maintains mitochondrial homeostasis, but whether increased mitophagy contributes to brain injury after CA-CPR and which upstream factors regulate it remain unclear. Transcriptomic analysis of hippocampal tissue from rats subjected to asphyxial CA-CPR identified tribbles pseudokinase 3 (TRIB3) as one of the most strongly upregulated genes, with its expression approximately 68-fold higher than that in sham controls. TRIB3 was knocked down by adeno-associated virus (AAV) injection into the hippocampal CA1 region 4 weeks before CA-CPR and by lentiviral transduction in H19-7 cells before oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R). TRIB3 knockdown improved neurological function and attenuated hippocampal CA1 neuronal injury in CA-CPR rats. It also attenuated mitophagy, alleviated mitochondrial dysfunction, and reduced neuronal apoptosis in vivo and in vitro. Valproic acid partially counteracted these mitochondrial and anti-apoptotic effects in vitro. Mechanistic analyses in OGD/R-treated cells showed that TRIB3 knockdown increased the p-AKT/AKT and p-FOXO3a/FOXO3a ratios, reduced FOXO3a nuclear accumulation and BNIP3 expression, and decreased FOXO3a enrichment at the Bnip3 promoter. Co-immunoprecipitation assays showed increased TRIB3-AKT association and reduced AKT-FOXO3a association after OGD/R. In vivo, TIC10 treatment partially counteracted the improvements in mitochondrial function and neurological outcomes following TRIB3 knockdown. Together, these findings suggest that TRIB3 may act as a previously unrecognized upstream modulator of mitophagy after CA-CPR, implicate AKT-FOXO3a-BNIP3 signaling, and support further evaluation of TRIB3 as a potential neuroprotective target.

secondary.title: Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal cord D2R expression via the PP2A/AKT-dependent NMDA receptor phosphorylation.
secondary.abstract: Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 48-h continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

best.title: Drp-1 Participates in LPS-Induced Neuroinflammation and Microglia-Neuron Interaction Through mtDNA-cGAS-STING Axis.
best.abstract: To investigate the role of dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp-1) in the process of LPS-induced microglial injury and its initiated neuroinflammation. C57BL/6J mice or BV2 microglia were challenged with LPS, and the behavioral performance and the cell viability were tested, respectively. The expression of Drp-1, inflammatory factors, and key molecules of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway was measured in the mouse hippocampus or in microglia in vitro, together with the abundance of mtDNA. Moreover, the effect of Drp-1 was further explored by siRNA in vitro and its selective inhibitor Mdivi-1 in vivo. Furthermore, a co-culture system of microglia and neurons was used to observe the potential role of cell-free mtDNA in the microglia-neuron crosstalk. Meanwhile, the plasma levels of cell-free mitochondrial DNA (cf-mtDNA) were detected in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). In vivo, intraperitoneal injection of LPS could result in anxious-like and depression-like behaviors in mice, together with a significant microglial activation and its related neuroinflammation, mtDNA release, and the imbalanced expression of synaptic plasticity, Drp-1, cGAS, STING, p-STING, and IRF3 in the hippocampus. All these behavioral and neuropathological changes could be reversed by treatment with Mdivi-1. Moreover, LPS-induced behavioral dysfunction and neuropathological injuries were also observed in mice that received hippocampal stereotactic injection of mtDNA. In vitro, besides the detrimental effect of LPS on microglia, our results indicated a crucial role of microglia-derived mtDNA in linking Drp-1-associated mitochondrial dysfunction to LPS-induced microglial injury and neuroinflammation, and in the crosstalk between HT22 and BV2 cells. Additionally, the plasma concentration of cf-mtDNA was increased in MDD patients, with a significant positive correlation with plasma levels of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IFN-γ. As a key regulator of mitochondrial fission, the imbalanced expression of Drp-1 participates in LPS-induced microglial injury and neuroinflammation via the Drp-1-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis.

best.title: Motor neuron disease due to a novel PIK3R1 mutation.
best.abstract: Mutations in PIK3R1, which encodes the regulatory subunit (p85α) of class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), are associated with immunologic and developmental disorders, but their effects on the nervous system have not been studied. We identified a novel heterozygous frameshift mutation (PIK3R1 c.1710dup) in a patient with common variable immunodeficiency who developed adult-onset, slowly progressive ALS-like motor-neuron disease. Studies of patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) demonstrated PIK3R1 haploinsufficiency with selective AKT activation. Investigation of patient's iPSC-derived motor neurons (iMNs) showed reduced neuronal electrical activity, and markedly increased apoptosis. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed coordinated up-regulation of differentiation and apoptosis programs across neuronal and glial clusters. Engineering the PIK3R1 c.1710dup mutation into healthy-control iPSCs reproduced the impaired electrical activity, increased apoptosis, and transcriptional vulnerability, confirming the variant's cell-intrinsic pathogenicity. In contrast, introduction of canonical APDS2-associated PIK3R1 splice mutations into the same genetic background did not produce these abnormalities, establishing a variant-class-specific mechanism of PI3K dysfunction. Together, these findings define PIK3R1 c.1710dup as a distinct pathogenic variant that links PI3K-pathway dysregulation to human motor-neuron degeneration and expands the mechanistic spectrum of PIK3R1-associated disease.

Co-immunoprecipitation assays showed increased TRIB3-AKT association and reduced AKT-FOXO3a association after OGD/R. In vivo, TIC10 treatment partially counteracted the improvements in mitochondrial function and neurological outcomes following TRIB3 knockdown. Together, these findings suggest that TRIB3 may act as a previously unrecognized upstream modulator of mitophagy after CA-CPR, implicate AKT-FOXO3a-BNIP3 signaling, and support further evaluation of TRIB3 as a potential neuroprotective target.

best.title: Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal cord D2R expression via the PP2A/AKT-dependent NMDA receptor phosphorylation.
best.abstract: Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 48-h continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

primary.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
primary.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

primary.title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
primary.abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

primary.title: Serum Extracellular Vesicle Proteomics Identifies Candidate Protein Biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder with a Diagnostic Specificity Assessment against Schizophrenia.
primary.abstract: Diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD) relies on subjective criteria and lacks objective biomarkers. Serum extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry stable cargo and can cross the blood-brain barrier, making them attractive biomarker sources. We therefore profiled serum EVs from a discovery cohort of 60 participants (40 healthy controls [HCs], 20 MDD patients) by size-exclusion chromatography and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and subsequently validated candidate proteins by ELISA in an independent cohort of 60 participants (20 HCs, 20 MDD, 20 patients with schizophrenia [SCZ]). Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were defined by |log2 fold change| > 1 and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted q < 0.05. Using these criteria, we identified 358 DEPs (235 upregulated, 123 downregulated), which were enriched in complement activation, coagulation, and immune-inflammatory pathways. However, several of the most significant DEPs are abundant circulating plasma proteins that are common co-isolates of serum EVs, so part of this signal may reflect residual soluble serum protein, and-given that EVs were isolated from serum rather than platelet-poor plasma-the pathway enrichment should be interpreted with caution. In the validation cohort, EV-associated TNC and APLP1 were elevated and EV-associated TF was reduced in MDD relative to HCs (P < 0.05), whereas only serum APLP1 was elevated. Notably, EV-associated TNC was also elevated in SCZ, while APLP1 and TF were unchanged; moreover, direct MDD-versus-SCZ comparisons were not significant, indicating that the data do not support MDD-specific alterations. In addition, a logistic-regression model combining EV-associated APLP1, TF and TNC distinguished MDD from HCs with an area under the curve of 0.905 (95% CI 0.812-0.998; 0.830 by leave-one-out cross-validation), outperforming individual proteins (TF 0.725; TNC 0.758; APLP1 0.725). Collectively, these findings define a serum EV-associated proteomic signature in MDD and preliminarily validate TF, TNC and APLP1 as candidate diagnostic biomarkers, implicating immune-inflammatory and complement-related pathways. Nevertheless, the panel remains exploratory and requires validation in larger, multi-center cohorts with diverse psychiatric controls.

primary.title: Mechanism of Autophagic Extracellular Vesicles Revealed.
primary.abstract: Recent work by Mao and colleagues identifies a distinct class of small extracellular vesicles, termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs), generated from amphisomes upon autophagy induction. In this commentary, we discuss how this study provides important mechanistic insight into the coupling between autophagy and secretion. AEVs are molecularly and functionally distinct from canonical exosomes, being enriched in autophagy-related components such as LC3 and p62, and dependent on core ATG machinery for their biogenesis. Notably, their secretion is enhanced by autophagy induction and contributes to intercellular communication, particularly in the context of viral infection. These findings position amphisomes as critical sorting hubs that direct cargo toward either degradation or secretion, thereby integrating autophagic and endolysosomal pathways. We further highlight how these results intersect with prior evidence implicating SNARE-dependent mechanisms, including VAMP7 and stress-responsive regulators such as GRASP55, in unconventional secretion. Finally, we discuss key unresolved questions, particularly the mechanisms underlying the generation of small intraluminal vesicles within amphisomes and the role of ESCRT machinery in this process. Overall, the identification of AEVs adds a new layer of complexity to extracellular vesicle biology and opens new avenues for understanding how autophagy contributes to intercellular signaling in health and disease.

primary.title: Glycoprotein-induced phase separation drives unconventional secretion of galectin-3.
primary.abstract: The mechanism of unconventional protein secretion remains an unresolved issue. Here, we describe an unconventional protein secretion pathway for galectin-3 that is mediated by phase separation and condensation. Using four lysosomal damage models, we observed a rapid, pronounced release of galectin-3 in large, non-exosomal particles. This secretion is driven by glycoprotein-induced galectin-3 phase separation and is independent of pyroptosis and secretory autophagy. During phase separation, the S-face of galectin-3 carbohydrate recognition domain binds glycoproteins that triggers galectin-3 N-terminal tail release and condensation. These condensates then recruit ALG-2 via the exposed N-terminal tail. ALG-2 directs the condensates to the endoplasmic reticulum-late endosome interface. After translocation into late endosomes, galectin-3 condensates are secreted into the extracellular milieu by SNARE-dependent vesicular transport. This mechanism of exporting phase-separated protein condensates may serve as a clean-up response to membrane damage.

primary.title: A protective role for APP in nuclear waste clearance via lysosomal exocytosis.
primary.abstract: Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is widely known for its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis through its proteolytic processing into amyloid-β peptides. However, its physiological functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a protective role for full-length APP in facilitating the disposal of nuclear-derived debris under genotoxic stress. In both cultured cells and in vivo mouse models, loss of APP leads to nuclear waste accumulation, increased inflammation, and cell death, whereas APP overexpression mitigates these effects. Mechanistically, we show that APP supports the extracellular release of nuclear waste material through lysosomal exocytosis. APP mutants associated with familial AD fail to mediate this process. Consistently, human AD brain tissue exhibits abnormal nuclear morphology, accumulation of nuclear waste in the cytoplasm, and reduced APP levels per neuron. These findings highlight a conserved cellular mechanism by which APP contributes to nuclear and cellular homeostasis, and suggest that impaired nuclear waste clearance may represent an underappreciated contributor to neurodegeneration.

primary.title: GPNMB is a biomarker for lysosomal dysfunction and is secreted via LRRK2-modulated lysosomal exocytosis.
primary.abstract: Genome-wide association studies have identified Glycoprotein Nmb (GPNMB) as a risk factor for Parkinson's disease. The risk allele increases GPNMB transcription and GPNMB protein levels in the CSF highlighting GPMNB as a potential biomarker for Parkinson's disease. However, a lack of knowledge of GPNMB's function and mechanism of secretion has hindered an interpretation of secreted GPNMB levels. In this study, we assessed the mechanism of GPNMB secretion by macrophages, the primary cell type expressing GPNMB in the brain. We show that GPNMB is secreted in response to lysosomal stress via lysosomal exocytosis and highlight the Parkinson's disease risk factor LRRK2 as a strong modulator of GPNMB secretion.

primary.title: Autophagic extracellular vesicles: a distinct secretory route linking autophagy to extracellular communication.
primary.abstract: Macroautophagy/autophagy is classically defined as a degradative pathway that delivers cytoplasmic material to lysosomes. However, accumulating evidence indicates that autophagy can also support unconventional secretion. A recent study identifies a previously unrecognized subtype of small extracellular vesicles termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs). These vesicles originate from amphisomes formed by the fusion of autophagosomes with multivesicular bodies and are characterized by a size below 100 nm together with the presence of autophagic cargos, ESCRT-III components and RAB13. Importantly, biogenesis of AEVs is distinct from that of classical exosomes, which requires specific components of the ESCRT III complex and the GTPase RAB27A. The further finding that enterovirus can exploit AEVs to infect receptor-negative cells, thereby expanding viral tropism, suggests that secretory autophagy serves as a pivotal mechanism driving pathogen dissemination. This work provides the conceptual framework of extracellular vesicle heterogeneity and positions secretory autophagy as an important contributor to intercellular communication.

primary.title: MYO18B promotes lysosomal exocytosis by facilitating focal adhesion maturation.
primary.abstract: Many cancer cells exhibit increased amounts of paucimannose glycans, which are truncated N-glycan structures rarely found in mammals. Paucimannosidic proteins are proposedly generated within lysosomes and exposed on the cell surface through a yet uncertain mechanism. In this study, we revealed that paucimannosidic proteins are produced by lysosomal glycosidases and secreted via lysosomal exocytosis. Interestingly, lysosomal exocytosis preferentially occurred in the vicinity of focal adhesions, protein complexes connecting the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix. Through genome-wide knockout screening, we identified that MYO18B, an actin crosslinker, is required for focal adhesion maturation, facilitating lysosomal exocytosis and the release of paucimannosidic lysosomal proteins to the extracellular milieu. Moreover, a mechanosensitive cation channel PIEZO1 locally activated at focal adhesions imports Ca2+ necessary for lysosome-plasma membrane fusion. Collectively, our study unveiled an intimate relationship between lysosomal exocytosis and focal adhesion, shedding light on the unexpected interplay between lysosomal activities and cellular mechanosensing.

primary.title: RYR:ATP6V0A1 complexes couple ER-lysosome contact sites to dynamic autophagy control.
primary.abstract: Ryanodine receptors (RYRs) are ER-resident Ca2+-release channels enriched in excitable cells, including neurons. RYR hyperactivity is implicated in early pathogenesis of disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), which is associated with impaired autophagy. We recently uncovered a mechanism linking RYR activity to lysosome availability for autophagy. RYRs localize to ER-lysosome contact sites via direct binding to ATP6V0A1, a V-ATPase subunit that also suppresses RYR-mediated Ca2+ release. In human iPSC-derived cortical neurons, spontaneous RYR activity promotes lysosomal secretion, depleting the intracellular lysosomal pool and inhibiting autophagic flux. RYR inhibition promotes ERlysosome contacts, limits lysosomal secretion, and restores lysosome availability for autophagosome fusion and cargo degradation (including APP). Conversely, disrupting the RYR:ATP6V0A1 interaction using a RYR-derived protein fragment serving as a "decoy" for ATP6V0A1 evokes RYR hyperactivity and stimulates lysosomal secretion. In this Punctum, we discuss how this RYR2:ATP6V0A1 "contact-site hub" may be perturbed in disease and highlight open questions on how lysosomes decode RYR-derived Ca2+ signals.

primary.title: Molecular mechanisms underlying p62-dependent secretion of the Alzheimer-associated ubiquitin variant UBB+1.
primary.abstract: UBB+1, a ubiquitin variant protein resulting from a frameshift in the ubiquitin-B gene, is a pathological hallmark of Alzheimer disease (AD). At the cellular level, UBB+1 disrupts the ubiquitin-proteasome system while inducing autophagy. Notably, UBB+1 itself is secreted via autophagosome-like vesicles. Here, we demonstrate that UBB+1 can be removed from the cell by degradative and secretory autophagy. Sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1)/p62 functions as a pivotal ubiquitin receptor for UBB+1, recognizing its ubiquitin domain and facilitating loading into autophagosomes. Oligomerization of SQSTM1/p62 was critical to isolate UBB+1 in bodies preventing its aggregation. Intriguingly, both gain- and loss-of-function SQSTM1/p62 suppressed UBB+1 secretion, causing intracellular retention: SQSTM1/p62 knockout led to UBB+1 accumulation in insoluble aggregates, while its overexpression promoted the formation of p62-UBB+1 bodies. We further identified distinct roles for SNARE-mediated membrane fusion in secretory autophagy of UBB+1. Specifically, the R-SNARE SEC22B and the Q-SNAREs Syntaxin-4 and SNAP23 participated in UBB+1 exocytosis. Disruption of SEC22B impaired the fusion of UBB+1-containing autophagosomes with the plasma membrane, reducing UBB+1 secretion without affecting its intracellular turnover. Inhibition of lysosomes partially stabilized UBB+1 indicating that degradation and secretion are complementary processes that determine the fate of UBB+1. This study elucidates the dual roles of autophagy in managing neurotoxic proteins, highlighting SQSTM1/p62 as a key mediator of UBB+1 trafficking and secretion. Although ubiquitin typically acts as a degradation signal, our findings reveal a rare instance of a ubiquitin-related protein driving secretory autophagy. These findings advance our understanding of cellular mechanisms underlying the clearance of misfolded proteins in neurodegenerative diseases.

primary.title: Impaired MAPT/tau-secretory lysosomes are linked to cognitive vulnerability in Alzheimer patients.
primary.abstract: MAPT/tau proteins propagate between brain regions in a prion-like manner, driving the onset and progression of dementia in Alzheimer disease (AD). However, the basis for variability in dementia progression among AD patients remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that cognitively resilient AD patients, characterized by reduced MAPT/tau pathology, maintain lysosomal integrity, whereas cognitively vulnerable patients, exhibiting greater MAPT/tau burden, display lysosomal dysfunction. Lysosomes in cognitively vulnerable AD brains contain partially digested, seed-competent MAPT/tau species composed mainly of the amyloidogenic core with degraded peripheral regions. These pathogenic MAPT/tau forms are secreted via lysosomal exocytosis, facilitating MAPT/tau propagation and contributing to cognitive decline. Cognitively vulnerable female AD patients show increased lysosome-mediated MAPT/tau secretion relative to their male counterparts. Our findings suggest that lysosomal dysfunction, marked by altered protein expression, pH dysregulation, and MAPT/tau accumulation, underlies the heterogeneity in dementia severity. primary.title: Inactive ryanodine receptors sustain lysosomal availability for autophagy by promoting ER-lysosomal contact site formation.
primary.abstract: Lysosomal and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ release mutually influence each other's functions. Recent work revealed that ER-located ryanodine receptor(s) (RyR(s)) Ca2+ release channels suppress autophagosome turnover by the lysosomes. In familial Alzheimer's disease, inhibiting RyR hyperactivity restored autophagic flux by normalizing lysosomal vacuolar H+-ATPase (vATPase) levels. However, the mechanisms by which RyRs control lysosomal function and how this involves the vATPase remain unknown. Here, we show that RyRs interact with the ATP6v0a1 subunit of the vATPase, contributing to ER-lysosomal contact site formation. This interaction suppresses RyR-mediated Ca²⁺ release, leading to reduced lysosomal exocytosis. Pharmacological inhibition of RyR activity mimics these effects on lysosomal exocytosis. Retaining lysosomes inside cells via RyR inhibition increases ER-lysosomal contact site formation, rendering lysosomes more available for autophagic flux. In summary, these findings establish RyR/ATP6v0a1 complexes as ER-lysosomal tethers that dynamically and Ca2+ dependently regulate the intracellular availability of lysosomes to participate in autophagic flux.

secondary.title: Extracellular vesicle-mediated neuroimmune remodeling across synucleinopathies: Therapeutic implications of cell-type specificity and central-peripheral crosstalk.
secondary.abstract: Synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy, are characterized by convergent α-synuclein misfolding, impaired proteostasis, and chronic neuroinflammation. Despite these shared pathological features, these disorders exhibit distinct inclusion-bearing cell profiles, vulnerable neural circuits, immune phenotypes, and clinical progression rates, with neuronal inclusions dominating in Parkinson's disease/dementia with Lewy bodies and oligodendrocyte pathology predominating in multiple system atrophy. Extracellular vesicles have emerged as critical modulators integrating these multifaceted pathogenic processes. Secreted by neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, extracellular vesicles cross biological boundaries to deliver diverse bioactive molecules and mediate intercellular communication. This review synthesizes current evidence to propose that extracellular vesicles serve as context-dependent mediators connecting intracellular proteostatic stress to local glial reactivity and systemic immune regulation. Extracellular vesicle-associated α-synuclein maintains a seeding-competent conformation, enters recipient cells, and triggers templated aggregation and inflammatory signaling, although its exact pathogenic contribution relative to free α-synuclein and non-vesicular transmission routes remains undefined. Extracellular vesicle cargo dynamically reshapes microglial and astrocytic activation, oligodendroglial homeostasis, neuronal survival, blood-brain barrier integrity, and peripheral immune recruitment. Extracellular vesicles exert bidirectional effects: pathological extracellular vesicles amplify neurotoxicity, while homeostatic or engineered extracellular vesicles restore proteostasis, optimize immune homeostasis, and facilitate neural tissue repair. Advanced techniques including immunocapture, real-time quaking-induced conversion, and single-vesicle profiling enhance the sensitivity and resolution of extracellular vesicle-based biomarkers, enabling improved discrimination among synucleinopathy subtypes. However, clinical translation is hampered by extracellular vesicle heterogeneity, inaccurate cell-origin tracing, pre-analytical variability, insufficient standardization, and limited causal in vivo and longitudinal evidence. It is concluded that extracellular vesicles function as integral components of a dynamic, multilayered communication network, with their outcomes determined by cellular origin, cargo, recipient type, disease stage, and anatomical context. Standardized protocols, longitudinal cohorts, and mechanistic models are indispensable for developing reliable extracellular vesicle biomarkers and safe extracellular vesicle-targeted therapies for synucleinopathies.

secondary.title: Exosomes derived from N2 neutrophils reprogram the immune microenvironment to promote spinal cord injury repair.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Spinal cord injury induces irreversible neurological impairments via secondary pathological cascades dominated by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, and neuronal apoptosis. As the first-responder immune cells following spinal cord trauma, neutrophils can acquire an N2-like reparative phenotype, yet direct neutrophil transplantation is hampered by poor cellular survival. Exosomes, nanoscale cell-secreted vesicles with low immunogenicity and favourable biostability, constitute promising cell-free candidates for regenerative therapy. Nevertheless, the therapeutic potential of exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils remains poorly defined for spinal cord injury repair. secondary.title: Metabolomics Profiling of Serum Small Extracellular Vesicle-Enriched Fractions Across Early Post-Injury Intervals Following Severe Traumatic Brain Injury.
secondary.abstract: Severe traumatic brain injury (sTBI) induces metabolic disturbances that remain difficult to assess non-invasively. This exploratory study compared metabolomics profiles of serum small extracellular vesicle-enriched fractions from healthy controls and patients with sTBI sampled at days 1, 3, and 5 post-injury. Using high-resolution liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), we identified metabolite differences associated with each sampled post-injury interval. Principal component analysis showed group-level separation between controls and the individual post-injury interval groups, with the largest separation observed in the day 1 comparison. N-Acetyl-l-aspartic acid, a canonical marker of neuronal integrity, showed lower abundance in the day 1 group relative to controls, whereas PGF2α ethanolamide showed lower abundance relative to controls in all three interval-specific comparisons. Glu-ser and tryptophan also met the differential-abundance criteria in more than one interval vs. control comparison. Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) linked the day 1 metabolite alterations to literature-curated neurological functions, including demyelination and neurodegeneration; however, these associations are presented as hypothesis-generating. Collectively, these findings identify serum small extracellular vesicle-enriched fraction metabolite alterations associated with sTBI for further investigation in fully longitudinal sTBI cohorts.

secondary.title: Serum Exosomes from Subacute Phase Post-cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Promote Microglial Pro-inflammatory Phenotype Polarization and Exacerbate Blood-Brain Barrier Disruption in Mice.
secondary.abstract: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) restores circulation but induces cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury characterized by blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption and microglial-mediated neuroinflammation. Exosomes circulate systemically following CPR, yet their temporal profiles and specific roles remain poorly understood. C57BL/6 mice (n = 5/group) underwent asphyxial cardiac arrest and CPR. BBB permeability was assessed longitudinally (3 h to 14 d) using Evans blue extravasation. Serum exosomes were isolated at 1 d and 3 d post-CPR and characterized. To determine immunomodulatory effects, exosomes were administered via intracerebroventricular injection into recipient mice, and BBB integrity and microglial polarization (CD86, CD206) were evaluated by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry. Additionally, primary cultures of microglia cells isolated from CPR mice were exposed to exosomes in vitro (n = 3/group), and pro-inflammatory phenotype/anti-inflammatory phenotype markers and inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, iNOS, TGF-β, Arg1, IL-10) were quantified. CPR induced transient BBB disruption peaking at 3 d post-resuscitation. Serum exosomes isolated at both 1 d and 3 d exhibited characteristic cup-shaped morphology. Intracerebroventricular administration of post-CPR exosomes significantly exacerbated BBB leakage and skewed microglial polarization toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype (elevated CD86⁺; reduced CD206⁺), with 3-day exosomes eliciting more potent detrimental effects than 1-day exosomes. In vitro, exposure to 3-day exosomes similarly produced stronger pro-inflammatory transcriptional responses and increased nitric oxide (NO) production compared with 1-day exosomes. Serum exosomes derived from post-CPR mice exhibit pro-inflammatory activity, aggravating BBB disruption and promoting microglial pro-inflammatory phenotype polarization upon central delivery. These findings suggest that circulating exosomes may contribute to post-resuscitation neuroinflammatory injury, and highlight exosome-related pathways as candidate targets worthy of further investigation.

secondary.title: TRPML3 and TRPML1/3 differentially regulate unconventional MIF secretion through TMED10 and secretory autophagy.
secondary.abstract: The intracellular Ca2+ channel TRPML3 regulates autophagy by multimerization in a phosphoinositide (PIP)-dependent manner; however, its role in other membrane dynamics remains unclear. Here, we report that TRPML3 regulates type III unconventional protein secretion (UcPS) through two distinct pathways: TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy. TRPML3 interacted with TMED10 and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), a signal sequence-lacking pleiotropic cytokine whose secretion mechanism has remained undefined. We found that cytosolic MIF is transported to membrane-enclosed compartments through TMED10-channeled UcPS. Notably, TRPML3, but not TRPML1 or TRPML1/3, promoted TMED10 oligomerization, thereby enhancing MIF secretion in a Ca2+-independent manner. Furthermore, once translocated into vesicular compartments, MIF colocalized with LC3, and its secretion was dependent on secretory autophagy. Mechanistically, we identified PI(3,4)P2 as a key regulator of secretory autophagy, with TRPML1/3 acting downstream of PI(3,4)P2 to mediate Ca2+-dependent MIF secretion. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that MIF is a novel cargo of type III UcPS, operating through TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy, which are regulated by TRPML3 in a Ca2+-independent manner and by the PI(3,4)P2-TRPML1/3 axis in a Ca2+-dependent manner, respectively.

secondary.title: Extracellular exosome signature links hypertension and Alzheimer's disease.
secondary.abstract: Untreated hypertension is a risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD); however, this association is not well understood. The aim of this study was to reveal protein signatures that bridge the pathophysiological changes in hypertension to AD. Using untargeted proteomics, we analyzed brain samples from aged (30- and 40-week-old) spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs, n = 12), and age-matched normotensive Wistar Kyoto (WKY, n = 8) controls, and human AD patients (Braak stages 4-6) (n = 30), cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) (n = 5), non-demented controls (Braak stages 0-3) (n = 37). Differential expression and pathway analyses in SHRs highlighted the 'extracellular exosome' pathway. This pathway also showed significant associations to differentially expressed proteins in AD and CAA patients. Comparison between species identified 24 proteins in SHRs and AD, whose trajectory pattern over the progression of hypertension, aligned with those observed during AD Braak stage progression, compared to respective controls. The proteins were similarly associated with extracellular exosomes. Immunostaining and spatial proteomics support vesicle accumulation and dysregulated exosome protein signatures in the cerebrovasculature of both SHR and AD brains. Additionally, the extracellular exosome pathway-association was not identified in a traditional model of familial AD (5xFAD). Our findings demonstrate cross-species translatability between AD and the SHR and provide novel mechanistic insights into a shared dysregulation of cerebral artery-associated exosomes.

best.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
best.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

best.title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
best.abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

best.title: Serum Extracellular Vesicle Proteomics Identifies Candidate Protein Biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder with a Diagnostic Specificity Assessment against Schizophrenia.
best.abstract: Diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD) relies on subjective criteria and lacks objective biomarkers. Serum extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry stable cargo and can cross the blood-brain barrier, making them attractive biomarker sources. We therefore profiled serum EVs from a discovery cohort of 60 participants (40 healthy controls [HCs], 20 MDD patients) by size-exclusion chromatography and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and subsequently validated candidate proteins by ELISA in an independent cohort of 60 participants (20 HCs, 20 MDD, 20 patients with schizophrenia [SCZ]). Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were defined by |log2 fold change| > 1 and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted q < 0.05. Using these criteria, we identified 358 DEPs (235 upregulated, 123 downregulated), which were enriched in complement activation, coagulation, and immune-inflammatory pathways. However, several of the most significant DEPs are abundant circulating plasma proteins that are common co-isolates of serum EVs, so part of this signal may reflect residual soluble serum protein, and-given that EVs were isolated from serum rather than platelet-poor plasma-the pathway enrichment should be interpreted with caution. In the validation cohort, EV-associated TNC and APLP1 were elevated and EV-associated TF was reduced in MDD relative to HCs (P < 0.05), whereas only serum APLP1 was elevated. Notably, EV-associated TNC was also elevated in SCZ, while APLP1 and TF were unchanged; moreover, direct MDD-versus-SCZ comparisons were not significant, indicating that the data do not support MDD-specific alterations. In addition, a logistic-regression model combining EV-associated APLP1, TF and TNC distinguished MDD from HCs with an area under the curve of 0.905 (95% CI 0.812-0.998; 0.830 by leave-one-out cross-validation), outperforming individual proteins (TF 0.725; TNC 0.758; APLP1 0.725). Collectively, these findings define a serum EV-associated proteomic signature in MDD and preliminarily validate TF, TNC and APLP1 as candidate diagnostic biomarkers, implicating immune-inflammatory and complement-related pathways. Nevertheless, the panel remains exploratory and requires validation in larger, multi-center cohorts with diverse psychiatric controls.

best.title: Mechanism of Autophagic Extracellular Vesicles Revealed.
best.abstract: Recent work by Mao and colleagues identifies a distinct class of small extracellular vesicles, termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs), generated from amphisomes upon autophagy induction. In this commentary, we discuss how this study provides important mechanistic insight into the coupling between autophagy and secretion. AEVs are molecularly and functionally distinct from canonical exosomes, being enriched in autophagy-related components such as LC3 and p62, and dependent on core ATG machinery for their biogenesis. Notably, their secretion is enhanced by autophagy induction and contributes to intercellular communication, particularly in the context of viral infection. These findings position amphisomes as critical sorting hubs that direct cargo toward either degradation or secretion, thereby integrating autophagic and endolysosomal pathways. We further highlight how these results intersect with prior evidence implicating SNARE-dependent mechanisms, including VAMP7 and stress-responsive regulators such as GRASP55, in unconventional secretion. Finally, we discuss key unresolved questions, particularly the mechanisms underlying the generation of small intraluminal vesicles within amphisomes and the role of ESCRT machinery in this process. Overall, the identification of AEVs adds a new layer of complexity to extracellular vesicle biology and opens new avenues for understanding how autophagy contributes to intercellular signaling in health and disease.

best.title: Glycoprotein-induced phase separation drives unconventional secretion of galectin-3.
best.abstract: The mechanism of unconventional protein secretion remains an unresolved issue. Here, we describe an unconventional protein secretion pathway for galectin-3 that is mediated by phase separation and condensation. Using four lysosomal damage models, we observed a rapid, pronounced release of galectin-3 in large, non-exosomal particles. This secretion is driven by glycoprotein-induced galectin-3 phase separation and is independent of pyroptosis and secretory autophagy. During phase separation, the S-face of galectin-3 carbohydrate recognition domain binds glycoproteins that triggers galectin-3 N-terminal tail release and condensation. These condensates then recruit ALG-2 via the exposed N-terminal tail. ALG-2 directs the condensates to the endoplasmic reticulum-late endosome interface. After translocation into late endosomes, galectin-3 condensates are secreted into the extracellular milieu by SNARE-dependent vesicular transport. This mechanism of exporting phase-separated protein condensates may serve as a clean-up response to membrane damage.

best.title: A protective role for APP in nuclear waste clearance via lysosomal exocytosis.
best.abstract: Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is widely known for its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis through its proteolytic processing into amyloid-β peptides. However, its physiological functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a protective role for full-length APP in facilitating the disposal of nuclear-derived debris under genotoxic stress. In both cultured cells and in vivo mouse models, loss of APP leads to nuclear waste accumulation, increased inflammation, and cell death, whereas APP overexpression mitigates these effects. Mechanistically, we show that APP supports the extracellular release of nuclear waste material through lysosomal exocytosis. APP mutants associated with familial AD fail to mediate this process. Consistently, human AD brain tissue exhibits abnormal nuclear morphology, accumulation of nuclear waste in the cytoplasm, and reduced APP levels per neuron. These findings highlight a conserved cellular mechanism by which APP contributes to nuclear and cellular homeostasis, and suggest that impaired nuclear waste clearance may represent an underappreciated contributor to neurodegeneration.

best.title: Extracellular vesicle-mediated neuroimmune remodeling across synucleinopathies: Therapeutic implications of cell-type specificity and central-peripheral crosstalk.
best.abstract: Synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy, are characterized by convergent α-synuclein misfolding, impaired proteostasis, and chronic neuroinflammation. Despite these shared pathological features, these disorders exhibit distinct inclusion-bearing cell profiles, vulnerable neural circuits, immune phenotypes, and clinical progression rates, with neuronal inclusions dominating in Parkinson's disease/dementia with Lewy bodies and oligodendrocyte pathology predominating in multiple system atrophy. Extracellular vesicles have emerged as critical modulators integrating these multifaceted pathogenic processes. Secreted by neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, extracellular vesicles cross biological boundaries to deliver diverse bioactive molecules and mediate intercellular communication. This review synthesizes current evidence to propose that extracellular vesicles serve as context-dependent mediators connecting intracellular proteostatic stress to local glial reactivity and systemic immune regulation. Extracellular vesicle-associated α-synuclein maintains a seeding-competent conformation, enters recipient cells, and triggers templated aggregation and inflammatory signaling, although its exact pathogenic contribution relative to free α-synuclein and non-vesicular transmission routes remains undefined. Extracellular vesicle cargo dynamically reshapes microglial and astrocytic activation, oligodendroglial homeostasis, neuronal survival, blood-brain barrier integrity, and peripheral immune recruitment. Extracellular vesicles exert bidirectional effects: pathological extracellular vesicles amplify neurotoxicity, while homeostatic or engineered extracellular vesicles restore proteostasis, optimize immune homeostasis, and facilitate neural tissue repair. Advanced techniques including immunocapture, real-time quaking-induced conversion, and single-vesicle profiling enhance the sensitivity and resolution of extracellular vesicle-based biomarkers, enabling improved discrimination among synucleinopathy subtypes. However, clinical translation is hampered by extracellular vesicle heterogeneity, inaccurate cell-origin tracing, pre-analytical variability, insufficient standardization, and limited causal in vivo and longitudinal evidence. It is concluded that extracellular vesicles function as integral components of a dynamic, multilayered communication network, with their outcomes determined by cellular origin, cargo, recipient type, disease stage, and anatomical context. Standardized protocols, longitudinal cohorts, and mechanistic models are indispensable for developing reliable extracellular vesicle biomarkers and safe extracellular vesicle-targeted therapies for synucleinopathies.
