best.title: Galectin-3 links microglial neuroinflammation to Aβ aggregation and lysosomal processing.
best.abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the molecular mechanisms linking microglial dysfunction to amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify galectin-3 (Gal3) as a regulator of plaque-associated microglial responses, linking Aβ aggregation, lysosomal function, and neuritic pathology. Using postmortem brain tissue from AD patients, we found that Gal3+ microglia preferentially associate with cored plaques and correlate with increased LAMP1+ dystrophic neurites. Gal3 was also detected in microglial lysosomal compartments, extramicroglial dystrophic structures, and in association with extracellular amyloid fibrils, suggesting roles in both intracellular and extracellular Aβ processing. In APP mice, Gal3 deficiency reduced plaque burden and neuritic dystrophy, increased plaque compaction, and enhanced TREM2 coverage around amyloid plaques. Mechanistically, in vitro microglial experiments showed that Gal3 modulates Aβ uptake and lysosomal processing, whereas lysosomal dysfunction promoted the accumulation of fibrillar Aβ from initially monomeric species, particularly in Gal3-deficient cells. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Gal3 preferentially binds fibrillar Aβ, inhibits secondary nucleation, and alters fibril morphology, while Gal3-modified fibrillar Aβ reduces N2a neuronal cell number. Finally, in silico structural analyses identified candidate Gal3 interactors enriched in leucine-rich-repeat and immunoglobulin-like proteins, supporting a role for this lectin in immune receptor regulation. Complementary in vivo transcriptomic profiling showed that Gal3 deletion suppresses type I interferon and microglial neurodegenerative transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings position Gal3 at the interface between Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and plaque-associated microglial responses in AD.

best.title: Markers of Blood-Brain Barrier Integrity and Neurodegeneration Across Alzheimer's and Non-Alzheimer Neurodegenerative Diseases.
best.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is increasingly recognized as an early feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, the relationship between BBB integrity, glial activation, and neuronal injury is not fully understood, particularly in non-Alzheimer's disorders such as frontotemporal dementia (NADD/FTD). This exploratory study investigated the relationships between BBB integrity, astroglial activation, and neuronal and tau-related injury in AD, NDD/FTD, and cognitively healthy controls (HCs). METHODS: Of the 105 individuals who were screened, the final analytic cohort, which was characterized using PET and CSF, comprised 63 participants. These included 34 individuals with AD, 16 HCs, and 13 participants with NADD/FTD. BBB integrity was assessed using platelet-derived growth factor receptor β (PDGFRβ), CSF fibrinogen, and the CSF/serum albumin ratio (QAlb). Plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), and phosphorylated tau 217 (pTau217) were assessed as markers of astroglial activation, axonal injury and tau pathology, respectively. Exploratory statistical analyses were adjusted for age and sex. RESULTS: Markers of BBB integrity did not significantly distinguish between the diagnostic groups (all p > 0.05). Significant associations were observed across the full cohort between CSF fibrinogen and CSF total tau and QAlb, and between plasma GFAP, NfL, and pTau217 (r = 0.65-0.70, all p < 0.001 for GFAP). In exploratory mediation analyses, neither tested model showed a significant indirect effect. No comparable amyloid-related mediation effects were observed. Exploratory mediation analyses involving other markers of BBB dysfunction likewise showed no significant indirect effects. CONCLUSION: BBB-related markers did not demonstrate consistent associations with astroglial activation and neuronal injury across diagnostic groups within this cross-sectional cohort. While these findings do not exclude a role for BBB alterations in neurodegenerative processes, they do suggest that their biological significance and potential relevance across disease stages remain unclear. Further research is required in the form of larger longitudinal studies to investigate these relationships.

best.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
best.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

best.title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
best.abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

best.title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
best.abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

best.title: Astrocytic cathepsin D promotes α-synuclein processing and Lewy neurite-like aggregate maturation.
best.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) and related synucleinopathies are marked by the accumulation and propagation of α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregates, a process primarily studied in neurons. Whether astrocytes actively contribute to α-syn processing and intercellular transfer remains unclear. Here, using a physiologically relevant neuron-astrocyte co-culture system that recapitulates tripartite synapse architecture, we show that astrocytes process α-syn and influence the morphological maturation of neuronal aggregates. Astrocytes internalize α-syn pre-formed fibrils (PFFs) and generate C-terminally truncated α-syn species via a Cathepsin D (CtsD)-dependent process. PFF-loaded astrocytes transfer α-syn-containing material to neurons and promote the formation and maturation of pS129-α-syn-positive Lewy neurite (LN)-like aggregates. Notably, α-syn PFF exposure induces lysosomal membrane damage, a senescence-like reactive state, and CtsD upregulation in astrocytes. Although PFF-containing lysosomes undergo autophagic engulfment, they persist within astrocytes, and a subset is detected beyond the astrocytic membrane boundary. Together, our findings support a model in which astrocytic lysosomal remodeling of internalized α-syn contributes to the morphological maturation and intercellular propagation of neuronal α-syn pathology in this co-culture system.

best.title: Hyperactive KIF5A in Neurodegeneration.
best.abstract: The highly polarised morphology of neurons and the sheer length of their axons make transport of cargoes throughout the cell a formidable task. Decades of evidence obtained from genetic studies on patients and animal models highlight deficits in axonal transport as a recurrent cause, or early contributing factor, in a plethora of neurodegenerative diseases. Axonal transport abnormalities usually manifest as a slowing of cargo trafficked by molecular motors along microtubules; however, hyperactivation of motors can also lead to disease. That is the case for the kinesin-1 protein KIF5A, in which hyperactive mutations are linked to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and neonatal intractable myoclonus (NEIMY). In this Perspective, we summarise the latest insights into the impact of KIF5A hyperactivity, such as loss of autoinhibition, aggregation, altered cargo binding and microtubule damage. We conclude by discussing possible strategies to counteract these disruptions, with an emphasis on the necessity of restoring axonal transport to physiological levels, a key requirement to maintain neuronal homeostasis.

best.title: Engineered autophagy receptors for selective protein clearance in neurodegeneration.
best.abstract: Engineered autophagy receptors offer a way to direct intracellular degradation toward proteins implicated in neurodegeneration. Guo and colleagues fused cytoplasm-stable antibody fragments to microtubule-associated protein 1A/1B-light chain 3 alpha (LC3A) and delivered the resulting constructs using small extracellular vesicles. Their experiments show reduced pathological tau and cytoplasmic TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) in neuronal cultures and reduced tau pathology in mice. A separate adeno-associated virus experiment reduces TDP-43 pathology and improves motor performance in mice. These findings connect selective cargo recognition with intracellular delivery and raise questions about how engineered autophagy receptors might be adapted to different disease contexts. Here, we discuss which pathological protein assemblies are most accessible to these receptors, how selective clearance interacts with neuronal autophagic capacity, and how intracellular exposure relates to sustained functional benefit. We consider these questions with particular attention to preserving physiological protein function and linking cargo turnover to neuronal outcomes.

best.title: Alzheimer's disease-associated presenilin 2 N141I mutation impairs neuronal lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial dynamics through selective downregulation of the Golgi exchange factor Gbf1.
best.abstract: Presenilin 2 (PS2) mutations cause familial Alzheimer's disease, yet their effects beyond amyloid processing remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how PS2 deletion and the N141I mutation affect neuronal lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial dynamics in mouse primary neurons. Both PS2 deletion and N141I mutation reduced neuronal lipid content. However, exogenous lipid supplementation rescued this deficit only in N141I-expressing neurons, indicating a partial loss-of-function effect. N141I neurons also displayed reduced OPA1, a mitochondrial fusion regulator, restored by lipid supplementation. RNA-sequencing identified Gbf1, a Golgi-specific guanine nucleotide exchange factor, as selectively downregulated in N141I but not knockout tissue, which was confirmed at the protein level in mouse brain and primary neurons. Gbf1 knockdown in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) recapitulated the N141I lipid profile. Together, these findings reveal a PS2-GBF1-lipid-mitochondria axis disrupted specifically by the N141I mutation, suggesting an amyloid-independent pathway contributing to neurodegeneration and identifying potential therapeutic targets for familial Alzheimer's disease.

best.title: VPS35 mutation inhibits PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy via increased LRRK2 kinase activity.
best.abstract: The p.D620N mutation in VPS35 causes an autosomal dominant form of Parkinson's disease via mechanisms that are poorly understood. PINK1 and parkin, two proteins whose loss-of-function underlies autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease, cooperate to mediate mitophagy, a quality control pathway for selective elimination of damaged mitochondria. PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy is disrupted by LRRK2 mutations, which are the most prevalent cause of autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease. Here, we investigated whether the p.D620N VPS35 mutation has an effect on PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy. We identified a novel family with autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease caused by a p.D620N VPS35 mutation. We cultured skin fibroblasts and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived dopaminergic neurons from the proband and from a second, unrelated Parkinson's disease patient with the p.D620N VPS35 mutation, and compared them with isogenic and non-isogenic control cells. PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy was severely impaired in VPS35 mutant fibroblasts and neurons, while non-selective, starvation-induced autophagy and lysosomal degradative capacity were preserved. siRNA-mediated VPS35 knockdown rescued the mitophagy defect in VPS35 mutant cells, whereas overexpression of wild-type VPS35 did not, suggesting a gain-of-function mechanism of the mutation. The VPS35 mutation did not interfere with activation of PINK1 or parkin after mitochondrial depolarization, but impaired mitochondrial recruitment of the autophagy receptor optineurin. LRRK2 kinase activity was increased in the VPS35 mutant cells, as shown by enhanced levels of the T73-phosphorylated form of the LRRK2 substrate RAB10. The enhanced level of phosphorylated RAB10 in VPS35 mutant cells was decreased by treatment with LRRK2 kinase inhibitors and by VPS35 knockdown. Importantly, the mitophagy defect of VPS35 mutant fibroblasts and neurons was fully rescued by LRRK2 kinase inhibitors as well as by overexpression of PPM1H, a phosphatase that dephosphorylates multiple RAB substrates of LRRK2. Finally, in situ proximity ligation experiments revealed that endogenous VPS35 and LRRK2 are proximity partners in human dopaminergic neurons and that this proximity relationship is enhanced by the VPS35 mutation. In conclusion, the VPS35 mutation impairs PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy via a gain-of-function mechanism that involves stimulation of LRRK2 kinase activity. Thus, a VPS35/LRRK2 axis linked to dominant Parkinson's disease intersects with a pathway mediated by proteins encoded by the recessive Parkinson's disease genes.

best.title: Lipid regulation of autophagy flux and neurodegeneration.
best.abstract: Autophagy is a lysosomal degradation pathway crucial for the maintenance of proteostasis, organelle quality control, and stress adaptation. Autophagosomes form from finger-like structures emanating from the recycling endosome, called phagophores, which capture cytoplasmic cargo before closing like a fist. These closed structures are then released from the recycling endosome by dynamin 2 to form autophagosomes that ultimately fuse with lysosomes, where their contents are degraded. In the central nervous system, autophagy protects against the cytoplasmic accumulation of toxic, aggregate-prone proteins and damaged organelles, common features of neurodegenerative diseases such as Huntington's and Alzheimer's disease. Lipids have emerged as crucial mediators of autophagosome biogenesis and have multifaceted effects on autophagic flux. At the edges of the phagophore, coordinated lipid transfer from donor membranes and scramblase activity support appropriate lipid bilayer formation and membrane expansion. In addition, the highly curved, loosely packed lipids at the phagophore edges act as a platform for binding of key autophagy effectors via their amphipathic domains and promote autophagosome maturation. The role of lipids extends beyond structural support in autophagosome formation and includes modulation of upstream signalling pathways, establishment of autophagic membrane identity, and lysosomal maintenance. Autophagy itself contributes to the maintenance of lipid homeostasis via the selective lipid droplet degradation pathway termed lipophagy. Importantly, alterations in lipid composition and metabolism have been demonstrated to impair autophagic flux and contribute to the development of several sporadic and inherited neurological disorders.

best.title: Intranasal delivery of a ROS-activatable myeloperoxidase inhibitor alleviates Alzheimer's-like symptoms and pathology.
best.abstract: Chronic neuroinflammation and oxidative stress are important contributors to Alzheimer's disease (AD). Myeloperoxidase (MPO), a key driver of oxidative inflammation released mainly by activated microglia in the neurodegenerative brain, is a potential therapeutic target to inhibit the neuroinflammatory cascade and oxidative damage in AD, but the underlying mechanisms remain unexplored, and achieving targeted brain delivery of an MPO inhibitor and minimizing systemic effects remain significant challenges. We addressed these limitations by first establishing that genetic deletion of MPO in the 5XFAD mouse model improved memory performance and reduced amyloid deposition, validating MPO as a therapeutic target. We then developed a liposome-encapsulated reactive oxygen species (ROS)-activatable MPO inhibitor (LERAMI). LERAMI uniquely combines targeted delivery with on-demand drug release, utilizing a ROS-sensitive linker to selectively release MPO inhibitors in ROS-rich regions within the AD microenvironment, minimizing off-target effects and systemic toxicity. In the 5XFAD mouse model. By reducing MPO expression and activity, LERAMI significantly improved cognitive performance, accompanied by decreased microglial activation, attenuated oxidative DNA damage, improved synaptic and neuronal density, and reduced amyloid burden. RNA sequencing revealed a robust hippocampal transcriptomic reprogramming, with upregulation of pathways critical for synaptic plasticity, calcium signaling, axon guidance, and neuroprotection, along with downregulation of inflammatory and immune response pathways. These findings demonstrate that targeted ROS-activatable MPO inhibition with LERAMI represents a promising therapeutic strategy for AD and potentially other neuroinflammatory diseases, offering a unique approach to mitigate neuroinflammation, preserve synaptic integrity, and restore cognitive function.

best.title: Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 participates in the internalization of arginine-rich dipeptide repeat proteins.
best.abstract: Microsatellite repeat expansion of the 5' GGGGCC 3' sequence in the C9orf72 gene is the most common monogenic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. Dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) translated from the mutant allele can be detected in postmortem brains of afflicted individuals. The arginine containing peptides, poly proline-arginine (poly-PR) and poly glycine-arginine (poly-GR), are particularly noxious to cells. Both can undergo cell-to-cell transmission, but underlying mechanisms are not understood. We found rapid internalization and nucleolar localization of bath-applied hemagglutinin (HA) tagged poly-PR with twenty repeats (HA-PR20) in cell lines and neurons. Small molecule and RNAi approaches implicated a temperature-dependent, fluid phase endocytosis mechanism for HA-PR20. We sought to identify DPR-related cell surface uptake factors using µMap high-resolution proximity labeling. DPR-iridium conjugates identified candidate cell-surface proteins which were interrogated in a secondary RNAi screen. Focusing on our strongest candidate, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 (CSPG4), we showed cellular uptake of HA-PR20 is reduced by inhibition of glycosaminoglycan chain synthesis and knockdown or ablation of CSPG4. Knockdown of CSPG4 protected PR20-induced neuronal toxicity. Using a dual reporter system to interrogate in vitro neuron-to-neuron transmission of PR50, we found PR50 synthesized by one neuron readily spread to neighboring cells. Transmission was significantly reduced with CSPG4 knockdown. Similarly conditioned media from PR50 or GR50 expressing neurons contained transmissible protein that was internalized into neurons in a CSPG4-dependent manner. These results suggest CSPG4 participates in poly-PR/poly-GR internalization and transmission.

best.abstract: Mutations in several genes are known to cause familial forms of Parkinson's disease (PD), including mutations in the vacuolar protein sorting 35 ortholog (VPS35) gene linked to late-onset, autosomal dominant PD. VPS35 encodes a core subunit of the retromer complex which functions in endosomal sorting and recycling. It remains unclear how the pathogenic D620N mutation in VPS35 disrupts retromer function to induce neurodegeneration in PD. Using cell- and rodent-based models expressing D620N VPS35, we performed interactome proteomics to identify alterations underlying the pathogenic effects of D620N VPS35 in PD. Using overexpression of VPS35 variants in HEK-293 T cells, we conducted tandem affinity purification (TAP) or co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) with protein chemical crosslinking to determine the native and non-native protein interactomes of wild-type (WT) and D620N VPS35, respectively. Notably, we can confirm the reduced interaction of D620N VPS35 with components of the WASH complex. Additionally, using a viral-mediated gene transfer model of human D620N VPS35 overexpression in adult rat brain, we identify the first brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35. These overexpression models reveal remarkably similar interaction profiles of WT and D620N VPS35, suggesting that the D620N mutation has a subtle effect on the overall VPS35 protein interactome. We also conducted proteomic analysis of brain tissue from a D620N VPS35 knockin (KI) mouse model that expresses VPS35 at endogenous levels. Using co-IP from hemibrain or striatal extracts of WT and D620N VPS35 KI mice, we reveal a high degree of similarity between the brain interactomes of WT and D620N VPS35, further suggesting a subtle effect of the D620N mutation on VPS35 protein interactions. Notably, in both hemibrain and striatum, we find a selective decrease in the interaction of two known interactors, TBC1D5 and VPS29, with D620N VPS35. We also performed global proteomic analysis of striatal tissue from D620N VPS35 KI mice and reveal a high degree of similarity between WT and D620N, further suggesting a subtle effect of this mutation. Together, our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the VPS35 protein interactome and reveals a selective effect of the PD-linked D620N mutation in mammalian cells and brain. Our study provides key insight into the mechanisms of retromer dysfunction in VPS35-linked PD.

best.title: BAG3 coordinates astrocytic proteostasis of Alzheimer's disease-linked proteins via proteasome, autophagy, and retromer interactions.
best.abstract: Bcl-2-associated athanogene 3 (BAG3) is a mediator of chaperone-assisted selective autophagy, and in the brain, is most highly expressed in astrocytes. However, its role in astrocytes remains poorly defined. Given the genetic and pathological links of BAG3 to proteostasis and neurodegenerative diseases, we investigated how BAG3 contributes to astrocyte function and Alzheimer's disease (AD). To define its function and relevance, we used single-nucleus RNA sequencing to confirm BAG3 enrichment in astrocytes and employed CRISPR/Cas9 editing of human induced pluripotent stem cells followed by proteomic and transcriptomic profiling, which revealed that BAG3 loss caused greater disruption in astrocytes than in neurons. BAG3-deficient astrocytes displayed reduced autophagy, lysosomal abundance and activity, and proteasome function. Coimmunoprecipitation identified BAG3 known binding partners (e.g., HSPB8, proteasome regulators), as well as an interactor in the retromer complex, VPS35. BAG3 deficiency resulted in altered retromer activity as measured by amyloid precursor protein (APP) localization in endosomes. In addition to validating these binding partners, integrative -omics analyses showed that BAG3 regulates AD-relevant proteins (GFAP, BIN1), as well as HSPB8. Functionally, BAG3 knockout astrocytes exhibited impaired amyloid-β proteostasis when cocultured with APP/PSEN1 mutant neurons, directly linking BAG3 to a disease-relevant astrocyte phenotype. Finally, analysis of postmortem human brain revealed that BAG3 expression marks a stress-responsive astrocyte subtype in aged individuals. Together, these findings demonstrate that BAG3 coordinates astrocyte proteostasis through interactions with regulators of autophagy, proteasome activity, and retromer function, positioning it as a potential therapeutic target and central node of astrocytic protein quality control in neurodegeneration.

best.title: Plasma P-Tau217 and NfL Longitudinal Changes Across Neurodegenerative Diseases: Impact of α-Synuclein in Alzheimer Disease.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Plasma phospho-tau217 (p-tau 217) is a validated biomarker of Alzheimer disease (AD), and its longitudinal dynamics may reflect AD progression. Plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) reflects axonal injury and neurodegeneration. Their trajectories may be modulated by concomitant proteinopathies such as α-synuclein (aSyn). We aimed to characterize longitudinal changes (36 months) in plasma p-tau217 and NfL across neurodegenerative and non-neurodegenerative cognitive disorders and to examine biomarker trajectories according to aSyn pathology status within AD. METHODS: In this prospective single-center cohort, participants were recruited from a memory clinic in Barcelona, Spain. Participants were eligible if they had cognitive impairment because of neurodegenerative or non-neurodegenerative conditions between 2019 and 2022 and if baseline and 3-year follow-up blood samples were available. CSF AD biomarkers measured with Lumipulse and aSyn pathology assessed using real-time quaking-induced conversion assay were determined at baseline and used for patient diagnosis. Plasma p-tau217 and NfL were measured with Lumipulse at baseline and 36 months and analyzed as study outcomes. Between-group differences at longitudinal level were assessed using linear mixed-effects models. RESULTS: A total of 223 participants were included: 92 AD-aSyn- (69.6 [5.6] years, 57.8% female), 15 AD-aSyn+ (69.1 [5.8] years, 53.3% female), 17 dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)-AD- (70.9 [6.8] years, 23.5% female), 13 DLB-AD+ (age 72.3 [5.0] years, 30.8% female), 48 frontotemporal lobar dementia (FTD) (65.5 [8.8] years, 45.8% female), and 38 non-neurodegenerative cognitive impairment (NNCI) (65.3 [7.7] years, 35.9% female). At baseline, AD-aSyn+ and AD-aSyn- groups showed the highest plasma p-tau217, whereas DLB-AD+ showed intermediate levels and DLB-AD-, FTD, and NNCI the lowest. Over 36 months, AD-aSyn+ exhibited the steepest increase in p-tau217 (2.19 pg/mL; p < 0.001), whereas AD-aSyn- and DLB-AD+ showed smaller increases; DLB-AD-, FTD, and NNCI remained stable. For NfL, FTD and AD-aSyn+ had the highest levels at baseline and follow-up (both p < 0.001), with similar increases. AD-aSyn-, DLB-AD+, and DLB-AD- showed intermediate values with moderate increases, whereas NNCI displayed limited changes. DISCUSSION: Plasma p-tau217 changes longitudinally in AD, and its trajectory is modulated by α-synuclein pathology. Patients with AD-aSyn+ show higher levels of NfL, similar to FTD, highlighting greater neuroaxonal injury. α-synuclein positivity identifies an AD-aSyn+ subgroup with steeper increases in p-tau217 and NfL, supporting biomarker-based stratification for prognosis and trial enrichment.

best.title: VPS35 Regulates Microglial Lipid Droplet Accumulation in Parkinson's Disease via Rab7.
best.abstract: Microglial dysfunction and aberrant lipid metabolism are emerging as key contributors to Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, the specific role and regulation of lipid droplets (LDs) within microglia remain poorly defined. In this study, we employed MPTP- and LPS-induced PD mouse models and an in vitro system utilizing astrocyte-conditioned medium to model disease-relevant lipid stress and found enhanced LD accumulation in microglia. VPS35 expression was decreased in microglia, correlating with elevated microglial LD levels in PD mouse models. We then performed genetic manipulations (knockdown and overexpression) of VPS35, including the PD-associated D620N mutant, in primary microglia and assessed LD accumulation, phagocytic function, inflammatory responses, and integrated stress pathways. We showed that VPS35 knockdown exacerbated the accumulation of LDs in microglia. Conversely, VPS35 overexpression ameliorated LD formation, improved phagocytic function, and reduced inflammatory and integrated stress responses in microglia. The PD-related VPS35[D620N] mutation abolished these protective effects. We further found that VPS35 interacts with Rab7 to maintain lysosomal function, and the D620N mutation disrupts this interaction, leading to defective LD clearance. Our findings reveal VPS35 dysfunction as a key pathogenic mechanism in PD, where the D620N mutation disrupts microglial lipid handling to promote disease progression, thereby nominating VPS35 restoration as a promising therapeutic strategy.

best.title: Early reduction of myelin-associated glycoprotein at myelin membranes in Huntington's disease.
best.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is marked by progressive neuronal loss and atrophy of grey matter structures, particularly the caudate and putamen. Brain imaging studies reveal that the white matter starts to decay in the brain of individuals bearing the HD mutation many years before symptomatic onset. However, the mechanism by which the HD mutation causes white matter loss remains to be further defined. In this study, we examined white matter pathology and explored the underlying mechanism in the HDQ140 knock-in mouse model of HD. Western blot analysis of proteins localized at different layers of the myelin sheath showed that myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), which is localized at the innermost myelin layer, was decreased earlier than proteins localized at outer layers of the myelin. The loss of MAG occurred at fully myelinated axons and was progressive with age. In postmortem symptomatic human HD brains, the level of MAG as well as other myelin proteins was also decreased. In HD mouse brains, MAG labeling was reduced at fiber bundles but accumulated in perinuclear structures of cells that expressed breast carcinoma amplified sequence 1, a marker for new oligodendrocytes. While their abundance was normal, new oligodendrocytes in HD brains were impeded in acquiring the expression of MAG. Compared with those in wild-type mouse brains, oligodendrocytes in HD mouse brains had a reduced frequency of MAG-bearing small vesicles and an increased abundance and enlargement of MAG-containing perinuclear structures. Further studies suggest that the MAG-accumulating perinuclear structures were derived from the late endosomal lysosomal compartment. Our study suggests that white matter decay in HD brains involves an early progressive loss of MAG in myelin membranes.

best.title: Impaired cellular stress adaptability in Alzheimer's disease patient-derived fibroblasts: a PFKFB3-linked transcriptomic response to oxidative stress.
best.abstract: Aging-related impairment in cellular stress adaptability may contribute to vulnerability to Alzheimer's disease (AD), but patient-derived experimental models that preserve agingassociated molecular features remain underused. Here, we investigated transcriptomic responses to oxidative stress in ex vivo dermal fibroblasts derived from patients with AD and control participants matched for age and sex. Fibroblasts were exposed to hydrogen peroxide to induce reactive oxygen species-mediated stress, followed by RNA sequencing to identify disease-associated differences in stress-responsive gene regulation. AD-derived fibroblasts exhibited distinct oxidative stress response patterns, with altered regulation of pathways related to endoplasmic reticulum stress, immune activation, autophagy, protein synthesis, and cell cycle control. Systematic candidate gene prioritization identified PFKFB3 as a key stress-responsive gene showing reduced induction in AD fibroblasts. Lower PFKFB3 responsiveness was associated with poorer cognitive performance and higher levels of neurodegeneration-related blood biomarkers, including plasma pTau217, neurofilament light chain, and glial fibrillary acidic protein. In immortalized human astrocytes, PFKFB3 knockdown reduced cell viability under oxidative stress and altered transcriptional programs related to proteostasis, metabolic regulation, and immune activation. These findings suggest that AD is associated with impaired cellular stress adaptability in patient-derived fibroblasts and highlight PFKFB3 as a candidate node linking oxidative stress responsiveness, glial vulnerability, and AD-related pathological burden.

best.title: Extracellular vesicle-mediated neuroimmune remodeling across synucleinopathies: Therapeutic implications of cell-type specificity and central-peripheral crosstalk.
best.abstract: Synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy, are characterized by convergent α-synuclein misfolding, impaired proteostasis, and chronic neuroinflammation. Despite these shared pathological features, these disorders exhibit distinct inclusion-bearing cell profiles, vulnerable neural circuits, immune phenotypes, and clinical progression rates, with neuronal inclusions dominating in Parkinson's disease/dementia with Lewy bodies and oligodendrocyte pathology predominating in multiple system atrophy. Extracellular vesicles have emerged as critical modulators integrating these multifaceted pathogenic processes. Secreted by neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, extracellular vesicles cross biological boundaries to deliver diverse bioactive molecules and mediate intercellular communication. This review synthesizes current evidence to propose that extracellular vesicles serve as context-dependent mediators connecting intracellular proteostatic stress to local glial reactivity and systemic immune regulation. Extracellular vesicle-associated α-synuclein maintains a seeding-competent conformation, enters recipient cells, and triggers templated aggregation and inflammatory signaling, although its exact pathogenic contribution relative to free α-synuclein and non-vesicular transmission routes remains undefined. Extracellular vesicle cargo dynamically reshapes microglial and astrocytic activation, oligodendroglial homeostasis, neuronal survival, blood-brain barrier integrity, and peripheral immune recruitment. Extracellular vesicles exert bidirectional effects: pathological extracellular vesicles amplify neurotoxicity, while homeostatic or engineered extracellular vesicles restore proteostasis, optimize immune homeostasis, and facilitate neural tissue repair. Advanced techniques including immunocapture, real-time quaking-induced conversion, and single-vesicle profiling enhance the sensitivity and resolution of extracellular vesicle-based biomarkers, enabling improved discrimination among synucleinopathy subtypes. However, clinical translation is hampered by extracellular vesicle heterogeneity, inaccurate cell-origin tracing, pre-analytical variability, insufficient standardization, and limited causal in vivo and longitudinal evidence. It is concluded that extracellular vesicles function as integral components of a dynamic, multilayered communication network, with their outcomes determined by cellular origin, cargo, recipient type, disease stage, and anatomical context. Standardized protocols, longitudinal cohorts, and mechanistic models are indispensable for developing reliable extracellular vesicle biomarkers and safe extracellular vesicle-targeted therapies for synucleinopathies.

best.title: A rare TMEM175 mutation drives Parkinson's disease pathology by disrupting proton gating and lysosomal acidification.
best.abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175), implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, has been variably proposed to function as a background K+ "leak" channel or a proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Here, we identified the rare TMEM175 variant p.L275R in a patient with early onset PD. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that TMEM175-L275R mutant proteins retain normal lysosomal expression and K+ "leak" activity, but specifically lose proton- and agonist-dependent activation gating. In skin fibroblasts isolated from the patient with PD harboring the monoallelic p.L275R mutation (TMEM175+/L275R), and in derived induced pluripotent stem cells and induced dopaminergic neurons, lysosomal H+ flux, acidification, and degradation were impaired. These lysosomal defects were corrected upon genome editing to produce the isogenic WT allele (+/+Cor), but appeared when the mutant allele was introduced onto a WT background (+/L275RMut). Pathological α-synuclein aggregation was facilitated in patient-derived (+/L275R) and mutation-introduced (+/L275RMut) neurons. Consistent with these genetic findings, pharmacological activation of TMEM175 with small-molecule agonists restored lysosomal functions and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in TMEM175+/L275R neurons. In in-vivo studies, equivalent-site-mutation knock-in mice demonstrated synucleinopathy and PD-like motor phenotypes. Collectively, our work provides genetic and pharmacological evidence that severe loss-of-function mutations may contribute causally to the onset age and pathogenesis of PD and identifies lysosomal proton channels and transporters as potential therapeutic targets for PD intervention.

Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b‑mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. best.title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
best.abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

best.title: Aging impairs CX3CL1 neuroprotection in α-synuclein-induced Parkinson's disease pathology.
best.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most prevalent movement disorder, is pathologically defined by the accumulation of α-synuclein (α-syn), loss of dopaminergic neuron and inflammation in the substantia nigra pars compacta. The neuronally expressed chemokine CX3CL1 (fractalkine, FKN), when delivered as the soluble form (sFKN) via AAV-mediated overexpression, protects dopamine neurons in several animal models of PD. Since aging is a major risk factor for PD, we examined the effects of sFKN overexpression in both young and aged PD models. To model PD, young (3-month) and aged (15-month) male F344 rats received unilateral intracranial injections of recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (rAAV9) encoding either human wild-type α-synuclein (α-syn) or green fluorescent protein (GFP). Motor performance was evaluated at baseline, 1 month, and 2 months post-injection. Behavioral deficits and neuropathological changes were compared across treatment and age groups. CX3CL1 involvement in PD-related neuroinflammation was assessed using immunohistochemistry and biochemical analyses and bulk RNA-seq was used to characterize transcriptomic changes. We found that sFKN rescued both motor deficits and dopaminergic neuron loss in young PD animals but not in aged animals. Analysis of the transcriptomics revealed age-dependent alterations in inflammatory, immune, and neurogenic signaling in response to sFKN treatment. In conclusion, while sFKN effectively ameliorates behavioral deficits and dopaminergic neurodegeneration in young PD animals, its protective effects are lost in aged animals. These findings emphasize the necessity of rigorous age-inclusive preclinical evaluation and suggest that targeting CX3CL1 signaling alone may be insufficient as a therapeutic strategy in age-related neurodegenerative disease.

best.title: Up-regulation of the kinase LRRK2, in enteric glia contributes to mucosal barrier impairment in Parkinson's disease via secretory autophagy.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) show intestinal epithelial barrier (IEB) alterations, enteric gliosis and inflammation that could contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms. Moreover, changes in leucine rich-repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) expression/activity have been associated with PD development and related intestinal inflammation. However, the molecular determinants linking LRRK2, enteric gliosis and IEB impairment remain unclear. Therefore, we investigated the role of LRRK2 in IEB changes associated with PD, focusing on its role in the interplay between enteric glial cells (EGCs) and intestinal epithelial cells (IECs). Intestinal motility, colonic α-synuclein and LRRK2 expression were assessed. Enteric gliosis was evaluated by detection of GFAP+ cells co-expressing LRRK2; IEB was tested by mucins detection and quantification of Muc-2, tight junction proteins and secretory autophagy. In vitro co-cultures between EGCs and IECs were performed to investigate glial LRRK2-mediated gut barrier alterations. KEY RESULTS: A53T mice, without central neuroinflammation, showed intestinal disturbances, colonic α-synuclein accumulation and an increase in colonic GFAP+/LRRK2+ glial cells before brain pathology. Moreover, PD animals displayed IEB alterations and increased colonic autophagosomes, suggesting a shift towards secretory autophagy. In co-culture experiments, α-synuclein and lipopolysaccharide promoted enteric gliosis and LRRK2 up-regulation in glial cells, contributing to IEB impairment via secretory autophagy. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: These changes could influence bowel symptoms and central pathology associated with PD, via the gut-brain axis.

best.title: Cerebrospinal fluid sTREM2 and PGRN in the early diagnosis and progression monitoring of Alzheimer's disease: A longitudinal study.
best.abstract: BackgroundAlzheimer's disease (AD) features amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition and tau pathology, with microglial dysfunction and neuroinflammation increasingly implicated. Soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-2 (sTREM2) and progranulin (PGRN) regulate microglial function and lysosomal homeostasis, but their dynamics across the AD continuum remain unclear.ObjectiveTo investigate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sTREM2 and PGRN in the early diagnosis and progression monitoring of AD, and their associations with Aβ pathology and other biomarkers.MethodsData were from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). Based on CSF Aβ42 and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores, subjects were categorized into Aβ-CN (n = 196), Aβ+CN (n = 101), Aβ+MCI (n = 378), and Aβ+AD (n = 96). Baseline demographics, neuropsychological assessments, imaging indices, and CSF biomarkers were compared. Spearman correlation, ROC curve analysis, and linear mixed-effects models (n = 255) were used.ResultsBaseline CSF sTREM2 was lower in Aβ+CN than Aβ-CN. PGRN was lower in Aβ+CN and Aβ+MCI than Aβ-CN. Over 2 years, sTREM2 increased most in Aβ+MCI and moderately in Aβ+CN, while PGRN declined in Aβ-CN, Aβ+MCI, and Aβ+AD. Both biomarkers correlated with CSF tau and p-tau in Aβ+ individuals.ConclusionsBaseline CSF sTREM2 and PGRN have limited cross-sectional diagnostic value for AD. However, their longitudinal trajectories raise the possibility that they may reflect the microglia-lysosome axis. best.title: Neuropathological and functional impact of astrocyte-derived extracellular vesicles in an aged model of Alzheimer's disease.
best.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are lipid-bound particles that transfer cargos between cells. While plasma neuronal-derived EVs (NEVs) from individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) have been reported to exhibit high pathogenic potential, this study examined the impact of astrocyte-derived EVs (AEVs) in an aged AD mouse model. Plasma AEVs were isolated from cognitively normal control (CNC), MCI, and AD individuals using GLAST-based immunocapture and AEV size, purity, and tetraspanin were validated by flow cytometry, nanoparticle tracking, and super-resolution microscopy. AEVs pooled by clinical cohort were injected into the hippocampus of 6-month-old female PSAPP mice. Behavioral, biochemical, and neuropathological outcomes were assessed 6 months later. Rotarod assessment revealed significant impairment in motor coordination (p < 0.0001) in mice receiving MCI- and AD-AEVs compared with those receiving CNC-AEVs. While Morris water maze (MWM) also demonstrated that CNC-AEVs injected mice exhibited a trend toward increased target quadrant entries and faster escape latencies, these measures did not reach did not reach statistical significance. No overt changes were observed in the staining of amyloid plaque burden (6E10), and astrogliosis (GFAP). Immunoblotting of 82E1 and 22C11 confirmed Aβ/AAP levels remained similar across all injected mice, whereas increased cortical tau accumulation was observed in MCI- and AD-AEV injected mice. Cerebellar synaptic density (SY-38) remained unchanged. These findings suggest that while human-derived AEVs can precipitate early tau-related changes and motor coordination deficits, they do not significantly alter overall amyloidosis or astrocyte-reactivity at this time point. Further investigation is required to determine the viability of AEVs as biomarkers or therapeutic targets given the subtle nature of the observed structural pathology.

best.title: Lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe ROCL enables dynamic hypochlorous acid imaging in living cells and a mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
best.abstract: Hypochlorous acid (HClO) plays critical roles in oxidative stress and is strongly implicated in the progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). Here, we report ROCL, a new lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe for sensitive and selective detection of HClO in living systems. ROCL displays rapid response, excellent selectivity, and a low detection limit of 49 nM, based on an HClO-induced spirolactam ring-opening mechanism. The probe enables real-time imaging of exogenous and endogenous HClO in SH-SY5Y and PC12 cells, exhibits low cytotoxicity, and effectively visualizes elevated HClO levels in MPTP- and rotenone-induced PD models. ROCL also shows favorable blood-brain barrier permeability and allows noninvasive in vivo HClO imaging in PD model mice. These results establish ROCL as a valuable tool for probing HClO-associated oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases.

best.title: Gut bacterial isolates from individuals with Alzheimer's disease induce strain-specific intestinal, inflammatory, and neurobehavioral phenotypes in mice.
best.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which alterations in the microbiota-gut-brain axis has been increasingly investigated. However, the effects of individual cultivable bacterial isolates recovered from individuals with AD on host intestinal and neurobehavioral phenotypes remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, three bacterial isolates, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Citrobacter pasteurii, were recovered from fecal samples collected from individuals diagnosed with AD and evaluated in healthy BALB/c mice following long-term oral administration. The effects of the isolates on physiological parameters, intestinal morphology and barrier-associated markers, inflammatory responses, gut microbial community composition, and neurobehavioral outcomes were assessed. The three isolates produced strain-specific effects, with C. pasteurii producing the most pronounced overall phenotype. Mice receiving C. pasteurii showed reduced body weight gain, increased spleen index, and shortened colon length, accompanied by elevated circulating inflammatory cytokines. Alterations in goblet cells, MUC2 expression, and tight-junction-associated proteins, including ZO-1 and claudin-1, were also observed, indicating alterations in intestinal barrier-associated structures. Gut microbiota analysis revealed strain-specific changes in microbial diversity and community composition, with the most pronounced alterations observed in the C. pasteurii group. In addition, C. pasteurii administration was associated with increased hippocampal inflammatory responses and astrocytic activation, whereas no apparent hippocampal neuronal loss was detected. Neurobehavioral testing revealed reduced locomotor activity and altered exploratory and behavioral responses, particularly in the C. pasteurii group. However, because reduced locomotor activity may influence performance in the novel object recognition and tail suspension tests, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. K. pneumoniae produced intermediate effects, whereas E. coli showed comparatively milder effects under the experimental conditions used. Collectively, these findings indicate that the tested bacterial isolates recovered from individuals with AD can produce strain-specific intestinal, inflammatory, microbial, and neurobehavioral alterations in healthy mice, with C. pasteurii producing the strongest overall phenotype. Importantly, the observed changes in gut microbial composition do not establish specific bacterial functions or pathogenicity, as microbial functional activity was not directly assessed. The present study does not establish that these bacteria are specifically associated with AD or that they cause AD progression; rather, it provides experimental evidence that individual cultivable bacterial isolates recovered from individuals with AD may differentially influence host phenotypes relevant to processes implicated in neurodegenerative disease. Further studies using larger human cohorts with appropriate healthy controls, validated AD models, and direct functional and mechanistic investigations are required to clarify the relevance of these observations to AD pathophysiology.

primary.title: Brain organoids: Experimental access to human-specific brain development.
primary.abstract: Human cerebral cortical development includes species-divergent cellular programs and unusually prolonged trajectories that remain difficult to investigate experimentally. These processes support human-specific cognitive abilities and are thought to be associated with vulnerability to neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain organoids provide a tractable system for studying these processes across developmental time and under controlled perturbation. Here, we review how cortical organoids model human-specific features of progenitor biology and cell diversification, as well as progressive cellular maturation and circuit formation. We consider the limitations that constrain later-stage maturation and how approaches including the addition of missing cell types, the use of assembloids, and transplantation can extend the developmental processes accessible to study. Finally, we examine how patient-derived, isogenic, chimeric, and perturbation-based organoid systems are being used to investigate neurodevelopmental disorders and, in turn, reveal mechanisms of typical human development.

primary.title: Integrating Cytoskeletal Systems in Neurons and Glia: Dynamic Orchestration of Structure and Function.
primary.abstract: Neurons and glia form the circuitry of our nervous system, allowing nerve cells to communicate with each other and other cell types throughout the body in a highly specific manner to integrate sensory, motor, and cognitive functions. The ability of these cells to do this is profoundly dependent on an elaborate and dynamic cytoskeleton which allows these cells to adopt complex shapes and specialized structures such as myelin sheaths, the blood-brain barrier, axonal growth cones, dendritic spines, nodes of Ranvier, synapses, and elaborate sensory organs. The cytoskeleton is also critical for morphogenetic movements, the migration of neuronal precursors, and axon growth, which together establish the organization and wiring pattern of the central and peripheral nervous system during development. This review provides a primer on our current understanding of the cytoskeleton of neurons and glia, with an emphasis on how the protein polymers of the cytoskeleton-microtubules, actin filaments, intermediate filaments, and septins-work together to orchestrate the remarkable shapes and functions of these cells. We also highlight key questions and challenges for the field and technological advances that may help address them.

primary.title: Cytoskeletal alterations underlying dendritic and synaptic plasticity in epilepsy.
primary.abstract: Aberrant dendritic changes in epilepsy, morphologically measured by the complexity and length of dendrite, as well as the density of dendritic spines, are dynamic and various considering disease course, developmental stages, and various neuronal type across different brain regions. Correspondingly, imbalanced excitatory and inhibitory synapses in epilepsy, quantitatively measured by the expression level and location of synaptic proteins, still vary considering etiology, disease course, and brain regions. And, various mechanisms involved in synaptic pruning add to the complexity of synaptic alterations in epilepsy. Still, sharing mechanisms underlying aberrant dendritic and synaptic plasticity in epilepsy exist, and cytoskeletal alterations can serve as a tool to decipher alterations of dendritic morphology and synaptic plasticity in epilepsy. Evidences supporting aberrant microtubule dynamics and post-translational modifications of tubulin in epilepsy emerge, combined with their involvement in dendritic morphology and synaptic plasticity. In conclusion, this review respectively summarizes the characteristics of dendritic pathology, synaptic alterations, microtubule dynamics, and tubulin's post-translational modifications in epilepsy, and discusses their interplay and correlation in epilepsy, providing insight into how cytoskeletal organization contributes to macroscopic changes in epilepsy.

primary.title: Mammalian lysophagy: mechanisms and pathophysiological implications.
primary.abstract: Lysophagy is a form of selective macroautophagy/autophagy that preserves lysosomal integrity by eliminating damaged lysosomes. Lysosomal membrane permeabilization can arise from diverse physiological and pathological insults, including proteotoxic stress, crystalline particles, pathogens and chemical perturbations, and occurs along a continuum ranging from transient nanoscale lesions to catastrophic rupture. Cells respond to lysosomal injury through a hierarchical quality-control network in which membrane repair, lysophagic removal and lysosomal regeneration operate in a coordinated manner. Damage recognition involves sensing of exposed lumenal glycans and membrane lipids, followed by ubiquitin-dependent tagging that recruits selective autophagy receptors and activates the core autophagy machinery to form lysophagosomes. Lysophagy is closely integrated with membrane repair pathways, metabolic signaling and innate immune responses that together determine lysosomal fate. Dysregulated lysosomal quality control has been implicated in diverse diseases, including neurodegeneration, infection, cancer and chronic inflammatory disorders. primary.title: Prenatal origins of neurodegeneration: The role of maternal immune activation in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's pathobiology.
primary.abstract: Recent evidence suggests that prenatal environmental factors, particularly maternal infection or maternal immune activation (MIA), may influence the progression of brain aging and lifetime risk for neurodegenerative disorders. The hypothesis is that even a short-lived inflammatory event during pregnancy may leave a lasting imprint on the developing brain and immune system of the fetus, such that aging or subsequent insults may later unmask neurodegenerative disorders. Support for this hypothesis comes largely from animal studies, where gestational inflammation has been shown to potentiate the onset of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases (AD/PD), by increasing amyloid/tau pathology, reducing synaptic connections, and damaging nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons. We review convergent mechanisms, including microglial priming, chronic cytokine excess, oxidative stress, epigenetic marks and proteostatic deficits, through which maternal immune activation may embed a latent "hit" that synergizes with aging to precipitate AD or PD. Furthermore, we appraise experimental models and available human data linking MIA to AD versus PD, noting shared and distinct pathways. Despite growing preclinical evidence, translation to human cohorts remains limited by heterogeneity in MIA exposure timing and outcome measures. An understanding of MIA's impact on neurodegeneration could suggest preventive strategies and interventions for early diagnosis and treatment.

primary.title: Dynamic contributions of astrocytes in Alzheimer's disease.
primary.abstract: In Alzheimer's disease, pathological stimuli reshape astrocyte functions, which in turn act on neurons, making astrocytes critical modulators of disease progression. A comprehensive understanding of how astrocytes dynamically shift from physiology to pathology across multiple functional domains remains to be established. This review synthesizes recent findings across four key domains: proteostasis, gliotransmission/synapse regulation, blood-brain barrier integrity and metabolism, and microglial crosstalk. For each domain, we compare homeostatic and pathological functions, analyze how supportive roles turn detrimental, and discuss effects on neuronal fate. We also examine signaling pathways that govern astrocyte reactivity and the potential of astrocyte-derived biomarkers. By tracing these dynamic transitions, we aim to refine Alzheimer's disease mechanisms and identify state-targeted therapeutic opportunities.

primary.title: Axon-guidance factors and their receptors could be potential targets to promote functional recovery via stimulating angiogenesis and blood-brain barrier repair after ischemic stroke.
primary.abstract: Angiogenesis and blood-brain barrier (BBB) repair play important roles in neural functional recovery after ischemic stroke. The formation of new blood vessels improves the local blood supply, enhancing the oxygen and nutrient supply of newly formed neurons. Despite advances in the mechanistic understanding of vascular growth and repair, there are no safe and effective angiogenic treatments that currently exist because of the immature vessel-induced BBB leakage. In addition to the most studied angiogenic growth factors, the process of vascular budding and migration requires the involvement of guiding factors, many of which were initially identified as regulators of axon growth. In this review, the inhibitory and promoting effects of axon-guiding factors on the vascular system are summarized, and their roles in angiogenesis, BBB repair and neural functional recovery after ischemic stroke are discussed.

primary.title: Midbrain organoids as next-generation models for Parkinson's disease: From pathogenesis to therapeutic discovery.
primary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by selective degeneration of dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and pathological aggregation of α-synuclein. Traditional two-dimensional (2D) cell cultures and animal models have provided valuable insights but fail to recapitulate the cellular architecture and pathophysiology of the human midbrain. Three-dimensional (3D) midbrain organoids self-organize into neural structures that mimic key aspects of human midbrain development and disease pathology. This review examines midbrain organoid-based PD modeling through a concept-driven lens, addressing five questions: (i) Which aspects of PD can organoids model? (ii) How are technological advances reshaping the field? (iii) How do organoids complement existing model systems? (iv) What are the current limitations, and how can they be addressed? (v) What is the path toward clinical translation? Organoids reliably reproduce mitochondrial and lysosomal dysfunction and, in SNCA triplication models, α-synuclein accumulation, but seldom progressive neurodegeneration or mature Lewy pathology. By distinguishing established findings from emerging technologies and providing a realistic assessment of current limitations, this review offers a framework for prioritizing organoid applications in PD research and translation.

primary.title: Analysis of multidimensional molecular mechanisms in Parkinson's disease and precise therapeutic strategies.
primary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, is characterized by progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and striatal dopamine deficiency, leading to motor dysfunction. The complex pathogenesis involves impaired protein homeostasis with α-synuclein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, including NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Newly identified regulated cell death pathways - including ferroptosis, cuproptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis - have further expanded current understanding of PD pathology, while gut-brain axis interactions may contribute to peripheral-central communication and disease progression. These mechanistic insights inspire targeted therapeutic strategies comprising α-synuclein inhibitors, mitochondrial protectants, anti-inflammatory agents, and novel cell death pathway blockers, alongside gut-brain axis interventions. However, these approaches face substantial challenges including limited blood-brain barrier penetration, insufficient target specificity, and individual genetic heterogeneity. Future research should prioritize developing multi-target combination therapies, integrating multi-omics and computational approaches for biomarker identification and patient stratification, while advancing clinical translation of gene- and cell-based therapies. Through interdisciplinary collaboration and precision medicine implementation, disease-modifying treatments for PD may become increasingly feasible.

primary.title: Convergent molecular mechanisms of chronic heavy metal exposure and repetitive mild traumatic brain injury in neurodegenerative processes.
primary.abstract: Repetitive mild traumatic brain injury (rmTBI) and chronic environmental exposure to heavy metals represent widespread contributors to neurological dysfunction that are typically studied independently. However, emerging evidence indicates that these insults converge on overlapping cellular pathways that disrupt neuronal homeostasis, redox balance, genomic stability and proteostasis, including tau regulation. Notably, environmental metals including mercury, lead, arsenic, cadmium, and hexavalent chromium induce oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroinflammatory signaling, processes that are also central to rmTBI pathophysiology. In this review, we synthesize mechanistic and clinical evidence linking chronic heavy metal exposure and rmTBI and examine how their interaction may influence long-term vulnerability to neurodegeneration. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate these two domains within a unified mechanistic framework. We first summarize shared and metal-specific mechanisms of heavy metal neurotoxicity and integrate these findings with the cellular and systemic consequences of rmTBI. Attention is given to higher-order convergent processes, including disruption of the blood-brain barrier, dysregulation of the gut-brain axis, protein misfolding and tau pathology, ferroptosis, and impairment of proteostatic and autophagic pathways. We also discuss emerging biomarker signatures and therapeutic targets relevant to combined environmental and traumatic exposures. Collectively, current evidence supports a model in which chronic heavy metal burden may diminish neural resilience and could increase vulnerability to the cumulative effects of rmTBI. Although direct evidence of their interaction remains limited, the substantial mechanistic overlap provides a framework for future studies investigating environmental contributions to post-traumatic neurodegeneration, biomarker discovery, and potential therapeutic strategies.

primary.title: Roles of autophagy in brain homeostasis and disease.
primary.abstract: Macroautophagy (autophagy) is a lysosome-dependent degradative pathway that encapsulates proteins and organelles within double-membraned vesicles and recycles the contents back into the cell. The interplay of autophagy with various membrane trafficking pathways is crucial for maintaining cellular homeostasis both under basal conditions and in response to environmental stress. In the CNS, neurons and glial cells rely on a spectrum of quality-control and recycling pathways, notably autophagy, to sustain the intricate functions of the brain. Genetic variants in autophagy genes are known to cause Mendelian disorders primarily affecting the human nervous system, underscoring the critical role of autophagy in brain function. We review the latest research delineating the landscape and network of autophagy in developing and mature neurons, elucidating how conserved autophagy pathways regulate neuronal homeostasis and functions at different ages. We examine the increasing evidence of dysfunctional autophagy that contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders, neurodegenerative diseases and psychiatric conditions. Recent insights into the dysregulation of autophagy provide valuable avenues for biomarker identification and therapeutic development, particularly targeting autophagy-lysosome pathways for neurological disorders.

secondary.title: Lysosomal dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.
secondary.abstract: Examination of genetic risk factors associated with neurodegenerative diseases has provided important mechanistic insights into the pathophysiology of these disorders, and it has implicated defects in lysosomal function as a key component of the neurodegenerative process. The lysosome has a primary role in mediating degradation of both intracellular contents and endocytosed material from the extracellular space. Aggregation of misfolded proteins is a pathological mechanism that is observed across neurodegenerative disorders, and aberrant lysosomal degradation of such proteins plays a pivotal part in driving neuronal dysfunction and cell loss. In addition to the crucial role of the endolysosomal system in degradation of intracellular constituents, lysosomes also serve as important nodes for intracellular signalling, participating in nutrient sensing, lipid metabolism, membrane repair and neuroinflammation. In this Review, we provide an overview of mechanisms of lysosomal dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease, with a particular focus on Parkinson disease, Alzheimer disease, frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

secondary.title: Mechanism of the lysosomal calcium signaling TRPML1-TFEB axis in Parkinson's disease.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a prevalent chronic neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive apoptosis of midbrain substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons, striatal dopamine depletion, and α-synuclein (α-syn)-positive Lewy-body formation. Patients exhibit motor deficits (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability) plus non-motor manifestations such as cognitive and sleep impairment. PD pathogenesis arises from intertwined mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, defective protein degradation and disrupted calcium homeostasis, whose precise mechanisms remain incompletely defined. As both a degradative organelle and signaling hub, lysosomes govern clearance of proteins and damaged organelles and mediate key neuronal events through calcium-dependent signaling. Transient Receptor Potential Mucolipin 1 (TRPML1), a lysosomal calcium-release channel, and Transcription Factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosome biogenesis and autophagic flux, constitute the conserved TRPML1-TFEB axis that couples lysosomal calcium signaling to transcriptional control of cellular degradation. Physiologically, TRPML1-triggered calcium release activates calcineurin to drive TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation, one of several convergent routes that maintain neuronal protein and organelle homeostasis; TFEB is likewise engaged by the second lysosomal calcium channel TPC2, by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) inhibition and by oxidative-stress-dependent phosphatases. Pathological TRPML1 malfunction perturbs lysosomal calcium signaling and suppresses TFEB activity, triggering lysosomal defects, autophagic blockage, α-syn buildup, mitochondrial damage and oxidative stress, which culminate in dopaminergic neuronal death and PD progression. Mounting data identify dysregulation of this axis as a core pathogenic driver bridging lysosomal failure and neurodegeneration across genetic, toxic and ageing-related PD, although for several disease genes the available evidence documents TFEB-dependent lysosomal failure without direct TRPML1 perturbation. This review summarizes this axis' molecular-physiological features, its pathological crosstalk with major PD events, targeted therapeutic progress, research limitations and future directions, offering theoretical clues for PD mechanistic study and novel therapeutic development.

secondary.title: Rab GTPases and the Rabopathy framework: from synaptic trafficking to neurodegeneration via LRRK2-driven pathology.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and Huntington's disease (HD) show significant differences in their clinical manifestations, but they all seem to share a common upstream problem: malfunction in the membrane transport controlled by Rab GTPases. This review introduces the concept of Rabopathy, a framework that connects developmental synaptic maturation defects with late-onset protein aggregation. The LRRK2-Rab phosphorylation axis is emerging as a potential common amplifying mechanism across these disorders, with the strongest mechanistic support in PD and growing implications in AD and HD. When Rab substrates are excessively phosphorylated at specific sites, vesicular transport is impaired or arrested, leading to progressive depletion of the reserve pool of synaptic vesicles and the surface pool of receptors, and severe compromise of the autophagy-lysosome flux. The failure of distinct Rab sub-networks also produces disease-specific signatures, including Rab5-driven endosomal congestion in AD, Rab35-mediated α-synuclein secretion in PD, and Rab11/Rab7 trafficking collapse in HD. Restoration of Rab flux may be a therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases, which can be achieved through calibration of LRRK2 activity, modulation of selective Rab subtypes, and rescue of the trafficking network at the systems level.

secondary.title: Disulfidptosis in neurological disorders: from disulfide stress to actin cytoskeletal collapse.
secondary.abstract: The mechanisms driving irreversible neural cell loss in neurodegenerative diseases remain elusive. The collapse of cellular redox balance has unveiled a complex network of emerging metabolic cell death modalities that extend far beyond classical apoptosis. Disulfidptosis, a newly identified form of regulated cell death driven by disulfide stress and uniquely marked by actin cytoskeletal collapse, adds a critical dimension to this network. This review establishes an integrative framework-from sulfur metabolic imbalance to cytoskeletal collapse-for understanding this lethal pathway specifically within the nervous system. we focus on three features that are distinctive to neural tissue: the neuron-glia metabolic coupling that dictates which cell type is most vulnerable; the contrast between chronic disulfide stress dynamics in neurodegeneration and acute stress dynamics in ischemic stroke; and the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and cellular heterogeneity constraints that shape translational strategies. We first establish the cystine/cysteine cycle as the central hub of sulfur metabolism, revealing how it transforms from an antioxidant defense into a lethal driver of disulfide stress upon crossing a critical threshold. We then systematically dissect the molecular machinery of disulfidptosis, centered on NADPH depletion, the SLC7A11 bidirectional paradox, and aberrant cytoskeletal crosslinking. By systematically comparing disulfidptosis with ferroptosis and cuproptosis, we identify the SLC7A11-cystine-NADPH axis as a shared regulatory node. We further discuss how this mechanism may converge to contribute to neural cell injury across chronic neurodegenerative and acute neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, and may also extend to acute neurological conditions such as ischemic stroke. Finally, we propose a dual neuroprotective strategy targeting disulfidptosis and highlight its biomarker potential. Collectively, this review offers a new paradigm for understanding metabolic cell death in neurodegenerative diseases and lays a theoretical foundation for neuroprotective strategies targeting disulfide homeostasis.

secondary.title: [Building and maintaining the muscle fiber: new perspectives on the microtubule network].
secondary.abstract: The motor unit is a unique structure, formed by the association of highly specialized cells: a motor neuron transmitting information from the brain, and a muscle fiber enabling muscle contraction. This functional specialization relies on a complex cellular architecture, notably supported by the microtubule cytoskeleton, whose role is now better characterized in neurons than in muscle fibers. In this context, recent data on the links between different regulators of the microtubule network in neurons enrich our understanding of cellular homeostasis. These advances suggest the existence of similar processes in muscle fibers, opening new perspectives for neuromuscular physiology and our view of the motor unit.

secondary.title: STMN2: Membrane-Binding Microtubule Regulator or Tubulin Effector?
secondary.abstract: STMN2, a protein implicated in motor neuron degeneration, is widely viewed as a membrane-associated microtubule inhibitor, but emerging evidence challenges whether this activity defined its cellular function. Three alternative models integrates available evidence to offer perspectives beyond microtubule regulation. The vesicle cargo adaptor model proposes that STMN2 recruits diverse cargos to transport vesicles for axonal delivery. The membrane-bound signaling messenger model links STMN2 turnover to local signaling, effector, degradation, or effector release. The traffic director model proposes that STMN2 regulates cargo routing between delivery and degradative pathways. These models are not mutually exclusive and position tubulin binding as a regulator of STMN2 function rather than its defining activity.
