secondary.title: Effects of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus on the Offspring's Neurodevelopment.
secondary.abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a major global health concern that affects up to 14% of pregnancies. Traditionally, it has been characterized by hyperglycemia and insulin resistance. However, GDM can also lead to long-term health consequences in offspring, particularly affecting neurodevelopment. It has been associated with an increased risk of cognitive deficits, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and emotional dysregulation in GDM-exposed offspring. Findings from human and experimental studies suggest that GDM disrupts cortical and hippocampal architecture, impairs synaptic plasticity, and induces epigenetic alterations in key neurodevelopmental genes. These mechanistic pathways include oxidative stress, inflammation, apoptosis, and altered neurotrophin expression and receptor signaling. Maternal metabolism, diet, and genetic background may negatively affect neurotrophin expression, which could impact fetal brain development. Lower levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and nerve growth factor (NGF) in maternal blood, placental tissue, and cord blood have been linked to poor neurodevelopmental outcomes. This suggests that neurotrophins could be considered potential biomarkers. This narrative review compiles the latest evidence on the effects of GDM on fetal brain development, emphasizing the role of neurotrophins, especially BDNF and NGF, as critical mediators in this process. Emerging data also suggest that glycemic control during pregnancy may partially restore neurotrophin levels and improve neurodevelopmental outcomes. Understanding the interaction between maternal glucose metabolism and fetal brain signaling pathways is essential for pregnancy care and the design of neuroprotective strategies.

secondary.title: The pathological roles of intrinsically disordered proteins in lysosomal acidification dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and Parkinson's disease (PD) are characterized by the accumulation of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), including amyloid-β (Aβ), tau, and α-synuclein (αSyn). These proteins disrupt neuronal homeostasis through toxic aggregation, impaired proteostasis, and progressive neurodegeneration, in part via dysfunction of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (ALP). A central feature of this impairment is defective vacuolar-type (H+)-ATPase (V-ATPase) function, leading to lysosomal deacidification and reduced degradative capacity. Pathological IDP species converge on V-ATPase through direct interactions with its subunits or by perturbing its assembly, while also exerting protein-specific effects, including lysosomal membrane destabilization, impaired hydrolase activity, and disrupted endolysosomal trafficking. These combined mechanisms create a reciprocal relationship between lysosomal dysfunction and IDP accumulation, in which impaired lysosomal degradation further promotes the persistence and aggregation of pathological IDP species. This review synthesizes current insights into the molecular interplay between IDPs and lysosomal acidification across AD, FTD, and PD, and highlights how these processes contribute to disease progression. We further discuss emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring lysosomal function. These findings underscore lysosomal dysfunction as a common feature of IDP-driven neurodegeneration and a potential therapeutic target across these disorders.

secondary.title: PINK1‑regulated mitophagy dysfunction in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease (Review).
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and the accumulation of misfolded α‑synuclein forming Lewy bodies. Emerging evidence highlights mitochondrial dysfunction as an important and early event in PD pathogenesis. Among the key regulators of mitochondrial quality control, PTEN‑induced kinase 1 (PINK1) plays a pivotal role by initiating mitophagy, the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria. Under physiological conditions, PINK1 is rapidly degraded, whereas mitochondrial depolarization stabilizes PINK1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane, where it recruits and activates Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, to promote mitophagy. Loss‑of‑function mutations in PINK1 also disrupt this process, leading to the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, oxidative stress, abnormal calcium homeostasis and neuronal apoptosis. Furthermore, PINK1 deficiency has been shown to exacerbate α‑synuclein aggregation, impair synaptic transmission and activate neuroinflammatory pathways, collectively accelerating dopaminergic neurodegeneration. Therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring or enhancing PINK1‑mediated mitophagy through pharmacological activation, gene delivery or modulation of parallel pathways‑represent a promising avenue for PD intervention. Continued elucidation of the molecular functions of PINK1 will provide critical insights into mitochondrial homeostasis and novel therapeutic targets for PD.

secondary.title: Genetic Susceptibility, Neurodevelopmental Abnormalities, and Neuroimmune Interactions Across Major Psychiatric Disorders.
secondary.abstract: Major psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and autism spectrum disorder, share overlapping genetic, neurodevelopmental, and neuroimmune underpinnings that challenge traditional diagnostic boundaries. This review synthesizes evidence across three interconnected domains: convergent genetic risk affecting synaptic and immune pathways, neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities shaped by early-life insults, and neuroimmune crosstalk involving blood-brain barrier dysfunction, sustained inflammation, and complement-mediated pathology. We propose a multidimensional developmental-immune framework in which genetic liability, environmental exposure timing, and peripheral immune status jointly shape transdiagnostic trajectories. This framework reframes psychiatric disorders as dynamic interactions among stable trait-like susceptibilities and fluctuating biological states, offering a roadmap for biomarker-driven stratification and early immune-targeted interventions.

secondary.title: Spontaneous Neuronal Activity in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Insights from Human and Animal Studies.
secondary.abstract: Developmental spontaneous neuronal activity (SNA) plays an instrumental role in the generation of precise brain circuits. Spontaneous activity patterns guide neuronal differentiation, synaptic refinement, and circuit formation; consequently, perturbations in these activity patterns can profoundly influence brain network organization. Growing evidence suggests that mutations in autism-associated genes lead to alterations of the SNA pattern during early brain development, thereby giving rise to the behavioral features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This review integrates findings from neuroimaging studies, which reveal widespread alterations in neuronal excitability in individuals with ASD. Regional homogeneity and functional connectivity analyses consistently demonstrate region-specific abnormalities, including hyperactivity in higher-order cortical regions, hypoactivity in sensorimotor areas, and disrupted long-range connectivity. These functional alterations are closely linked to the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms such as excitation-inhibition (E/I) imbalance, impaired GABAergic signaling, glutamatergic dysregulation, and abnormalities in calcium-dependent signaling pathways. Identification of activity-based biomarkers, together with advanced neuroimaging techniques and computational and machine learning (ML) approaches, may facilitate early diagnosis of ASD. Understanding the origin and consequences of alterations in SNA provides a unifying framework for identifying novel targets for designing pharmacological intervention strategies.

secondary.title: Lipid homeostasis and cellular metabolism in neurodegenerative diseases: A maturing framework to guide therapeutic development.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and dementia with Lewy bodies have long been viewed through the lens of protein aggregation. Emerging evidence, however, highlights lipid transfer, load, metabolism, and cellular homeostasis as upstream drivers of pathology. This perspective integrates established neurobiological, genetic, and mechanistic evidence of lipid dysfunction and outlines how these pathways can guide patient stratification, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic development. Of critical importance, lipid transport and lysosomal and trafficking networks are at the center of cholesterol regulation, glycosphingolipid clearance, endolysosomal function, and neuron-glia lipid exchange across genetic and sporadic neurodegenerative diseases. We present an integrated framework where correcting lipid imbalances and metabolic dysregulation may complement or obviate protein-targeted approaches, creating more precise clinical trials and combination strategies. By re-centering the therapeutic focus on lipid and cellular metabolism, we aim to catalyze translational advances in neurodegenerative disease treatment.

secondary.title: TLDc proteins: Stress-responsive nexus regulators of redox signaling, V-ATPase dynamics, and organellar crosstalk in neurodegeneration.
secondary.abstract: Many age-related neurodegenerative disorders are marked by progressive defects in cellular energy metabolism and protein homeostasis that converge on mitochondrial and lysosomal dysfunction. TLDc domain-containing proteins, such as OXR1, NCOA7, and related family members, have emerged as crucial modulators of organellar physiology and cellular stress responses. Growing evidence indicates that TLDc proteins physically interact with vacuolar ATPases (V-ATPases) to modulate their assembly and catalytic activity, linking TLDc function directly to the maintenance of lysosomal and Golgi lumen pH. This organellar pH homeostasis, in turn, is fundamental to intracellular iron handling and metabolic regulation, processes essential for mitochondrial bioenergetics, lysosomal functions, and cellular viability. Lysosomes maintain an acidic lumen via V-ATPase proton pumping, counterbalanced by specific ion channels, including TMEM175. This acidic environment is required for ferric iron reduction and subsequent release into the cytosol; when acidification fails, cells develop cytosolic iron deficiency, mitochondrial defects, pseudohypoxia via HIF-1α activation, and inflammation. Conversely, iron flux from lysosomes to mitochondria depends on acidic conditions and direct organelle contact, as exemplified by BDH2-driven siderophore transport, a V-ATPase-dependent but not TLDc-regulated process, which supports mitochondrial bioenergetics and sustains lysosomal acidity. Iron and pH dysregulation synergize to drive ferroptosis, lipid peroxidation, and neurotoxicity. Emerging studies link lysosomal deacidification and iron dyshomeostasis to the pathogenesis of major neurodegenerative diseases. These mechanisms collectively shape neuronal resilience, survival, and aging trajectories. This review integrates recent insights into how TLDc proteins coordinate organellar pH regulation and iron homeostasis and discusses how disruption of these interconnected pathways contributes to age-related neurodegeneration.

secondary.title: Decoding and Rewiring Neurovascular Communication in Spinal Cord Injury via Computational Extracellular Vesicle Dynamics.
secondary.abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts the neurovascular unit (NVU), notably impairing the blood-spinal cord barrier (BSCB), which undergoes a biphasic transformation from acute hyperpermeability to chronic fibrotic sclerosis. This dynamic remodeling creates a heterogeneous barrier that hinders effective drug delivery and limits therapeutic success. Here we integrate pathological characterization with computational molecular dynamics to rationally engineer extracellular vesicles (EVs) capable of receptor-mediated transcytosis across the fibrotic BSCB. Coupled with computational fluid dynamics-optimized hydrogel scaffolds and neuromodulation techniques, this approach promotes NVU repair, restores synaptic homeostasis, and facilitates neural circuit rewiring. This integrated framework advances precision SCI interventions by overcoming the evolving BSCB, offering a novel paradigm for enhancing functional recovery after traumatic SCI and informing therapeutic strategies for central nervous system disorders characterized by barrier dysfunction.

secondary.title: Maternal circulating cytokine and chemokine levels during pregnancy and risk of autism spectrum disorder in offspring: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Maternal immune activation (MIA) during pregnancy has been implicated in offspring neurodevelopment, but evidence linking maternal gestational immune mediators with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains heterogeneous. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether maternal circulating cytokine and chemokine levels during pregnancy are associated with autism in offspring. METHODS: Five databases were searched for human observational studies measuring maternal blood cytokines or chemokines during pregnancy and reporting autism outcomes in offspring. Eligible studies included autism versus control comparisons using maternal serum or plasma samples. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted using odds ratios (ORs) as the primary effect measure. Standardised mean differences (SMDs) were also analysed where group-level concentration data were available. Heterogeneity was assessed using I² statistics, and small-study effects were explored using Egger's test where estimable. RESULTS: Seven studies met the eligibility criteria. In OR-based analyses, nominal associations with autism were observed for IL-10 (OR 1.34, 95% CI 1.06-1.69), CXCL10 (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.24-2.11), IL-1α (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.23-1.65), IL-5 (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.18-1.89), and IL-17A (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.70-0.94). CCL4 showed a borderline association. Supportive SMD analyses indicated higher IL-6 and lower IL-1β concentrations in autism-associated pregnancies. Heterogeneity varied across analytes and was substantial for IL-10 and CCL4. CONCLUSION: Maternal gestational immune profiles may differ in pregnancies later associated with autism, but current evidence does not support a single robust cytokine biomarker. Progress requires larger prospective cohorts with repeated sampling, harmonised assays, pathway-level analyses, and integrated placental-foetal neurodevelopmental phenotyping.

secondary.title: AKAP12 as a signal-compartmentalizing Hub across diseases: Context-dependent functions and translational potential.
secondary.abstract: A-kinase anchoring protein 12 (AKAP12; Gravin/SSeCKS) is a multidomain scaffold that coordinates spatially restricted signaling rather than acting as a single linear effector. By organizing protein kinase A (PKA), protein kinase C (PKC), phosphodiesterases (PDEs), proto-oncogenic non-receptor tyrosine kinase (Src)-related modules, and cytoskeleton- or adhesion-associated proteins within local signaling microdomains, AKAP12 regulates kinase output, PDE-dependent cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) gradients, cytoskeletal remodeling, cell migration, barrier integrity, inflammatory activation, fibrosis, and tissue repair. However, AKAP12-related evidence remains dispersed across oncology, cardiovascular biology, neurovascular research, and inflammatory disease. Its apparent protective or pathogenic roles are often interpreted without sufficient attention to cell type, isoform usage, post-translational modification, disease stage, or microenvironmental stress. This review integrates mechanistic and translational evidence for AKAP12 across cancer, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, neurological disorders, and inflammation-related conditions. In malignant tumors, AKAP12 most often acts as a tumor suppressor by restraining oncogenic signaling, invasion, cytoskeletal reorganization, and metastatic niche formation; however, emerging studies also reveal pro-tumor functions in hypoxia-adapted melanoma, drug-resistant ovarian cancer, and AKAP12-positive cancer-associated fibroblast niches that drive macrophage-mediated immunosuppression. In the cardiovascular and neurovascular systems, AKAP12 shapes beta-adrenergic cAMP microdomains, PDE-dependent contractile responses, endothelial migration, blood-brain barrier stability, oligodendrocyte differentiation, and injury repair. In inflammatory and fibrotic disorders, AKAP12 links immune polarization, stromal remodeling, metabolic homeostasis, and organ repair. We propose that AKAP12 should be viewed as a dynamic signaling-interface module whose functional output depends on cellular origin, isoform context, and microenvironmental state. Future studies integrating single-cell and spatial omics, interactome proteomics, isoform-specific perturbation, organoid models, and precision delivery strategies will be essential to define when AKAP12 is protective, pathogenic, or therapeutically targetable.

secondary.title: Glial handling of alpha-synuclein seeds: uptake, degradation and redistribution in pathological propagation.
secondary.abstract: α-synuclein (αS) aggregation and propagation are central features of Parkinson's disease pathology. Preformed fibril (PFF) models have shown that extracellular αS aggregates can enter neurons and seed aggregation of endogenous αS. Within the brain, these seeds also encounter microglia and astrocytes, which efficiently internalise fibrillar αS and can influence its subsequent fate. This review examines the mechanisms through which glial cells take up, process, degrade and redistribute extracellular αS seeds. When lysosomal trafficking and degradation are effective, glia can act as a sink for seed-competent αS and restrict neuronal seeding and propagation. In contrast, lysosomal dysfunction, incomplete proteolysis or excessive aggregate burden can promote persistence, modification and redistribution of seed-competent αS, including through extracellular vesicles and intercellular transfer. Evidence from microglial and astrocytic models therefore indicates that the outcome of glial uptake depends on the balance between internalisation, intracellular processing and subsequent release. Differences in αS conformation, fibril preparation, inflammatory state, genetic background and experimental model may further explain the apparently protective and pathogenic effects of glia reported across different studies. Understanding the factors that determine whether glial uptake results in productive clearance or continued propagation may identify therapeutic strategies that enhance the removal of pathogenic αS without broadly suppressing glial function.

secondary.title: Immunometabolic dysregulation of reactive microglia and astrocytes in neurodegenerative diseases: Mechanistic insights and therapeutic implications.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) are increasingly understood as multifactorial disorders characterized by intertwined pathological processes, in which metabolic dysfunction may act as a critical and potentially disease-amplifying contributor to the proteinopathy-driven pathological cascade. Despite growing recognition that microglial and astrocytic metabolism governs central nervous system tissue damage-repair homeostasis, intercellular metabolic crosstalk between glia and neurons remains insufficiently synthesized across major NDDs. This review delineates how core metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, mitochondrial respiration, lipid processing, and amino acid transport, shape glial reactivity in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. We highlight glial metabolic reprogramming, a proposed theoretical framework arising from severe glial metabolic dysregulation. Within this framework, persistent pathological stress may drive reactive glia to sequester local energy substrates in excess, which is hypothesized to trigger bioenergetic failure in neighboring neurons. Broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory agents show poor clinical performance because they only block cytokine outputs rather than reverse glial metabolic exhaustion. Therapeutic efforts should therefore shift toward restoring glial metabolic flexibility. Cell-type-specific metabolic reprogramming, instead of pan-metabolic suppression, may circumvent systemic adverse effects. Precision strategies targeting such intercellular metabolic imbalance could provide promising cell-resolved metabolic avenues to retard NDD progression.

secondary.title: Emerging role of cGAS-STING in the pathogenesis of allergic diseases.
secondary.abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) signaling pathway, classically recognized as a crucial cytosolic DNA-sensing mechanism in innate antiviral immunity, is now emerging as a pivotal regulator of sterile inflammation and immune dysregulation. Recent evidence has shifted the paradigm, revealing its significant involvement in the pathogenesis of various allergic diseases, including asthma, atopic dermatitis, and allergic rhinitis. Beyond its canonical role in infection, aberrant activation of cGAS by endogenous DNA from mitochondrial stress, cellular damage, or neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) can drive pro-inflammatory cytokine responses and, depending on context, type I interferon responses; however, stimulus-induced type I interferon production is impaired in asthmatic airway epithelium and is further suppressed by type 2 inflammatory mediators. This review synthesizes current findings on how dysregulated cGAS-STING signaling contributes to allergic inflammation by amplifying Th2 responses, promoting airway remodeling, enhancing epithelial barrier dysfunction, and modulating the activity of key immune cells such as eosinophils, macrophages, mast cells, dendritic cells, and fibroblasts. We further explore the interplay between this pathway and other allergic signaling cascades, highlighting its role as an innate immune amplifier of allergic sensitization and chronicity Finally, we discuss the translational potential of targeting the cGAS-STING axis as an emerging therapeutic strategy for managing severe, steroid-resistant, or type-2-low allergic endotypes, while emphasizing the need for further validation, particularly in settings where type I interferon responses are impaired and where direct evidence for type-2-low endotypes remains limited.Understanding the emerging role of cGAS-STING provides critical insights into the complex immunobiology of allergic diseases and opens new avenues for intervention.

secondary.title: AI-driven transcriptomics for neurodegenerative disease research: A systematic review.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), present a growing global health challenge, with traditional diagnostic and therapeutic approaches facing significant limitations in early detection and mechanistic resolution. OBJECTIVES: Innovations in transcriptomic technologies-spanning bulk RNA sequencing, single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq), and spatially resolved transcriptomics-provide unprecedented insights into cellular heterogeneity and microenvironmental dysregulation. This systematic review synthesizes recent applications of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) across transcriptomic tiers to benchmark computational models for biomarker identification, disease diagnosis, patient subtyping, and drug repurposing. METHODS & ELIGIBILITY: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines for qualitative systematic reviews, literature published between 2016 and 2025 was systematically searched across PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, and bioRxiv/medRxiv. Of 1058 records identified, 19 core empirical studies met all eligibility criteria and were synthesized in depth alongside contextual reference benchmarks. SYNTHESIS & KEY FINDINGS: Traditional ML algorithms (SVM, RF, Elastic Net) demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.72-0.98) in blood-based biomarker selection, while deep architectures (autoencoders, LSTMs, and Graph Neural Networks) excel at modeling continuous disease trajectories and resolving spatial transcriptomic niches (e.g., STAGATE, SpaGCN, cell2location). Emerging spatial deep learning models successfully localize disease-associated microglia (DAM) around amyloid plaques and trace axonal degeneration pathways. LIMITATIONS & CONCLUSIONS: Key translational hurdles include data scarcity in rare NDD subtypes, lack of cross-platform spatial benchmarks, and the black-box nature of deep neural networks. Integrating explainable AI (XAI) and prospective multi-modal cohorts is essential for translating computational transcriptomics into clinical diagnostics and targeted therapeutics.

secondary.title: Dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier and neurovascular unit in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis - From advanced human models to treatments.
secondary.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by the degeneration of motor neurons, resulting in progressive and eventually complete loss of motor function. The phenotypical heterogeneity of ALS poses a challenge to early diagnosis and treatment, with currently available therapeutics only capable of relieving symptoms and slowing progression. While ALS is classified as a motor neuron disease (MND), research has identified significant impairment to the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and neurovascular unit (NVU) of ALS patients. The BBB along with supporting cells of the NVU selectively control the entry of substances into the central nervous system (CNS) and maintain brain homeostasis, with its many cellular components demonstrating impaired function, specifically relating to inflammation, oxidative stress and TDP-43 proteinopathy. The advent of more advanced in vitro techniques as well as use of patient-derived BBB cells has presented a promising alternative to recreate the in vivo structure of the BBB/NVU in a highly controlled platform. Such approaches have ranged from simple 2-dimensional (2D) cell culture to intricate 3-dimensional (3D) co-culture systems, as well as microfluidic systems and organoids, with a potential to investigate ALS associated BBB/NVU dysfunction and drug discovery. This review provides a comprehensive assessment of known BBB/NVU dysfunction in ALS and methods of investigating this using in vitro and in vivo platforms with a focus on inflammation, oxidative stress and pathological TDP-43 expression. This review also presents a future perspective to overcoming barriers to treatment of ALS using new patient-derived BBB/NVU model systems.

secondary.title: The spectrum within the spectrum: Neural heterogeneity in autism.
secondary.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses diverse behavioral, cognitive, and neural profiles that vary widely across individuals. Because diagnosis remains predominantly behavior-based, clinically meaningful within-spectrum differences are often missed. Recent advances in neuroimaging analysis have created opportunities for the identification of distinct neural profiles within ASD. These new avenues provide ways to examine intra-ASD heterogeneity directly, identifying person-specific brain-behavior patterns that group-level comparisons fail to capture. The present systematic review focused on neuroimaging methods (i.e., resting-state fMRI; rs-fMRI, cortical morphology) that emphasized heterogeneity-informed outcomes based on normative modeling, data-driven subtyping, clustering analysis and similar analytic choices. For rs-fMRI, findings showed that differences in connectivity within the default mode and salience networks were linked to social-communication and language impairments, with subtype-specific patterns emerging across samples. In cortical thickness and surface area, studies identified distinct developmental trajectories and individual deviation profiles, with prefrontal and temporal regions often tied to repetitive behaviors and social-communication difficulties. Voxel-based analyses revealed subgroup-specific gray matter alterations, including cerebellar and cortical differences, that aligned with variation in repetitive behaviors and social difficulties. Collectively, this emerging evidence supports the notion that neural heterogeneity in autism is a core feature rather than a limitation. Embracing individual variability can provide crucial insight into the inconsistencies and contradictions of earlier case-control and group-level findings. Moving forward, autism research must prioritize heterogeneity-based methods to establish reproducible subtypes and individualized brain-behavior links.

secondary.title: Effects of PPAR modulation on cognitive function and oxidative stress in experimental Alzheimer's disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
secondary.abstract: Oxidative stress is a key pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), characterized by increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), 4-hydroxynonenal, and protein carbonyls, alongside impaired antioxidant defenses such as superoxide dismutase (SOD). These alterations contribute to endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, and cognitive decline. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) have been recognized for their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties; however, their effects on oxidative stress in AD have not been systematically evaluated. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, with an updated search performed in February 2026. Twenty-nine eligible studies were included. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for outcomes reported in at least three studies. Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q and I² statistics, and random-effects models were applied when necessary. PPAR agonists significantly improved cognitive performance in the Morris water maze, reducing escape latency (p = 0.02). Protein and gene expression levels of PPARs were significantly increased compared to controls (p < 0.001). Experimental studies showed enhanced antioxidant capacity, including increased SOD levels and reduced MDA and ROS production. PPAR activation also decreased BAX expression, suggesting reduced apoptosis and improved cell viability. In addition, PPAR agonists attenuated amyloid-β deposition and improved neuronal morphology, whereas receptor antagonists largely reversed these beneficial effects. Current preclinical evidence suggests that PPAR modulation exerts beneficial effects on cognition, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammatory pathways in experimental AD. Nevertheless, substantial methodological heterogeneity and the absence of clinical evidence warrant cautious interpretation and further translational studies.

secondary.title: Nitric oxide signaling and mitophagy in Parkinson's disease: implications for aerobic exercise-related neuroprotection.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease is strongly associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitochondrial quality control, including defective mitophagy. Aerobic exercise is increasingly recognized as a safe and accessible intervention that can improve motor and non-motor outcomes in Parkinson's disease and may also engage mechanisms relevant to disease modification. In this review, we propose a context-dependent framework in which aerobic exercise reshapes nitric oxide signaling toward a more adaptive profile, characterized by relatively moderate, transient, and spatially restricted nitric oxide bioactivity, and we discuss how this shift may influence mitochondrial biogenesis, mitophagy initiation, and autophagic flux regulation. Rather than treating nitric oxide as uniformly protective or deleterious, we argue that its biological effects in Parkinson's disease depend on source, concentration, duration, subcellular localization, cellular target, and surrounding redox milieu. However, direct evidence that exercise-derived nitric oxide activates these pathways in Parkinson's disease-relevant neural tissue is still limited. We further highlight major translational gaps, including cell-type and brain-region heterogeneity, incomplete definition of exercise dose-response relationships, and the lack of validated in vivo biomarkers of neuronal mitophagy and nitric oxide dynamics in patients with Parkinson's disease. Overall, aerobic exercise is a plausible modulator of mitophagy-related pathways in Parkinson's disease, and nitric oxide is a credible contributor to this effect; however, the current evidence supports a multi-node, context-dependent model rather than a simple linear mechanism.

secondary.title: VPS13C-mediated endoplasmic reticulum-lysosome tethering in neuronal stress responses.
secondary.abstract: Organelle contact sites are increasingly recognized as regulatory interfaces that coordinate lipid transfer, ion signaling, and metabolic adaptation. In neurons, communication among the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), lysosomes, and mitochondria is essential for cellular homeostasis. Recent studies have identified vacuolar protein sorting 13 homolog C (VPS13C), a lipid transport protein, as a key mediator of ER-lysosome tethering and as an important component of the response to lysosomal stress. Structural analyses show that VPS13 family proteins form elongated lipid transport channels that are proposed to facilitate phospholipid transfer between adjacent membranes. Following lysosomal damage, VPS13C is recruited to ER-lysosome contact interfaces, where it forms tethering bridges that may support membrane repair by enabling high-capacity lipid transfer from the ER to lysosomal membranes. Beyond membrane repair, these contact interfaces may also participate in broader organelle communication networks. ER-lysosome contacts can occur in proximity to ER-mitochondria junctions, potentially forming multi organelle signaling hubs that coordinate lipid redistribution, calcium signaling, and mitochondrial adaptation. These signals may influence downstream responses, including activation of TFEB and TFE3, which regulate lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Disruption of this contact site network has emerged as a potential contributor to Parkinson's disease. Loss of VPS13C function is associated with altered lysosomal homeostasis and intersects with pathogenic pathways involving α-synuclein aggregation, PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, and LRRK2 signaling. This review presents a framework in which ER-lysosome tethering is considered part of a staged cellular damage response linking membrane repair, metabolic coordination, and transcriptional adaptation.

secondary.title: Axonemal dynein gene dysfunction as a cause of male infertility: insights from DNAH family mutations.
secondary.abstract: Male infertility is a complex disorder and defective sperm motility is one of the most common reasons for impaired fertility. The dynein axonemal heavy chain (DNAH) gene family encode molecular motors that form the structure of cilia and sperm flagella. Abnormalities in several DNAH genes have already been confirmed to be causative factors responsible for male infertility conditions, mainly including asthenozoospermia, multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF), and reproductive failure related to primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). Here, this review illustrates the current evidence regarding the involvement of members of the DNAH family in male infertility, along with summarizing their biological functions, genotypic and phenotypic correlations and clinical significance. Due to the breakthroughs of the technologies of whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing along with research with animal models and functional investigations, the diversity of reported causative DNAH mutations and their implications for the organization and function of sperm axonemes are currently better understood. DNAH1, DNAH8 and DNAH17 are the DNAH genes most frequently described as being involved in male infertility, though growing evidence also indicated that DNAH3, DNAH11, DNAH12 and DNAH14 also contribute to the male reproductive disorders. Implementation of testing DNAH genes into molecular diagnostics enhances the assessment of genes causing severe sperm motility disorders and aids genetic counseling of the affected families. Together with the genomic and functional data, further research will elucidate additional details for disease mechanisms and will bring benefit to more precise diagnosis and treatments of DNAH-associated male infertility.

secondary.title: UBE3A Dosage Imbalance as a Molecular Framework Linking Angelman Syndrome and Dup15q-Associated Autism Phenotypes.
secondary.abstract: UBE3A is a dosage-sensitive HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase whose neuronal expression is shaped by genomic imprinting at the 15q11.2-q13 locus. Opposite directions of UBE3A dosage imbalance contribute to distinct neurodevelopmental phenotypes: loss of maternal UBE3A underlies Angelman syndrome, whereas maternally derived 15q11.2-q13 copy-number gains, including interstitial duplications and isodicentric inv. dup(15)/idic(15) rearrangements, contribute to Dup15q-associated syndromic autism phenotypes. This review synthesizes evidence across molecular architecture, isoform biology, neuronal imprinting, synaptic regulation, circuit excitability, and therapeutic development. The central argument is that UBE3A should not be interpreted as a general explanation for autism, but as a mechanistically informative model for a defined subset of neurodevelopmental disorders in which parent-of-origin effects and copy-number state are central. In Angelman syndrome, UBE3A loss disrupts proteostasis, synaptic plasticity, inhibitory circuit function, and neuronal excitability through distributed rather than single-pathway mechanisms. In the maternally derived Dup15q spectrum, increased UBE3A dosage is strongly implicated in neuronal and synaptic abnormalities, although interval-wide dosage effects also contribute. Therapeutically, the direction of dosage change creates opposite translational requirements: restoration or paternal reactivation in Angelman syndrome versus dosage normalization in Dup15q-associated overdosage states. A dosage-directionality framework may therefore clarify how UBE3A biology connects molecular mechanism, developmental timing, and precision therapeutic design.

secondary.title: Cortical transcriptomic dysregulation in Autism spectrum disorder: A conceptual synthesis.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition in which human post-mortem cortical transcriptomic studies have identified recurrent but context-sensitive molecular abnormalities. This narrative review synthesises RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) evidence from ASD cortex and organises recurrent findings into three interacting cortical domains: synaptic/neuronal programmes, immune-glial programmes, and RNA-regulatory processes. Across bulk cortical datasets, the most reproducible signals include relative downregulation of neuronal and synaptic expression programmes together with upregulation of glial-associated and neuroimmune signatures, whereas transcript-level analyses further implicate alternative splicing, microexon dysregulation, differential transcript usage, and isoform-level perturbation. Single-nucleus and related cell-resolved approaches localise these abnormalities to defined neuronal and glial populations, while long-read strategies strengthen inference on transcript structure and isoform complexity. Within this framework, mitochondrial-related findings are best interpreted as a linked bioenergetic component rather than an equally established standalone transcriptomic domain. The review also summarise the principal interpretive constraints of cortical ASD transcriptomics, including region specificity, developmental stage, cohort heterogeneity, cell-type composition, post-mortem tissue quality, and cross-platform comparability.

secondary.title: Research Progress of Low-Intensity Pulsed Ultrasound in Parkinson's Disease.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder where current pharmacological and surgical interventions, including Deep Brain Stimulation, often fail to reverse neuronal degeneration or halt disease progression. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) has emerged as a novel, non-invasive neuromodulation technology with significant therapeutic potential. This review synthesizes current research on the key acoustic parameters, biological mechanisms, and clinical applications of LIPUS in PD. Unlike High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU), which relies on thermal ablation to destroy target nuclei (e.g., Vim, STN), LIPUS utilizes low-energy mechanical waves (typically <3 W/cm²) to exert non-thermal regulatory effects without damaging tissue. Mechanisms of action include the modulation of mechanosensitive ion channels (e.g., Piezo1), enhancement of neuroplasticity via brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), promotion of autophagy, and regulation of microglial phenotypes to reduce neuroinflammation. We further compare LIPUS with HIFU, highlighting the superiority of LIPUS regarding safety, reversibility, and the absence of requirement for MRI-based thermal monitoring. While preliminary clinical studies using wearable LIPUS devices indicate improvements in motor and cognitive functions, a unified consensus on optimal stimulation parameters and targeting strategies is lacking. Future research should focus on large-scale, standardized clinical trials to establish precise protocols for LIPUS as a disease-modifying therapy for PD.

secondary.title: Disruptions in axonal lysosome transport and its contribution to neurological disease.
secondary.abstract: Lysosomes are central to the maintenance of protein and organelle homeostasis in cells. Optimal lysosome function is particularly critical for neurons which are long-lived, non-dividing and highly polarized with specialized compartments such as axons and dendrites with distinct architecture, cargo, and turnover requirements. In recent years, there has been a growing appreciation for the role played by axonal lysosome transport in regulating neuronal development, its maintenance and functioning. Perturbations to optimal axonal lysosome abundance leading to either strong accumulations or dearth of lysosomes are both linked to altered neuronal health and functioning. In this review we highlight how two critical regulators of axonal lysosome transport and abundance, the small GTPase Arl8 and the adaptor protein JIP3, aid in maintaining axonal lysosome homeostasis and how alterations to their levels and activity could contribute to neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases.

secondary.title: Pathogenesis and therapeutic targets of neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease mediated by microglia lysosomal dysfunction.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by two core pathological features: senile plaques formed by amyloid-β protein (Aβ) deposits and neurofibrillary tangles formed by hyperphosphorylated tau protein. In recent years, neuroinflammation has been recognized as a key driver in the pathogenesis of AD, and microglia, as innate immune cells of the central nervous system, play a central role in regulating the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Lysosomes are key organelles within microglia responsible for degrading pathological proteins and regulating inflammatory signaling; dysfunction of lysosomes in microglia severely impairs their ability to clear Aβ, damaged proteins, and cellular debris, thereby promoting inflammatory responses. This manuscript summarizes upstream mechanisms that may influence microglial lysosomal dysfunction from four perspectives: pathological proteins, genetic factors, lipid metabolism disorders, and proinflammatory cytokines. Pathological proteins can impair lysosomal acidification and biogenesis by interfering with key pathways such as the TFEB-v-ATPase axis; various genetic factors exacerbate functional dysregulation by influencing the expression of lysosome-related genes and lipid metabolism; lipid metabolism disorders promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, block the autophagy cascade and activate the inflammasome; proinflammatory cytokines can exert varying effects on the clearance of pathological substrates and by regulating lysosomal function. The aforementioned factors can influence microglial lysosomal function through various mechanisms, thereby contributing to impaired clearance of pathological substrates and the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Intervention strategies targeting microglial lysosomal dysfunction, including enhancing lysosomal degradation capacity, regulating autophagy related pathways, correcting cellular metabolic dysregulation and suppressing excessive neuroinflammation, may offer new avenues for AD treatment.

secondary.title: Targeting Nrf2 signaling in Parkinson's disease: Mechanisms, strategies, and therapeutic perspectives.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective loss of dopaminergic neurons and the accumulation of α-synuclein. Disease progression is driven by a complex interplay of chronic oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired proteostasis. As a central regulator of the cellular antioxidant response, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) protects against these cellular insults by driving the expression of various cytoprotective genes. In this review, we summarize the regulatory mechanisms of the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway and evaluate how its activation counteracts core PD pathologies. We also highlight the extensive crosstalk between Nrf2 and other major signaling networks that collectively determine dopaminergic neuronal survival. Finally, we examine the therapeutic potential of current Nrf2 modulators, including natural phytochemicals, clinical-stage candidates, and repurposed drugs, and critically discuss the pharmacokinetic barriers, electrophilic off-target toxicities, and the Nrf2 paradox that must be overcome to successfully translate these compounds into disease-modifying therapies for PD, highlighting the transition toward non-covalent PPI inhibitors.

secondary.title: The early MALDI years and how "microscopy-grade" transmission-mode MALDI-2 mass spectrometry imaging was realized after a long delay: a personal retrospective and review.
secondary.abstract: Since its invention in the mid-1980s, matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization (MALDI) mass spectrometry (MS) has developed into a key bioanalytical technique for numerous research areas in the life sciences. One remarkable application shift that began in the mid-1990s is the increasing use of the label-free MALDI technique as a molecular microscope. One holy grail of MALDI-MS Imaging (MALDI-MSI) is to reach a true single-cell or even a sub-cellular resolution to visualize the molecular content of individual cells and organelles thereof. This requires pixel sizes in the low to sub-micrometer range. These are difficult to achieve, such that new irradiation concepts are needed. Another contemporary research focus is on the advancement of multimodal imaging, especially in the combination of immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy and highly-resolved MALDI-MSI. Drawing upon four decades of active research in the MALDI field, I structured this review to offer both a personal (retro-)perspective and a comprehensive exploration of both historical and contemporary aspects. The initial chapter provides a historical overview of the development of the first laser microprobe mass analyzer (LAMMA 500), while the subsequent chapter chronicles the discovery of the MALDI technique and its initial applications in biological research. The third and fourth sections then direct the reader's attention to selected recent advancements in MALDI-imaging, highlighting pioneering contributions from both in-house and external laboratories. These developments include the utilization of laser postionization for MALDI-2 and the resurgence of the LAMMA 500 concept in the form of transmission (t-) mode MALDI-2. The recently introduced direct coupling of t-MALDI-2 with IF microscopy holds significant promise in unveiling novel avenues for cell biology research.

secondary.title: Intermittent fasting as a therapeutic strategy in Alzheimer's disease: Understanding of brain-derived neurotrophic factor modulation.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques, tau tangles, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress, and it causes cognitive impairment and neuronal loss. The pharmacological treatment is of limited effectiveness, therefore the interest in novel approaches such as intermittent fasting (IF). IF, a nutritional regimen of periodic caloric restriction, has shown a potential to modulate neurodegenerative alterations by metabolic and molecular mechanisms. This review presents the implications of IF in the etiopathogenesis of AD, specifically in controlling brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). BDNF is a major neurotrophin that plays a key role in synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, and cognition. Evidence indicates that BDNF is drastically decreased in AD, therefore enhancing disease progression. IF enhances BDNF expression via mechanisms such as improved mitochondrial function, increased ketone body production, and reduced systemic inflammation. Preclinical studies indicate that IF not only upregulates BDNF but also alleviates key AD pathologies, including Aβ deposition and tau hyperphosphorylation. Additionally, clinical data highlight the cognitive benefits of IF and its role in modulating metabolic health, although studies specifically linking IF, BDNF and AD in humans remain limited. This review underscores the need for further research to determine optimal IF protocols and clarify its long-term impact on AD progression. IF's ability to modulate BDNF and other neuroprotective pathways positions it as a promising non-pharmacological intervention for AD management. By bridging metabolic health and neuroprotection, IF offers potential therapeutic synergy for mitigating AD's complex etiopathogenesis.

secondary.title: Stem Cell and Extracellular Vesicle Therapies for Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: Pathophysiology, Preclinical Evidence, and Translational Challenges.
secondary.abstract: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) remains a devastating neurological condition with high mortality and morbidity, largely due to secondary brain injury mechanisms such as early brain injury (EBI) and secondary white matter injury (SWMI). Conventional surgical and medical interventions have not been sufficient to prevent long-term disability, prompting investigation into novel regenerative strategies. We conducted a narrative review of preclinical and limited clinical evidence on stem cell- and extracellular vesicle/exosome-based therapies for SAH, with emphasis on MSCs and their derivatives. PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase were searched between February and March 2025 for studies examining mechanisms, therapeutic targets, dosing, timing, and routes of administration. Stem cell-based therapies, particularly MSCs and their exosomes, have shown the ability to attenuate neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, excitotoxicity, and BBB disruption. Key mechanisms include modulation of the HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB axis, polarization of microglia toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype, and secretion of trophic factors such as TSG-6, BDNF, and NT-3. Preclinical studies demonstrate improvements in neurological function, cognitive outcomes, and histological preservation across multiple SAH models. Exosome delivery of microRNAs (e.g., miR-129-5p, miR-193b-3p) has emerged as a potent cell-free strategy. Benefits have been reported after both early and delayed administration; however, differences in experimental models, therapeutic products, dosing methods, routes of administration, and outcome measures prevent direct cross-study comparisons and preclude identification of an optimal treatment window. MSC-derived therapies, hold significant promise for mitigating secondary injury and improving outcomes after SAH. Despite this promise, significant translational challenges concerning optimal dosing, delivery methods, and long-term safety must still be addressed. The path to clinical use requires rigorous validation in large animal models before advancing to human trials. Such validation may support the future clinical development of stem cell-based therapies for SAH.

secondary.title: Oxidative stress in neurodegeneration: from a simple insult to a dynamic regulator.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the central role of oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases, and to explore its dynamic regulatory features, underlying signaling pathways, and molecular mechanisms, as well as advanced technological strategies for antioxidant intervention. METHODS: This review comprehensively evaluated existing literature on oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases. It analyzed key regulatory pathways (Nrf2, Keap1, AMPK, mTOR) and molecular processes, including ferroptosis, NETosis, and mitochondrial quality control systems, along with oxidative damage to DNA, lipids, and proteins. The review also assessed advanced technological approaches such as subcellular organelle targeting, nanocarrier delivery systems (e.g. gold nanoparticles, liposomes for glutathione delivery), and single-cell/spatial omics technologies (e.g. single-cell redoxomics, spatial transcriptomics). RESULTS: Oxidative stress exhibits dynamic features, generating protective signals in early stages but transitioning into destructive factors later. A major obstacle for current antioxidant therapies is the blood-brain barrier. Breakthrough strategies identified include precision targeting at the subcellular level, functionalized nanoparticles for efficient antioxidant delivery, and the integration of single-cell redoxomics with spatial transcriptomics to identify specific biomarkers and enable personalized treatments. DISCUSSION: By integrating novel molecular mechanisms and advanced technological resources, this review redefines oxidative stress not as a singular event but as a complex, dynamically regulated system in neurodegenerative diseases. This reconceptualization provides new perspectives for developing targeted and personalized therapeutic interventions.

secondary.title: Brain aging in neurodevelopmental disorders: a narrative review of oxidative, inflammatory, and mitochondrial mechanisms.
secondary.abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), including autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, intellectual disability, and Down syndrome, are increasingly examined through the lens of aging. Emerging evidence indicates that individuals with NDDs may exhibit accelerated or atypical brain aging, characterized by cognitive decline and increased vulnerability to neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. This narrative review synthesizes current findings on biological mechanisms implicated in altered aging trajectories, with emphasis on oxidative stress, chronic neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cellular senescence. These processes, detectable from early development, mirror pathways involved in neurodegeneration, suggesting shared molecular cascades that increase susceptibility to early aging. Biomarker studies report telomere shortening, elevated plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein and neurofilament light chain levels, and deviations in neuroimaging-derived brain age, supporting the hypothesis of altered biological aging in NDDs. However, the limited number of longitudinal lifespan studies, along with marked heterogeneity in etiology, clinical profiles, and comorbidities, constrains causal inference. Psychosocial and environmental factors, including chronic stress, social exclusion, medical comorbidities, and lifestyle influences, further shape aging outcomes. Integrating biological, behavioral, and environmental markers is essential to advance monitoring and inform early interventions aimed at promoting healthier cognitive and functional aging in neurodivergent populations.

secondary.title: Multi-omics integration deciphers arsenic-induced multi-organ toxicity and the novel ferroptosis axis.
secondary.abstract: Chronic arsenic exposure threatens over 200 million people worldwide and induces multi-organ injury, yet the panoramic molecular reprogramming across organs remains incompletely understood, and traditional single-omics approaches fail to capture cross-level and cross-organ regulatory associations. This review systematically integrates evidence from global epidemiology to single-cell spatial omics, tracing the evolution of multi-omics technologies-from single-platform profiling to data fusion strategies such as coupled matrix factorization (CMF) and the DIABLO framework, two complementary multi-omics integration approaches-and to cutting-edge spatial transcriptomics. We highlight ferroptosis as a common mechanism in arsenic-induced multi-organ injury. At the molecular level, we propose a mechanistic model wherein arsenic (AsIII) disrupts selenium metabolism by inhibiting Sec-tRNASec synthesis, thereby impairing selenoprotein (especially GPX4) biosynthesis, a paradigm distinct from the traditional "ROS burst → lipid peroxidation" theory. Supporting evidence includes reduced 75Se incorporation into cellular RNA, genetic deletion of PRDX6 exacerbating ferroptosis, and rescue by selenium supplementation via Nrf2 activation. At the organ level, we compare toxicity features and propose that tissue-intrinsic ferroptosis thresholds-determined by iron content, PUFA-phospholipid composition, GSH reserves, GPX4 redundancy, and selenium availability-govern differential organ susceptibility; the brain shows extreme vulnerability, whereas the liver exhibits relative resistance. Emerging spatial omics further reveals elevated arsenic-responsive gene expression in tumor-adjacent regions. This systems toxicology paradigm offers mechanistic grounding for combinatorial biomarker panels and genotype-guided precision selenium supplementation, although definitive causal validation through tissue-specific Gpx4 knockout or Sec-tRNASec rescue experiments remains a critical next step. We also discuss prospects for AI-driven toxicity prediction models.

papers.title: Pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants drive distinct motor and behavioral phenotypes in humans and mice
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Pathogenic variants in MAPK8IP3 (JIP3) cause Neurodevelopmental Disorder with or without variable Brain Abnormalities (NEDBA), characterized by cognitive impairment, global developmental delay, motor dysfunction, abnormal muscle tone, behavioral dysregulation including autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), seizures, and structural brain abnormalities. While more than 30 largely de novo MAPK8IP3 variants have been reported, the functional impact of variants across JIP3 protein structural domains is poorly defined. To address this knowledge gap, we compare clinical features of individuals with a truncating (p.E27X) or one of two missense (p.R578C and p.R1146C) variants from distinct JIP3 functional protein domains to corresponding knock-in mouse models. Our findings showed that all individuals, regardless of variant type, exhibited delays in language and gross motor function, but individual variants were associated with distinct motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms. Corresponding homozygous p.E27X and p.R1147C variant mice resulted in embryonic lethality, consistent with essential roles for JIP3 in early neurodevelopment. Behavioral characterization of viable heterozygous mice revealed variant-specific locomotor, motor coordination, and hindlimb clasping defects that closely recapitulate clinical observations. Heterozygous p.R579C mice exhibited reduced locomotion, impaired motor performance, and hypertonia-like clasping, mirroring human motor deficits. In contrast, p.R1147C mice displayed hyperactivity, hindlimb clasping, and decreased brain weight, paralleling human clinical features. Together, our findings demonstrate that while distinct MAPK8IP3 variants lead to some shared phenotypes, they are also associated with distinct phenotypes that could reveal domain-specific aspects of JIP3 function. This work establishes the first domain-resolved in vivo rodent models of NEDBA and provides a validated translational platform for mechanistic investigation and preclinical therapeutic testing.

papers.title: Cross-species phosphoproteomic mapping of mTORC1 signalling reveals RNA splicing regulation during neurodevelopment
papers.abstract: Mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) regulates diverse cellular processes through its kinase activity and is essential for nervous system development. Although mTORC1 hyperactivation causes numerous neurodevelopmental disorders, its downstream targets in the developing nervous system remain poorly defined. Here, by profiling thousands of proteins and tens of thousands of phosphosites during the neurogenic phase in mouse and human models, we systematically define the proteomic and phosphoproteomic landscape downstream of mTORC1 during neurodevelopment. To facilitate community access, we developed PhosphoTargets, an interactive platform comprising protein and phosphoprotein expression data from mTORC1 models and patient tissue. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by identifying the deubiquitylating enzyme USP9X as a novel mTORC1 substrate and showing that mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation of USP9X regulates human neural progenitor cell proliferation. Furthermore, integration with gene expression datasets reveals a new role for mTORC1 in the regulation of mRNA splicing. Together, these data provide a comprehensive resource for investigating mTORC1 signalling mechanisms and reveal novel processes through which mTORC1 regulates neurodevelopment.

papers.title: RhoA Overexpression in Nucleus Accumbens-to-Ventral Tegmental Area Spiny Projection Neurons Induces Negative Affective-like Behavior
papers.abstract: Rationale. Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is increasingly affecting populations worldwide and becoming a leading cause of psychological disabilities. However, MDD patients do not respond to current medications, resulting in treatment resistance. This situation demands more basic research to identify targetable molecules and the specific brain circuits and cell types that underlie negative affective pathology. Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) mediates negative affective-like behaviors via dendritic atrophy of nucleus accumbens (NAc) D1 (dopamine receptor 1)-Spiny Projection Neurons (SPNs), making RhoA a promising target for new depression therapeutics. However, the sufficiency of RhoA elevation in NAc projection-specific D1-SPNs is yet to be investigated. Objectives. Whether RhoA overexpression selectively in NAc-to-ventral tegmental area (VTA) SPNs (NAc-VTA SPNs) is sufficient to induce negative affective-like behavior. Whether chronic stress (CS) induces RhoA mRNA expression in this specific projection. Methods. A retrograde (Rg) vector expressing Cre recombinase was infused into the VTA together with Cre-dependent vectors overexpressing either a control expressing only enhanced Yellow Fluorescent Protein (eYFP) or RhoA-eYFP in NAc-VTA neurons. Mice then underwent a battery of affective assays (social interaction, etc.) and a two-choice sucrose operant task assessing motivation. RNA in situ hybridization (RHA-ish) quantified RhoA mRNA in NAc-VTA D1-SPNs of chronically stressed versus unstressed (control) mice. Results. RhoA overexpression in NAc-VTA SPNs, which are primarily D1-SPNs, elicited negative affective-like phenotypes, including social avoidance, reduced open-arm exploration, decreased grooming, and increased latency to approach food. RhoA and control groups acquired a food operant task similarly. However, RhoA overexpression significantly reduced operant responding and breakpoint during progressive-ratio testing. RhoA overexpression in the NAc-VTA projection neurons also diminished persistent sucrose-seeking behavior. Chronic stress induced RhoA mRNA expression selectively in NAc-VTA neurons.

papers.title: Transcriptional aging across CNS tissues in the ALS-FTD spectrum reflects clock architecture and disease-associated cellular signatures
papers.abstract: Background: We examined transcriptomic (gene expression-based) aging in postmortem central nervous system (CNS) tissues from donors across the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-frontotemporal dementia (FTD) spectrum and investigated the molecular and cellular features underlying disease-associated differences in transcriptional aging clocks. Methods. Six transcriptomic clocks (RNAAgeCalc DESeq2, GTExAge, Pearson and GenAge; Pasta REG and age-shift) were applied to 2,235 RNA-sequencing samples from 609 donors across 11 CNS regions, with adjustment for age and tissue-specific technical variables. We compared transcriptional age across ALS, ALS-FTD, FTD, and controls, examining regional variation, gene-level contributions, cell composition, disease duration, and C9orf72 status, with independent validation of gene contributions in a cervical spinal cord cohort. Results. Disease-associated differences in transcriptional age varied by diagnosis, tissue, and clock. ALS and ALS-FTD showed the strongest differences in spinal cord, while FTD differences localized primarily to the frontal and temporal cortex. In ALS spinal cord, RNAAgeCalc DESeq2 estimates were lower than controls, whereas other clocks estimated higher transcriptional age when significant. CHIT1 was identified as the primary contributor to the DESeq2 transcriptional age decrease in ALS. Cell composition adjustment attenuated ALS spinal cord differences, reflecting microglial, lymphocyte, oligodendrocyte, and astrocyte signatures, though the lumbar GenAge increase in transcriptional age and DESeq2 decrease remained significant. The higher transcriptional age in ALS motor cortex also remained significantafter adjustment. Clinical associations were likewise clock dependent. Higher spinal DESeq2 age acceleration (AA) was associated with longer ALS duration, though this association was strongly influenced by the CHIT1 term. Higher GTExAge AA in cervical spinal cord, thoracic spinal cord, and occipital cortex was associated with shorter disease duration; no significant associations were observed for the other clock-tissue combinations or for ALS-FTD. No clock differed by C9orf72 repeat expansion status. Conclusions. In this study we found disease-associated differences in transcriptional age that localize to clinically relevant tissues. Differences in transcriptional aging across the ALS-FTD spectrum reflect interactions among clock architecture, disease-associated gene expression, tissue region, and cellular composition. Resolving these components reveals the biological context underlying divergent clock estimates and provides a framework for interpreting changes in transcriptional aging.

papers.title: A GPNMB-associated lysosomal program tracks neurodegeneration across the DAM continuum
papers.abstract: Summary Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) profoundly remodel microglial states, yet how the heterogeneity of disease-associated microglia (DAM) relates to neurodegeneration remains incompletely understood. Using a progranulin (PGRN) and TMEM106B-deficient mouse model recapitulating key features of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), including lysosomal impairment, we demonstrated that CSF1R inhibition reduced microgliosis yet accelerated neurodegeneration, suggesting a protective microglia contribution under lysosomal stress. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed that increasing Gpnmb expression within DAM was associated with a shift from immune and inflammatory processes toward a lysosomal, autolysosomal, and lipid-catabolic program. Across disease models, engagement of the GPNMB-associated program correlated with neurodegeneration. Consistently, Aβ-driven models with limited neurodegeneration exhibited prominent DAM activation but comparatively limited GPNMB expression and engagement of this program. The GPNMB-associated program was TREM2-dependent, while loss of TREM2 signaling under lysosomal stress was associated with exacerbated neuronal damage. Conversely, lysosomal rescue markedly reduced the GPNMB-associated program, demonstrating its reversibility. CSF proteomics identified a convergent lysosomal and microglial signature across models overlapping with alterations reported in human FTD. Together, GPNMB marks reversible, TREM2-regulated lysosomal transcriptional adaptation along the DAM continuum that scales with lysosomal burden and neurodegenerative severity, consistent with a potentially protective microglial response under lysosomal stress.

papers.title: Microglia and microglia activation are protective in an LSD1-induced model of neurodegeneration
papers.abstract: Attempts to determine the function of microglia activation and the immune system in neurodegenerative diseases have yielded conflicting results, with some data showing a protective effect, while other data shows a detrimental effect. This discrepancy in the function of microglia activation and the immune system in neurodegeneration likely stems from differing functions during the build-up of pathological proteins versus later stage defects. Therefore, we investigated the function of microglia activation and the immune system in Lsd1 inducible deletion mice, which serve as a late-stage tau-associated neurodegeneration model without the build-up of pathological proteins. We found that loss of LSD1 causes the morphological and transcriptional activation of microglia, accompanied by astrocyte activation and a broader immune response. Blocking microglia activation by inactivating Trem2 inhibited the entire Lsd1-induced immune response, while pharmacologically inhibiting microglia via PLX3397 treatment eliminated microglia but did not block astrocyte reactivity or the broader immune response. Surprisingly, despite these effects, neither blocking microglia activation nor depleting microglia prevented Lsd1-induced neurodegeneration, paralysis and death. Instead, we found in both cases that survival was significantly reduced. These results suggest that microglia and microglial activation, independent of astrocyte reactivity and the broader inflammatory response, is neuroprotective in a late-stage tau-associated neurodegeneration model.

papers.title: Doublecortin compacts the microtubule lattice through a DC1-dependent mechanism
papers.abstract: SUMMARY Doublecortin (DCX) is a microtubule-associated protein essential for neuronal migration during brain development, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its function on the microtubule remain incompletely understood. Here we show that DCX compacts the microtubule lattice, with the DC1 domain serving as the main driver of lattice compaction. Using in vitro reconstitution, optical trapping, and molecular dynamics simulations, we demonstrate that although DCX preferentially binds compacted microtubule lattices, it can also bind expanded lattices and remodel them by inducing ∼2-3 Å compaction at interdimer interfaces. This compaction stiffens microtubules and inhibits kinesin-1 and αTAT1 binding. The DC1 domain is necessary for lattice compaction, whereas DC2 is dispensable for this function. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that DC1 binding induces shearing and hinge motions that stabilize compacted conformations absent from apo tubulin, thereby reducing lattice heterogeneity. Our findings establish DCX as a bona fide microtubule remodeler and provide a molecular framework for understanding how DCX contributes to neuronal development through the control of microtubule lattice conformation.

papers.title: Disrupted mannosidase enzymes in C9orf72 ALS/FTD
papers.abstract: Summary Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is an age-related neurodegenerative disorder resulting from the loss of motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord. Neuroinflammation, induced by glial cells including microglia (MG) and astrocytes, is an acknowledged aspect of this neurodegeneration. Generating induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) neuroinflammatory models of ALS may help elucidate non-neuronal mechanisms of disease. Here, we analyze human postmortem tissue and an iPSC derived glia-crosstalk model identifying a reduction in Golgi enzymes MAN1A1 and MAN1A2 in addition to other glycan enzymes from ALS-associated microglia and astrocytes. Impaired Golgi and glycan metabolism is linked to inflammation and other related ALS disease mechanisms including impaired lysosomal proteostasis, altered extracellular matrix, disrupted secretion, and altered cell-cell signaling.

papers.title: Disrupting SORL1-retromer endosomal recycling in mice drives the age-dependent neurodegenerative signature of Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: MRI studies have mapped the atrophic signature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD), isolating regions differentially vulnerable to its age-dependent neurodegenerative process. An endosomal recycling pathway regulated by the interaction of SORL1 with retromer is pathogenically disrupted in AD. Here we test the hypothesis, that the pathway might drive the neurodegenerative process, via multiple yearlong studies in over 140 wildtype and SORL1 deficient mice, modeling SORL1's causative mutations. MRI studies revealed that SORL1 deficiency induced an age-dependent AD-pattern of atrophy, centered on the trans-entorhinal cortex, and that atrophy was prevented by SORL1 restoration, secondary to overexpressing the retromer protein VPS26b. Postmortem studies validated that the atrophy reflects neuronal loss. Proteomic profiling revealed that the atrophy is associated with reductions in cell death suppressors, one of which was then found deficient in the trans-entorhinal cortex of AD patients. Besides supporting the hypothesis, when taken together with other findings the results suggest that SORL1-retromer disruptions represent a therapeutically-amenable common 'neurodegeneration pathway' in AD.

papers.title: KIF1A-driven entry of degradative lysosomes into the axon is developmentally regulated by the microtubule environment at the axon initial segment.
papers.abstract: Neuronal function requires precise transport of lysosomal vesicles along highly polarized processes, yet how this trafficking is spatially and developmentally regulated remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the neuronally enriched kinesin-3 motor KIF1A is required for dendritic and axonal localization of lysosomal vesicles in both immature and mature rat hippocampal neurons. Remarkably, the specialized microtubule environment of the axon initial segment (AIS) restricts KIF1A-driven transport of degradative, cathepsin D-positive lysosomal vesicles while permitting less degradative lysosomal vesicles to enter axons in mature neurons. Disrupting the AIS microtubule environment or expressing a hereditary spastic paraplegia type 30-associated KIF1A variant with increased affinity for GTP-tubulin bypasses this restriction, enabling degradative lysosomal vesicles to enter mature axons. In human iPSC-derived neurons, KIF1A depletion similarly disrupts axonal lysosomal vesicle transport, causes autophagic vesicle accumulation, and triggers axonal degeneration. Together, our findings reveal a developmentally regulated AIS gate that selectively controls KIF1A-driven lysosomal vesicle transport into axons and link its subversion to KIF1A-associated neurological disease.

papers.title: Parkinson’s disease genetic risk converges on Lewy body pathology-associated microglial states
papers.abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) and related α-synucleinopathies are defined by the spread of Lewy body (LB) pathology across vulnerable brain regions, yet how substantia nigra (SN) myeloid cells respond remains unresolved. Using SOX10-based oligodendrocyte depletion and CD11b-based myeloid enrichment, we profiled 169,799 brain myeloid cells and nuclei from 96 donors spanning the LB continuum, including 86,427 from the SN, and integrated them with AMP PD for a total of 298,592 profiles. Across eight conserved states, α-synucleinopathy is associated with a bidirectional signature: upregulated glycolytic and proteostatic-stress programs alongside downregulated lysosomal and mitochondrial pathways. Microglia shift from P2RY12-high sensome cells toward an HSP90AA1-high proteostatic stress state, a transition that intensifies at late Braak LB stages. Immunohistochemistry confirmed that HSP60 + proteostatic microglia state proportions increase with SN neuron loss. A rare NUCKS1-high state (∼1% of myeloid cells), more abundant in late-stage disease, carried the strongest PD polygenic-risk loading. The PD-protective rs3732765-A allele, a microglial cis-eQTL that lowers P2RY12 expression, was nominally associated with a higher proportion of P2RY12-high microglia and higher lysosomal program activity. These findings frame microglial involvement as structured and genetically tractable, nominating the P2RY12 genetic axis and NUCKS1-high microglia for mechanistic studies.
