papers.title: A plasma proteomic atlas of rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders reveals convergent molecular signatures, neurodegenerative overlap, and a cross-disorder severity index
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders (RGNDs) are individually too small for well-powered biomarker studies. We profiled over 10,000 plasma proteins across 27 RGNDs and unaffected family controls, alongside standardized adaptive function measures, to identify shared molecular features. Cross-disorder analysis revealed two proteomic clusters distinguished by cytoskeletal and vesicle-trafficking versus metabolic and hepatic proteins. We identified recurrent protein changes and a shared 32-protein epilepsy signature largely undetectable within individual disorders. RGND proteomic signatures also overlapped extensively with those of adult neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, frontotemporal dementia, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, often in opposing directions. A 186-protein plasma index tracked communication ability in disorders excluded from model training and among individuals with the same diagnosis, independently of age. Twenty-four prioritized proteins have existing drug interactions, including targets of approved agents. These findings demonstrate that cross-disorder proteomics reveals otherwise inaccessible molecular signatures, clinically relevant biomarkers, and potentially actionable biology across genetically distinct RGNDs.

papers.title: In silico designed small molecule targets misfolded TDP-43 to rescue function and ALS pathology
papers.abstract: The DNA/RNA binding protein TARDBP or TDP-43 is a key driver of pathology in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), a motor neuron disease with no known cure. In >97% of sporadic ALS patients, nuclear TDP-43 in motor neurons mislocalizes and aggregates in the cellular cytoplasm (gain-of-function). A parallel reduction in nuclear TDP-43 in ALS patients leads to a loss-of-function in mRNA binding and splicing regulation. Using our machine learning platform, we discovered ACE-339, a novel, orally bioavailable small molecule that disrupts insoluble TDP-43 aggregates. Using in vitro , in vivo and in silico models, we show that ACE-339 directly targets aggregated forms of TDP-43. ACE-339 interacts directly with TDP-43 hexamers, disaggregates recombinant TDP-43 and rescues both gain- and loss-of-function phenotypes of TDP-43 in cells. ACE-339 functionally rescues TDP-43 dependent mis-splicing and synaptic activity. Lastly, ACE-339 rescues disease associated phenotypes in two independent mouse models of TDP-43 pathology. In addition, we now have a catalog of TDP-43 disaggregating compounds that are being developed further to be tested in clinical trials in patients with ALS and other TDP-43 proteinopathies.

papers.title: Brain Cell-Type-Specific X-Chromosome Gene Regulation Reveals Sex-Biased Candidate Genes in Neurodegeneration
papers.abstract: The impact of X-chromosome dosage on gene regulation in specific brain cell-types may importantly shape sex differences in neurodegenerative diseases but remains poorly resolved. We therefore mapped X-chromosome genetic effects on gene expression, i.e. cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTL), across seven brain cell-types from 423 old-age individuals. We identified 212 X-linked genes whose expression was genetically regulated, with the majority being cell-type specific. Notably, 10 of these genes (~5%) showed sex-heterogeneous genetic regulation. Through sex-differential expression analyses we further discovered 101 sex-biased genes that were predominantly female-upregulated most strikingly in microglia. Sex-biased gene expression showed both shared and distinct cell-type effects, appearing most divergent in non-neuronal populations. Many female-biased genes overlapped known escape-from-X-inactivation genes and were enriched for links to Alzheimer's disease. Finally, we integrated our resource with X-chromosome-wide association studies of neurodegenerative diseases through causal inference approaches including transcriptome-wide association, mendelian randomization, and colocalization analyses to nominate 11 candidate causal genes, linked to their respective cell-types and sex-informed mechanisms, for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Multiple System Atrophy. Altogether, our findings suggest escape from X chromosome inactivation may contribute to sex differences in neurodegeneration and provide a resource to advance sex-informed insights into disease pathogenesis and therapeutic opportunities.

papers.title: PolyMorph3D: A flexible MATLAB-based tool for quantifying microglia morphology and multi-colocalization in three dimensions
papers.abstract: As the principle immune cell of the central nervous system (CNS), microglia have been extensively studied throughout development and in a wide range of disease states. Of special focus have been their morphological features such as branching complexity, physical cell-cell interactions with surroundings, and gene expression readouts relating to phagocytosis and cytokine signaling. Each of these domains offers a window onto microglia function, and high-resolution confocal microscopy has long been a workhorse technique to visualize all three. A comprehensive view of microglia function requires both high-fidelity quantification with 3D resolution and colocalization of microglia with functional proteins such as those related to phagocytosis and with nearby structures such as synapses. Accordingly, a number of analytical tools have been developed to measure these features. However, existing open-source options lack either colocalization or 3D capability, while commercial solutions can be costly. Here, we sought to develop an open-source solution that addresses each of these limitations. PolyMorph3D is a MATLAB-based program capable of yielding individual cell-level data of microglia morphology and overlap with up to 4 other sources, all in 3D. The pipeline can be used effectively in mouse tissue and in human postmortem brain, thereby offering a flexible, low cost, and high-fidelity solution for the analysis of microglial morphology and function.

papers.title: Evolutionarily conserved coupling of lysosomal response sensing and disease-associated microglial reprogramming scales with pathological timescales
papers.abstract: Background: Microglia transition into disease-associated microglia (DAM) during central nervous system (CNS) injury and neurodegeneration, yet the upstream intracellular logic driving this state conversion in vivo remains unclear. The lysosome acts as a signaling hub, but whether physiological phagocytic load universally initiates and quantitatively couples to DAM reprogramming across different pathological timescales is unknown. Methods We established a rigorous, unit-corrected analytical framework to overcome pseudo-replication in public single-cell data, anchoring statistical inferences at the level of independent biological units (animals, sequencing plates, or donors). We integrated six transcriptomic datasets spanning three murine injury/amyloidosis models and three large-scale human neurodegenerative cohorts (>320,000 microglial nuclei), alongside human Alzheimer's disease (AD) GWAS summary statistics. Results We demonstrate that the MiT/TFE-regulated lysosomal biogenesis program temporally precedes DAM reprogramming and maintains an evolutionarily conserved baseline coupling even in uninjured homeostatic tissue. In human microglia, MITF and TFE3 transcripts closely track DAM activation, whereas post-translationally regulated TFEB mRNA does not. Genetic enrichment analysis (MAGMA) reveals that common AD risk does not act upon the upstream lysosomal program, but is strongly anchored downstream at APOE. Furthermore, Trem2-knockout models demonstrate that disease-induced coupling amplification retains roughly half its magnitude even when the mature DAM subpopulation collapses. Cross-system comparisons reveal a state-transition synchrony model: disease-driven amplification of lysosomal-DAM coupling (Δ) scales with pathological timescales, showing strong amplification in acute murine injury and aggressive amyloidosis (5xFAD Δ = +0.252), but manifesting primarily as steady baseline maintenance across decades-long asynchronous human AD progression (SEA-AD Δ = +0.072). Conclusions Our study establishes the lysosomal stress-DAM coupling as an evolutionarily conserved pacemaking module for microglial state transitions, providing a quantitative framework for therapeutically targeting neuroinflammation and tissue repair.

papers.title: Stathmin-2 regulates microtubule dynamics and axonal resilience in human motor neurons.
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by the selective degeneration of motor neurons, yet the mechanisms that either induce neurodegeneration or confer neuronal resilience remain poorly understood. Loss of the microtubule-associated protein Stathmin-2 (STMN2) is a downstream consequence of TDP-43 pathology present in nearly all cases of ALS and has emerged as a central feature of disease. However, the mechanisms by which STMN2 maintains homeostasis in motor neurons remain incompletely defined. Here, we investigated the role of STMN2 in regulating cytoskeletal organization and axonal function. Using TIRF microscopy at a single molecule resolution, we found that increasing STMN2 concentrations suppressed microtubule polymerization and increased catastrophe. In human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons, STMN2 depletion increased baseline rates of microtubule polymerization. However, STMN2 depletion impaired recovery of axonal microtubules following transient nocodazole-induced depolymerization, indicating that STMN2 is required for efficient cytoskeletal remodeling after stress. Consistent with these findings, STMN2-depleted neurons exhibited impaired microtubule recovery following acute depolymerization and reduced axonal recoil after optically induced local microtubule severing. Finally, STMN2 depletion disrupted the formation of neuromuscular junction-like contacts in human motor neuron-myocyte co-cultures, linking impaired cytoskeletal homeostasis to loss of distal neuronal connectivity. Together, these findings identify STMN2 as a key regulator of cytoskeletal resilience that coordinates microtubule remodeling, mitochondrial transport, and maintenance of neuromuscular junctions. We propose that impaired resilience of the axonal cytoskeleton represents a critical point of vulnerability in motor neurons in patients with ALS, establishing cytoskeletal resilience as a potential therapeutic target downstream of TDP-43 pathology.

papers.title: Structure-Based Discovery of GTP-Enhanced Rab10 Modulators and Their Effects on Alzheimer's Disease-Relevant Cellular Phenotypes.
papers.abstract: Rab10-mediated membrane trafficking has been implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but pharmacological tools for investigating its function remain limited. Here, we screened more than 80 million compounds using structure-based virtual screening and prioritized five candidate Rab10 modulators ( R1-R5 ). These compounds exhibited favorable docking scores, stable modeled protein-ligand complexes in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and predicted acceptable ADME/toxicity profiles. Comparative docking against Rab5, Rab8, and Rab11 predicted preferential interactions with GTP-associated Rab10. R1 and R2 yielded the most favorable Rab10 scores, whereas R3 showed the largest differences between GTP-associated, GDP-containing, and nucleotide-free Rab10 models. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) revealed micromolar apparent affinities of R1-R4 without added GTP and nanomolar apparent affinities under GTP-containing conditions, generally favoring GTP-bound Rab10 over Rab5. In a cell-based GTP quantification assay, R1 , R2 , R3 , and R5 reduced GTP-bound Rab10, whereas R4 increased it. R3 produced dose- and time-dependent reductions in GTP-bound Rab10 and was selected for functional studies. R3 altered endosomal organization and reduced EEA1 and LAMP1 expressions. In amyloid precursor protein (APP)/presenilin-1-expressing CHO cells, R3 redistributed intracellular APP, reduced APP carboxyl-terminal fragments (APP-CTFs), and decreased enlarged endosome-like structures. In neuronal differentiated PC12 cells, R1 - R3 attenuated NGF withdrawal-induced cytoskeletal disruption and cell death, accompanied by reduced APP-CTF accumulation and tau phosphorylation. These studies highlight novel Rab10 modulators and support their further validation as candidate pharmacological probes for investigating Rab10-associated trafficking and AD-relevant cellular phenotypes.

papers.title: Rare protein-disrupting variants in NPY5R, DLGAP1 and MAPK8IP3 segregate with OCD in two multiplex pedigrees.
papers.abstract: Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) is significantly heritable, but only a fraction of the contributory genetic variation has been identified, and the molecular etiology involved remains obscure. Identifying rare contributory variants of large effect would be an important milestone in helping to elucidate the mechanisms involved. Analysis of densely affected pedigrees is a potentially useful strategy to bypass the sample size challenges of standard case-control approaches. Here we performed whole genome sequencing (WGS) of 25 individuals across two multiplex OCD pedigrees. We prioritised rare variants using a Bayesian inference approach which incorporates variant pathogenicity and co-segregation with OCD. In the first pedigree, we identified a highly deleterious missense variant in NPY5R, carried by the majority of affected individuals. This gene is brain-expressed and has previously been implicated in panic disorder and internet addiction GWAS studies. In the second pedigree, we identified a large deletion of DLGAP1 and a missense variant in MAPK8IP3, that perfectly co-segregated in a specific branch of the family: both genes have previously been implicated in OCD and autism. Both genes contribute to a protein interaction network including ERBB4 and RAPGEF1 which we had previously identified in a large Tourette Syndrome pedigree. Our analysis suggests that both energy homeostasis and downstream signalling from the post-synaptic density may both be important avenues for future research.

papers.title: Anti-Parkinsonian Drugs Rescue Locomotor Deficits in JIP3 Knockout Zebrafish: Implications for Treating Patients with MAPK8IP3 -related Neurodevelopmental Disorders
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT MAPK8IP3- related neurodevelopmental disorders are a spectrum of rare conditions caused by de novo mutations in the MAPK8IP3 gene that encodes the JIP3 protein. These disorders are associated with a spectrum of neurodevelopmental symptoms that manifest in children and cause brain abnormalities, profound intellectual disabilities, movement disorders, and developmental delays. JIP3 is required for axonal transport of proteins and organelles between the soma and the synaptic terminal of neurons, a process critical for normal brain development and function. Homozygous loss-of-function mutations in JIP3 lead to impaired axonal transport and aggregation of cargo, which result in axonal swelling and stunted elongation. Despite these severe outcomes, disease mechanisms are poorly understood, and no current treatments are available. Here we conduct thorough morphological, behavioral, and motility phenotyping in the JIP3 knockout zebrafish and identify locomotor deficits and morphological abnormalities. To identify treatment options, we used insights from expert clinicians and the artificial intelligence tool, mediKanren, to identify drug candidates hypothesized to improve patient symptoms or compensate for the loss of JIP3 at the molecular level. We then prioritized drugs that are FDA-approved, safe for children, and readily available. These collective efforts identified amantadine and levodopa as candidate therapies and rescued motor phenotypes associated with JIP3 loss-of-function in zebrafish.

papers.title: Axon initial segment as an axonal lysosome trafficking control gate
papers.abstract: Spatial subcellular distributions of lysosomes are intricately coupled with their functional heterogeneities, yet how neurons preferentially allocate distinct subtypes of lysosomes between the soma and axons remains largely unknown. Here, we discover that the axon initial segment (AIS) may function as a lysosomal quality-control checkpoint by actively sorting lysosomes based on their functional states. Central to this checkpoint is MCF2L, a specific lysosome-associated protein enriched in AIS, that anchors clustered lysosomes at AIS via high-affinity binding to giant ankyrin-G (gAnkG, encoded by Ank3). Selective ablation of the MCF2L-gAnkG interaction accelerates disease progression in a mouse Parkinson's disease model. By clustering lysosomes, MCF2L restricts kinesin-mediated transport and regulates lysosomal positioning. In neurons, MCF2L-mediated lysosome clustering may act as a lysosomal quality-control checkpoint, by which less acidic (e.g., impaired) lysosomes are retained in AIS and functionally intact lysosomes are released for transport. Thus, AIS may impart neurons with a unique mechanism for axonal lysosome compartmentalization and quality control.

papers.title: Transcriptomic and Lipidomic Profiling of Human iPSC-Derived Microglia Reveals TREM2-Dependent and -Independent Processes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT TREM2 has been implicated in AD as a critical regulator of microglial functions and loss of function mutations in TREM2 increases one’s risk of developing AD. Given the diverse functional roles of TREM2, we sought to unravel how it affects downstream pathways using human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs) derived from TREM2 knockout (KO) and isogenic control lines and assessing the response to oligomeric amyloid-β 42 (oAβ42). While previous studies have primarily used fibrillar Aβ, we focused on microglial responses to oAβ42 given their disease relevance and potent cytotoxic effects. At baseline, we identified a set of TREM2-dependent genes, which corresponded to the DAM signature in mice and disease-associated signatures in humans. Additionally, loss of TREM2 resulted in increased expression of cholesterol biosynthesis genes. In response to oAβ42, we found that the transcriptional response was largely TREM2-independent and corresponded to a strong induction of inflammatory pathways, with TREM2 also being downregulated in control iMGLs. We identified subsets of genes and pathways that were unique to either control, such as mitochondrial DNA and RNA degradation, or TREM2 KO iMGLs, such as the senescence-associated secretory pathway and adipogenesis, suggesting some differences in gene expression driven by TREM2 in response to oAβ42. Given that the inflammatory response was TREM2-independent, we sought to identify signaling pathways that contributed to inflammation. Inhibition of toll-like receptor signaling significantly reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory genes and modestly increased expression of TREM2 and TREM2-dependent genes. Consistent with our transcriptional data, cytokine production and secretion in response to oAβ42 was significantly increased to similar levels in both controls and TREM2 KO iMGLs. Lipidomic profiling of microglia revealed that triglycerides and lactosylceramides were significantly increased in both control and TREM2 KO iMGLs in response to oAβ42. TREM2 KO iMGLs had decreased levels of BMPs and increased levels of cholesterol esters across all conditions, further highlighting a role for TREM2 in maintaining lipid homeostasis in microglia. Taken together, we describe genes, pathways, and lipids that are associated with TREM2 expression that likely influence microglial responses to oAβ42.

Increased excitatory neuronal contacts with pre-myelinating OLLCs accompanied ultrastructural myelin abnormalities in trisomic assembloids. papers.title: Autophagy activator AA-20 engages CDK5 to promote lipophagy and improve neurodegeneration-associated phenotypes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Lipophagy, the selective degradation of lipid droplets (LDs) by autophagy, has the potential to ameliorate neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s (PD) and Alzheimer’s (AD), wherein LD accumulation has been linked to the exacerbation of the proteinopathy component of neurodegeneration. Pharmacological lipophagy inducers remain scarce. We previously identified AA-20 as a novel autophagy activator that acts independently of mTORC1 inhibition, thereby providing a means of stimulating autophagy while avoiding the immunosuppressive side effects associated with direct mTORC1 inhibition. Prior work also showed that AA-20 treatment reduces PolyQ aggregate levels in several C. elegans tissues. Here, we demonstrate that AA-20 enhances LD recruitment to autophagosomes and promotes LD degradation via lysosomal acid lipase activation in murine hippocampal neuronal cells, consistent with lipophagy activation. In human Swedish Amyloid Precursor Protein mutated cerebral organoids, two weeks of AA-20 treatment normalized aberrant lipidomic profiles by selectively reducing various disease-associated lipids, while also correcting the AD-associated electrical hyperexcitability phenotype. Moreover, we identified cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5), a neuronal kinase linked to AD hyperexcitability and PD pathology, as a target of AA-20. AA-20-induced autophagy and lipid clearance in HT22 cells require CDK5. In a neuronal seeding model of α-synuclein pathology, AA-20 reduced pS129-α-synuclein levels. Collectively, these findings indicate AA-20 can promote lipophagic clearance of LDs and mitigate multiple cellular phenotypes associated with lipidopathy and proteinopathy in neurodegenerative disease models. SIGNIFICANCE Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s are associated with impaired autophagy and abnormal lipid droplet (LD) accumulation. Few small molecules enhance neuronal lipid clearance without inhibiting mTORC1, but chronic blockade of which is associated with immunosuppressive and metabolic side effects. This study shows that AA-20, an mTORC1-independent autophagy activator, promotes lipophagic LD clearance in neuronal cells and reduces selected disease-associated lipids in human Alzheimer’s cerebral organoids in a lysosomal acid lipase-dependent manner. AA-20 binds CDK5 and appears to modulate, rather than classically inhibit, this neuron-enriched kinase. In an exploratory Parkinson’s neuron model, AA-20 also reduced pathological α-synuclein phosphorylation. These findings support further investigation of AA-20 as a tool to probe neuronal lipid clearance and neurodegeneration-associated phenotypes.

papers.title: Cell-Corr: Fast and coding-free quantification of intracellular dynamics in confocal microscopy time series
papers.abstract: Abstract The dynamic organization of intracellular components, including cytoskeleton and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is essential for cell architecture, intracellular trafficking and organelle positioning. Overall temporal dynamics of these components can be analyzed in appropriate time series by virtue of progressive exponential decay of Pearson’s correlation coefficient. However, quantifying these dynamics from live-cell fluorescence microscopy time-series, remains challenging, particularly when analysis requires multiple software or programming expertise. Here, Cell-Corr, a standalone, coding-free software for rapid and reproducible quantification of intracellular dynamics is introduced. Cell-Corr integrates image processing, calculation of Pearson’s coefficient, statistical analysis, curve fitting and graphical visualization into a streamlined workflow. The software was evaluated using time series of fluorescently labelled actin filaments and ER, under various conditions including the chemical inhibition of actin nucleation and/or bundling with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 or the formin inhibitor SMIFH2. Comparison with existing analysis tools demonstrated improved processing efficiency and simplified data handling. By integrating established correlation-based approach into an accessible platform, Cell-Corr provides a fast, user-friendly solution for quantitative analysis of intracellular dynamics in live-cell fluorescence microscopy.

papers.title: Maternal Micronutrient Deficiency, DNA Methylation, and Fetal Neurodevelopment in Low-Resource Settings: A Secondary Analysis of Growth-Associated EWAS Signatures
papers.abstract: Maternal undernutrition is common in urban slums and other low-resource settings, where both low birthweight and childhood stunting have been associated with poorer brain development. One proposed explanation is epigenetic: a shortage of folate and related nutrients lowers the methyl-group supply during the period when the fetal brain is being programmed, altering DNA methylation. This is hard to test directly, because no epigenome-wide association study (EWAS) has yet measured neurodevelopmental outcomes in these populations. We therefore re-annotated published methylation signals for two nutrition-sensitive growth phenotypes: neonatal birthweight from the PACE consortium meta-analysis (914 CpG sites, 729 genes) and child height at the SOCS3 gene in low- and middle-income cohorts. The birthweight genes were sorted into functional categories, compared with three studies of methylation in undernourished children, and annotated against fetal-brain and placental chromatin states and fetal-brain expression. We found no enrichment for one-carbon metabolism; DNMT3A was the only related gene present, and the core folate-cycle enzymes were absent. Neurodevelopmental and synaptic genes made up a sizeable fraction of the signature (92 genes, 12.6%), but this reflects the composition of the gene set rather than a tested over-representation, and the fetal-brain enhancer enrichment we observed applied to the whole birthweight signal, not to these genes in particular, and was not specific to fetal brain. The most consistent finding was SOCS3, a nutrition-responsive locus that recurred across independent undernutrition datasets, altered its expression with methylation in vitro, and is expressed in the prenatal brain. Overall, the data support a nutrition-sensitive methylation signature at growth and immune loci that overlaps enhancers in fetal brain as in other tissues, with SOCS3 as a candidate link to neurodevelopment. The one-carbon-to-neurodevelopment pathway remains plausible but hypothesis-generating, and testing it will need formal enrichment analysis and primary methylation studies where undernutrition is most common.

papers.title: Autism-Related Language Preferences of Turkish-Speaking Autistic Adults
papers.abstract: Autism-related terminology is contested, and preferences vary across linguistic and cultural contexts. However, evidence from Turkish-speaking autistic communities is currently limited. This mixed-methods study examined terminology preferences among 127 native Turkish-speaking autistic participants aged 15–66 years. Participants selected all terms they felt comfortable using across seven categories of autism-related language. Eighty-one participants also provided open-ended responses, which were analysed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Participants most frequently endorsed otizm (“autism”; 79.30%) as the nomenclature of autism and nörolojik/beyin farklılığı (“neurological/brain difference”; 77.49%) as a broader conceptualisation. Farklılıklar (“differences”) was the most frequently endorsed term for both autism-related difficulties (82.45%) and strengths (71.19%). No single expression for an autistic person was endorsed by majority: otistik (“autistic”; 49.33%), nöroçeşitli kişi (“neurodivergent person”; 47.40%), and otizmli (“[person] with autism”; 45.48%) received similar support. Individual-difference measures showed few consistent associations with terminology endorsement after correction for multiple comparisons. Six qualitative themes concerned autonomy, social impact, identity, accuracy, context, and respect. Turkish-speaking autistic adults generally favoured direct and non-deficit-oriented language while emphasising individual choice. Researchers and professionals should therefore ask about personal preferences whenever possible and avoid imposing a single terminology on the wider community.

papers.title: Temperature-dependent Fano resonance in Microtubules and Tubulin investigated with Spontaneous Raman Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Microtubules are self-assembled biological hollow nanotubes composed by protein tubulin. They are essential for many biological functions, including cell motility, cell division, and act as intracellular track for organelle transport. In turn, through dynamic assembly and disassembly, they form spindle fibers for chromosome segregation during mitosis and meiosis. In this paper, we have measured the Raman spectra of microtubules and their constituent protein tubulin in dry powder form for a range of temperatures, from nitrogen liquid T =77 K up to room and physiological temperature T =310 K, to determine if molecular bond vibrations present potential Fano resonance asymmetry. We have found nontrivial persistence of Fano resonances, q <5, at room and physiological temperatures for some specific vibrational modes.

papers.title: TMEM55B promotes anterograde transport and distal axonal distribution of LAMP1-positive organelles
papers.abstract: Lysosomal function throughout life is vital for the proper functioning and survival of post-mitotic neurons by mediating cellular signaling, degradation, and recycling processes. Their intracellular transport relies on microtubule-dependent mechanisms involving kinesin and dynein motors. While lysosomes were long thought absent from axons, recent studies have demonstrated the importance of LAMP1-positive endo-/lysosomal organelles in axonal compartments. This study investigates the physiological role of TMEM55B, a lysosomal membrane protein involved in lysosome positioning and motor coupling in neurons. TMEM55B is highly expressed in LAMP1-positive organelles in cortical neurons. We generated viable Tmem55b knockout mice that exhibited altered lysosomal positioning in neurons. Lysosomes clustered abnormally in the pre-axonal exclusion zone and the proximal axon, with many forming elongated tubular structures. Similarly, in primary rat neurons, TMEM55B depletion resulted in lysosomal tubulation and impaired bidirectional lysosomal transport, particularly in distal axon segments, without affecting lysosome velocity in the proximal and mid-axon. These transport defects were consistent with disrupted JIP4 function, a scaffold linking TMEM55B to both dynein and kinesin motors. TMEM55B deficiency did not result in neurodegeneration, behavioral deficits, or reduced lifespan in mice. As an orthogonal approach, we analyzed TMEM55B function in C. elegans . Worms lacking the TMEM55B homolog Y71H2AM.2 showed altered lysosomal dynamics in cholinergic neurons, supporting an evolutionarily conserved role. To test the involvement of TMEM55B’s paralog, TMEM55A, in regulating neuronal lysosome positioning, we generated Tmem55a/b double-knockout mice, which exhibit impaired growth, premature death, and an overall aggravated phenotype. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that both TMEM55B and TMEM55A regulate lysosome distribution in neurons, particularly in axons, by influencing JIP4-dependent retro- and, notably, anterograde motor protein-mediated transport. This function is critical for spatial lysosomal homeostasis. Our study underscores the importance of TMEM55A/TMEM55B in regulating neuronal organelle dynamics and may be a factor considered in neurodegenerative diseases involving lysosomal trafficking defects.

papers.title: Rab10 and Arhgef7 interact to promote axon extension by linking vesicle supply and exocytosis
papers.abstract: The formation of functional neural circuits begins with the extension of a single axon by immature neurons. Axon elongation requires an expansion of the plasma membrane that depends on the polarization of vesicle trafficking and exocytosis. It is not completely understood how the increased transport of vesicles into the growing axon is linked to their subsequent insertion into the plasma membrane. An analysis of early stages of neuronal differentiation indicates that an asymmetry in neurite length precedes axon specification and the accumulation of PPVs in the nascent axon. We show that increasing the transport of vesicles in unpolarized neurons is sufficient to promote the extension of additional axons. This effect indicates that an increased supply of vesicles stimulates their subsequent insertion into the membrane to allow neurite growth. The link between vesicle transport and exocytosis is mediated by the interaction of Rab10 with Arhgef7. Rab10 stimulates Arhgef7 activity on PPVs as a GEF for Cdc42b to promote axon extension through exocyst-dependent exocytosis, suggesting that their interaction links the increased supply of PPVs to their exocytosis.

papers.title: High-content imaging of live microglia-containing Alzheimer's disease brain organoids.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common progressive neurodegenerative disease for which there is currently no safe and effective treatment. AD is characterized by the pathological aggregation of amyloid-β (Aβ) in the brain resulting in neuronal dysfunction/death and cognitive decline. Modeling these processes in vitro remains challenging due to the lack of an immune-competent 3D in vitro human model of AD amenable to high-throughput analyses. Conventional cerebral organoids (COs) lack microglia and are optically dense which precludes real-time longitudinal analyses. Here, we employ the fluorescent amyloid probe PyrPeg to selectively monitor Aβ aggregation, and calcein AM and propidium iodide to assess cellular viability within microglia-containing COs (MCOs). We identify age-dependent DS-AD-associated phenotypes within T21 MCOs including Aβ neuropathology, neurodegeneration, and glial cell dysregulation. Our platform supports real-time, multiplexed tracking of disease progression and provides a scalable platform for longitudinal analyses studying disease mechanisms and targeted approaches to treatment. MOTIVATION: High-throughput in vitro drug screening using cerebral organoids (COs) has great potential to accelerate drug discovery efforts for treating Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative diseases. However, live fluorescence imaging of COs has proved challenging due to their dense, optically opaque tissue. Furthermore, conventional COs lack microglia which are key immunomodulators of pathogenesis in the AD brain. To address these limitations, we developed and optimized a live organoid imaging approach employing the fluorescent amyloid-binding probe PyrPeg to label amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregates within human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived microglia-containing COs (MCOs). We achieved selective labeling and visualization of Aβ neuropathology in intact live MCOs and observed increased age-associated Aβ accumulation in MCOs derived from donors with trisomy 21 (T21) relative to disomy 21 (D21), consistent with the Down syndrome-associated AD (DS-AD) phenotype in the human brain. This method establishes a platform for high-throughput longitudinal drug screening in immunocompetent human COs that will enable the identification of new therapeutic candidates to modulate Aβ aggregation, glial reactivity, and neurodegeneration. HIGHLIGHTS: A platform was developed for high-resolution in vitro visualization of insoluble Aβ aggregates in live MCOs. The approach enables deep tissue imaging of Aβ pathology in intact 3D MCOs, allowing spatial mapping of Aβ aggregate distribution over time.Differences in Aβ burden and viability of neurons, neural progenitors, and astrocytes were quantified, distinguishing T21 COs from D21 control MCOs.The platform is positioned to support high-throughput longitudinal drug screening, providing a scalable tool to identify novel therapeutics targeting Aβ-mediated neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Glial involvement in mitochondrial metabolic alterations in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Metabolic alterations in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) emerge early in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but their molecular and cellular basis remains unclear. We hypothesized that impaired glial energy metabolism, particularly mitochondrial oxidative metabolism in astrocytes, underlies the metabolic vulnerability of the PCC in AD. To test this hypothesis, we integrated human PCC proteomics and transcriptomics with magnetic resonance spectroscopy in App NL-G-F knock-in (APP-KI) mice. Human proteomic and transcriptomic analyses converged on reduced mitochondrial oxidative-metabolism signatures associated with AD pathology and cognition. APP-KI hippocampus showed proteomic and 1 H-MRS alterations resembling those in the human AD PCC. Spatial transcriptomics identified widespread metabolic transcriptional changes and reduced mitochondrial pathway signatures in glia-enriched hippocampal clusters. Hyperpolarized [1- 13 C]pyruvate spectroscopy showed reduced bicarbonate labelling in APP-KI mice, consistent with impaired oxidative pyruvate metabolism. These findings reveal convergent mitochondrial alterations in human AD and APP-KI mice, implicating glial cells, particularly astrocytes, in the associated dysfunction.

papers.title: Scalable, unsupervised, and annotation-free discovery of cell–cell communication modules across 2D and 3D spatial omics with STARComm
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Spatial transcriptomics enables cell–cell communication to be studied within intact tissue, but most spatially aware methods score individual ligand–receptor pairs, depend on prior cell-type annotation, scale poorly to large datasets, or do not support three-dimensional data. Methods that identify higher-order communication programs directly from spatial coordinates are lacking. Results We present STARComm, an unsupervised, annotation-free method that detects cell-level ligand–receptor proximity events, converts them into kernel density profiles, and clusters co-localized profiles into multicellular communication interaction modules (MCIMs). In simulations with known ground truth, STARComm recovered modules more accurately than COMMOT, SpatialDM, and an expression-only baseline, particularly under sparse and low-signal conditions (adjusted Rand index 0.70 versus 0.20, 0.01, and 0.01 at 10% communication density), and its modules were more spatially coherent. In tissue benchmarks, STARComm produced more spatially coherent modules than COMMOT and SpatialDM (Moran’s I 0.91 versus 0.19 and 0.13 in a uterine cancer region) while reducing runtime from hours to minutes. We then demonstrated generalizability across platforms, scales, and dimensions: a 35-tissue Xenium cohort of chronic graft-versus-host disease salivary glands, a 16-region MERSCOPE pan-cancer dataset of more than 14.5 million cells, more than 2.5 million Visium HD bins, and a 362,704-cell three-dimensional mouse-brain volume with paired Deep-STARmap transcriptomic and Deep-RIBOmap translatomic layers, in which virtual two-dimensional sections retained approximately 7% of the communication events detected in three dimensions. Conclusions STARComm is a scalable method for identifying higher-order spatial communication programs in two- and three-dimensional spatial omics data. It is designed for communication-module discovery rather than for every cell–cell communication task, and the modules it identifies provide hypotheses for downstream biological and therapeutic validation.

papers.title: Targeting STAU1 ameliorates disease phenotypes in TDP-43 ALS mice
papers.abstract: Abstract Altered RNA metabolism and impaired proteostasis are central to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). STAU1 is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein that regulates mRNA decay and trafficking, interacts with ATXN2, and is overabundant in neurodegenerative disease models. STAU1 overabundance activates mTOR signaling, impairs autophagy and stress-granule turnover, and thereby participates in a feed-forward circuit that further elevates STAU1 abundance. Here, we tested whether genetic and antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-mediated STAU1 lowering can interrupt this circuit in TDP-43-associated disease. Stau1 haploinsufficiency in Prp -TDP-43 Q331K mice improved motor performance and open-field measures, reduced TDP-43 and gliosis, normalized neuronal, apoptotic, and autophagy markers, restored TDP-43-dependent splicing, and attenuated transcriptomic abnormalities. Screening 2′- O -methoxyethyl (MOE) gapmer ASOs identified ASO-45, which lowered STAU1 in patient-derived fibroblasts and mouse CNS. Intracerebroventricular ASO-45 improved spinal-cord and motor-cortex phenotypes, restored splicing, and attenuated cortical transcriptomic abnormalities. In independent Thy1 -TDP-43 models, ASO-45 improved molecular markers and extended survival by 9.5–15.7%. These findings show that STAU1 lowering can disrupt a self-amplifying mTOR–autophagy–stress-granule axis and nominate STAU1-directed ASOs as a disease-modifying strategy for ALS/FTD.

papers.title: An isogenic human stem cell model reveals NGLY1-dependent control of microglial development
papers.abstract: NGLY1 is a cytosolic N-glycanase involved in glycoprotein quality control and proteasome-mediated protein degradation and is critical for normal brain development and function. Although neuronal alterations caused by NGLY1 deficiency have been extensively characterized in animal and human cell models, how NGLY1 deficiency affects human glial cells, particularly microglia, the brain-resident innate immune cells, remains largely unknown. Using patient-derived NGLY1-deficient human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines and their corresponding CRISPR-mediated gene-corrected isogenic lines, we found that NGLY1-deficient primitive macrophage progenitors (PMPs) exhibited increased GlcNAc-Asn (GNA) accumulation and elevated expression of RUNX1, a key transcription factor regulating myeloid lineage development, accompanied by abnormal proliferation. Following further differentiation, NGLY1-deficient human microglia exhibited reduced morphological complexity and impaired phagocytic capacity. In addition, NGLY1-deficient microglia showed increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1β, IL-6, and TNFα, under both basal and stimulated conditions, indicative of a heightened inflammatory state. Mechanistically, our data showed that RUNX1 upregulation induced by NGLY1 deficiency partially mediated impaired PMP proliferation and subsequent microglial abnormalities, implicating RUNX1 dysregulation in NGLY1-associated microglial dysfunction and identifying RUNX1 as a potential therapeutic target. Together, using patient-derived and gene-corrected isogenic hiPSCs, our study establishes a human stem cell platform for modeling NGLY1 deficiency and reveals that impaired deglycosylation alters human microglial developmental trajectories and ultimately compromises microglial homeostasis and function. These microglial abnormalities may contribute to the neurological deficits observed in patients carrying loss-of-function variants in NGLY1.

papers.title: Investigating the causal and consequential role of the nuclear encoded mitochondrial genome in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but which mitochondrial pathways are involved, and whether their involvement is a cause or a consequence of disease remains unclear. We investigated whether nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene (NEMG) pathways are enriched for ALS genetic risk, which are dysregulated in ALS tissue, whether pathway activity defines patient subgroups that differ in survival, and whether co-expression between the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes is altered. We tested MitoCarta3.0 pathways for enrichment of ALS genetic risk using MAGMA and the largest European ALS GWAS to date (27,205 cases and 110,881 controls), using hierarchical testing across pathway tiers, and annotated the direction of gene-level effects using published TWAS and SMR results. In >1,500 bulk RNA-seq samples from post-mortem motor cortex and spinal cord (KCL Brain Bank, NYGC ALS Consortium) and iPSC-derived motor neurones (Answer ALS), we performed cell type adjusted gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), gene set variation analysis (GSVA)-based clustering with exploratory survival analysis, and nuclear-mitochondrial co-expression analysis. Of seven broad mitochondrial categories, only the mitochondrial central dogma was enriched for ALS risk after correction (P adj = 0.044). Hierarchical testing within this pathway localised the signal to translation (P adj = 0.008) and the mitoribosome (P adj = 0.014). Genetically predicted expression pointed in opposite directions for different mitoribosomal genes (lower MRPS33 and higher MRPL28 expression with increased risk), and did not agree in direction with differential expression in ALS tissue more often than expected by chance. A nominal enrichment in ROS and glutathione metabolism was largely attributable to SOD1 . In tissue, mitochondrial genes were broadly more highly expressed in ALS motor cortex in both cohorts, largely as a global shift across mitochondrial genes. OXPHOS subunits and the mitoribosome were enriched beyond this shift in ALS Consortium motor cortex (both P FDR = 0.027), as were OXPHOS subunits in iPSC-derived motor neurones (P FDR = 2.4 x 10⁻⁸), whereas spinal cord showed no genome-wide enrichment. GSVA based clusters were associated with diagnosis in motor cortex, and nominally with survival in lumbar spinal cord (adjusted HR 0.69, P unadj = 0.013), where cluster structure was weakest. No individual pathway was associated with survival after correction in adjusted models. In all four post-mortem tissues, nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes were more negatively co-expressed with mtDNA-encoded genes in ALS than in controls, most strongly in lumbar spinal cord, whereas iPSC-derived motor neurones showed the opposite pattern. In conclusion, inherited ALS risk shows a modest enrichment centred on mitochondrial translation, with gene specific rather than uniform directions of effect. The same pathway, alongside OXPHOS, is more highly expressed in end-stage ALS motor cortex, which may reflect a response to disease, residual differences in cell composition, or both. At the gene level, genetically predicted and observed expression changes did not agree in direction, so whether inherited risk and these tissue changes are linked remains unresolved.

papers.title: COG5-mediated Golgi organization coordinates neural progenitor fate during human brain development
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Apical radial glial cells (aRGs) are highly polarized epithelial cells that drive human cortical development through tightly regulated lineage progression. A distinctive feature of aRGs is their non-canonical Golgi organization, raising the possibility that specialized intracellular trafficking and secretory processes contribute to progenitor behaviour. However, how Golgi architecture contributes to human corticogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate this question in the context of COG5 deficiency, a rare congenital disorder of glycosylation associated with neurodevelopmental defects, using patient-derived fibroblasts and brain organoids, N-glycomics, glycolipidomics, and single-cell transcriptomics. We show that COG5 deficiency disrupts Golgi organization and impairs Golgi-to-ER retrograde trafficking. At the neurodevelopmental level, COG5-deficient organoids display altered ventricular organization and reduced basal progenitor abundance. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals rewired developmental trajectories characterized by premature differentiation from apical progenitors with activation of neuronal pathways. Despite the absence of major abnormalities in plasma glycoproteins glycosylation, glycolipidomic analysis identified marked defects in glycosphingolipid maturation within patient-derived brain organoids, indicating selective impairment of neural lipid glycosylation. Transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of developmental pathways, including reduced Notch signalling and altered localization of both cleaved Notch1 and the Golgi-associated protein ACBD3. Consistent with impaired progenitor maintenance, COG5-deficient organoids displayed altered cleavage plane orientation in apical progenitors. Together, our findings suggest a link between Golgi organization, intracellular trafficking, membrane glycosylation, and lineage progression in human neural progenitors, identifying Golgi architecture as an important regulator of apical radial glial cell biology and cortical development.

papers.title: JIP4 deficiency causes a lysosomal storage disease arising from impaired cystine efflux.
papers.abstract: Lysosomes break down macromolecules, clear cellular waste and recycle nutrients such as cystine. We describe a novel mechanism whereby JIP4 regulates lysosomal cystine storage by controlling the abundance of cystinosin (CTNS), the transporter responsible for lysosomal cystine efflux. To this end, JIP4, previously characterized as a motor adaptor and kinase signaling scaffold, suppresses TMEM55B-dependent ubiquitylation of CTNS. Loss of JIP4 reduces CTNS protein levels, leading to lysosomal cystine accumulation and lysosomal storage defects that phenocopy loss of CTNS in both human cells and the renal proximal tubules of JIP4 knockout mice. These phenotypes mirror cystinosis, the lysosomal storage disease caused by CTNS loss-of-function. Our findings thus reveal a fundamental process that controls the efflux of lysosomal cystine and has relevance to understanding human disease arising from JIP4 mutations.

papers.title: Lipidomic Profiling of L1CAM+ Extracellular Vesicles in Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) lacks minimally invasive biomarkers that reflect neuron-derived molecular alterations. Here, we performed a pilot study for untargeted Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS)-based lipidomics on serum total extracellular vesicles (tEVs) and L1CAM-enriched EVs (L1CAM+EVs) in patients with PD and healthy controls (n=10 per group; N=40). Partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) separated PD from control samples in both fractions L1CAM+EVs: R2Y = 0.998, Q2 = 0.879; tEVs: R2Y = 0.998, Q2 = 0.876), and distinguished L1CAM+EVs from tEVs within PD samples (R2Y = 0.999, Q2 = 0.925). In PD tEVs, triacylglycerols, fatty acids, phosphatidylcholines, sphingomyelins and phosphatidylserines were increased, and pathway analysis indicated enhanced conversion of phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) to phosphatidylserine (PS). In contrast, PD L1CAM+EVs showed increased DG, LPA and PS with reduced LPC; pathway reconstruction indicated enhanced PE-PC-DG and LPC-PC flux with reduced de novo PC and SM synthesis. Within PD, L1CAM+EVs were depleted of multiple sphingomyelin species (e.g., SM 41:2;O3, SM 35:2;O3, SM 41:3;O3) and glycerophospholipids relative to tEVs, whereas SPB 18:0;O2 and FA 16:4 were relatively enriched. These findings indicate that L1CAM-enriched EVs carry a PD-associated lipid signature that is qualitatively distinct from that of controls, supporting their evaluation as a complementary source of neuron-related lipid biomarkers.

papers.title: AAV-Mediated Astrogliosis Recapitulates Early Neuroinflammatory and Bioenergetic Features of Alzheimer″s Disease in Mice
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation and altered neuron-astrocyte metabolic interactions are increasingly recognized as early features of Alzheimer′s disease (AD). However, the underlying metabolic adaptations remain incompletely understood. This study employed deuterium magnetic resonance spectroscopy (DMRS) following administration of deuterium labeled glucose and acetate to investigate neuronal and astroglial substrate utilization and metabolic fluxes, respectively, in adenovirus-induced neuroinflammation and early-stage APP NL–F/NL–F mice. In adenovirus-induced astrogliosis, increased acetate derived [4,4′– 2 H 2 ]Glx (d 2 -Glx) production suggested enhanced astrocytic acetate utilization and TCA cycle activity. Conversely, reduced glucose derived d 2 –Glx despite comparable glucose uptake suggested a diminished neuronal activity due to potentially impaired neuronal oxidative metabolism. However, the glucose-derived lactate labeling remained unchanged, suggesting differential effects on oxidative and non-oxidative pathways of glucose metabolism. Similarly, 3-month-old APP NL–F/NL–F mice exhibited significantly increased [2,2′,2″- 2 H 3 ]acetate (d 3 -Ace) influx compared with wild-type controls, suggesting early alterations in astrocytic substrate utilization. While glucose uptake remained unchanged, glucose derived Glx and lactate showed modest, non-significant decreases, potentially reflecting early alterations in glucose metabolism. Overall, both models exhibited a metabolic pattern characterized by increased astrocytic acetate utilization with trends towards reduced glucose associated metabolism, with more pronounced changes in adenovirus-induced astrogliosis. These findings highlight the utility of DMRS for investigating dynamic metabolic adaptations during neuroinflammation and early AD pathogenesis. Importantly, the adenovirus-induced astrogliosis model recapitulates key metabolic alterations associated with the neuroinflammatory aspects of AD. As such, it provides a valuable complementary platform for investigating mechanisms driving early metabolic dysfunction and evaluating therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring neuron–astrocyte metabolic interactions prior to the onset of substantial neurodegeneration.

papers.title: N-terminal mutations R5L and R5H share a common mechanism in disrupting tau condensates on microtubule surfaces
papers.abstract: Tau, an intrinsically disordered protein abundant in neuronal axons, forms cooperative condensates on microtubule (MT) surfaces that regulate motor proteins and protect MTs from severing enzymes. Disease-associated mutations at residue 5 in the N-terminal projection domain of tau, far from the MT-tau binding interface, have been linked to progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) (R5L) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (R5H). While R5L was previously shown to disrupt tau condensate formation on MT surfaces, it remained unclear whether R5H shares this phenotype. Using total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, we show that both mutations reduce condensate packing density compared to WT tau under sub-saturating conditions at physiological pH (7.4), indicating impaired tau–tau cooperativity despite their distal location from the MT–tau binding interface. Single-molecule measurements further show both the dwell time and landing rate of tau within condensates are reduced while behavior on bare MTs remains unchanged, implicating weakened tau-tau cooperativity rather than disrupted binding to MTs. Strikingly, mutational analysis identifies the positive charge at residue 5 as critical for tau condensate formation: the charge-preserving R5K substitution retains WT-like behavior, whereas the charge-eliminating R5I substitution behaves like R5H/R5L. Further supporting this mechanism, R5H exhibits a pronounced pH dependence, transitioning from WT-like behavior at pH 6.4 to R5L-like behavior at pH 7.4 upon histidine deprotonation. Together, these findings establish that the positive charge at R5 is critical for tau condensate formation on MT surfaces and identify a common mechanism linking PSP and FTD. SIGNIFICANCE Tau, a protein that stabilizes microtubules in neurons, is central to Alzheimer’s disease and related neurodegenerative disorders. Many disease-associated tau mutations lie in its microtubule-binding region, but how mutations outside this region cause dysfunction remains unclear. We show that two such mutations, R5L (linked to progressive supranuclear palsy) and R5H (linked to frontotemporal dementia), weaken tau–tau interactions, so fewer tau molecules assemble together on microtubules, even though each molecule still binds microtubules with similar affinity. Restoring a positive charge at residue 5, either with another positively charged residue or by protonating R5H at lower pH, rescues assembly. These findings unite two mutations with distinct clinical presentations under a common molecular phenotype on microtubule surfaces.

papers.title: Deleterious coding variation in SFARI-associated genes among Indian individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorders: an exploratory exome-sequencing study
papers.abstract: Abstract Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder with impairment in social interaction, communication and restrictive, repetitive behaviours and interests. Considering limited genetic research on ASD in India, we are uncertain of whether its architecture is similar or dissimilar to what is observed globally. Therefore, utilizing SFARI- a well-curated database of ASD-associated genes, we investigated their mutation burden among Indian ASD subjects and studied the impact of variant stratification across populations. For this purpose, Whole Exome Sequencing and analysis was performed for 25 Indian ASD subjects. The findings revealed that only 15% of SFARI genes carried 241 common and rare deleterious variations in our ASD cohort. The most frequent variants were Protein Truncating Variants (PTVs) (69.7%). SFARI score-1 genes had more missense variants than PTVs, hinting at their evolutionarily conserved nature. Seven PTVs in genes, SON , KMT2C , EXOC6B, RBFOX1, CAPN12 and KIZ were found to be altered in multiple ASD individuals. papers.title: STING activation drives pericentrosomal positioning of acidic organelles via the VAIL-LRRK2-Rab35 pathway
papers.abstract: The cGAS-STING pathway is an innate immune system that responds to cytoplasmic double-stranded DNA, but recent studies have highlighted its noncanonical role in facilitating lysosomal stress responses. Specifically, STING activation has been shown to trigger V-ATPase-ATG16L1-induced LC3 lipidation (VAIL) and to activate LRRK2, a Parkinson disease-associated kinase, but the detailed molecular mechanism and the physiological roles of the activation have remained unclear. Here, we found that STING activation in microglia induces the translocation of LRRK2 to the pericentrosomal area, where lysosomes and recycling endosomes (REs) concentrate. This process was VAIL-dependent, and LRRK2 was found to be localized to the organelles. The translocation of LRRK2 required intact microtubule structures and was mediated by LRRK2 kinase activity, its substrate Rab35 and the motor adaptor proteins including JIP4. All these proteins were concentrated at the pericentrosomal area upon STING stimulation. The hyperactivating G2019S mutation of LRRK2 promoted the pericentrosomal translocation of these proteins. Overall, we propose a novel STING-induced noncanonical pathway that involves LRRK2 to facilitate pericentrosomal organelle positioning.

papers.title: A homozygous start-codon variant in PEX10 presenting as West syndrome: a case report
papers.abstract: Abstract Background PEX10-related peroxisome biogenesis disorder type 6 (PBD6) belongs to the Zellweger spectrum disorders (ZSDs), a group of rare autosomal recessive diseases caused by defective peroxisome biogenesis. PEX10-related cases presenting initially with infantile spasms (West syndrome) are extremely rare, and the genotype–phenotype relationship of start-codon variants has not been systematically characterized. Case presentation: We report a Chinese female infant with onset at 3 months of age of recurrent clusters of epileptic spasms, occurring more than 20 times per day, accompanied by delayed motor and cognitive development. Video-EEG showed atypical hypsarrhythmia, and epileptic spasms were recorded; West syndrome was diagnosed. Brain MRI showed diffuse bilateral T2-weighted hyperintensity of the cerebral white matter, ventricular enlargement, and a thin corpus callosum. After treatment with ACTH pulse therapy, topiramate, and clobazam, seizures decreased, but intermittent spasms persisted up to the last follow-up at 1 year of age. During follow-up, the patient developed global developmental delay, recurrent severe pneumonia (requiring non-invasive ventilation for respiratory failure), persistent liver dysfunction (peak ALT 453 U/L, peak AST 522 U/L), and hyperammonemia (peak 80 µmol/L). Tandem mass spectrometry and urine organic acid analysis showed no clearly specific abnormalities. Trio whole-exome sequencing (trio-WES) identified a homozygous start-codon variant in PEX10, NM_002617.4:c.3G > A (p.Met1?), with both parents being heterozygous carriers. The variant abolishes the normal translation initiation site; its pathogenic mechanism and its effect on protein function remain to be verified by functional studies. Conclusions This case expands the neurological phenotypic spectrum of PEX10-related disease and suggests that West syndrome may be an early manifestation of PEX10 start-codon variants. In infants with unexplained infantile spasms and developmental delay, genetic testing and screening for peroxisomal disorders should be considered even when routine metabolic screening is normal. The pathogenic mechanism of this variant requires functional validation.

papers.title: AKAP-CaN-NFATc3 signaling drives persistent inhibitory long-term potentiation
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT GABAergic inhibitory synaptic plasticity has critical roles in neuronal function, synaptic plasticity, and cognition. Activity-dependent alterations in gene expression are essential for generating long-term changes in inhibitory postsynaptic strength, yet the signaling mechanisms that drive inhibitory postsynaptic plasticity are not well understood. During an important form of inhibitory long-term potentiation (iLTP), NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activity promotes de novo synthesis of GABA A receptors (GABA A Rs) and the inhibitory scaffold, gephyrin, leading to persistent strengthening of inhibition. However, it remains unclear what activity-dependent signaling mechanisms control these changes in gene expression to maintain iLTP. In this study, we identify that activation of the transcription factor, nuclear-factor of activated T-cells (NFAT), and anchoring of the phosphatase, calcineurin (CaN), to A-kinase anchoring protein (AKAP79/150) are crucial in regulating long-term structural and functional GABAergic postsynaptic plasticity. Using short hairpin RNA (shRNA) to knock-down hippocampal NFAT isoform, NFATc3, we demonstrate its requirement for the synthesis of new inhibitory synaptic proteins, inhibitory synapse growth, and strengthening of synaptic currents during persistent iLTP. Additionally, using a knock-in mouse line containing a mutation in the CaN binding region of AKAP, we find that AKAP-CaN signaling lies upstream of NFATc3 activation and is required for increased inhibitory synapse clustering and synapse strengthening during iLTP via regulation of miRNA transcriptional activity and protein synthesis. Thus, we have identified an excitation-transcription coupling pathway that rapidly controls the synthesis of new inhibitory synaptic proteins and maintains persistent inhibitory synaptic plasticity, an essential process for memory formation and cognition in the brain.

papers.title: Brain and kidney Extracellular Vesicle Morphology and Complementary Brain proteomics after Inflammatory Challenge
papers.abstract: Shape, size variation, and protein composition describe different properties of tissue extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations. We compared brain and kidney EV shape and size using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). We also assessed repeated protein detection and reanalyzed a deposited brain proteomics cohort, with attribution to its original source. The study used intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and an intravenous miRNA-associated EV formulation. Each group contained three biological samples, as labelled in the source data. Source morphometry summaries included 385 brain and 101 kidney profiles. Kidney circularity was 0.9225, 0.8977, and 0.9288 in the control, LPS, and treatment groups, respectively. The corresponding values for diameter quartile dispersion, a measure of size variation, were 0.2603, 0.5334, and 0.6018. Thus, near-control outline shape coexisted with persistent size variation. None of the six primary morphology tests remained significant after Holm correction. Independent recalculation confirmed 1,527 eligible rat protein accessions across individual searches. The complete quantitative matrix contained 953 features. The main peptide filter combined unique and razor peptides. A stricter analysis retained 916 features. PTGFRN and LAMB2 remained the only significant treatment-versus-LPS findings. In the main analysis, PTGFRN increased 14.71-fold (q = 0.0365), and LAMB2 increased 6.23-fold (q = 0.00585). Their LPS levels were already close to control values. Exploratory normalization used the geometric mean of four measured EV-associated markers. The resulting treatment-versus-LPS increases were 16.43-fold and 6.96-fold, respectively. These ratios support selective changes in relative protein representation within the recovered mixture. They do not establish protein copies per EV. Analysis of the full protein profile and calibration of the complete selection process did not support an overall return to control. This study compares morphology and composition as separate outcomes. It identifies membrane and matrix associations as priorities for validation. Original TEM measurements were unavailable, sample matching remained unresolved, and kidney proteomics were absent. These limitations prevent causal conclusions and individual-sample comparisons between morphology and protein composition. Significance Statement This study contributes to exosome research by integrating particle morphology and proteomic analysis to characterize tissue-derived extracellular vesicle-enriched preparations following inflammation and miRNA-associated vesicle administration. The findings highlight that particle shape, size heterogeneity, and protein composition can follow different treatment-associated patterns, supporting their assessment as complementary features of exosome preparations. Selective enrichment of PTGFRN and LAMB2 prioritizes membrane and extracellular-matrix association for further investigation. This approach strengthens the interpretation of exosome characterization data and defines focused questions about particle identity, protein localization, and functional cargo delivery. It provides a foundation for evaluating how changes in recovered vesicle preparations relate to the biological activity of exosome-based interventions.

papers.title: Oligodendrocyte Development and Myelination in the 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome
papers.abstract: The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is associated with a high risk of neurodevelopmental disorders, including a 25% chance of developing schizophrenia (SCZ). SCZ is prevalent in 0.4-0.7% of the population. Evidence suggests that the cognitive deficits of SCZ may be caused by neurodevelopmental disconnection due to impaired oligodendrocyte (OL) maturation and myelination. We hypothesized that the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome impairs OL life cycle progression, halting oligodendrocytes in their immature phase and preventing advancement to the mature stage. This in turn creates myelination changes, demonstrated by a decrease in myelin. To test this, we utilized a 22q11.2 deletion mouse model focusing on the prefrontal cortex (PFC), a late-myelinating brain region. We evaluated PFC regions (mPFC, dlPFC, mOFC, lOFC) in adolescent (P14 and P28) mutant mice and controls. Additionally, we examined the two-hit hypothesis of schizophrenia using a maternal separation model. At P28, mutant mice displayed a significant increase in immature OLs and mature OLs in the PFC, and a decrease in myelination and myelin process length compared to controls. At P14, mutant mice showed subtle reductions in oligodendrocyte precursor cells and subtle myelination alterations in the mPFC. When considering the two-hit hypothesis, we saw equivalent reductions in myelination in the genetic-only, environmental-only, and two-hit groups. Together, these data demonstrate that the 22q11.2 deletion impairs OL maturation and functional myelination between P14 to P28, a critical window for neurodevelopment. Examining the impact of SCZ on OLs could reveal key intervention targets before SCZ symptom onset, and may determine the role of OLs and the 22q11.2 deletion in neural disconnectivity in schizophrenia.

papers.title: SACHET: seeded contour tracking measures Rab conversion kinetics on individual endosomes in live cells
papers.abstract: Membrane-labeled endosomes appear as hollow rings in a projection; they move, deform and exchange their coat, which population trackers — tools that detect every object of one kind and link the detections across frames — are not designed to follow. Here we introduce SACHET (Seeded Adaptive Contour & Hollow Endosome Tracking), a human-supervised Fiji tool that tracks one endosome at a time. On simulated ground truth it localizes the center to 10 nm, recovers transition time constants and lags without bias and holds the target among touching neighbors; comparisons with tuned TrackMate and Cellpose delineate where each is superior. In crowded spinning-disk projections, TrackMate followed one of seven marked Rab5-to-Rab7 conversions; supervised SACHET followed all 37. SACHET thus provides a stable per-endosome frame in which membrane morphology and protein exchange can be quantified: in five cell lines the conversion toggles like a digital switch within seconds to minutes, differing between lines.

papers.title: Using a 3-step semi-automated image analysis pipeline to quantify differences in VE-cadherin junction morphology in lymphatic endothelial cells in vitro.
papers.abstract: Lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) function is strongly tied to transitions between button- and zipper-like junctions that control fluid flow into vessels. Published methods quantifying junction morphology are limited to single cell analysis or use few quantitative metrics to describe junctions across LEC monolayers. Therefore, a novel 3-step image analysis pipeline was developed to identify new metrics that quantify differences in button- and zipper-like junctions in LECs. The pipeline used Cellpose, CellProfiler, and Fiji to analyze VE-cadherin expression across lymphatic vessels within a 3D microfluidic chip and quantify VE-cadherin radial intensity, number of objects, object size, branchpoints, endpoints, and junction thickness. Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α exposure produced button-like junctions, and unexposed cells were zippered. Radial intensity was heightened at the cell membrane in zipper-like junctions while perinuclear intensity increased for button-like junctions. Increased branchpoints, endpoints, objects per cell, and junction thickness were associated with junction buttoning, while increased object size was associated with junction zippering. Principle component analysis results reinforced these trends and identified metric combinations that represented each junctional state. Overall, this semi-automated pipeline quantified differences in VE-cadherin junction morphology across LEC monolayers and generated new quantitative metrics to expand the tools available for studying junction morphology in lymphatic vasculature.

papers.title: Whole-mount three-dimensional imaging and quantitative analysis platform for early brain development using dorsal forebrain spheroids
papers.abstract: SUMMARY Three-dimensional culture systems have emerged as a bridge between in vitro and in vivo models. Organoids and spheroids derived from human stem cells can model cellular interactions, morphology and organization of the neocortex, and provide a platform for future translational research into neurological disorders. However, the heterogeneity commonly found in 3D culture systems presents considerable challenges for identifying significant, reproducible, and disorder-relevant phenotypes. Here, we present a rigorous methodological framework for the longitudinal analysis of dorsal forebrain spheroids, beginning with gross spheroid morphology, extending to structural phenotypes in rosette morphogenesis, and culminating in cellular analyses of neural progenitor cell proliferation and cell cycle dynamics. This workflow integrates isogenic iPSC-derived spheroid culture, whole-mount optical clearing, high-resolution 3D imaging and reconstruction, and cumulative EdU-labeling assays. Testing the sensitivity of this approach in an isogenic Down syndrome model, we reliably detected new features of altered spheroid growth, delayed rosette emergence, reduced rosette density, and prolonged progenitor cell cycle progression. This approach provides a reproducible strategy for measuring complex developmental phenotypes in 3D culture models and can be applied to neurodevelopmentally altered cell lines beyond Down syndrome.
